label: Pitfall 8: cohort and sequencing platform differ; stratify and check direction
text: PITFALL: Pooled cohorts and assays with different sensitivity. The patient file has a COHORT column and sample IDs follow two naming schemes (targeted-panel style 'P-...-IM3/IM5' and 'DS-test-...'), although the gene panel matrix labels samples WXS; deep targeted panels detect low-allele-fraction mutations that ~50-100x exome sequencing misses, especially in low-purity tumours, so 'wild-type' is less certain on one platform, and if platform or cohort is also related to resistance (cohorts enriched for resistant cases) pooling can create or hide an association. Outcome-enriched sampling also means the resistant fraction is not a population rate, though the odds ratio stays valid. CHECK: tabulate COHORT and ID scheme against CHEMO_RESISTANT and TP53 status; compare t_depth and t_alt_count/t_depth of calls between schemes. IF FOUND: report the TP53 vs resistance odds ratio within each cohort/platform as well as pooled (Cochran-Mantel-Haenszel stratified by cohort), check that the direction is the same in both, and quote odds ratios rather than resistance 'rates' as population estimates. SOURCE: https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC3833702/ ; https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC7574938/ ; https://jhanley.biostat.mcgill.ca/Penrose/CaseControlStudiesBreslow2007.pdf

label: Pitfall 9: interpret effect size and interval, not just p; low power is not 'Not verifiable'
text: PITFALL: Misreading a non-significant or borderline result. With only a handful of TP53-altered patients, p > 0.05 does not show 'no association' (absence of evidence is not evidence of absence), and conversely a significant p from 3-5 events can hinge on one patient's classification. The task's 'Not verifiable' label is reserved for data that lack the variables, not for low power. CHECK: report the number of altered patients, the resistant fraction in altered vs unaltered patients, the odds ratio and its 95 percent confidence interval, and rerun after reclassifying the single most uncertain patient or event. IF FOUND: decide support vs contradiction from direction, effect size, interval and robustness across the pre-specified sensitivity analyses rather than from one p-value threshold; state plainly when the estimate points one way but the interval is wide; and do not pick the alteration definition or subgroup after seeing which gives p < 0.05. SOURCE: https://www.bmj.com/content/311/7003/485 ; https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC4877414/ ; https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC5726092/

text: PITFALL: Using DNA copy number (gain/amplification of the miRNA locus) as a proxy for miRNA upregulation. reason: A mis-coded event indicator or a blank time read as zero changes the survival comparison directly, and with few mutant patients the loss or mis-coding of a single one can change the result.
text: Survival fields need careful parsing. In data_clinical_patient.txt, OS_STATUS is a coded string such as '0:LIVING' / '1:DECEASED' (the event indicator is 1 only for DECEASED), and some patients have a blank OS_MONTHS (the library saw at least one LIVING patient with no OS_MONTHS). Do not treat blanks as 0 months or as events, and do not compare raw OS_MONTHS with a t-test or Mann-Whitney test, because that ignores censoring. Count the patients missing OS_MONTHS or OS_STATUS overall and inside the BRCA2-mutant group, confirm that the event indicator sums to the number of DECEASED rows, and check for zero or negative times. Drop patients lacking time or status from the survival analysis (say how many, and whether any were BRCA2-mutant), use censoring-aware methods only (Kaplan-Meier, log-rank, Cox), and report how many mutant patients remain evaluable.

reason: A careless join silently puts un-sequenced patients in the wild-type group or drops or duplicates patients, which alters both groups in a cohort this small.
text: Build the BRCA2 wild-type group only from patients whose tumour was actually sequenced. Patient-level survival (data_clinical_patient.txt) must be linked to mutations (data_mutations.txt, Tumor_Sample_Barcode) through data_clinical_sample.txt (PATIENT_ID to SAMPLE_ID). The library counted one more data row in the patient table (78) than in the sample table (77), so at least one patient appears to have no sequenced sample. Compare the ID sets across the three files, list IDs present in one and missing in another, and check for several samples per patient. Do not label an un-sequenced patient as BRCA2 wild-type; restrict to patients with a sequenced sample, collapse to one record per patient, and report the final N.

reason: Which patients count as BRCA2-mutant is the exposure variable of the whole analysis; including silent or non-coding rows can move patients between groups.
text: Not every BRCA2 row in the mutation file is a mutation in the usual sense. A study MAF can contain silent and non-coding calls (Variant_Classification values such as Silent, Intron, 3'UTR, 5'UTR, 3'Flank, 5'Flank, IGR, RNA) that cBioPortal-style analyses exclude when calling a gene altered. Filter data_mutations.txt to Hugo_Symbol == BRCA2 and tabulate Variant_Classification per Tumor_Sample_Barcode, and count a patient with several BRCA2 rows once. Define the mutant group as patients with at least one protein-altering BRCA2 variant (Missense_Mutation, Nonsense_Mutation, Frame_Shift_Ins/Del, In_Frame_Ins/Del, Splice_Site, Translation_Start_Site, Nonstop_Mutation), and state how many patients would change group if silent or non-coding calls were included.

reason: It prevents the label from being decided by a definition or test chosen after seeing the outcomes, which is the main way a small biomarker comparison goes wrong.
text: Fix the primary analysis before looking at any survival result. With only a handful of mutant patients, the conclusion can be flipped by analyst choices (all protein-altering BRCA2 variants versus truncating-only versus excluding missense variants of uncertain significance; which patients are kept; which test), and trying several until one is significant inflates false positives. The hypothesis says only 'BRCA2 mutations', so the primary analysis that matches its wording is: any protein-altering BRCA2 mutation versus none, overall survival, two-sided log-rank test. Run truncating-only and other definitions as clearly labelled sensitivity analyses. If the conclusion depends on the definition, base the label on the pre-specified primary analysis and report the disagreement rather than choosing whichever variant gives a significant result.

reason: The claim turns on statistical significance, and the default p-value and hazard ratio are the numbers most likely to be wrong when the mutant group is tiny.
text: The cohort is small (under 80 patients in the clinical tables), so a rarely mutated gene gives a very small mutant group, and the default asymptotic log-rank p-value is unreliable when groups are very unequal or events are few. Tabulate the number of patients and the number of deaths in the BRCA2-mutant and wild-type groups among patients with usable survival data. If the mutant group has fewer than about 10 patients or about 5 deaths, also compute a permutation or exact log-rank p-value (permute the mutant label many times, or enumerate all assignments if the group is tiny), report both p-values with group sizes and event counts, and treat any p near 0.05 as fragile. A standard Cox model can also fail in this setting (hazard ratio diverging to 0 or infinity, huge standard errors, convergence warnings, for example when all or none of the mutant patients died); if so, its Wald confidence interval and p-value are meaningless, and a Firth-penalized Cox fit with profile-likelihood intervals, or the permutation log-rank test with Kaplan-Meier estimates, should be reported instead.

reason: It shapes what must be computed and reported (direction as well as p-value) and how the outcome maps onto the task's three labels, without prejudging which outcome the data give.
text: The hypothesis makes two claims that must both be assessed: a direction (BRCA2-mutant patients survive for a shorter time: hazard ratio above 1, lower Kaplan-Meier curve) and statistical significance. Always report the direction of the effect (hazard ratio with 95% confidence interval, which curve is lower, medians if estimable) together with the two-sided p-value and the number of deaths in each group, because power depends on events rather than patients. A significant p-value is not enough by itself, since it does not say which group does worse, and a non-significant p-value in a small cohort is weak evidence rather than proof of no effect, so show the confidence interval. When choosing the label, re-read the task's definitions: the task text reserves 'Not verifiable' for data that lack the relevant variables or tables, which is a different situation from a comparison whose variables are present but which is underpowered.

reason: This is a confounder specific to BRCA2 in gastric cancer that a generic survival analysis would not think to check, and it affects how any observed association should be interpreted.
text: BRCA2 mutation status can be confounded by hypermutation or mismatch-repair deficiency. BRCA2 is a long gene with coding mononucleotide tracts, so in MSI-high or high-mutation-burden gastrointestinal tumours BRCA2 mutations (often frameshifts) are frequently passenger events, and such tumours tend to have a different prognosis from the rest. A naive mutant versus wild-type comparison may then reflect mutation burden or repair status rather than BRCA2, and the distortion can go in either direction. Check whether the BRCA2-mutant patients are concentrated among hypermutated or repair-deficient tumours, using the clinical columns the library reports (TMB_NONSYNONYMOUS, DNA_REPAIR_STATUS; confirm they exist) and per-sample mutation counts from the mutation file. Keep the unadjusted comparison as primary, add a sensitivity analysis stratified by or adjusted for repair status or mutation burden (or restricted to non-hypermutated tumours), and state whether the direction of the effect survives.

reason: Keeps the team from answering the wrong question: a systematic offset between assays must not be read as evidence about correlation in either direction.
text: Correlation is not agreement. If paired values exist, report the correlation coefficient with its confidence interval separately from bias (Bland-Altman mean difference and limits, regression slope and intercept), answer the hypothesis with the correlation coefficient, and report any bias as a separate finding rather than as absence of correlation.

reason: It sets the decision rule for a universal claim: what counts as support, what counts as a real counter-example, and what happens when no tumour is evaluable, which directly governs the label.
text: The hypothesis is a universal claim ('all'). It is not established by n-of-n in a small cohort, and it is refuted only by a well-supported counter-example. Report the number of evaluable tumours (correct tumour type, at least two same-tumour samples, comparable panels), the number showing ITH, and an exact binomial interval (with 0 exceptions in n the 95% upper bound on the exception rate is about 3/n; the exact lower bound on the proportion is 0.05^(1/n), e.g. 0.74 for n = 10). If the number of evaluable tumours is zero the proportion is undefined and the data do not address the claim. Detected ITH rises with the number of regions sampled, so a tumour with one or two samples or few compared genes that shows no heterogeneity is absence of evidence, not a homogeneous tumour: for every tumour scored 'no ITH' record the number of samples, the number of genes/mutations compared and the depth, and treat thinly sampled 'homogeneous' tumours as uninformative rather than as counter-examples. A single credible exception is what decides against a universal claim, so document its sampling depth and rule out technical explanations first.

reason: A filter that drops indels or matches a fixed protein string would make CALR mutations invisible and flip the count the label depends on.
text: CALR driver mutations in MPN are exon 9 insertions/deletions (commonly a 52-bp deletion, 'type 1', and a 5-bp insertion, 'type 2', plus more than 50 rarer variants), not point mutations. They are missed if you search for a specific protein-change string, filter to Variant_Type SNP or Variant_Classification Missense_Mutation, or drop indels. The same indel is written differently by different pipelines (e.g. L367fs*46 vs L367Tfs*46, K385fs*47 vs K385Nfs*47) and indel coordinates shift with left/right alignment. Select rows by Hugo_Symbol == 'CALR' with NO filter on Variant_Type or Variant_Classification, and as a backstop also look for rows on chromosome 19 with Start_Position inside the CALR locus (roughly 13.049-13.055 Mb on GRCh37). Then inspect Variant_Classification, Variant_Type, HGVSc/HGVSp and any study-specific DNA-change / protein-change columns for each row. Count CALR by gene and by frameshift/indel class, never by exact string match, and keep INS and DEL rows in every filter.

reason: Without panel matching and a power check, between-sample discordance would be manufactured by panel differences and low purity or depth, inflating the count of tumours called heterogeneous.
text: Apparent 'private' mutations between samples of one patient are often technical. (a) Panels: samples in this study may be sequenced on different targeted panels (the library's header read suggests the gene panel matrix lists IMPACT341, IMPACT410 and IMPACT468, and a FoundationOne panel file is supplied). A gene absent from a sample's panel is 'not profiled', not wild type. Join data_gene_panel_matrix.txt to the sample table and, for each within-patient pair, restrict mutation, CNA and SV comparisons to genes covered by both panels (IMPACT gene lists are not supplied, so use the union of genes mutated on that panel as a lower bound or restrict to the smallest panel). (b) Detection power: a MAF lists only called variants, so a missing row is not a genotype of zero; in a replicate study 34-80% of discordant variants that would be read as ITH were noise. For each mutation called in sample A but not in B, compare TUMOR_PURITY and coverage of the two samples and the alt count and VAF in A, and ask whether B could have detected it (expected alt reads = depth_B x VAF_A x purity_B/purity_A). Count as heterogeneous only discordances the partner sample was powered to detect, and report both the naive and the power-filtered result.

reason: Whether a CALR row counts as a somatic mutation decides whether it can bear on the claim; the per-row evidence columns for this are easy to overlook.
text: The claim says SOMATIC CALR mutations. A MAF can contain germline or unvalidated calls, and CALR variants that are not exon 9 frameshifts (in-frame exon 9 indels, missense, silent) are usually germline polymorphisms or non-drivers; the established pathogenic MPN CALR mutations are +1 frameshift indels in exon 9. For each CALR row check Mutation_Status, Validation_Status, the clinical SOMATIC_STATUS (matched vs unmatched), and any study-specific tumour/germline read-count or allele-percentage columns (the library reports columns named like 'Tumor reads', 'Tumor allele burden (%)', 'Germline reads', 'Germline allele percentage (%)' in data_mutations.txt; confirm in the header). Count as somatic CALR only variants with tumour support and no (or near-zero) support in the matched germline. Report in-frame, missense and silent CALR rows separately and say whether the conclusion changes if they are included.

reason: If the team falls back on single-sample VAF measures, the choice of score and threshold can make the universal claim trivially true or false; this steers them to evidence that can actually discriminate.
text: Be careful with single-sample, VAF-based evidence of ITH. Raw VAF is not the fraction of cancer cells carrying a mutation: it depends on purity, local copy number and multiplicity (including copy-neutral LOH), so low-VAF mutations in impure or copy-altered regions are easily mislabelled subclonal, and single-sample ITH methods disagree widely. If single-sample clonality is attempted, compute CCF = VAF x (purity x CN_tumour + 2 x (1 - purity)) / (purity x multiplicity) from TUMOR_PURITY and data_cna_hg19.seg with a binomial interval from t_alt_count/t_ref_count, and call a mutation subclonal only if the upper CCF bound is clearly below 1 under all plausible multiplicities; with missing purity, panel log-ratio segments without allele-specific copy number, or few mutations per sample these calls are low-confidence and should not carry a universal claim. VAF-dispersion scores such as MATH (100 x MAD/median of VAFs) are unstable or undefined with the handful of mutations a panel yields (a score of 0 for samples with 0-1 mutations means 'undefined', not 'homogeneous') and are positive for almost any sample, so 'score > 0 in every tumour' makes the hypothesis trivially true. Count mutations per sample; if a continuous score is used, fix the threshold before looking and show sensitivity to it. Prefer discrete evidence: a mutation or copy-number event confidently present in one same-tumour sample and confidently absent in another.

reason: JAK2 status defines the group the claim is about; a too-narrow or too-broad definition, or ignoring a curated status label, moves patients in or out of the JAK2-nonmutated row.
text: 'JAK2 mutated' can be defined too narrowly (V617F only) or too broadly (any JAK2 row). MPN JAK2 drivers are V617F (exon 14) plus exon 12 indels/missense around codons 537-547; a MAF may also hold silent, intronic or UTR JAK2 rows that are not mutations in the sense of the claim. List every JAK2 row with Variant_Classification, HGVSp_Short and Mutation_Status. The library also reports a study-supplied column 'JAK2/MPL mutation' in data_mutations.txt that is a sample-level label repeated on every row of the sample, not a per-variant field; confirm it exists and tabulate its unique values. Classify JAK2 status per patient two ways: (a) from nonsynonymous somatic JAK2 rows and (b) from the curated sample-level label; flag every patient where the two disagree, and run the conclusion under both definitions. Sequencing at ordinary exome depth does not detect low-burden JAK2 V617F (roughly below 2-5% allele fraction), so the curated label may reflect a more sensitive clinical assay; where the two disagree the curated label is the better guide, and 'nonmutated JAK2' should be stated as 'not detected at this assay's sensitivity'. Looking at the allele burden / alt-read counts of the JAK2 rows shows the lowest burden the study reports.

reason: Germline contamination in unmatched calls changes which mutations may be used for shared-versus-private and clonality comparisons, so it alters the filtering step of any ITH analysis.
text: Some mutation calls may have been made without a patient-matched normal: the library's header read of the mutation file saw Matched_Norm_Sample_Barcode values like 's_Normal_Pooled_FROZEN', Mutation_Status 'SOMATIC_VS_POOL', and Foundation rows with Variant_Type UNK and verification/validation status 'unknown'/'likely'. Such calls contain germline variants at VAF near 0.5 or 1.0 in every sample of a patient, which inflate apparent shared/clonal content and distort VAF-based ITH scores. Tabulate Center, Mutation_Status, Matched_Norm_Sample_Barcode and the SOMATIC_STATUS column of the sample table (Matched vs Unmatched); for unmatched samples look for a VAF spike at 0.5 and at n_alt_count and population-frequency columns. If found, analyse matched-normal samples separately, or drop variants with population allele frequency above about 0.1-1% and unknown-status Foundation calls, and state that unmatched samples cannot support clonality claims.

reason: Tells the team how much weight an absence of CALR rows can carry and what to check in the MAF to judge whether long indels were callable at all.
text: Short-read exome pipelines have poor sensitivity for long indels: reads carrying the 52-bp CALR deletion are often soft-clipped or mismapped, so a missing CALR call is weaker evidence than a present one. Check whether the MAF contains any indel longer than about 20 bp at all (compare lengths of Reference_Allele and Tumor_Seq_Allele2 on DEL/INS rows), whether CALR indels carry a Validation_Method or manual-curation flag, and how many JAK2-nonmutated patients have no JAK2, CALR or MPL row. reason: The verdict turns entirely on what 'high' is measured against. Without external benchmarks the team has no principled way to choose between True, False and Not verifiable, and the label could be decided by an arbitrary reading of the word.
text: The hypothesis says the median exonic mutation frequency is 'high' but gives no threshold, and the data carry no high/low flag. Do not call any non-zero rate 'high', and do not default to 'Not verifiable' just because no cut-off column exists: a per-megabase rate plus an external benchmark makes the claim testable. Compute the cohort median in mutations per Mb and place it on published scales, stating which benchmark you used. Reference scales reported by the library (from the literature, not from this dataset): across 27 tumour types the median rate varies more than 1,000-fold, lowest in haematological and paediatric tumours and highest in carcinogen-driven melanoma and lung cancer; the overall average is about 4.0 nonsilent coding mutations per Mb over about 30 Mb covered; per-tumour values span about 0.001 to more than 400 per Mb; common adult cancers sit at about 1-10 per Mb; paediatric tumour-type medians are about 0.02-0.8 per Mb (0.17 per Mb in AML and Wilms tumour up to 0.79 per Mb in osteosarcoma, in a 1,699-case paediatric pan-cancer set that included neuroblastoma); the clinical 'TMB-high' cut-off is 10 or more per Mb.

reason: This decides which comparison the team runs. Reading the claim as a between-risk-group contrast would lead either to an unwarranted 'Not verifiable' or to a proxy analysis that addresses a different question.
text: 'High' can be misread as 'higher in high-risk than in lower-risk neuroblastoma'. The library reports that the clinical tables have no explicit risk-group or stage column (it saw MYCN_AMP, AGE, GRADE, MKI and HYPERDIPLOID); check this yourself, and read the '#' header lines for any cohort description. If there is no risk column, an internal high-risk versus low-risk contrast is not possible, but that does not make the claim untestable, and a contrast built on proxies would not answer it. Treat the hypothesis as an absolute statement about the cohort's median, judged against external mutation-rate benchmarks. Mutation burden also rises with age at diagnosis, so within-cohort trends say nothing about whether the level is high. Tabulate MYCN_AMP and AGE and check whether the per-Mb rate varies with them; use those strata only as sensitivity analyses, to show whether the median falls on the same side of the benchmark in each stratum.

reason: The choice of denominator sets the number that is compared with the benchmark. It also points the team to the per-sample rate columns in the sample table, which they might otherwise overlook in favour of counting MAF rows.
text: A mutation count per sample is not a mutation frequency: frequency needs a per-megabase denominator, and a nominal exome size (30 or 38 Mb) differs from the bases actually covered well enough to call mutations in each tumour-normal pair. The library reports that data_clinical_sample.txt has COVERED_BASES, NUM_NONSILENT_MUTATION, SILENT_MUTATION and TOTAL_PER_MB. Recompute (NUM_NONSILENT_MUTATION + SILENT_MUTATION) / COVERED_BASES * 1e6 per sample and confirm it reproduces TOTAL_PER_MB (the library's spot check of the first row: 15 mutations over 28.58 Mb gives 0.52). Look at the spread of COVERED_BASES and whether it differs by PLATFORM. Report the median of per-sample mutations per Mb using each sample's own covered bases, not a median raw count and not count/30. If covered bases are missing or implausible for some samples, state the denominator used and show whether the result is stable under a 30 Mb versus a covered-bases denominator.

reason: The event definition decides the numerators. Counting all BRAF mutations, or deciding the variable is missing because no clinical column holds it, would each give a different label from a V600E-only count.
text: Define the event as exactly BRAF p.V600E, not 'any BRAF alteration'. In lung adenocarcinoma a large share of BRAF mutations are non-V600 (e.g. G469, G466, K601, L597, D594, N581) or variants of unknown significance, and these are not the targetable V600E; BRAF fusions in data_sv.txt and amplifications in data_cna.txt are not V600E either. A gene-level 'BRAF mutated' frequency can rank the groups differently from V600E itself. Filter data_mutations.txt to Hugo_Symbol == BRAF, tabulate HGVSp_Short, and take p.V600E (hg19 chr7:140453136 A>T, c.1799T>A) as the primary event. Look at any other codon-600 rows (V600K, V600_K601delinsE, dinucleotide calls) and report them separately. Base the verdict on V600E-only counts; show gene-level BRAF and all-codon-600 counts only as sensitivity analyses and say whether they agree in direction. reason: The sample table holds more than one burden-like column with different definitions. Picking the wrong one, or comparing one definition with a benchmark built on the other, shifts the median and could shift the verdict.
text: The column TMB_NONSYNONYMOUS in the sample table is a portal-derived value, not the study's exonic mutation frequency: it is the nonsynonymous mutation count divided by a fixed 30 Mb and excludes silent mutations, so it is systematically lower than a total (silent + nonsilent) rate per covered Mb. Take 'exonic mutation frequency' as all coding somatic mutations (silent + nonsilent) per covered Mb (TOTAL_PER_MB) as the primary measure and report the nonsilent-only rate as a sensitivity check. Do not mix the two measures, and match the variant classes to the benchmark you quote: clinical TMB cut-offs are usually nonsynonymous-only, while pan-cancer frequency plots usually count all exonic mutations.

reason: With a rare event, a wrong denominator shifts each group's percentage and can change which group looks lower.

Conversely, a sample not profiled for BRAF must not be counted as wild-type. Take the samples from data_clinical_sample.txt, join to data_gene_panel_matrix.txt (the 'mutations' column not NA), count how many clinical samples are absent from the mutation file, and confirm that every panel in the matrix covers BRAF exon 15. Join the mutation file's Tumor_Sample_Barcode to SAMPLE_ID, and read the clinical files by skipping the leading '#' lines. Frequency = unique profiled samples with the variant / all profiled samples in that subtype group, with profiled samples absent from the mutation file counted as wild-type and unprofiled samples excluded.

reason: It adds a stratified analysis the team would not otherwise run and a rule for how to conclude if platforms disagree, which guards the verdict against a technical artefact.
text: The library reports that the cohort mixes sequencing sources (PLATFORM / DATA_SOURCE values such as Exome_WGA, meaning whole-genome-amplified exome; native exome, WXS; and WGS). These differ in sensitivity and artefact rate: whole-genome amplification before exome capture adds amplification-only variants (in one published comparison only 74% of variants were seen in both amplified and unamplified DNA, and about 11% of amplified-DNA calls were absent from unamplified DNA), while low coverage or low tumour purity lowers sensitivity for low-allelic-fraction mutations. A pooled median can therefore reflect platform mix rather than biology. Tabulate samples by PLATFORM (and by WXS/WGS in the gene panel matrix), compute the median and IQR of TOTAL_PER_MB and COVERED_BASES within each platform, and test for a platform difference (for example Kruskal-Wallis). Report the pooled median together with the per-platform medians, and base the conclusion on whether every platform stratum falls on the same side of the benchmark rather than letting one stratum drive it.

reason: With only a handful of positive cases, one double-counted patient can move a group's frequency enough to change the direction of the comparison.
text: Check the unit of analysis. Sample IDs in this kind of panel-sequencing cohort carry tumour indices (e.g. -T01-, -T02-), so a patient may have more than one sequenced sample, and a mutation file can list the same variant more than once for one sample. Counting rows or samples instead of patients double-counts a rare event and breaks the independence that exact tests assume. Test whether PATIENT_ID is unique in data_clinical_sample.txt, look for duplicated (Tumor_Sample_Barcode, HGVSp_Short) BRAF rows, and compare the sample counts in the clinical sample file, the gene panel matrix and the patient file. If duplicates exist, analyse one sample per patient (the first sequenced or the primary resection sample), count a patient as V600E-positive once, and confirm the conclusion is the same at sample level.

reason: These are data-integrity checks that determine which samples and calls are valid inputs to the median; a genome-scale denominator or germline contamination in a subset would move the rate by orders of magnitude or inflate it.
text: 'Exonic' mutation frequency is the coding-sequence rate. For whole-genome samples, a genome-wide rate (all SNVs over about 3,000 Mb) or a covered-bases value that refers to the whole genome is a different quantity. Non-somatic calls (germline leakage in tumours without a matched normal) inflate burden, and duplicate MAF rows or more than one sample per patient distort per-sample counts. For WGS samples, check that COVERED_BASES is on the exome scale (about 30 Mb) like the exome samples; confirm SOMATIC_STATUS is 'Matched' for all samples; check Mutation_Status in the MAF; check that there is one sample per PATIENT_ID; de-duplicate MAF rows on sample + chromosome + position + alleles. If any of these fail: restrict to coding calls and exome-scale denominators for the WGS samples, exclude or separately report unmatched samples, and summarise one value per patient.

reason: The choice of pooled versus pairwise comparison can give different readings of the same counts, so the comparison structure has to match the wording of the claim.
text: The hypothesis is a three-group statement: MIP/SOL lower than LEP and lower than ACI/PAP. Testing only MIP/SOL against the two other groups pooled can hide that one comparator goes the other way, and an overall 3x2 test says nothing about direction. Report n mutated / n total and the percentage for each of the three groups separately, then compare (a) MIP/SOL vs LEP, (b) MIP/SOL vs ACI/PAP and (c) MIP/SOL vs LEP + ACI/PAP pooled, noting the direction in each. Treat the hypothesis as supported in direction only if the MIP/SOL frequency is lower than each comparator group, not just lower than the pooled one. If the pairwise directions disagree, say so and let the per-group table, not the pooled test, drive the verdict.

reason: The choice of test and of primary analysis determines whether the output is interpretable at all with so few events; a chi-square p-value or a separated regression model would be misleading inputs to the verdict.
text: BRAF V600E is rare in lung adenocarcinoma (a few percent of tumours), so each subtype group will hold only a handful of positives or none. Chi-square is invalid when expected cell counts are below 5, and Fisher's exact test is conservative with very low power here, so a large p-value is likely whether or not a real difference exists. Compute expected counts, state the total number of V600E-positive cases and how many fall in each group, and give exact (Clopper-Pearson or Wilson) 95% intervals for each group's proportion; for a group with 0/n events the upper bound is about 3/n. Use exact tests (scipy.stats.fisher_exact, and the more powerful unconditional barnard_exact or boschloo_exact) instead of chi-square. Report proportions with intervals, do not present an odds ratio of 0 or infinity as an estimate, and say how many events the conclusion rests on. Keep the unadjusted per-group frequency comparison as the primary analysis, because the claim is a descriptive statement about frequencies: a multivariable logistic regression (e.g. adjusting for smoking, stage, sex) with this few events gives separation and absurd odds ratios, so if adjustment is shown at all it should be a sensitivity analysis with at most one covariate, using Firth penalised regression or a stratified exact test.

label: Pitfall 1: resubstitution bias favours the study-derived genomic model over IPI
text: PITFALL: The study's genomic risk grouping (column PROGNOSTIC_MODEL in data_clinical_sample.txt, 'Genomic Risk Model Classification') was very likely fitted on this same cohort using its survival outcome, while the IPI was defined externally decades ago; scoring both on this cohort gives the genomic model a resubstitution (optimism) advantage, so its apparent C-index / KM separation / hazard ratios are biased upward relative to IPI. CHECK: look for any train/validation split flag (none is visible in the headers); quantify how large the genomic-vs-IPI margin is and whether it survives a paired bootstrap CI; if you build any genetic model yourself, put every step (gene selection, weights, cut-points) inside cross-validation folds and score only out-of-fold predictions. IF FOUND: treat a small apparent win of the genomic model as not demonstrating superiority, state the optimism caveat explicitly, and base the verdict on the size and robustness of the margin rather than on resubstitution statistics alone. SOURCE: https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC4410005/ ; https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC3105299/ ; https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC4312434/

label: Pitfall 2: do not compare models by eyeballing two C-indices; use LR tests both ways, AIC, paired bootstrap
text: PITFALL: Deciding 'model A outperforms model B' from two separately computed Harrell C-indices is unreliable: the C-index is a rank measure that is insensitive for comparing models, the naive difference of two Harrell C's can have inflated type-I error under censoring, and two C's from the same patients are correlated so non-overlapping/overlapping separate CIs are not a valid test. CHECK: on the identical set of patients fit Cox models (i) IPI only, (ii) genomic risk only, (iii) both; report likelihood-ratio chi-square of each term given the other (genomic | IPI and IPI | genomic), AIC of the two non-nested single-predictor models, and a paired bootstrap CI (resample patients, recompute both C's, take the difference). IF FOUND: base the comparison on the LR chi-squares/AIC and the paired bootstrap CI of the C difference; note that 'genomic adds significantly to IPI' shows complementary value only, it is NOT the same as outperforming IPI unless the reverse test (IPI adds to genomic) and the head-to-head measures also favour the genomic model. SOURCE: https://www.fharrell.com/post/addvalue/ ; https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC5909734/ ; https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC6460632/

label: Pitfall 5: Harrell C depends on censoring; check PH and use Uno C / time-dependent AUC
text: PITFALL: Harrell's C converges to a quantity that depends on the study's censoring distribution and over-weights early deaths (optimistic with heavy censoring), and a single global C or hazard ratio is misleading if hazards are non-proportional (e.g. risk groups that separate early and then converge or cross). CHECK: compute the censoring fraction and the follow-up distribution; test proportional hazards (Schoenfeld residuals) for both IPI and genomic risk; recompute discrimination with Uno's IPCW C truncated at a time tau within good follow-up (e.g. 5 years) and time-dependent AUC at 2 and 5 years. IF FOUND: report Uno's C / time-dependent AUC at fixed horizons alongside Harrell's C and require the ranking of the two models to agree across them before concluding one outperforms the other. SOURCE: https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC3079915/ ; https://scikit-survival.readthedocs.io/en/stable/user_guide/evaluating-survival-models.html ; https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC10219847/

label: Pathway mutation test: no silent mutations, so no dN/dS or MutSig-style BMR
text: PITFALL: The mutation table is essentially nonsynonymous-only (header scan: 4 'Silent' rows out of 1575; cBioPortal stores non-synonymous mutations), so tools that estimate each gene's background mutation rate from synonymous mutations (dNdScv, MutSigCV, OncodriveCLUST) cannot be run validly; dNdScv authors state that with synonymous calls filtered out dN/dS tends to infinity and everything looks selected. CHECK: tabulate Variant_Classification and confirm the Silent count is near zero. IF FOUND: do not compute dN/dS or a silent-based BMR; instead build the null from the nonsynonymous load itself (per-sample nonsynonymous count or TMB_NONSYNONYMOUS spread over the coding exome, scaled by each gene's coding length), state that this background includes drivers and ignores gene-specific covariates, and treat the resulting p-value as approximate. SOURCE: https://github.com/im3sanger/dndscv/issues/41 ; https://docs.cbioportal.org/user-guide/faq/

label: Pitfall 6: score direction, event coding and label ordering
text: PITFALL: Coding errors silently invert or corrupt the metric: lifelines.utils.concordance_index(event_times, predicted_scores, event_observed) assumes HIGHER score = LONGER survival, so a risk score (IPI 0-5, Low<Medium<High) must be negated or it returns 1-C; scikit-survival's concordance_index_censored assumes higher = higher risk; OS_STATUS is a string like '0:LIVING'/'1:DECEASED' that must be parsed to an event indicator; risk labels are text that sort alphabetically (High<Low<Medium) unless mapped explicitly; the sample file also has a separate CENSORED column whose description ('True or False') does not match its values. CHECK: confirm event = 1 for DECEASED, cross-tabulate OS_STATUS against CENSORED, map Low/Medium/High to 0/1/2 explicitly, and sanity-check that KM curves order as Low best, High worst and that IPI C is above 0.5 (published IPI C for OS in R-CHOP cohorts is about 0.63). IF FOUND: fix the direction/encoding before any comparison; a C below 0.5 for IPI or the genomic model means a coding bug, not a finding. SOURCE: https://lifelines.readthedocs.io/en/latest/lifelines.utils.html ; https://ashpublications.org/blood/article/135/23/2041/452696/International-prognostic-indices-in-diffuse-large

label: Pathway mutation test: raw frequency is not significance; correct for gene length
text: PITFALL: Reporting 'X% of tumours carry a mutation in the pathway' is not a significance test; a gene set with many or long genes is hit in a large share of tumours by chance alone, and tests that treat all genes as equally mutable ignore gene length. PathScan was written because earlier pathway tests neglected gene-length differences in mutation probability under the random-mutation null. CHECK: sum the coding length (bp) of the pathway genes and compute the expected number of tumours with at least one pathway mutation given each tumour's mutation rate; compare observed with expected. IF FOUND: use a length-aware null (per-gene Bernoulli/binomial with probability from coding length x background rate, as in PathScan) or an empirical null from random gene sets matched on number of genes and total coding length, rather than raw frequency or an unweighted hypergeometric test. SOURCE: https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC3106187/

text: Gene lookup: the library reports that Entrez_Gene_Id is empty in this MAF, so Hugo_Symbol is the only key. Match symbols exactly after stripping whitespace and ignoring case; do not match by substring, which would pull in antisense or readthrough loci such as EP300-AS1. Also search for older aliases (EP300 = p300/KAT3B; PBRM1 = BAF180/PB1; CHUK = IKKA/IKK1/IKBKA/TCF16) and confirm hits by location in the Chromosome/Start_Position columns (EP300 22q13, PBRM1 3p21, USP28 11q23, CHUK 10q24). Merge true aliases, exclude antisense/readthrough symbols. If a gene has no rows under any name, record it as 0/n mutated samples rather than treating the gene as absent from the data: the mutation table is exome-wide, so absence of rows for a gene is an observation, not a missing variable.

label: Pitfall 7: significance of genomic risk groups is not superiority; test within strata both ways
text: PITFALL: Showing that the genomic risk groups separate survival (significant log-rank p, large hazard ratio) does not show they OUTPERFORM established methods; p-values and hazard ratios from classifiers with different group sizes and cut-points are not comparable, and a significant new marker can still discriminate worse than IPI. CHECK: do the head-to-head the way the field does it: (a) KM/Cox of genomic risk groups WITHIN each IPI risk stratum and of IPI groups WITHIN each genomic risk stratum (stratified log-rank or stratified Cox), (b) absolute spread of 2- and 5-year OS between best and worst group for each system and the share of patients placed in the extreme groups, (c) the joint-model LR tests. IF FOUND: conclude 'outperforms' only if the genomic model stays prognostic within IPI strata AND IPI adds little within genomic strata AND global measures favour it; if both add to each other the evidence is for complementarity, not superiority. SOURCE: https://brb.nci.nih.gov/techreport/JCO_2005.pdf ; https://ashpublications.org/blood/article/135/23/2041/452696/International-prognostic-indices-in-diffuse-large

label: Pathway mutation test: per-sample mutation-rate heterogeneity and hypermutators
text: PITFALL: Pooling all tumours into one binomial with a single cohort-wide background mutation rate inflates significance when mutation load varies between tumours: a few high-load tumours contribute most pathway hits. Lawrence 2013 and Tokheim 2016 show unmodelled heterogeneity in background rate is the main source of false-positive 'significantly mutated' calls; PathScan computes a p-value per tumour and combines them with Fisher-Lancaster; MuSiC allows per-sample or grouped BMRs; Kandoth 2013 excluded hypermutators. CHECK: plot per-sample mutation counts (or TMB_NONSYNONYMOUS); see whether pathway-mutated tumours are the high-load ones, and whether the result survives dropping the top-load tumours. IF FOUND: use a per-sample background rate (per-sample p-values combined by Fisher/Lancaster, or a Poisson-binomial across samples), and report a sensitivity analysis without the outlier tumours. SOURCE: https://www.nature.com/articles/nature12213 ; https://www.pnas.org/doi/full/10.1073/pnas.1616440113 ; https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC3106187/ ; https://doi.org/10.1038/nature12634

label: Pitfall 8: which comparators count as established and which exist in this dataset
text: PITFALL: 'Current established methods' for DLBCL prognosis are the IPI family (IPI, R-IPI, NCCN-IPI), cell-of-origin (GCB vs ABC) and MYC/BCL2(/BCL6) rearrangement (double-hit) or double-expressor status; picking a weak or partial comparator, or declaring the claim untestable because one comparator is absent, both distort the verdict. From the file headers this dataset HAS IPI total plus its five component flags, MYC/BCL2/BCL6 FISH status, overall survival, and the study's genomic risk label, but shows NO cell-of-origin or expression column. CHECK: list which comparators are present and how complete each is (FISH columns may be sparsely filled); build double-hit status from MYC_FISH and BCL2_FISH_STATUS/BCL6_FISH_STATUS where available; keep IPI in full (0-5 or 4 groups). IF FOUND: make IPI the primary comparator, add FISH/double-hit as a secondary comparator on its own complete subset, and state plainly that cell-of-origin could not be compared; do not use raw mutation counts or TMB as a stand-in for 'the genetic alterations identified' when the study's own genomic risk label is provided. SOURCE: https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC6821591/ ; https://ashpublications.org/blood/article/135/23/2041/452696/International-prognostic-indices-in-diffuse-large ; https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12619815/

label: Pathway mutation test: gene-set definition changes the answer; pre-specify it
text: PITFALL: 'ERBB-PI3K pathway' has no single gene list, and the answer can flip with the definition: a broad database set (e.g. KEGG PI3K-Akt, hundreds of genes incl. collagens/laminins) dilutes signal and adds long passenger genes, while a narrow curated core (ERBB receptors, PI3K catalytic/regulatory subunits, PTEN, AKT, MTOR etc.) concentrates it. Sanchez-Vega 2018 kept only genes with recurrent or known driver alterations in curated pathway templates. Trying several lists and keeping the significant one is a forking-paths error. CHECK: write down the gene list before looking at counts; then rerun with one narrow and one broad definition and with Hugo symbol aliases resolved (check Hugo_Symbol vs SYMBOL columns). IF FOUND: report the result for each definition; base the label on the pre-specified core list and say explicitly if the conclusion depends on the definition. SOURCE: https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC6070353/

reason: Choosing the threshold after seeing the numbers lets the label go either way; a pre-set criterion and a stability check make the label defensible.
text: The cohort is only a few dozen tumours, so each gene's frequency rests on a handful of samples and one or two samples shift it by several percentage points. 'Frequently' has no fixed threshold. Fix the criterion for 'frequently mutated' before looking at the four genes' numbers (for example the gene's rank/percentile among all genes in this cohort and its frequency relative to accepted cutaneous SCC drivers), report k/n with a Wilson or Clopper-Pearson 95% interval for each gene (not a Wald interval), and check whether the verdict is the same under a stricter and a looser criterion and with plus or minus one mutated sample. If it flips, say so. The hypothesis is a conjunction: each of the four genes has to meet the criterion on its own.

reason: Gives the team an in-data yardstick for what a given percentage means in this tumour type, and a built-in check that their pipeline works.
text: Calibrate 'frequent' inside this cohort with controls run through the identical pipeline. Positive controls: established recurrently mutated cutaneous SCC genes (TP53, NOTCH1, NOTCH2, CDKN2A, HRAS, FAT1). Negative controls: known passengers (TTN, MUC16, an olfactory receptor gene) and, for each of the four hypothesis genes, a set of random genes of similar coding length. Place the four hypothesis genes on that scale. If the positive controls themselves come out implausibly low or absent, treat it as a sign that the pipeline (filters, symbol matching, denominator) is wrong and fix it before answering.

reason: The reading of 'frequently affect' (raw prevalence versus more than background) can change the conclusion; the team should compute both and be explicit about which one decides the label.
text: UV-driven cutaneous SCC has one of the highest mutation burdens of any cancer, so raw recurrence alone can arise from background mutation: long, late-replicating or low-expressed genes (TTN, MUC16, RYR2, CSMD3, olfactory receptors) top frequency lists by chance. Rank all genes by fraction of samples with a protein-altering mutation and see where the four genes fall relative to such passengers and relative to coding length (e.g. mutated-sample fraction per kb of coding sequence, or nonsynonymous versus synonymous counts within the gene); if feasible, compare with a simple expectation from each sample's burden and the gene's length (binomial/Poisson, or a dNdScv/MutSigCV-style test). Report both the raw prevalence and whether it exceeds what burden and length predict, and state explicitly which of the two definitions (raw prevalence versus excess over background) the final label rests on.

reason: The pooled frequency may not describe either subgroup; knowing where the mutated samples sit changes how the frequency should be interpreted.
text: The library reports that the cohort mixes subgroups with very different mutation burdens: the clinical tables have HERED_DISORDER (e.g. RDEB versus None), IMMUNE_STATUS, and TMB_NONSYNONYMOUS ranging from below 1 to above 50 per Mb. A pooled per-gene frequency may come entirely from a few hypermutated tumours or be diluted by a low-burden subgroup. For each of the four genes, list the mutated samples with their TMB, HERED_DISORDER and IMMUNE_STATUS; compute frequency within each subgroup and within TMB strata; and test whether mutated status simply tracks TMB (e.g. Mann-Whitney of TMB in mutated versus unmutated samples, or logistic regression on log TMB). Report subgroup frequencies alongside the pooled one and state which population the claim about cutaneous SCC is being judged on.

reason: In a small cohort, double-counting one person's related tumours changes both numerator and denominator of a gene's frequency.
text: The library reports that samples are not all independent patients: the clinical tables include more than one tumour from the same person under separate IDs (e.g. Patient9 and Patient9_2). Identify patients with more than one sample (also by ID stem such as a '_2' suffix). For the four genes, check whether the mutated samples include such pairs and whether the identical variant (chromosome, position, alleles) appears in both. Report frequency per patient (mutated if any of their tumours is) as well as per sample, and count an identical variant shared by tumours of one person once. An identical variant recurring in many unrelated samples should be inspected as a possible germline or artefact call before it is counted as recurrence.

reason: One or two low-confidence calls can decide a gene's frequency in a cohort this small, but over-filtering in the main analysis would be equally distorting; the team needs to know to treat it as sensitivity, not as the primary count.
text: Call quality as a sensitivity check only: the MAF has t_ref_count, t_alt_count, n_ref_count, n_alt_count and dbSNP_RS. For every protein-altering variant in the four genes compute VAF = t_alt_count/(t_alt_count+t_ref_count), tumour depth, n_alt_count and whether dbSNP_RS is filled, and check Matched_Norm_Sample_Barcode/Mutation_Status to see whether calls are tumour-normal or tumour-only. Rerun the frequencies with a conventional filter (e.g. t_alt_count of at least 3 to 5, VAF at least 0.05, n_alt_count at most 1) and report whether the conclusion survives. Do not drop variants in the main analysis: the deposited MAF is already the study's filtered call set.

label: Pitfall 9: self-built mutation models need nested cross-validation and correct wild-type denominators
text: PITFALL: If a team rebuilds a genetic predictor from data_mutations.txt / data_log2_cna.txt (about 140 genes, about 1000 exomes), fitting many gene indicators and then scoring on the same patients gives strongly optimistic results (pure-noise features can produce well-separated KM curves), and a MAF lists only mutated calls so a sample with no row for a gene is wild-type only if it was profiled (see data_gene_panel_matrix.txt); patients missing from the mutation or CNA tables must not be treated as wild-type. CHECK: compare the sample ID sets across clinical, gene-panel, mutation and CNA files; count events per candidate feature; drop very rare alterations; run penalised Cox with feature selection and tuning inside nested cross-validation and evaluate only out-of-fold (pre-validated) risk scores, with a permutation test for the cross-validated statistic. IF FOUND: report cross-validated, not apparent, performance for any self-built model and compare its out-of-fold score with IPI on the same patients; treat the supplied PROGNOSTIC_MODEL column as the primary representation of the study's model. SOURCE: https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC3105299/ ; https://doi.org/10.1093/jnci/95.1.14 ; https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC2394420/

label: Pathway mutation test: separate driver-like from passenger mutations
text: PITFALL: Counting every missense variant in a pathway gene as a pathway 'hit' mixes passengers with drivers. Expert pathway analyses (Sanchez-Vega 2018) count only activating hotspot mutations in oncogenes and truncating or recurrent mutations in tumour suppressors, filtering likely passengers with OncoKB; hotspot recurrence at the same residue (Chang 2016) is independent evidence of selection that does not need a silent-mutation background. CHECK: for each pathway gene list the protein changes (HGVSp_Short), the Hotspot column, Variant_Classification, and whether the same codon recurs across tumours or matches well-known activating residues. IF FOUND: report two tallies, all nonsynonymous and putative-driver-only, and note whether significance rests on recurrent/known-driver events or on scattered unique missense variants. SOURCE: https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC6070353/ ; https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC4744099/

label: Pathway mutation test: self-contained vs competitive null; one gene can carry a pathway
text: PITFALL: Self-contained and competitive nulls answer different questions and can disagree. Self-contained (pathway mutated more than a background rate predicts) can be significant because of a single highly mutated member gene; competitive (pathway mutated more than other genes of similar size) can be non-significant when many genes outside are also mutated. CHECK: after the pathway-level test, do leave-one-gene-out and look at the per-gene breakdown of mutated samples. IF FOUND: state which null was tested, say whether the signal is spread over several pathway genes or carried by one gene, and prefer a conclusion that holds under both nulls. SOURCE: https://doi.org/10.1093/bioinformatics/btm051 ; https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC4103537/

label: Pathway mutation test: small cohort, aggregate at pathway level and report power
text: PITFALL: With roughly 56 exomes the cohort has low power for genes mutated in a few percent of tumours (Lawrence 2014: most cancer genes are mutated at 2-20% and need hundreds of tumours per type to detect), which is exactly why pathway-level aggregation is used; a non-significant single-gene result is therefore not evidence that the pathway is not significantly mutated, and a non-significant pathway test is weak evidence of absence. label: Fraction LOH needs allele-specific copy number (lcn==0)
text: PITFALL: 'Fraction of LOH' is an allele-specific metric: in MSK facets-suite calculate_loh it is (autosomal length of segments with minor/lesser copy number lcn == 0) / (autosomal length of segments with non-missing lcn). It needs FACETS-style tcn/lcn from heterozygous-SNP allele ratios; it cannot be computed from a plain total-copy-number seg file. CHECK: list columns of data_cna_hg19.seg and the clinical tables for lcn/tcn/minor CN/BAF/FRACTION_LOH/purity/ploidy; the library's header read found the seg file has only ID, chrom, loc.start, loc.end, num.mark, seg.mean, data_cna.txt is gene-level discrete calls (-2..2), and no clinical column contains LOH, PURITY, PLOIDY or FRACTION. IF FOUND: treat fraction LOH as absent from the data; any number derived from seg.mean is a different variable (copy-number-loss burden), must be named as a proxy, and should not be silently presented as fraction LOH. SOURCE: https://github.com/mskcc/facets-suite/blob/master/R/copy-number-scores.R ; https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC5027494/

label: Deletions/negative seg.mean are not LOH (CN-LOH invisible, WGD)
text: PITFALL: Using negative seg.mean (deletions) as a stand-in for LOH is biased: copy-neutral LOH (mitotic recombination, uniparental disomy) and gain-LOH leave total copy number unchanged or raised and are invisible to log-ratio data; allele-specific reanalysis of TCGA reclassified about 9% of copy-number-wild-type and 7% of gain calls as LOH. Conversely in whole-genome-doubled tumours a relative loss (e.g. 3 of 4 copies) gives a negative log ratio without LOH. TP53-mutant tumours are enriched for WGD, so the proxy error differs between the two groups being compared. CHECK: confirm there is no allelic information (no lcn, no BAF, no germline het-SNP counts); if a loss-fraction proxy is computed anyway, examine whether the seg.mean distribution per sample is centred near 0 or shows multi-modal shifts suggestive of WGD. IF FOUND: do not equate fraction-of-genome-lost with fraction LOH; report it only as a sensitivity/proxy analysis with this caveat, and do not let it alone decide between True and False. SOURCE: https://www.cell.com/cell-systems/fulltext/S2405-4712(21)00383-5 ; https://journals.plos.org/ploscompbiol/article/file?id=10.1371%2Fjournal.pcbi.1001060&type=printable ; https://documents.thermofisher.com/TFS-Assets/LSG/brochures/copy_neutral_loh_appnote.pdf

label: FGA is not fraction LOH
text: PITFALL: Fraction Genome Altered (FGA) is easily confused with fraction LOH. cBioPortal FGA = total length of segments with |seg.mean| above a threshold (0.2 by the usual definition; 0.1 has also been quoted) divided by total length of all profiled segments; it counts gains and losses alike and says nothing about allelic state. TP53 mutation vs FGA/aneuploidy is a well-known positive association, so substituting FGA will almost always return 'supports' regardless of what is true for LOH. CHECK: if you compute a burden from data_cna_hg19.seg, write down exactly which segments enter the numerator (gains+losses vs losses only), the threshold, and that the denominator is summed segment length (length-weighted, not segment counts). IF FOUND: label the result 'FGA' or 'fraction genome lost', never 'fraction LOH', and treat it as answering a different question than the hypothesis. SOURCE: https://www.biostars.org/p/406584/ ; https://groups.google.com/g/cbioportal/c/SqtGhn-AZ4s ; https://docs.cbioportal.org/user-guide/faq/

label: LST column is not fraction LOH
text: PITFALL: The clinical sample table has an 'LST' column (integers 0,1,2,...; 178 of 471 NA) that could be mistaken for an LOH measure. If it is the genomic-scar score, LST = large-scale state transitions = number of chromosomal breakpoints between adjacent segments of at least 10 Mb, a count of breaks used for HRD scoring; it is distinct from HRD-LOH (number of LOH regions >15 Mb) and from fraction of genome under LOH. In a colorectal table 'LST' may also mean something unrelated; the column description only says 'LST'. CHECK: read the '#' description lines for LST and look at its value range and missingness pattern. IF FOUND: do not use LST as the fraction-LOH variable; at most mention it as a different instability score, and note its 38% missingness if used in any sensitivity analysis. SOURCE: https://github.com/sztup/scarHRD/blob/master/scarHRD.md ; https://link.springer.com/article/10.1186/s40364-015-0033-4 ; https://github.com/mskcc/facets-suite/blob/master/R/copy-number-scores.R

label: Purity confounds seg.mean burden vs mutation status
text: PITFALL: Tumour purity confounds any seg.mean-based burden versus mutation-status comparison in the same direction: normal-cell admixture compresses log ratios toward 0 (so fixed thresholds such as |0.2| miss single-copy changes in low-purity samples) and also lowers mutation VAF so TP53 mutations are missed; low-purity samples therefore look both 'copy-number quiet' and 'TP53 wild-type', manufacturing a positive association. cBioPortal itself warns that purity/ploidy differences cause false positive and false negative CNA calls. CHECK: there is no purity column, so use a proxy per sample (e.g. maximum or median VAF = t_alt_count/(t_alt_count+t_ref_count) of somatic mutations, or spread of seg.mean) and see whether the proxy differs between TP53-mutant and wild-type groups and correlates with the burden. IF FOUND: repeat the comparison restricted to adequately pure samples or adjust for the purity proxy in a regression; report whether the association survives. SOURCE: https://docs.cbioportal.org/user-guide/faq/ ; https://cnvkit.readthedocs.io/en/latest/tumor.html ; https://www.annalsofoncology.org/article/S0923-7534(19)31355-9/fulltext

reason: Whether a real income variable exists determines whether any association can be estimated at all; a team that silently regresses 8q gain on a proxy would report a test of a different hypothesis.
text: First step, before any modelling: establish whether the data contain the hypothesis exposure at all. The exposure is community-level (area-level) average income. The library's listing of the file headers reported that the patient table has only PATIENT_ID, AGE_AT_DIAGNOSIS, AGE_AT_PROCUREMENT, RACE, SMOKING, PSA, M_STAGE, VITAL_STATUS, DISEASE_EXTENT and the sample table only PATIENT_ID, SAMPLE_ID, TUMOR_SAMPLE_HISTOLOGY, TISSUE_TYPE, SAMPLE_TYPE, GLEASON_SCORE, ONCOTREE_CODE, CANCER_TYPE, CANCER_TYPE_DETAILED, SAMPLE_CLASS, GENE_PANEL, SOMATIC_STATUS, 8Q_ARM, TMB_NONSYNONYMOUS, and that a case-insensitive search for income|ancestry|zip|census|admixture across all seven files returned nothing. This is the library's report, not a verified fact: re-list every column yourself (including the '#' description lines of both clinical tables and the headers of the mutation, SV, CNA, seg and gene-panel files) and confirm whether any income, zip code, census tract, deprivation index or other socioeconomic field is present. Whatever you find, do not use a stand-in as the 'income' term: self-reported race, smoking, PSA or stage are not valid proxies for a socioeconomic exposure (race bundles ancestry, culture, discrimination and economic position, and in this hypothesis race is the adjustment covariate, so it cannot also be the exposure). A race-vs-8q result answers a different question and may be reported only as descriptive context, never as support for or against the income hypothesis. If the exposure column is absent, say explicitly which variable is missing and apply the task's own label definitions for that situation.

reason: The hypothesis names ancestry as a required adjustment covariate; the team needs to know it must check for it and that it cannot be reconstructed from the files provided.
text: The hypothesis requires adjustment for race AND genetic ancestry. Quantitative ancestry needs germline ancestry-informative SNP genotypes (matched normal or unfiltered tumour pileups) projected onto reference panels; it cannot be recovered from a filtered somatic mutation file, a gene-level CNA matrix or a seg file, because germline variants have been removed (the library notes a SOMATIC_STATUS column, suggesting matched-normal-filtered somatic calls, and found only a self-reported RACE column). Check whether any ancestry-fraction column exists and inspect RACE for small or Unknown/Other categories. If no ancestry column exists, do not attempt to infer ancestry from somatic calls and do not describe any estimate as 'ancestry-adjusted'; adjustment by self-reported race alone is at best partial and must be described as such.

reason: The three task labels hinge on the difference between 'analysed and found no effect' and 'could not be analysed'; this fixes the decision rule before the team looks at results.
text: Rule for choosing the label: a non-significant p-value is not evidence that a hypothesis is false, and a missing variable is not a null result. Before choosing a label, write down (a) which column is the exposure, (b) which column is the outcome, and (c) the adjusted effect estimate with its 95% confidence interval. Distinguish three states: supported (a real exposure measure, interval excludes the null); contradicted (a real exposure measure, interval tight around the null or pointing the other way); not testable (the exposure or a required covariate is absent from the data, so (a) cannot be filled in with a real income measure). A null result obtained on a proxy variable must not be reported as contradiction, and a wide interval means the data do not settle the question.

reason: Fixes which column is the outcome and prevents the team from substituting MYC amplification or an ad hoc seg threshold, either of which would change the result.
text: Outcome definition: arm-level 8q gain is not the same as gene-level amplification. Focal MYC amplification in data_cna.txt does not equal 8q arm gain, and re-deriving arm gain from the panel seg file is threshold-dependent with no consensus definition (e.g. ASCETS default |log2 ratio| 0.2 over at least 70% of the covered arm; others use 0.1/50% or >90% of arm). The library reports a curated 8Q_ARM column in data_clinical_sample.txt: use it as the primary outcome, tabulate its levels (e.g. Gain/Neutral/Loss and missing), define the binary as Gain vs not-Gain, and state how Loss and missing are handled. If you recompute from data_cna_hg19.seg (hg19 8q is roughly chr8:45.6Mb-146.4Mb), compare with 8Q_ARM in a confusion table and treat the seg-derived call as a sensitivity analysis only.

reason: The choice of covariates can create or remove an association; the library gave two facts pulling in opposite directions on sample type and stage, so the team needs both and a stated primary-versus-sensitivity ordering.
text: Adjustment set, applicable only if a real income exposure is found. State the adjustment set up front: the hypothesis names only race and ancestry, so the minimally adjusted model is the primary analysis. Two opposing concerns about clinical covariates: (1) 8q gain frequency in prostate cancer rises steeply with progression (grade, stage, metastatic and castration-resistant disease) and socioeconomic position affects stage at presentation, so disease extent is plausibly a mediator; adjusting for DISEASE_EXTENT, M_STAGE, GLEASON_SCORE or SAMPLE_TYPE is overadjustment for the total association. (2) Log2 ratios shrink toward zero as tumour purity falls, so arm gains are under-called in low-purity samples, and purity differs between primary and metastatic samples and between tissue sites, producing differential outcome misclassification correlated with sample type. Therefore: tabulate 8Q_ARM by DISEASE_EXTENT, M_STAGE, SAMPLE_TYPE, TISSUE_TYPE, Gleason group and GENE_PANEL (the library notes IM5 vs IM6 panels are visible in sample IDs); fit the model both without and with these clinical/technical variables; report the minimally adjusted model as primary and the clinically/technically adjusted or stratified model as a labelled sensitivity analysis. Do not interpret raw gain-frequency differences between groups with different sample-type mix, and do not read covariate coefficients from the same model as if each were itself an adjusted effect (Table 2 fallacy).

reason: Race is a mandatory covariate in this hypothesis, and small race strata can make an ordinary logistic model give misleading estimates and p-values.
text: Sparse-data caution for any race-adjusted model of a binary arm-gain outcome: institutional clinical-sequencing cohorts are heavily imbalanced by race, so logistic regression with small race categories suffers sparse-data bias or separation (maximum-likelihood odds ratios drift away from the null or become infinite as covariates are added; Wald p-values become unreliable). Print the full outcome x exposure x RACE cross-table; flag any cell under about 5-10, any coefficient with |log OR| > 3 or a huge standard error, and estimates that move away from the null as covariates are added. If found, use Firth penalized logistic regression with profile-likelihood intervals (or exact/stratified Cochran-Mantel-Haenszel), collapse or drop tiny race categories with the decision stated, and report likelihood-ratio rather than Wald tests.

reason: Sets the unit of analysis (one sample per patient) and limits how far any estimated association may be generalised.
text: Unit of analysis and scope: this is a single-centre clinical tumour-sequencing cohort, where patients are selected on referral, advanced disease and access to care; these relate to socioeconomic position and race, and to 8q gain through disease stage, so conditioning on being sequenced can induce or mask a socioeconomic-genomic association and under-represents minority and low-income patients. Describe the cohort mix (RACE counts, DISEASE_EXTENT, SAMPLE_TYPE) and check whether there is one sample per patient (the library reports both clinical tables have about 2068 data rows; confirm). Analyse one sample per patient, present any association as holding within this selected cohort only, and consider stratifying by disease extent to see whether an association is consistent within strata.

label: MSI/hypermutation confounds TP53 vs copy-number in CRC
text: PITFALL: In colorectal cancer, microsatellite-unstable (MSI-H) and POLE-hypermutated tumours form a separate pathway: near-diploid, few copy-number changes/LOH, and much less often TP53-mutant, whereas chromosomally unstable MSS tumours carry aneuploidy, 17p/18q/5q LOH and TP53 mutation. A pooled TP53-vs-copy-number comparison therefore partly just contrasts MSI with MSS tumours. CHECK: cross-tabulate TP53 status against MSI_TYPE (values seen: Stable 428, Instable 27, Indeterminate 8, Do not report 7, NA 1) and against TMB_NONSYNONYMOUS; compare the burden within MSS only. IF FOUND: report the MSS-only (and non-hypermutated) estimate as the primary within-cohort result, or adjust for MSI/TMB; do not attribute the pooled difference to TP53 alone. SOURCE: https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC4978761/ ; https://www.cancer.gov/types/colorectal/hp/colorectal-genetics-pdq

label: Mutation VAF cannot give genome-wide fraction LOH
text: PITFALL: Inferring LOH from the TP53 mutation's VAF (e.g. VAF > 0.5 means LOH) is unreliable and answers a different question: converting VAF to zygosity requires purity and allele-specific copy number at the locus, which are not in the data, and even if done it gives LOH at the TP53 locus (17p), not the genome-wide fraction of LOH; it is also undefined for TP53-wild-type tumours, so it cannot be compared between groups. CHECK: confirm whether any purity/ploidy/allele-specific columns exist (none were found in the headers). IF FOUND: do not build a fraction-LOH variable from mutation VAFs; mention VAF-based 17p LOH only as a locus-level side observation, if at all. SOURCE: https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC7867630/ ; https://link.springer.com/article/10.1186/s13039-025-00718-3

label: Define TP53 status per profiled sample; missing seg is not zero
text: PITFALL: Mis-defining the TP53 groups and the analysis set. Errors seen in this kind of cBioPortal analysis: counting variants instead of samples; including Silent/intronic/UTR rows; calling samples absent from data_mutations.txt 'wild-type' without confirming they were profiled; treating samples with no rows in the seg file as zero burden; mixing samples flagged as excluded. CHECK: (a) define TP53-mutant per sample from Hugo_Symbol == TP53 with non-silent Variant_Classification, optionally also TP53 deep deletion in data_cna.txt and TP53 events in data_sv.txt; (b) use data_gene_panel_matrix.txt to confirm every sample was profiled for mutations (panels IMPACT341/410/468 all include TP53); (c) note the header read found 471 samples = 471 patients (no repeated patients), 466 sample IDs in the seg file (5 lack seg data and must be dropped, not set to 0), and 41 samples with USED_IN_GENOMIC_ANALYSIS = No. IF FOUND: restrict to samples with both mutation and seg data, run the comparison with and without the USED_IN_GENOMIC_ANALYSIS = No samples, and report group sizes. SOURCE: https://docs.cbioportal.org/user-guide/faq/ ; https://api.oncokb.org/oncokb-annotator/gene-annotation

label: Panel version/batch and sparse segments affect burden
text: PITFALL: Genome-wide copy-number burden from a targeted panel depends on the panel version and probe density: the samples were run on three assay versions (IMPACT341 n=79, IMPACT410 n=239, IMPACT468 n=153), which differ in number of targets, so segment count, num.mark and resolution differ by batch; published MSK-IMPACT burden analyses adjust for panel version and purity. Short segments supported by few markers (small num.mark) are noisy and can inflate altered-fraction estimates. CHECK: compare the burden metric and TP53-mutant frequency across the three panels in data_gene_panel_matrix.txt; inspect the effect of dropping segments with very low num.mark; use a rank-based test (Wilcoxon/Mann-Whitney) because genome fractions are bounded in [0,1], skewed and zero-inflated. IF FOUND: stratify by or adjust for panel version, length-weight the fraction, and report a non-parametric test with medians and an effect size rather than a t-test alone. SOURCE: https://doi.org/10.1038/s41588-025-02371-3 ; https://www.jmdjournal.org/article/S1525-1578(15)00045-8/fulltext
