reason: This decides between 'Not verifiable' and a testable hypothesis; a team that simply finds no difference without checking for promoter rows could mislabel a missing variable as support for the hypothesis.
text: First establish whether a TERT promoter mutation variable exists in this dataset at all. In exome-based cBioPortal studies the TERT promoter is non-coding; its calls appear in data_mutations.txt only as Variant_Classification 5'Flank rows for TERT (the one non-coding class cBioPortal keeps), and in TCGA-style cohorts promoter status often came from a separate targeted assay or WGS that was never loaded into the mutation file, so the table may hold no promoter calls or only a partial set. Check: select Hugo_Symbol == TERT (Entrez_Gene_Id 7015) in data_mutations.txt and tabulate Variant_Classification, Start_Position and the number of distinct Tumor_Sample_Barcode; also scan the '#' header lines and column names of both clinical tables for any TERT status column. If there are zero promoter (5'Flank / hotspot) rows and no clinical TERT column, the mutation variable does not exist and the fitting label is 'Not verifiable', not 'True'. If promoter rows exist, the variable exists and the test can proceed, but treat only the positive (mutant) calls as trustworthy.

reason: The grouping variable is the core of the test; a mutant group contaminated with coding or non-activating TERT variants would change the comparison.
text: Do not define 'TERT promoter mutated' as any mutation row with Hugo_Symbol TERT. Coding TERT variants (missense, silent, etc.) are not promoter mutations, and non-hotspot upstream variants or the common germline promoter SNP rs2853669 (reported to lower, not raise, TERT expression) are not the activating events. The activating hotspots are C228T at hg19 chr5:1295228 and C250T at hg19 chr5:1295250 (TERT is on the minus strand, so they appear as G>A in the mutation file), plus rare neighbouring activating changes (another base change at 1295228, or the tandem CC>TT at 1295242-1295243). Check: list every TERT row with Variant_Classification, Start_Position, alleles and HGVSc; keep only 5'Flank rows at these positions as promoter mutants. Samples with only coding TERT variants should not go into the mutant group (note them separately). If numbers allow, report C228T and C250T pooled and separately, since the two hotspots may differ in effect size.

reason: Misclassifying unprofiled or uncovered samples as wild-type changes both group membership and how a null or positive result should be interpreted; this directly affects the label for a 'no correlation' hypothesis.
text: Be careful about who goes into the comparison ('wild-type') group. (a) The expression matrix, mutation table and copy-number table in cBioPortal data cover different sample sets (RNA-seq is often a small subset), and a sample absent from the mutation file may be unprofiled rather than unmutated. Build three sets - RNA-seq column IDs, samples whose 'mutations' entry in data_gene_panel_matrix.txt is not NA (profiled), and samples with a TERT promoter row - and report every intersection size; confirm sample IDs match exactly (TCGA-XX-XXXX-01 form) and that there is one sample per patient (primary vs recurrent). Restrict the analysis to samples that have RNA-seq AND are mutation-profiled; drop unprofiled samples rather than calling them wild-type; report n per group, because the usable overlap may be small. (b) Even among profiled samples, no TERT promoter call does not mean wild-type: the promoter is >80% GC and poorly captured by exome kits, and low tumour purity also hides calls. The literature frequency of TERT promoter mutation in glioblastoma is about 70-80%. Check the fraction of profiled samples carrying a promoter call against that expectation and inspect t_alt_count / t_ref_count on the called rows to see how thin the coverage is. If the call rate is far below 70%, describe the comparison group as 'no call detected', not wild-type: it then likely contains hidden mutants, which biases any mutant-vs-rest expression difference toward zero. Under that bias a non-significant result cannot be read as support for 'no correlation', whereas a difference that is still seen in called mutants is seen despite the dilution. Add a sensitivity analysis restricting the comparison group to samples with independent evidence of a non-TERT telomere mechanism (e.g. IDH1 or ATRX mutation).

reason: The choice of expression file and statistical test can make or erase a group difference for a near-zero, zero-inflated gene like TERT.
text: Handle the TERT expression measure with care. TERT mRNA is very low and zero-inflated in bulk RNA-seq (mean below 1 TPM in most cancer types; brain tumours often have 25% or more samples at zero) with a bimodal expressed / not-expressed pattern, so a t-test or Pearson correlation on raw RSEM values is driven by a few outliers and can miss or invent a difference. Pull the TERT row from data_mrna_seq_v2_rsem.txt by Entrez_Gene_Id 7015 (Hugo_Symbol can be blank or duplicated) and inspect the fraction of zeros, range and distribution shape in each group. If it is skewed with many zeros/ties, use a Mann-Whitney / Wilcoxon rank-sum test as the primary test on RSEM or log2(RSEM+1), report medians and a rank effect size (AUC or rank-biserial) with a bootstrap confidence interval, and add a Fisher exact test on TERT detectably expressed vs not. Use data_mrna_seq_v2_rsem.txt as the primary measure. The two z-score files are computed against tumour samples only (all samples, or only samples diploid for that gene), are not tumour-vs-normal and not normally distributed; the diploid-referenced file shifts with the gene's copy-number pattern and can be NA for low-variance genes. Confirm TERT is present and non-NA in each file, use the all-samples z-scores only as a cross-check, and do not define 'elevated' solely by a z > 2 cut-off.

reason: Confounding by IDH/G-CIMP/ATRX status and TERT copy number could drive or mask the primary comparison; the stratified checks determine how much weight the primary result can bear.
text: The TERT-promoter-non-mutant group in glioblastoma is biologically mixed, which can either inflate or hide a mutant-vs-rest expression difference. IDH-mutant / G-CIMP / ATRX-mutant tumours maintain telomeres by ALT and have near-absent TERT mRNA, whereas roughly half of IDH-wild-type, promoter-wild-type glioblastomas raise TERT through rearrangements upstream of TERT; TERT amplification and promoter methylation also raise it. Check: cross-tabulate TERT promoter status against the IDH1 mutation and G-CIMP methylation columns in the clinical tables, ATRX mutation in data_mutations.txt, and TERT copy number (GISTIC value in data_cna.txt and the value in data_linear_cna.txt). Keep the unadjusted mutant-vs-rest comparison as the primary answer, because the hypothesis is about correlation; then repeat it within IDH-wild-type / non-G-CIMP samples and with TERT copy number as a covariate (or excluding TERT-amplified samples). Call the result robust only if direction and rough size hold in the stratified analysis.

reason: Without an explicit rule for what counts as support for a null claim, a team could turn an underpowered non-significant test into 'True' or a trivial significant difference into 'False'.
text: The hypothesis is a claim of NO correlation, so interpret results accordingly. A non-significant p-value in a small sample overlap is not evidence for it (absence of evidence is not evidence of absence); equally, a tiny but statistically significant difference is not automatically 'elevated'. Report group sizes, the direction, and an effect size (median difference or fold change, AUC / rank-biserial) with a confidence interval, and ask whether the interval excludes a biologically meaningful increase. Reporter and tumour studies in the literature describe roughly 2- to 4-fold higher TERT transcription with promoter mutation, so about 2-fold is a reasonable smallest effect of interest. Decision logic: evidence contradicts the hypothesis when called mutants show clearly and significantly higher TERT expression; the data support it only if the estimate is near zero AND the interval excludes a meaningful increase (equivalence / TOST logic) with adequate n per group. If the test is non-significant but the interval is wide or a group has only a handful of samples, describe the data as underpowered rather than claiming support, and decide the label from the direction and size of the estimate together with the sensitivity analyses.

CHECK: Plot acquired count per patient by group and look for an outlier (also check TMB_NONSYNONYMOUS and MSI_TYPE of later samples); compute the interval between samples from AGE_AT_SEQ_REPORTED_YEARS (integer years only, so coarse) and compare it between groups. IF FOUND: Use medians and rank/permutation tests rather than means, report results with and without the outlier, and state interval/therapy as an uncontrolled confounder (therapy data are not in the tables). SOURCE: https://www.nature.com/articles/s41586-026-10803-1 ; https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC10240575/

label: Two-part claim, small n: judge by direction, test both halves
text: PITFALL: The hypothesis is a two-part claim (FN-RMS acquire fewer new alterations than the implicit comparator, FP-RMS; AND no acquired mutation recurs across FN patients), tested on roughly ten patients per group: a non-significant p-value is not evidence of 'no difference', and zero recurrences in n patients is still compatible with a true rate up to about 3/n (rule of three). Conversely, if the observed direction is opposite to the claim (FN acquire as many or more than FP, or the same gene is acquired in several FN patients), that is evidence against it regardless of p. CHECK: State the direction and effect size (median acquired per patient, FN vs FP, with exact Mann-Whitney/Fisher test and CI) and, separately, tabulate each gene acquired in >=2 FN patients (gene level and pathway level, e.g. RAS pathway, TP53, CDKN2A). IF FOUND: Decide the label from direction first and significance second, evaluate both halves of the claim explicitly, and reserve 'Not verifiable' for missing variables, not for small n: paired samples plus mutation/CNA/SV tables do make the claim testable. SOURCE: https://ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pmc/articles/PMC4877414/ ; https://www.biostathandbook.com/small.html

label: Private-to-later is not proof of acquisition (subclones, unmatched normals)
text: PITFALL: A mutation seen only in the later or metastatic sample need not have arisen after the first sample: single-region biopsies miss pre-existing subclones (spatial heterogeneity), and samples without a matched normal (SOMATIC_STATUS = Unmatched) can carry germline variants that look like private somatic mutations. CHECK: Flag pairs where both samples were reported at the same age or are primary-vs-synchronous-metastasis; check SOMATIC_STATUS per sample and flag private variants at VAF near 50% or 100% in unmatched samples. IF FOUND: Describe the quantity as 'alterations private to the later sample' (an upper bound on true acquisition, applied equally to FP and FN), drop likely-germline private variants from unmatched samples, and do not over-interpret low-VAF private mutations as resistance drivers. SOURCE: https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC7867630/ ; https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC9710689/

reason: Whether a PTC comparator exists in the tables decides what the analysis can and cannot measure and how the result must be reported; building a pseudo-PTC group from cytology columns or importing outside figures would give a wrong or unsupported comparison.
text: The hypothesis is comparative ('compared to PTCs'), so first establish whether the study tables contain a papillary thyroid carcinoma (PTC) group at all. The library's reading of the files is that the cohort may hold only advanced thyroid cancers (the patient table has a PDTC_DEFINITION column and sample rows show Anaplastic Thyroid Carcinoma); this is unconfirmed, so check it. Tabulate CANCER_TYPE_DETAILED and ONCOTREE_CODE in data_clinical_sample.txt, and look for any TERT-status clinical attribute. Columns such as CYTOLOGICAL_PHENOTYPE (e.g. 'tall cell variant') or GROWTH_PATTERN describe the cytology/architecture of an advanced tumour; they are not a PTC sample group and must not be used to build one. If there are no PTC samples, state explicitly which half of the claim is measured from the data (prevalence and clonality of TERT promoter mutations in the advanced tumours) and which half is not in the tables. Do not bring in a PTC prevalence or clonality figure from memory as if it were data: published PTC cohorts were mostly exome-sequenced, exome kits cover the TERT promoter poorly or not at all, so outside PTC numbers are not like-for-like with deep targeted-panel data. Anything taken from outside knowledge must be labelled as background, kept separate from the in-data result, and not tested statistically against the study data. Choose the label by applying the task's own label definitions as written to what you actually found.

reason: Without pre-stated criteria for both halves of the claim, the label can end up resting on only one half, or on thresholds chosen after seeing the numbers.
text: The hypothesis has two separate parts, 'clonal' and 'highly prevalent', and each needs its own criterion written down before looking at the results. For example: prevalence reported per histology and pooled with an exact binomial 95% CI; clonality reported as the proportion of TERT-promoter-mutant tumours whose cancer cell fraction interval includes 1. Fix these definitions first and report both parts separately instead of letting one stand in for the other.

reason: A routine coding-variant filter would delete the very variants the hypothesis is about and produce a false zero prevalence.
text: TERT promoter mutations are non-coding. Any filter that keeps only protein-changing variants (Missense/Nonsense classes, non-empty HGVSp_Short, 'nonsynonymous') silently removes them and yields a prevalence of zero. In a GRCh37/hg19 MAF they sit at chr5:1295228 (C228T, c.-124C>T) and chr5:1295250 (C250T, c.-146C>T), usually with Variant_Classification 5'Flank, Consequence upstream_gene_variant, empty HGVSp, and plus-strand alleles G>A. Rarer promoter variants include tandem CC>TT at 1295228-1295229 and 1295242-1295243, and c.-57A>C. The two hotspots are normally mutually exclusive and heterozygous. List every row with Hugo_Symbol == TERT in data_mutations.txt with Start_Position, Variant_Classification, Reference_Allele, Tumor_Seq_Allele2, t_ref_count and t_alt_count; define 'TERT promoter mutant' by genomic position / 5'Flank class, keep it separate from any coding TERT variants, and never pass the MAF through a nonsynonymous-only filter first.

reason: Stops the team from testing the wrong thing (enzyme abundance or non-histone acetylation) or from choosing a label without checking whether the measured histone sites and Wnt variables are actually there; fixes the primary comparison up front.
text: Where the variables are, and what counts as each. Histone acetylation is measured directly as lysine-acetylation site rows on histone proteins in data_acetylprotein_quantification.txt. Wnt variables are CTNNB1 mutations in data_mutations.txt, Wnt target genes in the mRNA table, and CTNNB1 protein/phosphosites. Confirm this yourself: count the histone site rows and the CTNNB1-mutant samples, and check that they overlap on the same sample ids (acetyl sample columns are patient-style ids such as C3L-00006). If both exist and overlap, the task's definition of 'Not verifiable' (no relevant variables) does not apply, and the label has to come from the test. Do not substitute proxies: mRNA or protein levels of acetyltransferases/deacetylases (EP300, CREBBP, KAT2A/B, HDAC1-3) and acetyl sites on non-histone proteins (EP300/CREBBP auto-acetylation, CTNNB1 K666/K671) are not histone acetylation; report them only as secondary context. Primary test: histone acetyl sites versus Wnt status. Pre-specify, before looking at p-values, that H2B N-terminal sites and H3/H4 tail sites (including H3 K18/K27) get priority, because these are the sites CBP/p300 writes when recruited by beta-catenin/TCF. That mechanism is a reason for choosing which sites to look at first, not evidence about this dataset.

reason: A search for modern histone names would find few or no rows and could wrongly suggest the data hold no histone acetylation; the paralog, numbering and correlated-site issues change how sites are grouped and counted.
text: Finding and reading the histone rows in data_acetylprotein_quantification.txt. Histones are listed under the OLD gene names (HIST1H2BB, HIST2H2BF, HIST1H4G, HIST2H4B, HIST3H3, H3F3A, H2AFZ, H2AFX, H2AFY, H1F0, HIST1H1B ...), not H3C1/H4C1 or plain 'H3'/'H4'. Select them with gene-symbol patterns ^HIST, ^H1F, ^H2AF, ^H3F3; the library expects roughly 130 site rows over roughly 30 gene symbols (confirm the count). A peptide shared by identical paralogs is assigned to one arbitrary paralog, so treat the gene label as a histone-family label (H2B, H3, H4, H2A, H1, macroH2A). Residue numbers may be shifted by +1 from textbook marks if the initiator methionine is counted; compare site numbers with canonical marks to detect this. Neighbouring lysines on one tail (H4 K5/K8/K12/K16; H3 K9/K14, K18/K23, K27/K36; H2B N-terminus) are measured on the same or overlapping multiply-acetylated peptides, so they are strongly correlated mixtures: compute the correlation matrix among histone sites, do not over-interpret one named lysine, and do not count correlated neighbours as independent confirmations. Keep linker histone H1 and macroH2A sites separate from core-histone tail acetylation when summarising.

reason: Prevalence is half the hypothesis and it changes directly with the choice of denominator, sample-versus-patient counting and whether every counted sample was actually assayed at the TERT promoter.
text: Get the prevalence denominator right. A MAF only has rows for samples with at least one called mutation, so counting distinct Tumor_Sample_Barcode values undercounts the profiled tumours. The library reports that in this study the '#sequenced_samples' header line of data_mutations.txt, data_gene_panel_matrix.txt, data_clinical_sample.txt and the .seg file do not obviously list the same sample set (it cites sample P-0000174-T01-IM3 as present in the panel matrix and seg file but not seen in the sequenced_samples header); verify this yourself. Patients may also have more than one sample, which double-counts. Compare the sample sets across those four sources, count samples per PATIENT_ID, and confirm that each sample's mutation panel covers the TERT promoter (MSK-IMPACT panels such as IMPACT341 do; a WES or NA panel may not). Use profiled samples (panel-matrix mutations column not NA) as the denominator, report prevalence per patient and per histology (each advanced histology and pooled) with exact binomial CIs, and say how the figure changes under each plausible denominator.

reason: The choice of Wnt definition decides which tumours are in each group; a pathway-level mutation flag would mix in hypermutated tumours and test mutation burden instead of Wnt.
text: Defining Wnt activation from mutations. Do not flag a tumour as Wnt-active for any non-silent mutation in any Wnt gene (CTNNB1, APC, AXIN1/2, RNF43 ...). In endometrial carcinoma the activating events are CTNNB1 exon 3 degron missense/in-frame mutations (codons D32, S33, G34, S37, T41, S45), while POLE-ultramutated and MSI-hypermutated tumours carry many passenger mutations in long genes such as APC, so an 'any Wnt gene mutated' flag mostly measures mutation burden. Check: list the CTNNB1 rows in data_mutations.txt with protein position and Variant_Classification and count exon 3 hotspot (codons 32-45) versus elsewhere; cross-tabulate any broader Wnt-mutation flag against GENOMICS_SUBTYPE / POLE_SUBTYPE / MSI_STATUS and LOG2_VARIANT_PER_MBP in data_clinical_sample.txt. Use CTNNB1 exon 3 hotspot mutation as the primary binary Wnt variable; treat non-hotspot CTNNB1 and other Wnt-gene mutations in hypermutated tumours as unclassified and run a sensitivity analysis with them excluded and with them included.

reason: It changes how TERT-negative samples are read and adds a sensitivity analysis that guards against a technically driven prevalence estimate or between-group difference.
text: Observed TERT promoter prevalence is a lower bound, because detection sensitivity depends on tumour purity and sequencing depth: variant callers lose sensitivity quickly when purity is below about 50% or VAF below about 10%, and the GC-rich promoter adds dropout. A low-purity tumour with no TERT call may be a false negative, not wild-type. Compare TUMOR_PURITY, specimen type (e.g. SPECIMEN_PRESERVATION_TYPE, frozen vs FFPE, if present) and the number of called mutations between TERT-mutant and TERT-wild-type samples and between histologies, and look for samples whose purity is so low that not even the main driver mutation was called. Report prevalence both in all profiled samples and restricted to samples with adequate purity or a detected driver, treat the all-sample figure as conservative, and do not interpret a prevalence difference between histologies without checking that it is not a purity difference.

reason: Clonality is the other half of the hypothesis; a raw-VAF threshold or a point-estimate CCF threshold would misclassify mutations in impure or low-depth samples, in a direction that can flip the conclusion.
text: Do not call clonality from raw VAF with a fixed cut-off (e.g. 'VAF >= 0.4 is clonal'). VAF depends on tumour purity and local copy number, and advanced/anaplastic tumours are often heavily diluted by stromal and immune cells, so a fixed cut-off labels clonal mutations in low-purity tumours as subclonal. Use the cancer cell fraction: CCF = VAF * (purity*N_T + 2*(1-purity)) / (m*purity), where N_T is the local total tumour copy number and m the number of mutated copies; for a heterozygous mutation in a diploid region this reduces to CCF = 2*VAF/purity. Compute VAF = t_alt_count/(t_ref_count+t_alt_count) for each TERT promoter call and plot it against TUMOR_PURITY from data_clinical_sample.txt: a clonal heterozygous mutation should lie near VAF = purity/2. Also allow for read-count noise: the TERT promoter is more than 80% GC and is captured less efficiently than exons, so its depth can be far below the sample's typical depth. Compare each TERT call's total depth with the median depth of that sample's other mutations, compute a binomial 95% interval for the VAF and propagate it to CCF. Use the interval rule that is standard in the field: clonal when the 95% CI of the CCF includes 1, subclonal only when the upper bound is below 1. Report how many calls are too imprecise to say either way, and do not report 'all clonal' if the intervals are too wide to exclude subclonality.

reason: There is no ready-made Wnt activity column, and the obvious substitutes (pathway gene sets, CTNNB1 level) do not measure activity; the positive control tells the team whether their score is usable.
text: Building a continuous Wnt activity variable. data_clinical_sample.txt has PATHWAY_ACTIVITY_* columns for EGFR, hypoxia, JAK-STAT, MAPK, NFkB, PI3K, TGFb, TNFa, TRAIL, VEGF and p53 but none for WNT, so a Wnt score must be built. Do not build it from pathway MEMBERS (ligands, receptors, CTNNB1 mRNA, the Hallmark WNT_BETA_CATENIN set): member expression does not track pathway activity. Build it from downstream feedback targets in data_mrna_seq_rsem.txt: z-score across samples and average those present of AXIN2, NKD1, LGR5, RNF43, ZNRF3, NOTUM, LEF1, TCF7, SP5, APCDD1. Positive control: the score must be clearly higher in CTNNB1 exon 3 hotspot-mutant tumours than in wild-type; a score that does not separate the mutants is not measuring Wnt and should not be used. Use the validated score as the continuous Wnt variable alongside hotspot status as the binary one, and check that the two definitions agree in direction before concluding. Do not use CTNNB1 mRNA or protein level alone, since activating mutations stabilise beta-catenin rather than induce its transcription.

reason: Copy-number change at the TERT locus can make a clonal mutation look subclonal or the reverse, and the copy-number files are easy to misuse (thresholded calls, purity-uncorrected log2 ratios).
text: Account for local copy number and multiplicity at TERT (chr5p15.33) when estimating clonality. 5p gain, TERT amplification or LOH changes the expected VAF of a clonal mutation: if the mutated allele is the gained one, VAF exceeds purity/2 (CCF above 1 if m=1 is assumed); if the other allele is gained, VAF is lower and the mutation looks subclonal. The discrete values in data_cna.txt (-2..2) are thresholded calls, not absolute copy number, and seg.mean in data_cna_hg19.seg is a log2 ratio that is NOT corrected for purity (low purity compresses it toward 0). For every TERT-promoter-mutant sample, look up the seg.mean of the segment covering chr5:1295228 and the data_cna.txt value for TERT, and convert to tumour copy number with n = (2*2^seg.mean - 2*(1-purity))/purity. If the segment is near 0, the simple diploid formula CCF = 2*VAF/purity is adequate. If it is not, compute CCF under each admissible multiplicity (m=1 and m=number of gained copies), cap at 1, and flag samples whose clonal/subclonal call flips with m.

reason: A pooled comparison can show or hide an association that is really a subtype difference; stratifying or adjusting can change the result.
text: Confounding by histology and genomic subtype. CTNNB1 mutation / Wnt activation in endometrial carcinoma sits almost entirely in endometrioid, copy-number-low tumours and is rare in serous / CNV-high tumours. Subtype and histology change thousands of proteins and modification sites, so a pooled Wnt-versus-histone-acetylation association can be only the endometrioid-versus-serous or subtype difference. Check: cross-tabulate Wnt status against GENOMICS_SUBTYPE (data_clinical_sample.txt) and HISTOLOGIC_TYPE and grade (data_clinical_patient.txt), and test whether the histone acetyl sites differ by subtype/histology on their own. Then repeat the Wnt test (a) within endometrioid tumours only and within CNV-low only, and (b) in a linear model with GENOMICS_SUBTYPE and histology as covariates. Base the conclusion on the stratified/adjusted effect and say explicitly if an association exists only in the pooled data.

reason: Without protein adjustment a change in histone amount is indistinguishable from a change in acetylation, which is what the hypothesis is about.
text: Acetyl-site values track parent-protein abundance. In enrichment TMT data a site's value rises and falls with the amount of its parent protein, so a histone acetyl-site difference by Wnt status may be only a histone (or chromatin/proliferation) abundance difference. Check: for each histone acetyl site, look up the parent protein in data_protein_quantification.txt (row ids look like 'GENE|GENE'), correlate site with protein across samples, and test whether the parent protein itself differs by Wnt status. Test each site adjusted for protein (site ~ Wnt + parent_protein, or the residual of site on protein, or site minus protein) and report both raw and protein-adjusted results. If the exact histone paralog is absent from the protein table, adjust with another measured paralog of the same histone family, or state that the adjustment could not be done. Treat a difference as an acetylation relationship only if it holds after this adjustment.

reason: Every CCF depends on the purity value; if it is biased the clonality call is biased, and a within-sample comparison against the truncal driver gives an independent check that does not depend on purity.
text: Do not rely on the purity column alone. Pathologist-estimated purity agrees only loosely with sequencing-derived purity and tends to be too high; an overestimated purity pushes every CCF down and makes clonal mutations look subclonal, while an underestimate gives CCF above 1. Find out what TUMOR_PURITY is (range, missing values; round numbers suggest a histological estimate). As a calibration, compute CCF for the known truncal driver in each tumour (BRAF V600E, or an NRAS/HRAS/KRAS hotspot): if those come out far from 1, the purity column is biased. Add a purity-free analysis: compare the TERT promoter VAF with the VAF of the truncal driver (or the highest/median VAF of the other somatic mutations) in the SAME sample; a ratio near 1 means TERT is as clonal as the founding driver. Exclude reference mutations in copy-number-altered or LOH regions (e.g. TP53 with 17p loss), and be careful with unmatched samples (see SOMATIC_STATUS if present), where a germline variant at VAF about 0.5 can masquerade as the top somatic VAF. Report both the purity-based and the relative result.

reason: Sets the evidence standard before the team sees p-values; without it either a chance hit or an underpowered null could be over-read.
text: Multiple testing and correlated sites. With roughly 130 histone acetyl sites and several possible Wnt definitions, about 6 sites are expected at p<0.05 by chance, so reporting whichever site/definition pair is significant manufactures a relationship. Histone sites are also strongly inter-correlated, so counting significant sites or permuting features gives inflated set-level significance. Do this: fix the Wnt variable(s) and the histone-site family before looking at p-values; apply Benjamini-Hochberg across all histone sites tested; get a set-level p-value by permuting SAMPLE labels (for example 10,000 permutations of Wnt status, with mean absolute t or the number of sites below p<0.05 as the statistic) so inter-site correlation is preserved; compare the histone-site result with the background of all acetyl sites in the table (the library expects about 10,800). Decision rule to apply whichever way it falls: treat the hypothesis as supported only if sites survive FDR or the sample-permutation set test is significant, with consistent direction across related sites; a few nominal hits that fail FDR are not support; and a null result from a small Wnt-active group is not by itself contradiction, so report the group sizes (the library expects about 95 tumours in total; confirm) and effect sizes with confidence intervals.

reason: The label depends entirely on how 'uncommon' is operationalised; fixing the rule in advance and reporting per gene with proper small-sample intervals prevents a threshold chosen after the fact from deciding the answer.
text: 'Uncommon' is a qualitative word and the hypothesis is a conjunction over three genes (TP53, RB1, ATRX), so the label can be steered by choosing the threshold after seeing the numbers. Before computing any frequency, write down a decision rule (for example: 'uncommon' = upper 95% confidence bound below about 10%; 'common' = lower bound above about 20%). Then, for each gene separately, report altered/profiled patients, the proportion, and a 95% Wilson or Clopper-Pearson interval (not Wald; the cohort is small, under 100 patients, so intervals are wide). Do not report only a pooled figure. If an interval straddles the threshold or the genes disagree, say which gene(s) drive the label: the claim that all three are uncommon is contradicted if any one of them is clearly common, and is supported only if each is clearly rare.

reason: Pooling other uterine sarcoma subtypes, which have different driver profiles, would change the frequencies the hypothesis is about.
text: The hypothesis is about uterine leiomyosarcoma only, but data_clinical_sample.txt has CANCER_TYPE = 'Uterine Sarcoma' with separate CANCER_TYPE_DETAILED / CANCER_TYPE_DETAILED_CODE / ONCOTREE_CODE columns, so the study may mix histologies; do not assume every sample is leiomyosarcoma. Check value_counts of CANCER_TYPE_DETAILED and ONCOTREE_CODE (skip the 4 '#' header lines). If more than one histology is present, restrict every numerator and denominator to uterine leiomyosarcoma (ONCOTREE_CODE ULMS / 'Uterine Leiomyosarcoma'); other subtypes may be shown only as contrast.

reason: The unit of analysis changes both numerator and denominator of the frequency and its confidence interval.
text: Samples are not patients. Sample IDs in this study carry T01/T02/T03 suffixes, so some patients may contribute more than one tumour (e.g. primary and metastasis); counting samples double-counts those patients and breaks independence in a prevalence estimate. Compare the number of unique PATIENT_ID with the number of SAMPLE_ID in data_clinical_sample.txt and list patients with more than one sample. If any exist, compute frequency per patient (a patient is altered if any of their profiled samples is altered, or use one pre-specified sample per patient) and give the per-sample figure only as a sensitivity check.

reason: It fixes what the primary analysis must be. A team that tests baseline ERBB2 against outcome would be analysing the wrong question and could reach any label for the wrong reason.
text: Answer the question that was asked: the hypothesis is about ACQUIRED trastuzumab resistance, i.e. progression after initial benefit on trastuzumab (response or durable stable disease, roughly >= 4 months), not primary resistance (progression at first assessment) and not baseline predictors of benefit. Relating pre-treatment ERBB2 level or heterogeneity to PFS or response tests primary resistance and cannot settle a claim about subclone selection under treatment. Check: use HER2_RESPONSE (CR/PR/SD/POD), HER2_TTP_ON_1ST_LINE_MONTHS and HER2_TX_STATUS to classify each patient who has paired samples, and check that the later sample was taken after progression rather than while the patient was still responding (ON TREATMENT). If so: make the primary analysis the within-patient pre->post change in ERBB2 amplification among patients who progressed after benefit, and report best-response=POD patients and on-treatment samples separately.

reason: A wrong denominator directly inflates or deflates the frequency on which the 'uncommon' judgement rests.
text: Use the right denominator. In cBioPortal-format data a sample with zero called mutations has no rows in data_mutations.txt but was still profiled; using 'samples appearing in the mutation file' (or in the CNA matrix) as the denominator inflates frequency, and counting un-profiled samples as wild-type deflates it. The authoritative record of who was profiled for what is data_gene_panel_matrix.txt (columns mutations, cna, structural_variants; NA = not profiled). Samples span panel versions IMPACT341/410/468 (IM3/IM5/IM6 suffixes). Denominator per data type = samples with a non-NA panel in that file; compare that count with the clinical-sample rows, the unique barcodes in the mutation file and the columns of data_cna.txt. Confirm TP53, RB1 and ATRX have rows in data_cna.txt with non-NA values for every panel version (a gene absent from a panel shows as NA, not 0). If counts differ, use profiled samples/patients as the denominator per gene and per data type; for a union of mutation + CNA + SV, use samples profiled for all three.

reason: The definition of 'loss-of-function mutation' is the numerator of the analysis; a loose or wrong filter changes the result.
text: Not every row in data_mutations.txt is a loss-of-function (LoF) event; the file also holds non-protein-altering rows (its first data row is a TERT 5'Flank promoter variant), so counting 'any row for the gene' overstates LoF. Standard truncating/LoF classes in Variant_Classification are Nonsense_Mutation, Frame_Shift_Del, Frame_Shift_Ins, Splice_Site, Translation_Start_Site (and Nonstop_Mutation). In_Frame_Del/Ins and Missense_Mutation alter the protein but are not automatically LoF. Silent, Intron, 3'UTR, 5'UTR, 3'Flank, 5'Flank, IGR, RNA and Splice_Region are low-consequence and must be excluded. Print value_counts of Variant_Classification for each of the three genes before filtering, confirm none of the low-consequence classes is being counted, and count each patient once per gene even if they carry several mutations in it.

reason: The obvious shortcut (PRE-TX vs POST-TX across all samples) uses the wrong population and the wrong exposure; this defines the cohort that actually bears on the hypothesis.
text: The sample column IMPACT_PRE_POST (PRE-TX / POST-TX) is not guaranteed to mean before/after trastuzumab; it may mean before/after any systemic therapy, and only HER2-positive patients received trastuzumab (look for patient TREATMENT values containing '+BIOLOGIC' and DETAILS_FIRST_LINE_COMMENTS mentioning trastuzumab). Comparing ERBB2-AMP frequency in all POST-TX versus all PRE-TX samples across the whole cohort (reported as ~341 samples, mostly HER2-negative and chemotherapy-only) answers a different question and is confounded by who gets re-biopsied. Check: restrict to patients with baseline HER2 positivity and documented trastuzumab exposure (HER2_RESPONSE / HER2_TTP_ON_1ST_LINE_MONTHS / HER2_TX_STATUS not NA, or trastuzumab in the treatment details) and confirm the POST-TX sample post-dates trastuzumab. If so: analyse only the trastuzumab-treated, baseline-amplified patients as within-patient pairs; treat a cohort-wide unpaired PRE vs POST comparison as supporting context at most. Verify the column names and counts against the files yourself.

reason: Pairing errors or pooled-sample tests would change the count of informative patients and the validity of any test; the heterogeneous sample-ID styles make missed pairs likely.
text: Do not treat samples as independent and do not pair them by sample-name parsing. The library reports roughly 341 samples from roughly 305 patients, with about 34 patients having 2-3 samples, and sample IDs in several styles (P-xxxx-T01-IMx, YJ-her-00x-P1/M1a, s_YJ_her_0xx_P/M/X), so string matching on sample ID can miss pairs; some same-patient pairs may be two PRE-TX regions rather than pre/post. Check: build pairs from PATIENT_ID in data_clinical_sample.txt, tabulate each multi-sample patient's combination of IMPACT_PRE_POST, SAMPLE_TYPE and HER2_IMPACT, and confirm every paired sample has a column in data_cna.txt and rows in data_cna_hg19.seg. If so: make the patient the unit of analysis and use paired methods (exact or mid-p McNemar on discordant pairs for binary AMP status, Wilcoxon signed-rank on the paired ERBB2 log-ratio); never run chi-square/Fisher on pooled samples as if independent; keep PRE-PRE pairs separate as a heterogeneity control.

reason: A single uniform filter across the three genes mis-estimates at least one of them; the gene-specific definition can move the TP53 frequency substantially.
text: TP53 needs a different LoF definition from RB1 and ATRX. Most inactivating TP53 hits are missense mutations in the DNA-binding domain, which saturation-mutagenesis work shows act by loss of function / dominant-negative effect; dropping all Missense_Mutation rows can cut the TP53 frequency by roughly half. For RB1 and ATRX the opposite holds: missense variants are mostly of uncertain significance, so including them would wrongly inflate those genes; only frameshift/nonsense/splice are safely LoF there. Tabulate Variant_Classification separately for TP53, RB1 and ATRX and compute the TP53 frequency two ways: (i) truncating only, (ii) truncating + missense (optionally restricting missense to DNA-binding-domain codons ~100-300 or known hotspots R175, G245, R248, R249, R273, R282). If TP53 missense rows are numerous, report both definitions, treat TP53 DNA-binding-domain missense as LoF in the primary analysis, and keep RB1/ATRX to truncating classes.

text: Read the discrete CNA matrix correctly. The library reports that data_cna.txt in this study holds only -2, 0, 2 and NA: 0 means 'no high-level amplification or deep deletion called', NOT diploid (low-level gains and borderline amplification, fold-change 1.5-2, are coded 0), and NA means the gene is not on that sample's panel version (IMPACT300/341/410/468), not copy-neutral. Check: confirm the ERBB2 row has no NA for the paired samples; cross-check the discrete ERBB2 call against the sample-level HER2_IMPACT (AMP/DIPLOID), HER2_IMPACT_LR and the seg.mean of the segment covering ERBB2 (chr17:37.84-37.89 Mb, hg19), and flag disagreements. If so: analyse the continuous log-ratio alongside the binary call (a drop from high-level to borderline is partial loss / a mixed population, not 'unchanged' or 'diploid'), and exclude NA rather than coding it 0.

reason: It tells the team how to count copy-number events (strict -2 only) and how asymmetrically to weigh a low versus a high observed frequency.
text: Targeted-panel calls are a lower bound on LoF frequency. The discrete CNA value -2 is a 'putative' deep deletion; low tumour purity pulls log-ratios toward 0 so true homozygous deletions can be called -1 or 0, and panels only detect SV breakpoints that fall in captured exons or selected introns. A low observed frequency is therefore weaker evidence for 'uncommon' than a high observed frequency is against it. A value of -1 (shallow loss) is not by itself LoF and must not be counted. In data_cna_hg19.seg, look at seg.mean for segments overlapping TP53 (chr17:7.57-7.59 Mb), RB1 (chr13:48.88-49.06 Mb) and ATRX (chrX:76.76-77.04 Mb), hg19 coordinates; list samples with strongly negative seg.mean (e.g. < -1) that are not -2 in data_cna.txt, and note how many samples are -1. Report the strict frequency (-2 only) as primary and a relaxed one as sensitivity. If the observed frequency is low, state explicitly that under-detection could not be ruled out.

reason: Without a purity check, an artefactual non-amplified call would be counted as evidence of subclone selection; this tells the team how to separate real loss from dilution using the tables they have.
text: Low tumour purity in a post-treatment biopsy can dilute the ERBB2 log-ratio below the panel's amplification threshold (MSK-IMPACT calls AMP at fold-change >= 2, log2 ratio about >= 1; fold-change 1.5-2 is 'borderline') and produce a false 'loss of amplification'. Check, for every post-treatment sample called non-amplified: (a) the continuous ERBB2 value (HER2_IMPACT_LR and the seg segment covering chr17:37.84-37.89 Mb hg19); (b) whether the rest of that sample's seg profile is flat (small spread of seg.mean, other CNAs seen in the paired pre sample also gone); (c) the VAFs, t_alt_count/(t_alt_count+t_ref_count), of mutations shared with the pre sample (e.g. TP53) as a purity proxy. If the profile is flat and shared-mutation VAFs have collapsed: treat the pair as indeterminate, not as loss, and run a sensitivity analysis excluding it; count true loss only when truncal mutations or other CNAs persist at a comparable level while ERBB2 falls.

reason: ATRX copy-number data may be missing or unreliable, which would bias one of the three genes in the conjunction if unnoticed.
text: ATRX is on chromosome X and subject to X-inactivation, so a single truncating hit can abolish function, and copy-number pipelines often treat chrX differently from autosomes: chrX may be missing from the seg file or the discrete CNA matrix, or be coded 'X' vs '23'. (That the pipeline behind this dataset does so is the library's inference, not a documented fact.) Treating a missing ATRX CNA row as 'no deletions' silently biases ATRX downward relative to TP53/RB1. Confirm that ATRX has a row in data_cna.txt with non-NA values, check whether chromosome X/23 occurs in data_cna_hg19.seg, and check SEX in data_clinical_patient.txt. If ATRX CNA is absent or all NA/0, base the ATRX frequency on mutations + SVs only, label it a lower bound, and do not compare it naively with the other two genes.

reason: It gives the operational definition of the hypothesis's key term and the test for whether the data can address it, which governs both the per-pair classification and the choice between a substantive label and 'Not verifiable'.
text: Bulk targeted-panel data cannot show a 'subclone' directly. Two opposite mistakes follow: over-claiming clonal selection from a single lost amplification call, or declaring the question unanswerable because no column is named 'subclone'. The accepted operational evidence for selection of a non-amplified subclone is: the paired samples are clonally related (shared truncal mutations such as TP53 in data_mutations.txt at comparable VAF), other clonal CNAs persist, and the ERBB2 amplicon (ERBB2 plus co-amplified 17q12 neighbours on the panel, e.g. CDK12) is high before treatment and absent after. Check: for each pre/post pair list shared versus private mutations with VAFs, and the 17q12 segment seg.mean in both samples. A pair with retained shared mutations and a lost amplicon counts as evidence of selection for an ERBB2-non-amplified population; a pair that shares no mutations, or whose post sample has no tumour signal, is uninformative and should be dropped. Before choosing 'Not verifiable', establish whether the three ingredients (pre/post pairs, per-sample ERBB2 copy number, trastuzumab exposure/outcome) exist in the tables.

reason: The choice of baseline definition changes the numerator and denominator of the loss rate. I removed the library's quoted loss rates from other published series so the team is not primed toward a result.
text: Guard against baseline misclassification and one-way change. Patients enter a trastuzumab cohort because they tested HER2-positive by IHC/FISH, so on retest status can only move toward negative (regression to the mean), and a tumour that was IHC/FISH-positive but never ERBB2-amplified by sequencing at baseline will look like 'loss' if the clinical HER2 status is used as the pre value. Check: define the pre value from the pre-treatment sequenced sample itself (HER2_IMPACT = AMP, ERBB2 = 2 in data_cna.txt), cross-tabulate it against HER2_IHC_OR_FISH / IHC_HER2, and stratify any loss by baseline IHC score and baseline ERBB2 log-ratio. Count 'loss' only as sequencing-amplified pre -> non-amplified post on the same assay; report separately the patients who were clinically HER2-positive but not amplified by sequencing at baseline, because they bear on primary, not acquired, resistance.

reason: Germline contamination or an ID mismatch between files can inflate or zero out the counts; these checks guard the numerator against artefacts.
text: Not every row is a confident somatic call, and joins between files can silently fail. data_clinical_sample.txt has a SOMATIC_STATUS column (Matched vs possibly Unmatched), the mutation file has Mutation_Status, and data_sv.txt has SV_Status; tumour-only samples can carry unfiltered germline variants. Check value_counts of SOMATIC_STATUS, Mutation_Status and SV_Status, and verify that the sample IDs in the mutation, CNA and SV files all match SAMPLE_ID in the clinical table. An implausibly extreme frequency (near 0% or near 100%) for any gene should first be suspected as a filtering or sample-ID join bug and re-checked before it is accepted. If unmatched samples or germline-flagged rows are found, rerun excluding them as a sensitivity analysis and report whether the frequency changes materially. The label must come from this study's data.

reason: The label hinges on how a null result in a low-event subgroup is read; treating p>0.05 or a significant/non-significant contrast as proof of no benefit would be an invalid basis for the label.
text: Applies only if exposure and outcome variables exist. The hypothesis is a claim of NO benefit in a subgroup, so a non-significant p-value for anticoagulation among ctDNA-negative patients is not by itself evidence for it. Power in time-to-event data comes from the number of events, and ctDNA-negative patients have a lower baseline VTE rate and so fewer events. Count VTE events in each cell (ctDNA-negative x anticoagulated yes/no), report the hazard or risk ratio with its 95% CI, and ask whether the CI excludes a meaningful benefit (roughly HR <= 0.7-0.8); if the CI spans both no effect and meaningful benefit, say the result is inconclusive rather than supportive, and weigh direction and CI, not p>0.05 alone. Do not infer 'works in ctDNA-positive, not in ctDNA-negative' from one subgroup being significant and the other not: fit one model with anticoagulation, ctDNA status and their interaction and report the interaction estimate with CI; also look at absolute risk differences, since the same relative effect gives a smaller absolute benefit at low baseline risk.

text: Applies only if exposure and outcome variables exist. Anticoagulation is not randomised, and three biases can reverse or exaggerate its apparent effect. (a) Confounding by indication: patients are anticoagulated because of a prior VTE, atrial fibrillation or judged high risk, so a naive comparison can show MORE VTE in the anticoagulated and falsely suggest no benefit. Look for prior VTE, indication (prophylactic vs therapeutic), and timing of anticoagulation relative to the blood draw; restrict to patients without prior VTE where possible, adjust for VTE risk factors, and state that residual confounding limits a causal reading. (b) Cancer type: in a pan-cancer cohort it drives both ctDNA detectability and baseline VTE risk (pancreatic, lung, gastric are high-risk), so pooling within ctDNA-negative mixes very different risks. Cross-tabulate CANCER_TYPE against ctDNA status, exposure and outcome; stratify or adjust for cancer type and check the direction of effect is consistent across the larger cancer types. (c) Immortal time: if anticoagulation started after cohort entry (the plasma draw) but patients are labelled anticoagulated from baseline, the pre-start time is VTE-free by construction and inflates benefit. Check whether exposure means 'on anticoagulation at blood draw' or 'ever during follow-up'; if the latter, use a time-varying covariate or a landmark analysis.

text: If an interval column exists, check how it is defined before comparing groups. Radiation-associated sarcoma criteria impose a minimum latent period (variously 6 months, 2 years, or 3-4 years), the start point may be first day of RT, end of RT, or diagnosis of the primary cancer, units may be months or years, and patients with several RT courses have several possible start dates. Read the column description for start event, end event and unit; inspect the minimum and any zero, negative or implausibly small values; check that all groups share the same floor and that there is one value per patient. If units or definitions are mixed across rows, harmonise before testing; if a minimum-latency floor is visible, say that the medians are conditional on it and compare groups only under one definition.

reason: The choice of test structure (omnibus or pooled versus two separate pairwise tests) can flip the conclusion for a claim that must hold against both comparison groups.
text: If the groups and interval exist: the hypothesis is a conjunction (RT-AS lower than RT-MPNST AND RT-AS lower than RT-UPS). A significant 3-group Kruskal-Wallis omnibus, or one test of AS against pooled MPNST+UPS, does not establish it: the omnibus can be driven by a single pair, and pooling lets the larger group mask a null result for the smaller one. Run the two pairwise comparisons separately (AS vs MPNST, AS vs UPS), check the direction of each median difference, and report n per group. Require both pairwise tests to be significant in the stated direction (intersection-union logic: each at alpha 0.05, no extra multiplicity penalty is needed for a conjunction), and also report Dunn or pairwise Wilcoxon p-values with Holm adjustment after the omnibus, so the verdict is shown not to depend on the adjustment choice.

reason: The hypothesis is worded about medians, so the team needs to know that the default rank test answers a slightly different question and when a median-specific check is needed.
text: If the groups and interval exist: rank tests are not tests of medians. Wilcoxon-Mann-Whitney and Kruskal-Wallis test stochastic ordering and can be significant with equal medians, or non-significant with different medians, unless the group distributions share shape and spread; latency intervals are typically right-skewed with unequal spread. Report each group's median with n, IQR and range, and compare distribution shapes. If shapes or spreads differ, support the 'median is lower' claim with a median-targeted analysis alongside the rank test (Mood's median test, a permutation test on the difference in medians, a bootstrap CI for the difference in medians, or quantile regression), and state which estimand each p-value refers to. Mood's test is robust but low-powered at small n.

text: If the groups and interval exist: expect small, unbalanced groups; in radiation-associated sarcoma series MPNST is usually much rarer than angiosarcoma or undifferentiated sarcoma, so the MPNST group may hold only a handful of patients. Count patients (not samples) with a non-missing interval per group and note ties. If any group has fewer than about 10, use exact or permutation p-values (for example scipy.stats.mannwhitneyu with method='exact', or scipy.stats.permutation_test), report an effect size with a confidence interval (Hodges-Lehmann shift or bootstrap median difference), and state the group sizes in the reasoning. Asymptotic p-values and Mood's median test are unreliable or underpowered at such sizes, and a non-significant result at n<10 is weak evidence.

label: Tumour-in-normal contamination: do not require zero germline reads for somatic CALR/JAK2
text: PITFALL: In blood cancers the matched 'germline' sample (buccal swab, saliva, T cells, skin) is often contaminated with tumour cells, so a true somatic driver shows a few percent of reads in the normal; an analyst who requires zero germline reads (or Germline allele percentage == 0) to call a CALR or JAK2 variant somatic will wrongly discard real somatic mutations and may then conclude no CALR mutation exists. CHECK: for every CALR and JAK2 row compare 'Germline allele percentage (%)' with 'Tumor allele burden (%)' (and 'Germline reads' with 'Tumor reads'); look at how much germline signal the study's own curated JAK2 V617F calls carry (the same patients' known drivers calibrate the contamination level). IF FOUND: treat a variant as somatic when the tumour burden is clearly higher than the germline percentage (germline near 0 or a small fraction of tumour), and as germline only when germline is around 50% or 100% or similar to tumour; do not use a hard 'germline == 0' filter, and report the conclusion with and without low-germline-signal rows. SOURCE: https://www.nature.com/articles/s41467-023-44158-2 and https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12672828/

label: Blank optional MAF columns make somatic/gene filters return zero rows
text: PITFALL: Optional MAF columns such as Mutation_Status, Validation_Status, Entrez_Gene_Id, t_alt_count and n_alt_count can be entirely blank in a cBioPortal study file; filtering with Mutation_Status == 'Somatic' (or on Entrez_Gene_Id, or on t_alt_count > 0) then silently returns zero rows, which looks like 'no CALR mutations' or 'no relevant data' and produces a wrong True or Not verifiable. cBioPortal's own convention is that only rows explicitly marked Germline are germline; blank or NA is treated as somatic. CHECK: print value_counts(dropna=False) for Mutation_Status, Validation_Status, Validation_Method and Entrez_Gene_Id before using any of them as a filter, and print the row count before and after each filter step; assert that the known JAK2 V617F rows survive the same filter chain you apply to CALR. IF FOUND: do not filter on blank columns; establish somatic status from the clinical SOMATIC_STATUS (Matched), the Validation_Method text and the study-specific germline/tumour read columns instead, and select genes by Hugo_Symbol. SOURCE: https://github.com/cBioPortal/cbioportal/pull/8692 and https://docs.cbioportal.org/file-formats/

label: TMB definitions shift values ~3-fold across studies
text: PITFALL: Mutation-burden values from different studies are not on one scale: the mutation classes counted and the pipeline move the number by a constant factor (in one whole-exome evaluation, counting all coding mutations including synonymous and indels gave values 3.1-fold higher than missense-only, though rank order was preserved, Spearman 0.99; germline subtraction by database instead of a matched normal inflates counts; laboratories running their own pipelines on the same samples report substantially different values). A verdict of 'high' or 'not high' that rests on a benchmark within about 3-fold of the cohort median is therefore not safe. CHECK: compute the cohort median under each definition available in data_clinical_sample.txt (TOTAL_PER_MB; TOTAL_PER_MB minus SILENT_PER_MB; NUM_NONSILENT_MUTATION/30; missense-only from MISSENSE_MUTATIONS over COVERED_BASES) and measure the ratio of each to the chosen external benchmark. IF FOUND: state the definition used for both the cohort value and the benchmark, compare on the order-of-magnitude scale, and call the result settled only if every definition puts the median on the same side of the benchmark by more than the roughly 3-fold definitional spread; otherwise report the dependence explicitly. SOURCE: https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s40291-019-00408-y ; https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC6618007/ ; https://www.annalsofoncology.org/article/S0923-7534(21)04495-1/fulltext

label: High-risk neuroblastoma criteria when no risk column exists
text: PITFALL: The hypothesis is about high-risk neuroblastoma but the tables carry no risk-group or stage column, so a team may either declare the claim untestable or carve out a wrong 'high-risk' subset (for example MYCN-amplified only). In the standard clinical classification, high-risk is mainly metastatic disease (stage M / INSS 4) in children older than 18 months, plus MYCN-amplified tumours of stage L2, M or MS at any age; MYCN amplification is sufficient but not necessary, and most high-risk patients are MYCN non-amplified older children. CHECK: tabulate AGE from data_clinical_patient.txt (in years; 18 months = 1.5) against MYCN_AMP from data_clinical_sample.txt (note the codes, e.g. 9 may mean unknown in GRADE/MKI) and count patients who are neither older than 1.5 years nor MYCN-amplified; these are the only ones whose high-risk status is doubtful without stage. IF FOUND: if nearly all patients are older than 18 months or MYCN-amplified, treat the whole cohort as the high-risk group and report the cohort median; as a sensitivity analysis recompute the median after dropping the doubtful patients, and do not restrict to MYCN-amplified cases as if that were the definition of high-risk. SOURCE: https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC8500606/ ; https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC10587593/ ; https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC2650388/

label: Sample ID conventions: T01/T02 are specimens not regions; mixed ID styles break joins
text: PITFALL: In MSK-IMPACT style sample IDs (P-0004401-T01-IM5, P-0004401-T02-IM6) the T01/T02 suffix is only a per-patient specimen counter and the IMx suffix tracks the assay version (the panel matrix here pairs IM3 with IMPACT341 and IM5 with IMPACT410); two T-numbers for a patient are separate clinical specimens (often primary and metastasis, or different dates), not multi-region biopsies of one tumour, and the standard IMPACT QA guidance is to ask whether using both samples even makes sense. This study also mixes three ID styles seen in the file headers (P-00xxxxx-T0x-IMx; s_DK_cac_001_P in the seg and mutation files versus p_DK_cac_001 in the patient table; Foundation TRFxxxxxx), so a naive join can silently drop samples or miscount patients. CHECK: Derive patient from the first 9 characters of P- IDs and confirm against PATIENT_ID; count patients versus samples; verify every Tumor_Sample_Barcode, seg ID and CNA column maps to a row of data_clinical_sample.txt; for each multi-sample patient list SAMPLE_TYPE, TISSUE_SEQUENCED and panel. IF FOUND (multi-sample patients are few and are primary/metastasis or cross-panel specimens): do not describe the cohort as multi-region sequenced, and report how many patients truly have two or more comparable samples of one lesion (possibly zero). SOURCE: https://mskcc-epi-bio.github.io/gnomeR/articles/qa-impact-data.html and https://www.synapse.org/Synapse:syn7222066/discussion/threadId=9817

label: CNA discordance between samples is confounded by purity and thresholds
text: PITFALL: Copy-number differences between two samples of one patient are easily manufactured by purity and ploidy: the observed log2 ratio of a real event shrinks toward 0 as tumour purity falls (a one-copy loss is log2(1/2) = -1 only at 100% purity, about -0.4 at 50%), so thresholded discrete calls in data_cna.txt (-2/-1/0/1/2) and seg.mean values in data_cna_hg19.seg flip between samples of differing purity without any biological heterogeneity; data_cna.txt here also contains NA for genes not on a sample's panel. CHECK: Before calling a CNA 'private' to one sample, compare TUMOR_PURITY of the two samples, look at the raw seg.mean of the same region in the partner (is it shifted in the same direction but below threshold?), and exclude genes that are NA in either sample. IF FOUND: count as copy-number heterogeneity only events with a clearly opposite or absent signal in a partner of adequate purity (roughly 30% or more), prefer segment-level log-ratio comparison after purity scaling over discrete calls, and report CNA-based and mutation-based heterogeneity separately. SOURCE: https://cnvkit.readthedocs.io/en/stable/calling.html and https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC5027494/ and https://www.nature.com/articles/s41467-020-17967-y

label: Independent primaries versus clonally related samples
text: PITFALL: Two tumour samples from one patient may be independent primaries rather than parts of one clonal tumour (multifocal synchronous or metachronous cancers arise from field cancerisation in chronic inflammation such as IBD); total genomic discordance between independent tumours is inter-tumour difference, not intratumour heterogeneity, and it would inflate any 'ITH present' count. CHECK: For each within-patient sample pair count shared versus private somatic mutations and shared copy-number breakpoints; a pair sharing no somatic mutation (after removing germline-looking and hotspot-only coincidences such as a common KRAS or TP53 hotspot) should be treated as possibly independent; formal clonality tests compare observed sharing with that expected by chance from population frequencies of each alteration. IF FOUND (pairs with zero or only hotspot sharing): exclude them from the ITH denominator or report them separately as likely independent tumours. SOURCE: https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC3145177/

label: Library verification status of earlier pitfall facts
text: LIBRARY NOTE (bd11, second session): Two of the earlier library facts were re-checked against their sources and hold as written: the Cell Reports replicate study states that a cancer-only pipeline gave about 69% false-positive somatic calls and that 34-80% of discordant variants readable as intratumour heterogeneity were technical noise (https://www.cell.com/cell-reports/fulltext/S2211-1247(18)31635-8), and the Scientific Reports TCGA study states that MATH/VAF-distribution heterogeneity measures are sensitive to the mutation caller and are largely driven by copy number (https://www.nature.com/articles/s41598-018-29154-7). The other source links in the earlier facts were not re-opened in this session. The library did not tabulate the data; the tumour-type observation (colitis-associated colorectal headers, no kidney columns seen) comes from file headers and first rows only and must be confirmed by tabulating CANCER_TYPE and ONCOTREE_CODE.

label: Pitfall: proliferation confounds histone acetylation vs Wnt
text: PITFALL: Proliferation rate is a hidden driver of bulk histone acetyl signals: newly synthesised histone H4 is diacetylated at K5 and K12 (by HAT1) before replication-coupled deposition and deacetylated within about an hour, and histone protein synthesis itself is S-phase coupled, so H4K5ac/K12ac and histone abundance rise with the fraction of cycling cells; a Wnt-versus-histone-acetylation association (or its absence) can therefore reflect how fast Wnt-active tumours proliferate (CTNNB1-mutant tumours are mostly low-grade) rather than Wnt-directed acetylation. CHECK: build a proliferation score from data_mrna_seq_rsem.txt (mean z-score of MKI67, TOP2A, PCNA, MCM2-7, CCNB1, BUB1, those present) or use MKI67/PCNA/MCM protein from data_protein_quantification.txt; correlate it with each histone acetyl site and compare it between Wnt groups; also compare HISTOLOGIC_GRADE_FIGO between Wnt groups. IF FOUND: add the proliferation score (and grade) as a covariate in site ~ Wnt, report the adjusted effect, and interpret H4 K5/K8/K12 N-terminal sites separately from p300/CBP-type marks (H3K18/K27, H2B N-terminus), since only the latter are the expected Wnt/beta-catenin readout. SOURCE: https://www.jbc.org/article/S0021-9258(19)56461-4/fulltext ; https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC10003558/ ; https://journals.plos.org/ploscompbiol/article?id=10.1371%2Fjournal.pcbi.1010604

label: Pitfall: EP300/CREBBP mutations confound Wnt vs histone acetylation
text: PITFALL: Mutations in the histone acetyltransferase genes themselves are a competing cause of histone acetylation differences: EP300 is mutated in roughly 7 percent of endometrial carcinomas (CREBBP also recurrently), p300/CBP are the enzymes that write H3K18ac, H3K27ac and H2B N-terminal acetylation, and in other tumour types CREBBP/EP300 coding mutations cluster in TMB-high / MSI tumours; if such mutations are unevenly spread between Wnt-active and Wnt-inactive tumours they can create or hide the Wnt association. CHECK: from data_mutations.txt flag tumours with truncating or HAT/bromodomain missense mutations in EP300 or CREBBP (and note KAT2A/KAT2B, HDAC1-3 if any), cross-tabulate against CTNNB1 hotspot status and GENOMICS_SUBTYPE, and test whether the flagged tumours differ in the p300/CBP-type histone sites. IF FOUND: rerun the Wnt test excluding HAT-mutant tumours or with HAT-mutation status as a covariate, and do not present a HAT-mutation effect as a Wnt effect. SOURCE: https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/27881443/ ; https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11812348/ ; https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12650065/

label: Pitfall: fragile tests with small unbalanced Wnt group and outliers
text: PITFALL: With a small Wnt-active group (CTNNB1 hotspot mutants are a minority of about 95 tumours) and heavy-tailed TMT log-ratios, a per-site Student t-test or Pearson correlation is fragile: the t-test is only robust to non-normality when groups are not small and there are no outliers, per-site variance estimates from few samples are erratic, and one or two extreme tumours can create or destroy a Pearson correlation between a Wnt score and an acetyl site. CHECK: for the top sites compare Welch t-test with Wilcoxon rank-sum and Pearson with Spearman, plot the values by group, and redo the test leaving out each of the most extreme samples; check group variances. IF FOUND: use Welch (unequal variance) or a moderated linear model (limma-style, which also takes covariates such as subtype, plex, purity and tolerates NA without imputation) as primary and require the rank-based test to agree in direction and rough significance; discard associations that disappear when a single sample is removed. SOURCE: https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC4373093/ ; https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC8015007/ ; https://mrctoxbioinformatics.github.io/Proteomics_data_analysis/Markdowns/Stats_diff_abundance_TMT.html

label: Selection tests underpowered at small n; non-significance is not contradiction
text: PITFALL: A formal driver/selection test (dNdScv, MutSigCV-style, binomial excess over background) is badly underpowered in a cohort of a few dozen tumours with a UV-level background rate: saturation analysis shows 600-5000 samples per tumour type are needed to find genes mutated at intermediate frequency (2-20%), the more the higher the background rate. A non-significant q-value for a gene here is therefore not evidence that the gene is rarely mutated, and treating it as a contradiction would wrongly reject a descriptive frequency claim. CHECK: run the same test on accepted cSCC drivers (TP53, NOTCH1, NOTCH2, CDKN2A, FAT1) in this cohort; note how many of them reach significance and at what mutated-sample fraction; compare the four hypothesis genes' effect sizes (observed/expected, dN/dS point estimate with interval) rather than only their p-values. IF FOUND: if known drivers at similar frequency also fail significance, the test cannot discriminate at this n; then judge the hypothesis ('mutations frequently affect gene X') on prevalence with a confidence interval and rank relative to controls, report the selection test as inconclusive rather than negative, and keep 'significantly mutated' and 'frequently mutated' as separate statements. SOURCE: https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC4048962/ ; https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC2820387/

label: Adjacent-skin / contaminated matched normal distorts calls; avoid hard n_alt filter
text: PITFALL: In skin cancer the matched 'normal' is often adjacent or nearby skin (or may be contaminated by tumour cells); sun-exposed normal skin carries UV-induced clonal mutations in cancer genes, and tumour-in-normal contamination puts tumour alleles into the normal. Tumour-normal subtraction then under-calls real somatic mutations, and an analyst's own strict filter on normal alt reads (n_alt_count = 0) removes more of them, lowering per-gene frequency. The opposite error also exists: a shallow normal (low n_ref_count+n_alt_count) cannot exclude germline variants. label: Mutation class pattern (truncating share, hotspots) vs raw counts
text: PITFALL: Counting mutated samples ignores what kind of mutations they are. A gene that is a real target usually shows a characteristic pattern (the 20/20 rule: tumour suppressors have >20% inactivating mutations - nonsense, frameshift, splice site - spread along the gene; oncogenes have >20% missense at recurrent positions), whereas a passenger shows scattered missense in proportion to silent mutations. But recurrence at one position is not proof either: UV and other processes create passenger hotspots at inherently mutable sites. CHECK: for each of the four genes tabulate protein-altering variants by class (truncating vs missense vs in-frame), count silent mutations in the same gene, compare the gene's truncating share to the cohort-wide truncating share among all protein-altering mutations (exact binomial test), list any amino-acid position hit in 2 or more patients, and note whether mutations are C>T / CC>TT at dipyrimidines (UV type). IF FOUND: use the pattern as supporting or weakening evidence alongside prevalence - a truncating share clearly above the cohort baseline supports the gene being 'affected' as a target, a missense-only profile with matching silent counts is what background predicts; state this as a qualifier, since the hypothesis as worded is about frequency and can be met on prevalence alone. label: PITFALL detection floor and hotspot rescue truncate VAFs
text: PITFALL: Calls in a clinical panel MAF are truncated by the caller's floor, and the floor differs for hotspots. The MSK-IMPACT pipeline requires depth >=20 and calls known hotspots at >=8 mutant reads and >=2% VAF but non-hotspot mutations only at >=10 mutant reads and >=5% VAF (detection limit about 2% for hotspots, 5% for others). So (a) subclonal mutations below the floor are never in the table, and 'every detected TERT promoter mutation is clonal' is partly a selection effect in low-purity tumours, and (b) a within-sample comparison of TERT VAF against other mutations is asymmetric because the comparators cannot appear below 5%. CHECK: look at the lowest t_alt_count and VAF among all calls and among TERT promoter calls (Hotspot column), and for each sample compute the smallest CCF that could have been detected, about 2*floor/purity. IF FOUND: state clonality as 'clonal among detected', compare TERT against the truncal driver hotspot (BRAF/RAS, same floor) rather than against all mutations, and say in which low-purity samples a subclonal TERT mutation could not have been seen at all. SOURCE: https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC4940024/ ; https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC5808190/

label: Tumour purity confounds TERT call vs TERT expression
text: PITFALL: Tumour purity is a shared cause of both variables in a mutation-vs-expression comparison on bulk tumour. Low purity lowers variant allele fraction so somatic calls are missed (mutation counts rise with purity across TCGA callers), and it also dilutes mRNA of a tumour-cell-specific gene such as TERT, which normal brain and immune cells do not express. Low-purity samples therefore land in the 'no call' group with low TERT expression for reasons unrelated to promoter biology, which can create or enlarge an apparent 'mutant is higher' difference; this acts in the opposite direction to the dilution of the wild-type group by hidden mutants. CHECK: the clinical tables have no purity column, so build a proxy per sample: the amplitude of clonal arm-level events in data_cna_hg19.seg (e.g. absolute seg.mean of chr10 loss / chr7 gain, or of CDKN2A deep deletion), the VAF (t_alt_count/(t_alt_count+t_ref_count)) of the sample's other clonal mutations, and TMB_NONSYNONYMOUS; compare the proxy between TERT-called and no-call groups and correlate it with TERT expression. IF FOUND (groups differ in purity proxy, or proxy correlates with TERT expression): keep the unadjusted comparison as the headline, then add a purity-adjusted check (rank regression or logistic model with the proxy as covariate, or restrict to samples above a purity-proxy threshold) and say whether direction and size hold; do not present a difference that vanishes after adjustment as proof of promoter-driven elevation, and do not present a null in low-purity data as support for 'no correlation'. SOURCE: https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC7785586/ ; https://www.nature.com/articles/ncomms9971 ; https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC8419469/ ; https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC10154864/

label: Ordered groups: exact trend test is supplementary only
text: PITFALL: Treating the three histologic groups as unordered when they are an ordered grade (LEP low < ACI/PAP intermediate < MIP/SOL high), or the opposite error of letting a trend test stand in for the hypothesis. An unordered 3x2 Fisher test wastes power on ordinal groups, but the asymptotic Cochran-Armitage trend test is unreliable when the event (BRAF V600E) has only a handful of cases, and a significant trend can be driven entirely by LEP vs the rest while ACI/PAP and MIP/SOL are equal, which would not support 'MIP/SOL lower than both'. CHECK: Lay out the 3x2 table in grade order and see whether the V600E proportion falls monotonically; if a trend test is run, use an exact/permutation p-value (e.g. permute the V600E labels 100,000 times and recompute the Cochran-Armitage statistic with scores 1,2,3, fixed seed), not the chi-square approximation. IF FOUND: Report the exact trend test only as a supplementary, more powerful check of direction; keep the two pairwise comparisons (MIP/SOL vs LEP, MIP/SOL vs ACI/PAP) with per-group proportions and exact CIs as the basis of the verdict. SOURCE: https://online.stat.psu.edu/stat504/Lesson04 ; https://www.stata.com/manuals/rnptrend.pdf ; https://doi.org/10.1515/ijb-2014-0013

label: Do not re-filter hotspot calls or drop panel versions
text: PITFALL: Re-filtering MSK-IMPACT calls with a home-made threshold or dropping older panel versions. MSK-IMPACT calls known hotspots such as BRAF V600E at a lower threshold (about 2% variant allele fraction with at least 8 alt reads) than non-hotspot variants (about 5% VAF, at least 10 alt reads, depth above 20), so imposing a blanket VAF>=5% or alt-read filter deletes legitimate low-purity V600E calls and can do so unevenly across subtypes; and the panel versions are nested (341 genes within 410 within 468; sample-ID suffixes IM3/IM5/IM6), with BRAF on every version, so no sample should be excluded from a BRAF denominator because of panel version. Samples called without a matched normal may carry germline variants, but V600E is not a germline polymorphism. CHECK: Tabulate panel version (gene panel matrix 'mutations' column or the IM3/IM5/IM6 suffix) by subtype group; list t_alt_count, depth and VAF of each V600E call; look at the Mutation_Status column for non-somatic entries. IF FOUND: Accept the MAF calls as delivered for the primary count (no extra VAF filter), keep all panel versions in the denominator, and mention any V600E call below 5% VAF as a caveat rather than removing it. label: Testing a no-correlation claim needs paired data and an interval, not a p-value
text: PITFALL: A claim of 'no correlation' cannot be supported by a non-significant p-value alone (absence of evidence), and it is contradicted only by a paired analysis that shows a positive correlation; lack of association needs an equivalence-style argument and often very large n. CHECK: first confirm that paired panel and WES TMB values exist on the same tumours; if they do, report the correlation with a 95 percent confidence interval and see whether the interval lies above zero (contradicts the claim), lies wholly inside a small band around zero such as |r| < 0.3 (supports it), or straddles both (inconclusive). IF FOUND (no paired values at all): neither support nor contradiction can be computed, so do not fill the gap with general knowledge that panel TMB usually tracks WES TMB; label by what the tables can test. SOURCE: https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC5502906/ ; https://doi.org/10.1348/000711009x475853 ; https://doi.org/10.5334/pb-51-2-109
