label: Compare the two GCB subsets head-to-head, not each vs rest
text: PITFALL: To claim that two GCB subsets have different outcomes they must be compared with each other directly; showing that one subset differs significantly from the remaining DLBCLs (or from a reference cluster) while the other does not is not evidence that the two differ, because a difference in significance is not a significant difference. CHECK: Run one head-to-head test restricted to the two GCB-enriched subsets (log-rank and a Cox hazard ratio with 95 percent CI for subset A versus subset B), not separate each-versus-rest tests. IF FOUND: Base the outcome half of the hypothesis on the direct two-group hazard ratio and its CI; report each-versus-rest results only as context. SOURCE: https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC5687944/ ; https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC1914513/ ; https://www.statisticsdonewrong.com/significant-differences.html

label: OS diluted by non-lymphoma deaths in older patients; PFS vs OS
text: PITFALL: Overall survival in a cohort that includes elderly-only trial patients (the patient table has AGE_AT_DIAGNOSIS and an IPI age factor, and one cohort is an older-patient trial series) is diluted by deaths unrelated to lymphoma, which can hide a real difference in lymphoma control between genetic subsets or create one if the subsets differ in age; in older lymphoma patients OS and lymphoma-specific survival can differ by tens of percentage points. The data carry no cause of death, so a competing-risk analysis is not possible. CHECK: Compare age distribution between the two subsets; analyse PFS and OS separately; count how many PFS events are deaths without a different PFS time (PFS time equal to OS time with both events). IF FOUND: Treat PFS as the endpoint closest to disease biology, adjust or stratify OS for age (or IPI), and do not read a null OS result alone as proof of equal outcome. SOURCE: https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC8882124/ ; https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC13530942/ ; https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC4562529/

label: Unequal follow-up and thin KM tails in small subsets
text: PITFALL: Kaplan-Meier curves for small subsets are unreliable in their right-hand tail, where few patients remain at risk, and pooled cohorts can have very different follow-up lengths, so a late separation or late crossing of curves (or a subset drawn mostly from a short-follow-up cohort) can drive or mask a log-rank difference. CHECK: Compute median follow-up per subset and per COHORT with the reverse Kaplan-Meier method (swap event and censoring), print numbers at risk at 12, 24, 36 and 60 months for each subset, and note the time after which fewer than about 10 to 20 percent of patients remain at risk. IF FOUND: Compare survival at fixed landmarks inside the well-observed window (for example 2-year or 3-year PFS with CIs), or truncate follow-up at a common horizon before the log-rank/Cox test, and say so. SOURCE: https://academic.oup.com/ije/article/47/3/850/4851146 ; https://doi.org/10.1002/pst.2300 ; https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC3932959/

label: Double-hit (MYC+BCL2) cases can drive GCB subset outcome gap
text: PITFALL: GCB-DLBCL is prognostically heterogeneous for a known reason: tumours with concurrent MYC and BCL2 rearrangements (double-hit, almost exclusively of germinal-centre origin, roughly 10 percent of DLBCL) do poorly on R-CHOP, so an outcome gap between two GCB subsets may be carried by a handful of double-hit cases rather than by the subset as a whole; MYC rearrangements are also under-called by exome/capture sequencing, so double-hit status is incompletely known. CHECK: From data_sv.txt flag samples with both a MYC and a BCL2 structural variant, tabulate them by subset, and rerun the head-to-head survival comparison with those cases removed or with double-hit as a covariate. IF FOUND: If the difference vanishes without double-hit cases, report that the outcome difference is real but concentrated in that group; if it persists, state that it is not explained by detected double-hit status (with the caveat about missed MYC events). SOURCE: https://ashpublications.org/thehematologist/article/doi/10.1182/hem.V16.2.9388/463104/Defining-the-Poor-Prognosis-of-Double-Hit ; https://ascopubs.org/doi/full/10.1200/JCO.18.01583 ; https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC5572137/

label: FFPE, purity and coverage confound mutation-frequency comparisons
text: PITFALL: Mutation detection depends on sample type and quality: FFPE DNA is degraded and carries artificial sequence changes, and low tumour purity or low coverage lowers the allele fraction and the sensitivity for real mutations; the sample table has SAMPLE_COLLECTION_SOURCE, PURITY_ABSOLUTE and MEAN_TARGET_COVERAGE_TUMOR, and the MAF has FFPE/oxoG filter columns, so apparent differences in alteration frequency between subsets can partly reflect which subset holds more FFPE, low-purity or low-coverage samples. CHECK: Tabulate SAMPLE_COLLECTION_SOURCE and compare purity and mean coverage between the two subsets (Fisher and Mann-Whitney); look at whether total and silent mutation density differ by sample type. IF FOUND: If the subsets are unbalanced, repeat the gene-frequency comparison within one sample type or stratified (Cochran-Mantel-Haenszel), and give more weight to clonal, recurrent driver-gene alterations than to total mutation counts. SOURCE: https://journals.plos.org/plosone/article?id=10.1371%2Fjournal.pone.0144162 ; https://www.nature.com/articles/s41587-021-00994-5 ; https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC4048335/

label: Multiple testing and low power in gene-level subset comparisons
text: PITFALL: Comparing every gene in an exome MAF between two small subsets runs thousands of Fisher tests, most on genes mutated in one or two samples where no p-value below 0.05 is even attainable; uncorrected p-values produce false positives, while correcting over all genes destroys power, and a gene that is non-significant in a small subset is not shown to be equally frequent. CHECK: Fix the gene list before testing (for example significantly mutated genes from data_mutsig.txt at q below 0.1 plus recurrent SV targets, or genes altered in at least about 5 percent of samples), count the tests, and apply Benjamini-Hochberg correction over that list. IF FOUND: Report per-subset frequencies and odds ratios with CIs for the pre-filtered list with FDR-adjusted p-values, and describe genes as enriched in a subset only when the effect size is large and the adjusted p-value supports it. SOURCE: https://doi.org/10.1214/10-aoas438 ; https://ashpublications.org/blood/article/142/6/561/495422/Genetic-subdivisions-of-follicular-lymphoma

label: Annotators disagree on actionability; driver is not actionable
text: PITFALL: Independent annotators do not agree on which variants are actionable, so a hand-built rule table is one opinion, not a measurement: for level-1 drug actionability of gene-variant-diagnosis combinations two services (Watson for Genomics and OncoKB) agreed only moderately (kappa 0.44; 27 combinations called by both, 58 by one alone, 6 by the other alone), and for pathogenicity agreement was 30-76% with kappa from -0.26 to 0.22. 'Oncogenic/driver' is also not the same as 'actionable': TP53, most KRAS and CDKN2A alterations are frequent drivers with limited or no actionability. CHECK: build the rule table twice, a strict one (standard-care, tumour-type matched) and a permissive one (any targetable driver in any tumour type), list the genes that contribute most hits under each, and confirm none of the count comes from TP53/CDKN2A/non-G12C KRAS style drivers. IF FOUND: if strict and permissive tables fall on opposite sides of 20%, the verdict rests on the definition; say so and choose the label on that basis rather than presenting one table's number as the data's answer. SOURCE: https://ascopubs.org/doi/10.1200/PO.19.00118 ; https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC10784742/

label: Do not VAF-filter plasma calls; classify by variant identity
text: PITFALL: In plasma cfDNA, true driver alterations are often present at very low allele fraction (in one advanced lung cancer series median cfDNA fraction was 0.7%, a quarter of samples had VAF below 1%, and 3 of 17 EGFR/ALK-positive samples were below 1% yet responded to treatment), so filtering mutations by a tissue-style VAF or read-depth threshold removes real actionable calls; about a third of plasma point mutations were variants of unknown significance, so counting every call inflates it. CHECK: look at t_alt_count/(t_alt_count+t_ref_count) for calls in actionable genes by panel (ACCESS129 vs IMPACT); see how many actionable calls would be lost at a 1%, 2% or 5% VAF cut. IF FOUND: do not add a VAF filter of your own to the released calls; classify by variant identity instead, and report the count with and without low-VAF calls only as a sensitivity check. SOURCE: https://www.annalsofoncology.org/article/S0923-7534(19)60121-3/fulltext

label: Pitfall: hypermutated samples as false carriers
text: PITFALL: Hypermutated / mismatch-repair-deficient tumours contaminate gene-altered groups. A small share of prostate tumours sequenced on targeted panels are hypermutated (MSI-high or replication-repair deficient) and carry many passenger mutations in cancer genes, so a hypermutated sample can be counted as AR-, SPOP- or TP53-'altered' through a passenger variant; with few AR and SPOP carriers, one or two such samples can move the hazard ratio. Even recurrent 'hotspot' sites can be passengers at highly mutable positions. CHECK: list MSI_TYPE, MSI_SCORE and TMB_NONSYNONYMOUS (data_clinical_sample.txt) for every carrier of each gene; flag carriers that are MSI Instable or have TMB far above the cohort median and whose only alteration in the gene is a non-hotspot missense. IF FOUND: rerun each gene's Cox/log-rank with those samples excluded or reclassified as wild-type, and report whether direction and size hold; do not let the verdict rest on them. label: Compound claim: two readings of 'focal amplifications', conjunction logic
text: PITFALL: The phrase 'KIT mutations and focal amplifications' can be read two ways (focal amplification of KIT itself at 4q12, usually co-amplified with PDGFRA and KDR; or focal amplifications of any gene as a general feature of the subtype), and in the literature both are measured with copy-number assays (array CGH, SNP arrays with GISTIC, qPCR, FISH) that are separate from mutation sequencing, so neither reading can be scored from a MAF, and an analyst who picks one reading silently or scores only the mutation half will mis-state what the label rests on. CHECK: write down which reading you adopt, confirm for BOTH readings whether any per-sample copy-number variable exists in the supplied files, and record the status of each conjunct separately (supported / contradicted / no variable). IF FOUND (one conjunct has no variable): apply conjunction logic explicitly when choosing the label, i.e. a compound claim is contradicted by the data if its testable conjunct is contradicted, whereas support for only the testable conjunct leaves the other conjunct unexamined; say in the reasoning exactly which part the label rests on and which part was not testable. SOURCE: https://aacrjournals.org/clincancerres/article/14/21/6821/73163/KIT-Gene-Mutations-and-Copy-Number-in-Melanoma and https://doi.org/10.1634/theoncologist.2018-0528 and https://doi.org/10.1200/jco.2006.06.2984.

label: Enrichment is relative: low absolute KIT frequency is not contradiction
text: PITFALL: 'Characterized by enrichment of KIT mutations' is a relative claim, not a majority claim: even in the melanoma classes where KIT is a recognised driver (acral, mucosal, chronically sun-damaged) only roughly 10 to 30 percent of tumours carry a KIT mutation and non-CSD cutaneous melanoma is below 5 percent, so judging the hypothesis false because most Triple-WT tumours are KIT wild-type, or true because a single KIT-mutant Triple-WT tumour exists, are both errors. CHECK: report the KIT-mutated fraction in Triple-WT and in each other subtype with exact (Clopper-Pearson) confidence intervals, the fold difference/odds ratio, and what share of all KIT hotspot mutations in the cohort fall in Triple-WT compared with the share of samples that are Triple-WT. IF FOUND (low absolute frequency but clearly higher rate than every other subtype): treat that as enrichment; if the Triple-WT rate is equal to or lower than the other subtypes for both any-nonsilent and hotspot-only definitions with adequate sample size, treat that as contradiction; if intervals are too wide to tell, say so. SOURCE: https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12650433/ and https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC4447200/.

label: Mutation-load bias runs against low-TMB subtype drivers; KIT hotspot ranges
text: PITFALL: Driver genes of a low-mutation-load subtype look anti-correlated with everything else because most genes are hit more often as tumour mutation load rises; here that bias runs AGAINST the hypothesis, since passenger KIT variants accumulate in the UV-high BRAF/RAS/NF1 tumours and raise the comparator's raw KIT frequency, so a raw any-nonsilent odds ratio near 1 must not be read as contradiction before passengers are separated from drivers. About 70 percent of genuine KIT driver mutations in melanoma fall in four hotspots: L576 (exon 11), K642 (exon 13), W557 to V560 (exon 11) and D816 to A829 (exon 17). CHECK: for every KIT variant list Protein_position, subtype and the sample's TMB; flag whether it lies in those four hotspot ranges; compare silent KIT mutation counts and median TMB of KIT-mutated versus KIT-wild-type samples within each subtype (KIT-mutant comparator samples with very high TMB and non-hotspot positions are probable passengers). IF FOUND: make the hotspot-restricted comparison (and/or a TMB-stratified or TMB-adjusted comparison) the primary analysis and report the any-nonsilent comparison as secondary; if the two disagree, explain which variants drive the difference. SOURCE: https://www.cell.com/cell/fulltext/S0092-8674(19)30503-3 and https://doi.org/10.1097/cmr.0000000000000116.

label: Pitfall: subset loss still counts as association
text: PITFALL: Reading 'most post-trastuzumab tumours keep ERBB2 amplification' as support for 'not associated'. Acquired trastuzumab resistance has several mechanisms, so loss of HER2 is expected only in a subset: paired pre/post-progression series in gastric/GEJ cancer report loss of HER2 positivity in 29% (14/48), 32% (7/22) and 61% (20/33) of patients, against ~7-12% discordance without anti-HER2 therapy; the rest progress with HER2 retained (some with other RTK/RAS/PI3K changes). CHECK: among baseline-amplified, trastuzumab-treated patients with a post-treatment sample, compute the fraction that lost amplification (with exact CI) and ask whether it exceeds background, not whether it exceeds 50%. IF FOUND (loss clearly above ~10% background in clonally related pairs): that is evidence FOR an association between selection of a non-amplified population and acquired resistance, i.e. it contradicts a 'not associated' claim even though the majority retain amplification; retained-amplification cases with new EGFR/MET/KRAS/PIK3CA alterations are a different mechanism and are neutral to this hypothesis. SOURCE: https://doi.org/10.1007/s10120-018-0891-1 ; https://www.ejcancer.com/article/S0959-8049(18)31394-7/abstract ; https://doi.org/10.1002/ijc.30408

label: Pitfall: unpaired PRE vs POST contrast with IHC/FISH baseline as fallback
text: PITFALL: Declaring the hypothesis 'Not verifiable' (or resting everything on a handful of NGS pairs) because few patients have both a pre- and a post-trastuzumab sequenced sample, and because there is no untreated 'non-resistant' comparison arm. The data also allow an unpaired second line of evidence: every trastuzumab-treated patient was clinically HER2-positive (HER2_IHC_OR_FISH = POS) before treatment, and each sequenced sample is flagged PRE-TX or POST-TX. On the same assay, NGS-vs-IHC/FISH concordance in untreated tumours is ~98% (248/252 in the MSK-IMPACT validation; discordances came from low tumour content and heterogeneity). label: Pitfall: germline variants and panel version confound clonal-relatedness check
text: PITFALL: The 'shared truncal mutation' test of clonal relatedness is corrupted by germline variants and by panel differences. In this study 318 of 341 samples are SOMATIC_STATUS = Unmatched (tumour-only; only the 23 retrospective YJ-her samples are Matched), and paired samples can be on different panel versions (IMPACT300/341/410/468). Tumour-only calls retain germline variants, which are shared by ANY two samples from the same person, so they prove sample identity, not that the non-amplified post-treatment tumour descends from the amplified clone; and a mutation 'private' to the later sample may just be in a gene absent from the earlier, smaller panel. CHECK: for each pair, list shared variants with VAF in both samples and dbSNP_RS; distrust shared variants with VAF ~0.5 (or ~1.0) in both samples or with an rs ID and no hotspot/driver annotation; for private variants confirm the gene is covered in both samples (gene row is non-NA in data_cna.txt for both, panel from data_gene_panel_matrix.txt). IF FOUND: base relatedness on recognised somatic drivers (e.g. TP53 truncating/hotspot, Hotspot = 1) and shared copy-number breakpoints in the seg file, weighting rare shared mutations more than common hotspots; restrict private-mutation claims to genes on both panels. SOURCE: https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC5477989/ ; https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC5677588/ ; https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC4649945/

CHECK: in data_mutations.txt read the HGVSc/HGVSp_Short/Transcript_ID columns for CDKN2A rows (all 17 CDKN2A rows, in 17 different samples of 108, are annotated on ENST00000304494 = p16INK4a, so the mutation calls are p16-level; 11 are truncating/splice, 2 in-frame deletions, 4 missense); then see whether CDKN2A protein and RNA are actually low in the truncating-mutant tumours, which tells you whether the gene-level row behaves like p16. IF FOUND: if the CDKN2A protein row does not drop in truncating mutants, do not use it as a p16 read-out or as a way to define 'p16-null' tumours, and rest the CDKN2A grouping on the mutation calls; state that p14ARF contribution cannot be separated. CHECK: build a proliferation score from the RNA or protein table (MKI67, TOP2A, MCM2-7, PCNA) and test whether RB1 phospho still differs by CDKN2A status after adjusting for it; cross-tabulate CDKN2A status against RB1 state (RB1 mutant or RB1-protein-low versus RB1 intact) and look at CDKN2A protein/RNA in the RB1-deficient tumours. IF FOUND: report RB1 phospho adjusted for both RB1 protein and proliferation, describe tumours by joint p16/RB state rather than by CDKN2A mutation alone, and treat a CDKN2A-altered tumour with low RB1 protein or low phospho as one where CDKN2A status alone would mislead about CDK4/6 dependence. SOURCE: https://doi.org/10.14670/hh-22.769 ; https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC5347397/ ; https://www.nature.com/articles/s41467-022-32828-6

label: Promoter window and alternative TSS choice
text: PITFALL: There is no single agreed 'promoter' window and a gene can have several annotated transcription start sites, so a window measured from one picked transcript (or the DISTANCE column, which is distance to the picked transcript only) can exclude a variant that sits at the promoter of another transcript of the same gene; published promoter-mutation screens use windows from a few hundred bp up to +/-1 kb of a RefSeq TSS and include bases just downstream of the TSS. CHECK: take the gene's 5'-most coordinate from its own rows (all transcripts in all_effects, not only Transcript_ID), list every row within +/-1 kb of it with its signed offset to the TSS, and repeat with a narrow window (about -500..+100 bp) and a wide one (+/-5 kb). IF FOUND: if hits appear at any reasonable window (within about 1 kb of a TSS, 5'Flank or 5'UTR), treat promoter mutations as present; if hits appear only several kb away, say the conclusion depends on the window and report both; do not let a single narrow window decide 'absent'. SOURCE: https://aacrjournals.org/mcr/article/13/8/1218/130542/Systematic-Screening-of-Promoter-Regions-Pinpoints ; https://www.gencodegenes.org/pages/promoter_windows/

label: MAF alleles are plus-strand; minus-strand genes
text: PITFALL: MAF alleles (Reference_Allele, Tumor_Seq_Allele2) are always given on the genome plus strand, while papers describe promoter hotspots on the gene's own strand; for a minus-strand gene a UV-type C>T reads as G>A and CC>TT as GG>AA in the file, and 'upstream' means higher genomic coordinate. Also Tumor_Seq_Allele1 often equals the reference, so the mutant base is in Tumor_Seq_Allele2. CHECK: work out the gene's strand from the file (HGVSc/cDNA_position direction versus Start_Position, or upstream_gene_variant rows lying above the gene's highest coordinate) before filtering; never filter promoter rows on a specific base change such as C>T. IF FOUND: match by genomic interval only, and when reporting describe each hit with both the plus-strand alleles from the file and the gene-strand equivalent. SOURCE: https://docs.gdc.cancer.gov/Encyclopedia/pages/Mutation_Annotation_Format_TCGAv2/ ; https://www.biostars.org/p/473393/

label: Xenograft response calls depend on design, duration and dropout
text: PITFALL: (Applies only if in-mouse tumour-growth response data are found.) Response classifications of chemotherapy-treated xenografts are not a fixed property of the model: they shift with initial tumour volume, untreated growth rate, mice per arm, study duration and analysis method, and mice killed at a tumour-size limit drop out informatively (fast growers leave first), which biases naive mean curves and mixed-model slopes. A study of 70 cisplatin-treated PDX models found about 8 mice per arm and 21 days of dosing were needed to call responders reliably; single-mouse-per-model designs give noisy per-model calls, so apparent between-model heterogeneity can be measurement noise and apparent uniformity can be a short, underpowered study. CHECK: Record mice per model per arm, follow-up length, starting volumes and how many animals were censored for tumour burden; see whether response calls change when the analysis is truncated at a common day or restricted to models with at least 3 mice per arm. IF FOUND: Compare models at a common time point before dropout begins or use a joint longitudinal-survival model; down-weight or exclude models with one mouse per arm; report between-model spread together with its replicate-noise floor instead of raw responder counts. SOURCE: https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC6441558/ ; https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC10035449/ ; https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC6643318/ ; https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC9685207/.

label: Recurrent identical variants may be artefacts
text: PITFALL: Counting recurrent identical variants as independent somatic hits. The same indel or SNV seen at exactly the same position in several tumours is, outside known hotspots, more often a sequencing/alignment artefact (polymerase slippage at mononucleotide repeats and low-complexity sequence) or germline leakage than true recurrence; this MAF already shows the same in-frame 3-bp deletion in one gene in two samples in its first rows, and its t_alt_count/t_ref_count columns look empty, so allele-fraction or depth filters cannot be applied after the fact. CHECK: for each gene of interest list every row (sample, position, ref/alt, Variant_Classification, HGVSp_Short, dbSNP_RS, Hotspot) and count DISTINCT variants versus mutated samples; cohort-wide, tabulate how many (Chromosome, Start_Position, alleles) keys occur in 2 or more samples and whether they are indels in repeats. IF FOUND: if a gene's mutated-sample count rests mainly on one identical indel repeated across samples, report the frequency both with and without that variant and do not call the gene frequently altered on that variant alone; if the gene's hits are different variants at different positions in different samples, treat them as independent and say so. SOURCE: https://www.pnas.org/doi/10.1073/pnas.1808403116 ; https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC5852328/

label: Frequency claim vs driver pattern (20/20 rule)
text: PITFALL: Confusing 'frequently altered' (a descriptive prevalence claim) with 'proven driver', in either direction. Vogelstein's 20/20 rule says driver genes are best recognised by mutation PATTERN, not frequency: a tumour suppressor has more than 20% of its mutations inactivating (nonsense, frameshift, splice-site), an oncogene has more than 20% of its mutations as missense at recurrent positions. An analyst can wrongly reject the hypothesis because a gene's mutations are scattered missense (not driver-like), or wrongly accept it on pattern alone when only one or two samples are hit; and with fewer than about 5-10 mutations in a gene the 20/20 fractions are too unstable to decide anything. CHECK: for each gene compute the truncating fraction and the number of distinct positions, alongside n/N mutated samples and the gene's rank among all genes in the cohort. IF FOUND: let the label rest on prevalence (n/N, interval, rank versus the cohort's top genes and versus background), and report the mutation pattern only as supporting context for whether the frequency reflects selection; do not demand both genes pass a driver test, and do not let a driver-like pattern rescue a gene mutated in only a sporadic sample or two. SOURCE: https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC3749880/

label: Left truncation / time zero at plasma draw
text: PITFALL: In clinico-genomic cohorts patients enter at the date of sequencing (here a plasma cfDNA draw), often months or years after diagnosis, so anyone who had the event or died before the draw is absent (left truncation / delayed entry); measuring time from diagnosis without adjusting inflates event-free time, and VTEs that happened before the draw are prevalent events that cannot be attributed to ctDNA status or to later anticoagulation. CHECK: see what the time origin of any follow-up variable is (diagnosis vs plasma draw), whether a VTE date relative to the draw exists, and how many VTEs precede the draw. IF FOUND: use the plasma draw as time zero and count only VTEs after it (exclude or separately handle patients with VTE before the draw); if time must run from diagnosis, use risk-set adjustment with delayed entry (Surv(entry, exit, event)) and note it assumes entry time is independent of outcome. If no dates exist at all, time-to-event analysis is impossible and this should be stated. SOURCE: https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC9190030/ ; https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC9377725/ ; https://jamanetwork.com/journals/jamanetworkopen/fullarticle/2766816

label: Sparse events / monotone likelihood in subgroup
text: PITFALL: With few VTE events in a subgroup cell (e.g. ctDNA-negative and anticoagulated), ordinary Cox or logistic maximum likelihood is biased away from the null, and with zero events in one cell the estimate diverges (monotone likelihood / separation): the software returns a huge or tiny HR with an enormous Wald CI and p near 1, which is easily misread as 'no effect'. Adjusting for many covariates with under ~10 events per variable makes this worse. CHECK: print the 2x2 table of events by anticoagulation within ctDNA-negative patients before modelling; look for zero cells, convergence warnings, coefficients with |beta| > ~5 or standard errors in the hundreds. IF FOUND: use Firth penalised likelihood (R coxphf / logistf; in Python a penalised or exact alternative) with profile-likelihood CIs, or Fisher's exact test / exact risk-ratio CI for the 2x2 table, keep the adjustment set small, and read the result by its CI width rather than its p-value. SOURCE: https://doi.org/10.1111/j.0006-341x.2001.00114.x ; https://www.jclinepi.com/article/S0895-4356(13)00051-6/abstract ; https://search.r-project.org/CRAN/refmans/coxphf/html/coxphf.html

label: Arm-level vs focal CNA event counting, with hg19 centromere table
text: PITFALL: Counting each threshold-crossing segment as one copy number alteration splits a single whole-arm or whole-chromosome gain/loss into several 'events' when it is fragmented, and there is no consensus definition of an arm-level alteration, so event counts depend on the rule used. CHECK: assign every autosomal segment to a p or q arm using hg19 centromeres (split segments that span the centromere), and for each sample and arm compute the fraction of the arm's measured length that is gained and the fraction that is lost at the chosen |seg.mean| cutoff; call the arm altered if the summed same-direction altered length exceeds a stated fraction (clinical validation found sum-of-segments > 90% best; GISTIC treats events longer than 0.5 arm as broad by common setting; aneuploidy-score work uses a loose |log2| > 0.1 cutoff), and count the remaining shorter altered runs as focal events after merging adjacent same-state segments. IF FOUND that the lesion-type ordering differs between raw altered-segment count and arm-level plus merged-focal event count: report both and rely on the arm-level/merged count, stating the arm fraction and cutoff used and showing the ordering at 50% and 90% arm fraction. hg19 centromere start-end per chromosome: 1 121535434-124535434; 2 92326171-95326171; 3 90504854-93504854; 4 49660117-52660117; 5 46405641-49405641; 6 58830166-61830166; 7 58054331-61054331; 8 43838887-46838887; 9 47367679-50367679; 10 39254935-42254935; 11 51644205-54644205; 12 34856694-37856694; 13 16000000-19000000; 14 16000000-19000000; 15 17000000-20000000; 16 35335801-38335801; 17 22263006-25263006; 18 15460898-18460898; 19 24681782-27681782; 20 26369569-29369569; 21 11288129-14288129; 22 13000000-16000000 (13, 14, 15, 21, 22 are acrocentric: use the q arm only). label: Check seg.mean scale; seg file is the only CNA source
text: PITFALL: The seg.mean column of a cBioPortal-style .seg file is not on a fixed scale across studies (it is normally a log2 tumour/normal ratio where 0 means unaltered, but some studies load linear or absolute copy number), and the gene panel matrix may list no CNA profile even when a seg file is present; applying log2 cutoffs to a linear-scale file, or looking for a discrete GISTIC-style -2..2 table that does not exist, gives a wrong count or a false 'Not verifiable'. CHECK: look at the distribution of seg.mean over all samples: values centred near 0 with both negative and positive values indicate log2 ratio; values centred near 2 and never negative indicate absolute copy number. Also note that a discrete CNA table (data_cna.txt) is absent, so calls must be derived from the seg file. IF FOUND log2 scale: threshold |seg.mean| as planned; if absolute scale: call gain/loss relative to 2 (or the sample's modal copy number) instead. In both cases the segmented file is a valid copy-number variable, so the hypothesis is testable from it. SOURCE: https://groups.google.com/g/cbioportal/c/oWO1LFXGHHs ; https://groups.google.com/g/cbioportal/c/Z2uSPv3EeUA ; https://docs.cbioportal.org/file-formats/

Also, ERG_FISH_RESULT is a coarse per-sample event class with the levels 'Translocation' and 'Translocation with deletion', and ETS_FUSION_SEQ gives the fusion partner and frame; these are the only columns that describe how a fusion looks, and neither says whether it belongs to a chain of interdependent rearrangements. CHECK: intersect sample IDs across all tables and name the one sample missing from data_cna.txt; confirm the 25 blank rows are exactly the samples without WGS tables; cross-tabulate ERG_FISH_RESULT against ETS_FUSION_SEQ and data_sv.txt. IF FOUND: use 57 as the denominator for fusion and segment-based statements and 56 for gene-level CNA statements, treat blank as not assessed and NA as assessed-negative only if that reading is stated as an assumption, and do not read the FISH label 'Translocation' as a chained or chromoplexy event. label: MAF read counts cannot give LOH; fraction-LOH definition and cohort re-verified
text: PITFALL: Trying to rebuild allelic (LOH) information from data_mutations.txt read counts. The MAF holds only somatic variant sites (columns t_ref_count, t_alt_count, n_ref_count, n_alt_count); the normal sample is homozygous reference at these sites, so they are not germline heterozygous SNPs and give no B-allele-frequency track. Fraction LOH in MSK facets-suite (code re-read 2026-11-15) is sum(length[lcn == 0]) / sum(length[!is.na(lcn)]) over chromosomes 1-22 and requires FACETS tcn/lcn segments plus het-SNP data, none of which are in the seven supplied files (seg columns are only ID, chrom, loc.start, loc.end, num.mark, seg.mean). A second header check on the same date also confirmed all 471 samples are Colorectal Cancer (COAD 347, READ 96, COADREAD 13, MACR 10, SRCCR 5) and that no file contains the strings pituit or PitNET. CHECK: list MAF columns for any germline/het-SNP/zygosity/LOH field before attempting an allelic estimate. IF FOUND (none present): state that fraction LOH and the PitNET population are both absent from the data rather than constructing a substitute from somatic read counts. SOURCE: https://github.com/mskcc/facets-suite/blob/master/R/copy-number-scores.R ; https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC5027494/

label: Pitfall 10: low tumour purity and false wild-type calls
text: PITFALL: Low tumour purity makes 'TP53 wild-type' unreliable. Stroma and inflammatory cells dilute the variant fraction, so mutation and copy-number callers lose sensitivity in low-cellularity specimens (number of called mutations correlates with purity); a negative result may be an artefact of low tumour input, and if purity differs between histologies or between resistant and sensitive cases the misclassification is differential. Germ cell tumours are highly aneuploid with few point mutations, so a sample with a flat copy-number profile and zero mutations is more likely low-purity than truly quiet, whereas TMB = 0 alone is not informative. CHECK: per sample, count rows in data_mutations.txt, look at TMB_NONSYNONYMOUS, and measure in data_cna_hg19.seg the fraction of the genome with |seg.mean| above about 0.2; flag samples with no mutations AND an essentially flat profile, and tabulate the flag against CHEMO_RESISTANT and histology; also look at t_alt_count/t_depth of the TP53 calls. IF FOUND: keep all profiled patients in the primary analysis, add a sensitivity analysis excluding flagged (uninformative) samples from the wild-type group, and say that undetected alterations in wild-type patients would normally bias the odds ratio toward the null rather than create an association. SOURCE: https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC6887630/ ; https://www.frontiersin.org/journals/molecular-biosciences/articles/10.3389/fmolb.2020.533196/full ; https://www.cell.com/cell-reports/pdf/S2211-1247(18)30785-X.pdf

label: Pitfall 11: specimen histology, teratoma and what 'resistant' means
text: PITFALL: The histology of the sequenced specimen can differ from the patient's overall histology, and 'resistance' lumps different biology. Non-seminomas are mixtures; teratoma is intrinsically resistant to chemotherapy and radiotherapy and is what commonly remains in post-chemotherapy residual masses (roughly necrosis 50 percent, teratoma 35 percent, viable tumour 15 percent), while clinical platinum-refractory disease has its own narrower definition. A resistant patient whose sequenced tissue is a post-chemo teratoma from a retroperitoneal dissection is a different case from one whose pre-chemo viable tumour was sequenced. CHECK: cross-tabulate DETAILED_SAMPLE_HISTOLOGY_CATEGORY, SAMPLE_DETAILED_SUBHISTOLOGIES, PC_RPLND and RPLND_PATH against CHEMO_RESISTANT and TP53 status, and tabulate CHEMO_RESISTANT against PROGRESSION_OF_DISEASE and SALVAGE_CHEMO to see what the study's resistance flag actually tracks. IF FOUND: keep the study's CHEMO_RESISTANT flag and all histologies for the primary test (the hypothesis says 'germ cell tumors' without restriction), describe which histology and specimen type the TP53-altered cases come from, and report a sensitivity analysis by sample histology rather than excluding any histology after seeing the results. SOURCE: https://ascopubs.org/doi/10.1200/JCO.23.00654 ; https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC2878447/ ; https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC8484155/ ; https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC7352163/

label: Pitfall 12: VUS, germline leakage and gene-level collapsing
text: PITFALL: Counting every TP53 call as a real somatic alteration, or testing variants one at a time. Most rare variants in cancer genes are variants of unknown significance, germline variants can leak into somatic call sets (matched normals can be contaminated with tumour DNA, and allele fractions near 50 percent suggest germline origin), and testing each rare variant separately against treatment response needs enormous sample sizes, so alterations must be collapsed to one gene-level indicator. CHECK: for each TP53 row in data_mutations.txt list Variant_Classification, HGVSp_Short, the Hotspot column, Mutation_Status, t_alt_count/t_depth and n_alt_count/n_depth (non-zero alternate reads in the normal are a warning), and note that the mutation file has no ready-made oncogenicity annotation. IF FOUND: use one pre-specified gene-level indicator (any somatic non-synonymous TP53 mutation, deep deletion or structural variant) for the primary test; as a sensitivity analysis keep only truncating, splice-site, hotspot or DNA-binding-domain missense calls and drop calls with clear normal-read support; if the conclusion changes with the stricter definition, report both and say which patients moved. SOURCE: https://academic.oup.com/oncolo/article/29/8/658/7710154 ; https://www.jmdjournal.org/article/S1525-1578(17)30313-6/fulltext ; https://ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pmc/articles/PMC3766744/

label: Entrez IDs are 0; match pathway genes by resolved Hugo symbol
text: PITFALL: Entrez_Gene_Id is 0 in the mutation table (seen in the header rows; a known cBioPortal MAF annotation issue), so selecting pathway genes by Entrez ID silently returns nothing, and matching by symbol can miss genes listed under an outdated or alias symbol (the file has both Hugo_Symbol and SYMBOL columns). CHECK: tabulate Entrez_Gene_Id; for every gene in the pathway list confirm by exact Hugo_Symbol match and also search aliases/previous symbols (e.g. ERBB2=HER2/NEU, ERBB3=HER3, PIK3CA/PIK3CB/PIK3CD/PIK3R1/PIK3R2, PTEN=MMAC1, MTOR=FRAP1) and compare Hugo_Symbol with SYMBOL. IF FOUND: match on Hugo_Symbol after alias resolution, never on Entrez ID, and list in the reasoning which pathway genes were found mutated and which had zero rows, so a zero is a real zero and not a failed join. SOURCE: https://github.com/cBioPortal/datahub/issues/1640 ; https://cran.r-project.org/web/packages/HGNChelper/vignettes/index.html

label: MAF barcodes (NPC015D) vs clinical IDs (NPC15F) may not join
text: PITFALL: Sample identifiers in the mutation table do not obviously equal those in the clinical tables: the first MAF row has Tumor_Sample_Barcode 'NPC015D' while the clinical sample/patient IDs look like 'NPC15F', 'NPC29F', 'NPC10F' (header rows only; clinical sample table has about 55 samples, patient table about 56, MAF 56 distinct barcodes). A naive merge on ID can drop most or all samples, or make the denominator wrong, and TMB_NONSYNONYMOUS would then not attach to the right tumour. CHECK: list distinct Tumor_Sample_Barcode and SAMPLE_ID/PATIENT_ID, compute the exact-match overlap, then try a normalised key (strip leading zeros in the number, drop the trailing letter) and see whether the mapping is one-to-one. IF FOUND: either build an explicit, verified ID map, or compute per-sample mutation load directly from the MAF (rows per barcode) instead of relying on the clinical TMB column; state the denominator used (number of tumours sequenced) and how it was derived. SOURCE: https://github.com/cBioPortal/cbioportal/issues/3067 (plus direct reading of file headers)

label: Low tumour purity under-calls mutations; frequency is a lower bound
text: PITFALL: Low tumour purity lowers sensitivity for somatic calls: the number of mutations called correlates positively with purity across callers and cancer types (Cheng 2020; Wilkerson 2014 shows exome sequencing has low sensitivity in low-purity tumours), so in tumours with heavy non-malignant infiltrate (typical for nasopharyngeal carcinoma) both pathway hits and background counts are under-called, and observed pathway frequency is a lower bound. The sample table has TUMOR_CELLULARITY_DOMINANT_CLONE_VAF and TUMOR_CELLULARITY_PATHOLOGY_REVIEW (some 'N.A.'). CHECK: correlate per-sample mutation count with cellularity; compare cellularity and t_alt_count/t_depth between pathway-mutated and non-mutated tumours; flag tumours with very few calls. IF FOUND: prefer a test that conditions on each tumour's own mutation count (per-sample background), since that cancels purity-driven under-calling in numerator and denominator alike; do not read a low raw frequency as evidence against significance, and mention the lower-bound caveat. SOURCE: https://www.frontiersin.org/journals/molecular-biosciences/articles/10.3389/fmolb.2020.533196/full ; https://doi.org/10.1093/nar/gku489 ; https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC10154864/

label: Mutual exclusivity tests are biased by mutation-load heterogeneity
text: PITFALL: Mutual exclusivity of mutations among pathway genes is often cited as supporting evidence that a pathway is selected (MEMo; one hit per tumour is enough), but the usual Fisher/hypergeometric exclusivity or co-occurrence test assumes every tumour has the same alteration probability; Canisius 2016 (DISCOVER) shows that with heterogeneous mutation loads this yields many spurious co-occurrences and misses true exclusivity, and CoMEt notes subtype mixtures create spurious exclusivity. With about 56 tumours and a handful of pathway-mutated cases the test also has almost no power. CHECK: build the tumour x pathway-gene binary matrix and count tumours with 0, 1 and 2+ mutated pathway genes; see whether the 2+ tumours are the high-load ones. IF FOUND: report the exclusivity pattern descriptively only, or use a test with per-tumour alteration rates (DISCOVER-style Poisson-binomial); do not let an exclusivity p-value, significant or not, decide the label - the enrichment-over-background test is primary. SOURCE: https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC5162102/ ; https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC3266046/ ; https://link.springer.com/article/10.1186/s13059-015-0700-7

label: Fix alpha and test family before calling a pathway significant
text: PITFALL: 'Significantly mutated' for a pathway is a statement about a p-value/q-value against a background model, and the threshold depends on how many gene sets were tested: a pathway scan over hundreds of gene sets needs FWER/FDR control, while a single pre-specified pathway is judged at a nominal alpha. Mixing the two (scanning many sets then quoting an uncorrected p for one, or Bonferroni-correcting a single pre-specified test by an imaginary family) can flip the call when the p-value is between about 1e-4 and 0.05. CHECK: fix the alpha and the family of tests before computing; if several pathway definitions or filters are run, count them. IF FOUND: report the nominal p for the pre-specified ERBB-PI3K core list as the primary result, say whether it would survive correction for a realistic number of canonical pathways (about 10, as in curated oncogenic-pathway templates), and call the result borderline in the reasoning if the label depends on that choice. SOURCE: https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC8286309/ ; https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC6070353/

label: Risk-group quality: size, ordering, Brier
text: PITFALL: A risk-group system can show a large hazard ratio or a wide best-vs-worst survival gap while being a poor classification, because its extreme groups are tiny, its groups are not monotonically ordered (e.g. Medium no better than High), or its predicted survival is inaccurate; C-index, D-index and Brier score each capture only one or two of the four properties a good prognostic classification needs (well-separated curves, stable ordering, reliably sized groups, accurate survival prediction). CHECK: for the genomic PROGNOSTIC_MODEL groups and for the IPI groups, on the same patients, tabulate group sizes and deaths per group, confirm the KM curves are ordered at every horizon (2 and 5 years) with CIs, and compute an overall-accuracy measure for each system (IPCW Brier score at 2 and 5 years or integrated Brier score, expressed as scaled Brier / explained variation against the pooled KM) in addition to discrimination. IF FOUND: do not credit a system for separation that comes from a group holding only a few percent of patients or from adjacent groups that do not differ; call the genomic model better only if it wins on overall accuracy as well as discrimination, and report disagreement between measures as mixed evidence. SOURCE: https://onlinelibrary.wiley.com/doi/10.1002/(SICI)1097-0258(19990915/30)18:17/18%3C2529::AID-SIM274%3E3.0.CO;2-5 ; https://riviste.unimi.it/index.php/ebph/article/view/29482 ; https://www.stratos-initiative.org/wp-content/uploads/2023/07/McLernonetal-2023.pdf

label: Follow-up maturity and horizon choice
text: PITFALL: Survival comparisons read from the unstable right-hand tail of the Kaplan-Meier curves, or fixed-horizon metrics (5-year OS, 5-year AUC/Brier) computed at a horizon most patients were never followed to, are unreliable; KM estimates are only stable in the time range where most subjects have had the event or are still under observation, and one extra death in a small risk set moves the curve a lot. CHECK: compute median follow-up by the reverse Kaplan-Meier method (flip the event indicator) and the number still at risk at 2, 3 and 5 years overall and per risk group; note OS_MONTHS is in months. IF FOUND: set the evaluation horizon tau for Uno's C, time-dependent AUC, Brier score and group survival differences inside the range with adequate numbers at risk (curtail where the risk set gets small), and do not base 'outperforms' on late curve separation or crossing beyond that range. SOURCE: https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC4506242/ ; https://academic.oup.com/ije/article/47/3/850/4851146

label: Do not rebuild IPI from partial components
text: PITFALL: A composite score built from partly missing components is silently wrong: in data_clinical_patient.txt some patients have a blank IPI total and blank ECOG/stage/LDH/extranodal flags but a filled IPI_AGE flag (age is always known), so summing the five component columns with missing treated as 0 (pandas sum skips NaN by default) fabricates low IPI scores for patients whose IPI is really unknown, deflating IPI's performance; missingness of IPI items is rarely completely at random. CHECK: verify that IPI equals the sum of the five flags wherever all five are present; count patients with 1-4 of 5 flags filled; never use sum(skipna=True) or fillna(0) on the components; also note that patients with blank OS appear to have a blank PROGNOSTIC_MODEL too. IF FOUND: use the supplied IPI total, recompute it only when all five components are non-missing, treat every other case as missing IPI (complete-case primary analysis, multiple imputation as sensitivity), and report how many patients were excluded. SOURCE: https://doi.org/10.1002/sim.9203 ; https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC5358992/ ; https://effectivehealthcare.ahrq.gov/sites/default/files/wysiwyg/missing-data-registries-guide-3rd-ed-addendum-white-paper.pdf

label: MYC-family CNA is not a subtype readout

label: Discrete CNA coding and mixed panel versions
text: PITFALL: The discrete CNA matrix uses the cBioPortal/GISTIC-style code (-2 deep deletion, -1 shallow loss, 0 diploid, 1 gain, 2 amplification) and mixes MSK-IMPACT panel versions (patient IDs ending IM3, IM5, IM6 = 341, 410, 468 genes; models listed as IMPACT468), so a 0 or blank can mean 'gene not on that sample's panel' rather than 'diploid', and a gene row exists only if the gene is on a panel; copy number of a gene also says nothing about its mRNA/protein level, which is what the subtype definition needs. CHECK: count rows of data_cna.txt (expect about the panel size, not about 20,000 genes), look for NA/blank cells per panel version, and confirm the three TF genes have no row. IF FOUND: never read a missing row or a 0 as 'TF not expressed' or 'subtype absent', and restrict any patient-vs-model genomic comparison to genes shared by all panel versions involved. reason: The exposure in the hypothesis is 'PTEN alterations that result in loss of function'. Which patients fall in the altered group depends entirely on this definition, and the group is small, so a few misclassified patients can change the result.
text: Defining 'PTEN loss of function' (task bd08). Do not count every PTEN row in data_mutations.txt as loss of function, and do not use mutations alone. The standard (OncoKB) definition is: truncating mutations (Nonsense_Mutation, Frame_Shift_Ins, Frame_Shift_Del, Splice_Site) and homozygous deletion (PTEN = -2 in data_cna.txt). A missense variant counts only if it is a known inactivating variant (for example phosphatase-core residues C124, G129, R130, R173); other missense variants are of unknown significance and are common UV passengers in melanoma. 5'Flank, intron, silent and in-frame calls do not count, and a CNA value of 2 is an amplification, not a loss. The library reports that data_cna.txt holds only the values -2, 0 and 2 (no -1), so hemizygous loss cannot be seen. What to do: list every PTEN row in the mutation file (Variant_Classification, HGVSp_Short, Hotspot, allele fraction t_alt_count/(t_alt_count+t_ref_count)) and the PTEN row of data_cna.txt. Build a patient-level strict flag = truncating mutation OR CNA -2 (primary), and a broad flag = any nonsynonymous PTEN mutation OR CNA -2 (sensitivity). If the two flags classify patients differently, report results under both, base the conclusion on the strict flag, and say whether the direction is the same.

text: Small, unbalanced groups make standard p-values unreliable (task bd08). The cohort is about 66 patients and the PTEN-altered group will be a small minority. reason: Reading the claim as the familiar 'mutual exclusivity' statement, or answering it with an association test, examines the wrong cell of the table and can give the wrong label.
text: The hypothesis is a universal negative about one specific group: 'no patient with nonmutated JAK2 carries a somatic CALR mutation'. It is NOT the textbook statement that CALR and JAK2 mutations are mutually exclusive, which concerns the opposite group (CALR in JAK2-MUTATED patients). Test it by building a patient-level 2x2 table of JAK2-mutated (yes/no) by somatic-CALR-mutated (yes/no) and reading the JAK2-nonmutated row: count how many JAK2-nonmutated patients carry a somatic CALR variant and report the size of that row. The decision rests on that count: a single credible case is enough to break a universal negative, and zero among a reasonable number of profiled JAK2-nonmutated patients is what support would look like. A test of association or an enrichment p-value does not answer the question.

reason: It sets when each label is legitimate and fixes group membership for MPL-mutated patients; a team that looks only for a clinical status column, or that drops MPL patients from the JAK2-nonmutated group, would be working on the wrong variables or the wrong group.
text: Do not choose 'Not verifiable' merely because data_clinical_sample.txt has no JAK2-status or CALR-status column, and do not choose any label from prior belief about MPN biology. The mutation table is itself the relevant variable: gene-level rows (Hugo_Symbol) for JAK2 and CALR, together with the list of sequenced samples, are enough to test a presence/absence claim. Confirm that both JAK2 and CALR can appear in Hugo_Symbol and that the cohort is MPN (CANCER_TYPE / ONCOTREE_CODE in the clinical file), and count the JAK2-nonmutated profiled patients so the denominator is visible. 'Not verifiable' fits only if CALR could not appear in the data at all (for example no indels in the mutation file, or no CALR coverage) or there are no JAK2-nonmutated patients. The claim conditions only on JAK2, not on MPL: an MPL-mutated patient without a JAK2 mutation belongs in the JAK2-nonmutated group.

reason: The JAK2-nonmutated group is defined by absence of rows, so who was actually sequenced and how rows map to patients decides who is in that group and how many there are.
text: Define the groups per patient and on sequenced samples only. In a cBioPortal-style data_mutations.txt a sample with no row for a gene is either wild-type or was not profiled, and a sample with zero called mutations does not appear in the file at all, so 'JAK2 nonmutated' cannot be defined from the mutation file alone. Compare the set of SAMPLE_ID in data_clinical_sample.txt with the set of Tumor_Sample_Barcode in data_mutations.txt (every barcode should map to a clinical SAMPLE_ID); check that each clinical sample has sequencing evidence (non-missing TMB_NONSYNONYMOUS, SOMATIC_STATUS) and that the mutation file looks exome-wide (many genes, silent rows present) rather than a small targeted panel. A sequenced sample with no JAK2 row is JAK2-nonmutated; report separately any clinical samples absent from the mutation file instead of silently counting them as wild-type for both genes. The claim is about patients, but rows are one per variant per sample: a patient may have several samples, a variant may appear on duplicate rows, and any sample-level annotation column is repeated on every row of that sample. Check whether PATIENT_ID and SAMPLE_ID are one-to-one, then collapse to one record per patient with boolean flags (has JAK2 mutation, has somatic CALR mutation, has MPL mutation), where a patient is positive if ANY of their samples is. Report counts of patients, not rows or samples.

reason: The whole test hinges on which patients count as JAK2-nonmutated; there are two sources for that status in the data and they may not agree, and a team that does not know the curated column is sample-level could misuse it as a per-variant field.
text: 'JAK2 mutated' can be defined too narrowly (V617F only) or too broadly (any JAK2 row). MPN JAK2 drivers are V617F (exon 14) plus exon 12 indels/missense around codons 537-547; a mutation file may also hold silent, intronic or UTR JAK2 rows that are not mutations in the sense of the claim. List every JAK2 row with its Variant_Classification, HGVSp_Short and Mutation_Status. The library also reports a study-supplied column named 'JAK2/MPL mutation' in data_mutations.txt that is a sample-level label repeated on every row of the sample, not a per-variant field; confirm it exists and tabulate its unique values. Classify JAK2 status per patient two ways, (a) from nonsynonymous JAK2 rows and (b) from the curated sample-level label, flag every patient where the two disagree, and run the conclusion under both definitions; it should be the same under both before it is trusted. Exome sequencing at ordinary depth does not detect low-burden JAK2 V617F (roughly below 2-5% allele fraction, versus 0.01-1% for allele-specific PCR), so the curated label may reflect a more sensitive clinical assay: where the two disagree the curated label is the better guide, and 'nonmutated JAK2' should be worded as 'not detected at this assay's sensitivity'. The allele burden / alt-read counts of the JAK2 rows show the lowest burden the study reports. This affects which patients fall in the JAK2-nonmutated group, not the logic of the test.

reason: Decides which samples the median is computed over. Without it the team may answer 'Not verifiable' for lack of a risk column, or compute the median on a MYCN-amplified subset that is not what 'high-risk' means.
text: The hypothesis is about high-risk neuroblastoma, but the library reports that the tables have no risk-group or stage column. Two opposite mistakes follow: declaring the claim untestable, or carving out a wrong 'high-risk' subset such as MYCN-amplified tumours only. In the standard clinical classification, high-risk is mainly metastatic disease (stage M / INSS 4) in children older than 18 months, plus MYCN-amplified tumours of stage L2, M or MS at any age. MYCN amplification is therefore sufficient but not necessary, and most high-risk patients are older children without MYCN amplification. First read the '#' header lines and column names for any risk, stage or cohort description. Then cross-tabulate AGE from data_clinical_patient.txt (the library reports it is in years, so 18 months = 1.5; confirm the unit) against MYCN_AMP from data_clinical_sample.txt, checking the codes first (in GRADE and MKI a code such as 9 may mean unknown). Count the patients who are neither older than 1.5 years nor MYCN-amplified: on the data available these are the ones with least support for high-risk status. If nearly all patients are older than 18 months or MYCN-amplified, the library advises treating the whole cohort as the high-risk group and reporting the cohort median, then recomputing the median after dropping the doubtful patients as a sensitivity analysis. Do not restrict to MYCN-amplified cases as if that defined high-risk. Director's caveat: age and MYCN status are proxies, because stage is missing; an older child with a localized, non-amplified tumour is not high-risk, so say in your reasoning that cohort membership rests on these proxies (and on any cohort description you find), not on a recorded risk group.

reason: A common filtering habit (SNVs or missense only, or matching a protein-change string) would silently remove exactly the variants the claim is about and make CALR look absent.
text: CALR driver mutations in MPN are exon 9 insertions/deletions (commonly a 52-bp deletion, 'type 1', and a 5-bp insertion, 'type 2', plus more than 50 rarer variants), not point mutations. They are missed if you search for a specific protein-change string, filter to Variant_Type SNP or Variant_Classification Missense_Mutation, or drop indels. The same indel is written differently by different pipelines (e.g. L367fs*46 vs L367Tfs*46, K385fs*47 vs K385Nfs*47) and indel coordinates shift with left/right alignment. Select rows by Hugo_Symbol == 'CALR' with NO filter on Variant_Type or Variant_Classification, and as a backstop also look for rows on chromosome 19 with Start_Position inside the CALR locus (roughly 13.049-13.055 Mb on GRCh37). Then inspect Variant_Classification, Variant_Type, HGVSc/HGVSp and any study-specific DNA-change / protein-change columns for each row. Count CALR by gene and by frameshift/indel class, never by exact string match, and keep INS and DEL rows in every filter.

reason: The team already holds external benchmarks for judging 'high'. This sets how large the gap between the cohort median and a benchmark must be before the comparison can carry the label, and adds a multi-definition robustness check.
text: Mutation-burden values from different studies are not on one scale. The mutation classes counted and the calling pipeline shift the number by a roughly constant factor: in one whole-exome evaluation, counting all coding mutations (including synonymous and indels) gave values 3.1-fold higher than counting missense only, although the rank order of samples was preserved (Spearman 0.99); subtracting germline variants by database instead of a matched normal inflates counts; and laboratories running their own pipelines on the same samples report substantially different values. A verdict of 'high' or 'not high' that rests on an external benchmark lying within about 3-fold of the cohort median is therefore not safe. Compute the cohort median under each definition the sample table allows (the library lists TOTAL_PER_MB; TOTAL_PER_MB minus SILENT_PER_MB; NUM_NONSILENT_MUTATION / 30; and missense-only, MISSENSE_MUTATIONS over COVERED_BASES) and take the ratio of each to the benchmark you chose. reason: Fixes the unit of analysis and the denominator; without it a team may mistake between-patient diversity for ITH.
text: Intratumour heterogeneity (ITH) is a within-tumour property. It is directly measurable only with several spatially separate samples of the same tumour (multi-region sequencing) or with per-mutation cancer cell fractions. A table with one sample per patient shows differences between patients, which is not ITH. Count samples per PATIENT_ID in data_clinical_sample.txt; for patients with more than one sample read SAMPLE_TYPE, TISSUE_SEQUENCED and METASTATIC_SITE to see what the samples are, and check whether any ITH/clonality column exists (CCF, clonal/subclonal flag, region ID). If most patients have one sample and there are no clonality columns, a per-tumour 'ITH present yes/no' call cannot be made for those patients; compute the fraction of tumours with ITH only over tumours with at least two same-tumour samples and state that denominator.

reason: Determines which within-patient comparisons count as evidence about ITH and guards against miscounting patients through ID mismatches.
text: Not every multi-sample patient is a multi-region case. (a) Differences between a primary and its metastasis, or between samples taken at different times (e.g. before and after therapy), are inter-lesion or temporal heterogeneity; some authors count them as ITH and some do not, so state the definition used and report same-lesion and cross-lesion results separately. (b) Two samples from one patient may be independent primaries (multifocal tumours from field cancerisation), whose total discordance is inter-tumour difference and would inflate an 'ITH present' count: for each within-patient pair count shared versus private somatic mutations and shared copy-number breakpoints, and treat a pair sharing nothing (or only a common hotspot such as KRAS/TP53) as possibly independent, excluded from the ITH denominator or reported separately. reason: Sets the evidential standard for supporting or refuting an 'all tumours' claim, which governs how counts are turned into a label.
text: The hypothesis is a universal claim ('all'). It is not established by n-of-n in a small cohort and is refuted only by a well-supported counter-example. Report the number of evaluable tumours (correct tumour type, at least two same-tumour samples, comparable panels), the number showing ITH, and an exact binomial interval (with 0 exceptions in n the 95% upper bound on the exception rate is about 3/n; the exact lower bound on the proportion is 0.05^(1/n), e.g. 0.74 for n = 10). If the number of evaluable tumours is zero, the proportion is undefined and the data do not address the claim. Detected ITH rises with the number of regions sampled, so a tumour with one or two samples or few compared genes that shows no heterogeneity is absence of evidence, not a homogeneous tumour: for every tumour scored 'no ITH' record the number of samples, the number of genes/mutations compared and the depth, and treat thinly sampled 'homogeneous' tumours as uninformative rather than as counter-examples. reason: The CNA and seg tables are an obvious second route to an ITH call, and this is the main way that route gives false positives.
text: Copy-number differences between two samples of one patient are easily manufactured by purity and ploidy. The observed log2 ratio of a real event shrinks toward 0 as purity falls (a one-copy loss is -1 only at 100% purity, about -0.4 at 50%), so the thresholded calls in data_cna.txt (-2/-1/0/1/2) and seg.mean values in data_cna_hg19.seg can flip between samples of differing purity with no biological difference; data_cna.txt may also hold NA for genes not on a sample's panel. Before calling a CNA private to one sample, compare TUMOR_PURITY of the two samples, look at the raw seg.mean of the same region in the partner (shifted the same way but below threshold?), and exclude genes that are NA in either sample. Count as copy-number heterogeneity only events with a clearly opposite or absent signal in a partner of adequate purity (roughly 30% or more), prefer segment-level log-ratio comparison after purity scaling over discrete calls, and report CNA-based and mutation-based heterogeneity separately.

reason: If the team falls back on single-sample measures, these are the ways such measures produce an artefactual 'ITH everywhere' or 'no ITH' result.
text: Be careful with single-sample, VAF-based evidence of ITH. Raw VAF is not the fraction of cancer cells carrying a mutation: it depends on purity, local copy number and multiplicity (including copy-neutral LOH), so low-VAF mutations in impure or copy-altered regions are easily mislabelled subclonal, and single-sample ITH methods disagree widely. If single-sample clonality is attempted, compute CCF = VAF x (purity x CN_tumour + 2 x (1 - purity)) / (purity x multiplicity) from TUMOR_PURITY and data_cna_hg19.seg, with a binomial interval from t_alt_count/t_ref_count, and call a mutation subclonal only if the upper CCF bound is clearly below 1 under all plausible multiplicities; with missing purity, panel log-ratio segments without allele-specific copy number, or few mutations per sample, such calls are low-confidence and should not carry a universal claim. VAF-dispersion scores such as MATH (100 x MAD/median of VAFs) are unstable or undefined with the handful of mutations a panel yields (a score of 0 for a sample with 0-1 mutations means 'undefined', not 'homogeneous') and are positive for almost any sample, so 'score > 0 in every tumour' makes the hypothesis trivially true. Count mutations per sample; if a continuous score is used, fix the threshold before looking and show sensitivity to it. Prefer discrete evidence: an event confidently present in one same-tumour sample and confidently absent in another.

reason: This limits how strongly 'clonal' can be claimed from detected calls and changes the comparator for the purity-free relative-VAF check I recommended earlier; without it the team could overstate clonality.
text: Calls in a clinical panel MAF are cut off at the variant caller's floor, and the floor differs between hotspot and non-hotspot mutations. The MSK-IMPACT pipeline requires depth of at least 20 and calls known hotspots at 8 or more mutant reads and VAF of 2% or more, but non-hotspot mutations only at 10 or more mutant reads and VAF of 5% or more. Two consequences. (a) Subclonal mutations below the floor never appear in the table, so in low-purity tumours a finding that 'every detected TERT promoter mutation is clonal' is partly a selection effect. (b) A within-sample comparison of the TERT promoter VAF against all other mutations is asymmetric, because non-hotspot comparators cannot appear below 5% VAF. Check the lowest t_alt_count and VAF among all calls and among TERT promoter calls (use the Hotspot column), and for each sample compute the smallest cancer cell fraction that could have been detected, roughly 2*floor/purity. State clonality as 'clonal among detected mutations'. For the relative comparison, compare TERT against the truncal driver hotspot in the same sample (BRAF V600E or a RAS hotspot, which has the same floor) in preference to all mutations, and name the low-purity samples in which a subclonal TERT mutation could not have been seen at all.

reason: A batch difference or FFPE artefact could create apparent subclonal TERT calls or a prevalence difference between histologies that is technical, which would distort both halves of the hypothesis.
text: The cohort appears to mix two specimen batches: research samples named s_JF_thy_* / s_JJ_thy_* (e.g. frozen) and clinical samples named P-xxxx-IM3 (see SPECIMEN_PRESERVATION_TYPE). Batch may be confounded with histology. Formalin fixation causes cytosine deamination, which produces artefactual C:G>T:A changes at low allele frequency (typically under 5-10%). Both TERT promoter hotspots are G>A on the plus strand, the same substitution class, so a low-VAF promoter call in an FFPE sample may be an artefact and not a true subclone; frozen and FFPE samples also differ in depth and sensitivity. Cross-tabulate specimen type/batch by histology and by TERT promoter status. List any TERT promoter call with VAF under 5% or fewer than about 10 alt reads together with its specimen type. Do not build a 'subclonal TERT' conclusion on a few low-VAF FFPE calls. Give prevalence and clonality stratified by batch and check that the conclusion holds in each.

reason: This is the only library finding the team does not yet hold, and it changes how the result must be read: the guidance the team already has says misclassification in the no-call group biases toward zero, so a mutant-vs-rest difference would look conservative. Purity confounding pushes the other way and could manufacture that difference, so the team needs a purity-proxy comparison and an adjusted sensitivity analysis before settling on a label.
text: Tumour purity (the fraction of the bulk sample that is tumour cells) can drive both variables in a TERT-promoter-mutation vs TERT-mRNA comparison, so check it before interpreting any difference. Low purity lowers variant allele fraction, so somatic calls (including TERT promoter calls) are missed; it also dilutes the mRNA of a tumour-cell-specific gene such as TERT, which normal brain and immune cells do not express. Low-purity samples therefore tend to land in the 'no promoter call' group with low TERT expression for reasons unrelated to promoter biology, which can create or enlarge an apparent 'mutant is higher' difference. This acts in the OPPOSITE direction to the bias from hidden mutants sitting in the no-call group (which shrinks the difference), so neither a positive nor a null result is automatically safe: a difference seen in called mutants should not be credited as 'seen despite dilution' until purity has been checked. Check: the clinical tables are reported to have no purity column (confirm by scanning their headers), so build a per-sample purity proxy from the data: (i) the amplitude of clonal arm-level copy-number events in data_cna_hg19.seg, e.g. absolute seg.mean of chromosome 10 loss or chromosome 7 gain, or of a CDKN2A deep deletion; (ii) the variant allele fraction, t_alt_count / (t_alt_count + t_ref_count), of the sample's other clonal mutations in data_mutations.txt; (iii) TMB_NONSYNONYMOUS. Compare the proxy between promoter-called and no-call samples, and correlate it with TERT expression. If the groups differ in the proxy, or the proxy correlates with TERT expression: keep the unadjusted comparison as the headline result, then add a purity-adjusted check (rank regression or a logistic model with the proxy as covariate, or restriction to samples above a purity-proxy threshold) and state whether the direction and size of the difference hold. Do not present a difference that vanishes after adjustment as proof of promoter-driven elevation, and do not present a null found in low-purity data as support for 'no correlation'.

reason: The verdict depends on a threshold that the task does not define; pre-specifying it and testing its robustness prevents a label driven by a post-hoc cutoff or by one sample.
text: The cohort is only a few dozen tumours, so each gene's frequency rests on a handful of samples and one or two samples shift it by several percentage points. reason: Two opposite errors are possible: calling a gene frequent on raw percent that passengers also reach, or rejecting a descriptive frequency claim because an underpowered driver test is non-significant. The team needs both halves to weigh the evidence correctly.
text: Background mutation versus prevalence (this extends any earlier note on background mutation). UV-driven cutaneous SCC has one of the highest mutation burdens of any cancer, so raw recurrence can arise from background alone: long, late-replicating or low-expressed genes (TTN, MUC16, RYR2, CSMD3, olfactory receptors) top frequency lists by chance. Rank all genes by fraction of samples with a protein-altering mutation and see where the four genes fall relative to such passengers and relative to coding length (mutated-sample fraction per kb of coding sequence, or nonsynonymous versus synonymous counts within the gene); if feasible compare with a simple expectation from each sample's burden and the gene's length (binomial/Poisson, or a dNdScv/MutSigCV-style test). However, any such formal selection test is badly underpowered here: published saturation analysis indicates 600 to 5000 samples per tumour type are needed to detect genes mutated in 2-20% of tumours, more at high background rates, and this cohort is a few dozen. A non-significant p- or q-value for a gene is therefore not evidence that the gene is rarely mutated. Run the same test on accepted drivers (TP53, NOTCH1, NOTCH2, CDKN2A, FAT1) in this cohort and note how many reach significance and at what mutated-sample fraction; compare effect sizes (observed/expected, dN/dS point estimate with interval), not only p-values. If known drivers at similar frequency also fail, report the selection test as inconclusive rather than negative and judge the claim on prevalence with a confidence interval and rank relative to controls. Keep 'significantly mutated' and 'frequently mutated' as separate statements, report both raw prevalence and whether it exceeds what burden and length predict, and state explicitly which definition the final label rests on.

Focal MYC amplification in data_cna.txt does not equal 8q arm gain, and re-deriving arm gain from the panel seg file is threshold-dependent with no consensus definition (e.g. ASCETS default |log2 ratio| 0.2 over at least 70% of the covered arm with a minimum breadth-of-coverage filter; others use 0.1/50% or >90% of the arm). text: Adjustment set, applicable only if a real income exposure is found. Two opposing concerns about clinical covariates: (1) 8q gain frequency in prostate cancer rises steeply with progression (grade, stage, metastatic and castration-resistant disease) and socioeconomic position affects stage at presentation, so disease extent is plausibly a mediator; adjusting for DISEASE_EXTENT, M_STAGE, GLEASON_SCORE or SAMPLE_TYPE is overadjustment for the total association, while not adjusting leaves an association that may only reflect who presents late. text: Sparse-data caution for any race-adjusted model of a binary arm-gain outcome: institutional clinical-sequencing cohorts are heavily imbalanced by race, so logistic regression with small race categories suffers sparse-data bias or separation (maximum-likelihood odds ratios drift away from the null or become infinite as covariates are added; Wald p-values become unreliable). text: Evidence standard for a 'do not correlate' claim. text: Two sample-level factors can weaken a TMB comparison for reasons that are not the targeted assay's fault; they matter only if a paired panel-vs-WES analysis turns out to be possible. text: PITFALL: tumour purity jumps at first engraftment because human stroma is rapidly replaced by mouse stroma, whose reads do not count toward the human genome. Published work attributes larger patient-vs-PDX than PDX-vs-PDX copy-number deviations to stromal dilution of the patient sample. CHECK: for each tumour/xenograft WGS pair, put both copy-number profiles on common bins and regress xenograft log2 on tumour log2; a high correlation with slope > 1 is pure amplitude scaling. Also check whether xenograft-only mutations outnumber tumour-only ones in nearly every pair and whether TMB is systematically higher in xenografts (the purity signature). IF SO: do not use fixed gain/loss thresholds (e.g. +/-0.3) or raw mutation-count/TMB differences as evidence of a clonal change; use scale-invariant comparisons (correlation, or rescale the tumour profile by the fitted slope) and look for bins that deviate from the fitted line (state changes). reason: Unequal follow-up across pooled cohorts and thin tails can produce or hide the survival difference the label depends on; the earlier briefing mentioned landmarks only as a fallback when proportional hazards fails and did not ask for follow-up or numbers-at-risk checks.
text: Check follow-up length and the tail of the Kaplan-Meier curves. KM curves for small subsets are unreliable on the right, where few patients remain at risk, and the pooled cohorts may have very different follow-up, so a late separation or late crossing, or a subset drawn mostly from a short-follow-up cohort, can drive or mask a log-rank difference. Compute median follow-up per subset and per COHORT by the reverse Kaplan-Meier method (swap event and censoring), print numbers at risk at 12, 24, 36 and 60 months for each subset, and note the time after which fewer than about 10-20% of patients remain at risk. If the result depends on the poorly observed tail, compare survival at fixed landmarks inside the well-observed window (for example 2- or 3-year PFS with CIs) or truncate follow-up at a common horizon before the log-rank/Cox test, and say that you did. Choose the landmark or horizon from the numbers at risk, before seeing its effect on the p-value, and report it as a sensitivity analysis of the pre-specified comparison.

reason: A single self-chosen definition can land almost anywhere relative to 20%; the team needs to bracket the estimate with strict and permissive definitions before judging the claim.
text: The fraction of samples called 'actionable' swings several-fold with the evidence-level cutoff, the knowledgebase date and who annotates. Re-annotating the same 47,271 tumours gave 8.9% (2017 OncoKB) versus 31.6% (2022 OncoKB) at level 1-2. The 2017 OncoKB abstract reads, as written and with nested wording: 'Forty-one percent of samples harbored at least one potentially actionable alteration, of which 7.5% were predictive of clinical benefit from a standard treatment'. Two annotation services agreed only moderately on level-1 actionability (kappa 0.44; 27 gene-variant-diagnosis combinations called by both, 58 by one alone, 6 by the other alone). 'Oncogenic/driver' is not 'actionable': TP53, CDKN2A and most KRAS alterations are frequent drivers with little or no actionability. So a hand-built rule table is one opinion, not a measurement. Compute the fraction under several named definitions: (a) strict standard-care only (FDA-label or guideline biomarker in that tumour type), (b) plus investigational level 3, (c) permissive: plus off-tumour-type (3B), biological-evidence level 4 and resistance markers. List the genes contributing most hits under each and confirm none of the count comes from TP53/CDKN2A/non-G12C-KRAS style drivers. Never report one number without naming its definition; prefer the definition that fits the era of the samples (panel versions indicate the era); if strict and permissive definitions fall on opposite sides of 20%, say that the verdict rests on the definition and choose the label on that basis.

text: The hypothesis denominator is 'samples with somatic alterations', not all samples.
