reason: The team needs a pre-set agreement criterion and an honest interval; repeated samples per patient and tumour-agnostic markers both affect whether an estimate can be told apart from 20%.
text: A point claim ('20%') cannot be judged by eye. Published sentences of this type are often nested ('X% had an alteration, of which Y% were actionable'), so the same data give different percentages for different denominators, and with about 1,000 samples a binomial interval is only about +/-2.5 points, so 20% is easily excluded by a rule set slightly too wide or too narrow. Fix in advance what counts as agreement (e.g. the estimate rounds to about 20%, or its interval covers 20%), then compute the estimate and an interval for each defensible definition and denominator. Tumour-agnostic biomarkers held in the clinical table rather than the alteration tables (MSI_TYPE unstable, high TMB_NONSYNONYMOUS) can move the count: run with and without them. Samples are not independent: the 1,446 samples come from about 617 patients (several plasma and tissue samples per patient), so a patient with many serial samples and a persistent driver is counted repeatedly and a naive binomial interval is too narrow. Keep the sample-level fraction as primary because the claim says 'samples', show a patient-level figure beside it (patient actionable if any altered sample is; also first-sample-only), and judge 20% against a cluster-aware interval (bootstrap resampling patients, or a cluster-adjusted Wilson interval). If every defensible definition lands far from 20% the claim is contradicted; if only some reach 20%, report that the verdict is definition-dependent and name the definition you rely on.

text: Build the denominator from the clinical and panel tables, not from the mutation file. In cBioPortal-format data, data_mutations.txt lists only samples with at least one called mutation, so using the samples present in it as the denominator drops mutation-free tumours and inflates the per-group frequencies, possibly unevenly across groups. Conversely, a sample that was not profiled for BRAF must not be counted as wild-type. Take the samples from data_clinical_sample.txt (skip the leading '#' lines), join to data_gene_panel_matrix.txt (the 'mutations' column not NA), join the mutation file's Tumor_Sample_Barcode to SAMPLE_ID, and count how many clinical samples are absent from the mutation file. Frequency = unique profiled samples with the variant / all profiled samples in that subtype group; profiled samples absent from the mutation file count as wild-type and unprofiled samples are excluded. reason: With a rare event, counting non-V600E BRAF mutations or filtering out one or two real V600E calls could reverse the direction of the comparison; and a team looking only for a clinical column could wrongly answer 'Not verifiable'.
text: Define the event as exactly BRAF p.V600E, not 'any BRAF alteration'. In lung adenocarcinoma a large share of BRAF mutations (roughly half or more) are non-V600 (e.g. G469, G466, K601, L597, D594, N581) or variants of unknown significance; these are not the targetable V600E, and neither are BRAF fusions in data_sv.txt or amplifications in data_cna.txt. A gene-level 'BRAF mutated' frequency can rank the groups differently from V600E itself. Filter data_mutations.txt to Hugo_Symbol == BRAF, tabulate HGVSp_Short, and take p.V600E (hg19 chr7:140453136 A>T, c.1799T>A) as the primary event, counting unique samples rather than rows. Look at any other codon-600 rows (V600K, V600_K601delinsE, dinucleotide calls) and report them separately. Base the verdict on V600E-only counts; show gene-level BRAF and all-codon-600 counts only as sensitivity analyses and say whether they agree in direction. Accept the mutation calls as delivered: MSK-IMPACT calls known hotspots such as V600E at a lower threshold (about 2% variant allele fraction with at least 8 alt reads) than other variants (about 5%, at least 10 alt reads), so adding your own blanket VAF >= 5% or alt-read filter deletes legitimate low-purity V600E calls and can do so unevenly across subtypes. List t_alt_count, depth and VAF for each V600E call and check Mutation_Status for non-somatic entries; mention a call below 5% VAF as a caveat rather than removing it. There may be no ready-made 'BRAF V600E' clinical column; the variable can be derived from the mutation file, so its absence as a column does not make the claim unverifiable.

reason: A string mismatch or a silently lumped 'other' category changes group sizes and proportions, and so can change the comparison the verdict rests on.
text: Define the three histologic groups carefully. Lung adenocarcinomas are grouped by predominant pattern: lepidic (LEP, low grade), acinar/papillary (ACI/PAP, intermediate) and micropapillary/solid (MIP/SOL, high grade). The library reports, and you should verify in the file, that data_clinical_sample.txt has a SUBTYPE_GROUP column and a PREDOMINANT_HISTOLOGIC_SUBTYPE column, and that the group label is written with a space after the slash (like 'Micropapillary/ Solid'), so an exact string match can silently drop a whole group. Strip and normalise whitespace before matching. Cross-tabulate the two columns including NA and blank, confirm that each predominant subtype maps to exactly one group, and note any tumours outside the three groups (invasive mucinous, colloid, other variants, missing subtype). Use the provided group column unless it is inconsistent; exclude samples that belong to none of the three groups and report how many, rather than folding them into a comparator.

reason: With only a handful of V600E events, one double-counted patient can shift a group's frequency enough to change the direction of a comparison.
text: Check the unit of analysis. Sample IDs in this kind of panel-sequencing cohort carry tumour indices (e.g. -T01-, -T02-), so a patient may have more than one sequenced sample, and a mutation file can list the same variant more than once for one sample. Counting rows or samples instead of patients double-counts a rare event and breaks the independence that exact tests assume. Test whether PATIENT_ID is unique in data_clinical_sample.txt, look for duplicated (Tumor_Sample_Barcode, HGVSp_Short) BRAF rows, and compare the sample counts in the clinical sample file, the gene panel matrix and the patient file. If a patient has more than one sample, analyse one sample per patient (the first sequenced or the primary resection sample), count a patient as V600E-positive once, and confirm that the conclusion is the same at sample level.

reason: Which comparison the verdict rests on (pairwise against each comparator versus pooled or trend) can give different answers to the same hypothesis, so the teams need the comparison structure fixed in advance.
text: The hypothesis is a three-group statement: MIP/SOL lower than LEP and lower than ACI/PAP. Testing only MIP/SOL against the two other groups pooled can hide that one comparator goes the other way, and an overall 3x2 test says nothing about direction. Report n mutated / n total and the percentage for each of the three groups separately, then compare (a) MIP/SOL vs LEP, (b) MIP/SOL vs ACI/PAP and (c) MIP/SOL vs LEP + ACI/PAP pooled, noting the direction in each. Treat the hypothesis as supported in direction only if the MIP/SOL frequency is lower than each comparator group, not just lower than the pooled one; if the pairwise directions disagree, say so and let the per-group table, not the pooled test, drive the verdict. The groups are also an ordered grade (LEP < ACI/PAP < MIP/SOL), so lay the table out in that order and see whether the frequency falls monotonically. A trend test may be added as a supplementary, more powerful check of direction, but only with an exact or permutation p-value (e.g. permute the V600E labels 100,000 times with a fixed seed and recompute the Cochran-Armitage statistic with scores 1, 2, 3); the chi-square approximation is unreliable with so few events. A significant trend does not stand in for the hypothesis, because it can be driven entirely by LEP versus the rest while ACI/PAP and MIP/SOL are equal. Keep the two pairwise comparisons, with per-group proportions and exact intervals, as the basis of the verdict.

reason: The choice of test and of primary analysis determines whether the output is interpretable at all with a rare event; an invalid chi-square or a separated regression could be mistaken for the answer.
text: BRAF V600E is rare in lung adenocarcinoma (about 1.5-3% of tumours in general), so each subtype group will probably hold only a handful of positives or none. Chi-square is invalid when expected cell counts are below 5, and Fisher's exact test is conservative with very low power here, so a large p-value is likely whether or not a real difference exists. reason: The hypothesis names RB1 protein expression and RB1 phosphorylation as two separate things; without protein adjustment the phospho result is not independent evidence.
text: A phospho log-ratio mixes two things: how much of the parent protein is present and what fraction of it is phosphorylated. A tumour with low RB1 protein will show low RB1 phospho even if the phosphorylated fraction is unchanged, so raw RB1 phospho differences can simply restate RB1 protein differences. Correlate RB1 phospho with RB1 protein across samples, then compute a protein-adjusted phospho value (phospho log-ratio minus protein log-ratio, or the residual from regressing phospho on protein) and repeat any group comparison with it. Report both: raw phospho means 'amount of phosphorylated RB', adjusted phospho means 'phosphorylation per RB molecule'. Do not infer altered CDK4/6 activity from raw phospho alone.

reason: The most common failure on this kind of task is drifting into testing something other than the stated outcome. The team needs a concrete definition of what a relevant variable looks like, a search procedure covering all six files, and the library's header read as a lead to confirm.
text: First step: decide whether the outcome of the hypothesis is measured at all. A claim about chemotherapy sensitivity of engrafted (in-mouse) tumoroids can only be tested with a functional response measurement: tumour volume or growth under drug versus vehicle in mice, or a derived metric (TGI, mRECIST category, AUC, endoluminal tumour size, survival). Inventory ALL six files, not just the clinical tables: print every header, read the '#' description rows, and print the distinct values of every string column. Search column names AND cell values for response-like terms: response, sensit, resist, AUC, IC50, viab, volume, growth, TGI, RECIST, TRG, regression, pCR, xenograft, engraft, mouse, treated, vehicle. A header read by the library (verify it yourself) described data_clinical_patient.txt as PATIENT_ID and SEX only; data_clinical_sample.txt as 27 columns (derivation age, prior therapy, derivation site, sample type/class, gene panel, purity, MSI, TMB, cancer type); data_mutations.txt as a standard 46-column MAF; data_cna.txt as a gene-by-sample discrete copy-number matrix of about 610 genes; data_cna_hg19.seg as ID, chrom, loc.start, loc.end, num.mark, seg.mean; data_gene_panel_matrix.txt as SAMPLE_ID, mutations, cna. State in your reasoning which variables you searched for and whether each was found. Then choose the label strictly by the task's own definitions of 'True', 'False' and 'Not verifiable', applied to what your inventory actually shows; do not test a stand-in variable and report that as the answer.

Testing it needs two separate readouts: a per-model in-vivo response and a per-patient clinical response (RECIST, tumour regression grade, pathologic or clinical complete response). The library reports that HER2_TTP_ON_1ST_LINE_MONTHS, HER2_RESPONSE, HER2_VITAL_STATUS and HER2_TX_STATUS are columns of data_clinical_sample.txt (not the patient table) and are filled for only about 60 of about 341 samples (HER2_RESPONSE: PR 29, SD 18, CR 9, POD 4; HER2_TX_STATUS: OFF TREATMENT 55, ON TREATMENT 5). The data also have no biopsy dates, so the interval between stopping trastuzumab and the POST-TX biopsy cannot be read directly (published re-biopsy studies required progression on trastuzumab and a biopsy within about 3 months). reason: It fixes the decision rule the team applies to its own numbers. Without it, a team could see a minority of pairs losing amplification and wrongly conclude the hypothesis is supported, or count retained-amplification cases with other alterations as evidence for the null.
text: Choose the right benchmark for 'associated'. Acquired trastuzumab resistance has several mechanisms, so even if selection of a HER2-negative population is one of them, it is expected in only a subset of patients; the rest progress with HER2 retained, some with other receptor-tyrosine-kinase / RAS / PI3K changes. Published paired pre/post-progression series in gastric and gastro-oesophageal cancer (other cohorts, not this dataset) report loss of HER2 positivity in 29% (14/48), 32% (7/22) and 61% (20/33) of patients, against about 7-12% discordance without anti-HER2 therapy. Therefore 'most post-trastuzumab tumours keep ERBB2 amplification' is not by itself support for 'not associated'. Check: among baseline-amplified, trastuzumab-treated patients with a post-treatment sample, compute the fraction that lost amplification with an exact CI, and ask whether it exceeds the background rate (internal PRE-PRE discordance, or about 10%), not whether it exceeds 50%. Reading the result: loss clearly above background in clonally related pairs is evidence for an association and contradicts a 'not associated' claim even when the majority retain amplification; loss at or below background supports the claim; retained-amplification cases that gained new EGFR / MET / KRAS / PIK3CA alterations are a different mechanism and are neutral to this hypothesis, so do not count them for or against. The label must come from what this dataset shows, not from the literature figures.

text: A prior-therapy column such as THERAPY_PRIOR_TO_DERIVATION records which regimens the PATIENT received before the tumoroid was derived (for example 'FOLFOX, FOLFIRI, SCRT and FUDR'). It is a treatment-exposure history, not a measure of how the patient's tumour or the engrafted tumoroid responded. Read its distinct values: do they name drugs or regimens only, or do they state an outcome (responder, progression, complete response)? Does any value refer to treatment given to mice? Searching for the word 'promoter', or only for 5'Flank, misses real promoter hits. For the gene of interest, pull every row with Variant_Classification in {5'Flank, 5'UTR, IGR, RNA, Intron} near its 5' end and inspect Consequence, DISTANCE (bp to the transcript for upstream variants), HGVSc (c.-N notation for 5'UTR) and cDNA_position. reason: The conclusion can flip with the window definition, so the team needs a defensible window and a sensitivity check agreed up front.
text: There is no single agreed 'promoter' window, and a gene can have several annotated transcription start sites. A window measured from one picked transcript (or the DISTANCE column, which is distance to the picked transcript only) can exclude a variant at the promoter of another transcript of the same gene. Published promoter-mutation screens use windows from a few hundred bp up to +/-1 kb of a RefSeq TSS and include bases just downstream of the TSS. Take the gene's 5'-most coordinate from its own rows (considering all transcripts listed in all_effects, not only Transcript_ID), list every row within +/-1 kb with its signed offset to the TSS, and repeat with a narrow window (about -500..+100 bp) and a wide one (+/-5 kb). If hits appear at any reasonable window (within about 1 kb of a TSS, 5'Flank or 5'UTR) treat promoter mutations as present; if hits appear only several kb away, say that the conclusion depends on the window and report both; do not let a single narrow window decide 'absent'.

reason: Prevents both under- and over-counting, and prevents discarding or missing rows because the alleles look 'wrong' for a UV signature on the plus strand.
text: Match promoter rows by genomic interval only, never by exact position, variant type or base change. In UV-exposed melanoma, promoter hotspot mutations often occur as C>T at several adjacent bases or as CC>TT dinucleotide changes, so one hotspot appears as SNP rows at neighbouring positions and as DNP rows whose Start_Position is one base off. Exact-position matching or Variant_Type == 'SNP' undercounts; counting rows instead of tumours overcounts (one tumour can carry two rows in the same promoter). Use interval overlap (Start_Position..End_Position) with the window, keep Variant_Type SNP, DNP, TNP, ONP, INS and DEL, and count distinct Tumor_Sample_Barcode / PATIENT_ID. Also, MAF alleles (Reference_Allele, Tumor_Seq_Allele2) are on the genome plus strand, while hotspots are usually described on the gene's own strand: for a minus-strand gene a UV-type C>T reads as G>A and CC>TT as GG>AA, and 'upstream' means higher genomic coordinate. reason: The hypothesis concerns a low-risk subgroup where the anticoagulated cell may hold very few or zero VTE events. A diverged model with p near 1 would look like support for 'no benefit' when it is a fitting failure, so this can change both the method used and how the output is read.
text: Applies only if an anticoagulation exposure and a VTE outcome exist in the data. Before fitting any model, print the 2x2 table of VTE events by anticoagulation (yes/no) among ctDNA-negative patients. With few events in a cell, ordinary Cox or logistic maximum likelihood is biased away from the null; with zero events in a cell the estimate diverges (monotone likelihood / separation) and the software returns a huge or tiny hazard ratio with an enormous Wald CI and a p-value near 1, which is easy to misread as 'no effect'. Adjusting for many covariates with fewer than about 10 events per variable makes this worse. Warning signs: a zero cell, convergence warnings, coefficients with |beta| above about 5, standard errors in the hundreds. If you see them, use Firth penalised likelihood with profile-likelihood CIs (R coxphf / logistf, or a penalised or exact alternative in Python), or Fisher's exact test / an exact risk-ratio CI on the 2x2 table; keep the adjustment set small; and read the result by the width of its CI, not by its p-value.

reason: If outcome data exist, the choice of time zero, the handling of VTEs that happened before the blood draw, and the handling of deaths decide which events are counted and which estimator is valid. In a small subgroup, a handful of miscounted prevalent events or unequal follow-up can move the estimate for ctDNA-negative patients.
text: Applies only if an anticoagulation exposure and a VTE outcome exist in the data. Setting up time and events: (a) In a clinico-genomic cohort patients enter at the plasma cfDNA draw, often months or years after diagnosis, so patients who had a VTE or died before the draw are missing or carry a prevalent event (left truncation). Check what the time origin of any follow-up variable is (diagnosis or plasma draw), whether VTE timing relative to the draw is recorded, and how many VTEs precede the draw. Use the plasma draw as time zero and count only VTEs after it; exclude or handle separately patients whose VTE came before the draw, since those events cannot be attributed to ctDNA status or to later anticoagulation. If time has to run from diagnosis, use delayed-entry risk sets (Surv(entry, exit, event)) and say that this assumes entry time is independent of outcome. If no dates exist at all, a time-to-event analysis is not possible and that should be stated. (b) Death is a competing risk for VTE. Plain VTE yes/no proportions ignore unequal follow-up, and 1 minus Kaplan-Meier with deaths censored overstates cumulative VTE incidence, more so in the group that dies sooner. Check whether follow-up time and death/censoring status exist and what share of each group dies without VTE. For the question of whether anticoagulation lowers the VTE rate, use cause-specific Cox hazards with deaths censored; for cumulative incidence use the Aalen-Johansen estimator with Gray's test or a Fine-Gray model; report both if they disagree.

text: The hypothesis variable is mature miRNA EXPRESSION (abundance of miR-452, miR-766, miR-1180 in HCA, in HCC and in normal liver). In cBioPortal-style study folders, expression lives in its own files (mRNA/miRNA expression or z-score matrices), separate from the mutation (MAF), discrete CNA, segment (.seg), gene-panel-matrix and clinical-sample files; many studies ship without any expression file. Before any statistics, inventory what is actually there: list every file and every column, search all tables case-insensitively for 'MIR', 'hsa-', 'miR', 'expression', 'zscore', 'RPM', and establish whether a numeric per-sample abundance matrix exists. Then write down the exact column(s) that measure the hypothesis variable; if you cannot name one, you do not have a test of the hypothesis. Finding zero mutations or amplifications in MIR452/MIR766/MIR1180, or finding that these genes are simply absent from the tables, is absence of measurement, not evidence that the miRNAs are not upregulated. reason: With only mutation, CNA and segment tables on hand, the tempting move is a substitute analysis from copy number or neighbouring-gene alterations; the team needs to know such a result cannot count as support for or against an expression claim, so that the label is not driven by a proxy.
text: DNA-level data are not a valid proxy for the level of a specific mature miRNA, in either direction. (a) Copy number: genome-wide studies find weak copy-number/expression correlation for miRNAs even inside copy-number-altered regions (in a TCGA analysis of 7 cancer types only about 80 of 971 miRNAs were mainly copy-number-driven), and tumour-vs-normal miRNA expression changes were not significantly related to miRNA copy number; so 'locus gained => miRNA up' and 'locus not gained => miRNA not up' are both unsound. (b) Host genes and machinery: status of a host gene (SEPT6/SEPTIN6 for miR-766, GABRE for miR-452/miR-224) or of upstream genes (DICER1, DROSHA, XPO5, TP53, CTNNB1) says nothing quantitative about these miRNAs; an estimated 35-50% of intronic miRNAs have independent promoters and promoter activity correlates with mature miRNA level only at about Spearman 0.25-0.27. (c) Coverage: a targeted DNA panel such as MSK-IMPACT assays exons/selected introns of a few hundred cancer genes and has no RNA component; data_cna.txt holds panel genes only and .seg segments are interpolated across large gaps between targeted genes. The loci are MIR452 at Xq28 (clustered with MIR224), MIR766 at Xq24 (intron of SEPT6) and MIR1180 at 17p11.2. Check whether Hugo_Symbol in data_cna.txt and data_mutations.txt contains ^MIR, GABRE, SEPT6/SEPTIN6 or B9D1; if not, say that the miRNA genes are not assayed even at DNA level, and do not report a segment value overlapping them (least of all a chrX value, which is confounded by sex and reference choice) as a measurement of the miRNA.

reason: The MSS restriction is part of the hypothesis and the filter directly moves the BRAF and RNF43 rates by side; a team that skips or mis-defines it would be testing a different claim.
text: The hypothesis is restricted to microsatellite-stable (MSS) tumours, and how MSS is defined can change the result: MSI-high tumours are predominantly right-sided and carry BRAF V600E and RNF43 frameshifts, so leaving MSI-high or POLE-hypermutated tumours in the cohort can create a right-sided enrichment that is not a property of MSS disease. The library's read of the sample table suggests MSI_STATUS can be NA while MSI_SCORE and a separate MOLECULAR_SUBTYPE column are filled, so one column alone may not define MSS (verify this in the data). Check: tabulate MSI_STATUS against MOLECULAR_SUBTYPE and look at MSI_SCORE and TMB_NONSYNONYMOUS within each group. Standard MSIsensor cutoffs for MSK-IMPACT are score <3 = MSS, 3 to <10 = indeterminate, >=10 = MSI-H; POLE-ultramutated tumours have very high TMB with a low MSI score. Define MSS explicitly (labelled MSS, or score <3 where the label is NA), exclude MSI-H and POLE/hypermutated cases, and rerun the comparison under a stricter and a looser MSS definition to show the conclusion does not depend on the choice.

reason: The exposure variable of the hypothesis is tumour side; the grouping rule and the handling of ambiguous sites decide who is in each arm of every test.
text: There is no single definition of right- versus left-sided colorectal cancer. The common rule is cecum through transverse colon = right and splenic flexure through rectum = left, but some studies drop transverse tumours, split the transverse colon, or treat rectum separately, so a side re-derived from the detailed site can disagree with a curated side variable. Check: cross-tabulate the curated side column (the library expects PRIMARY_TUMOR_LOCATION with Right/Left/other) against the detailed site column (the library expects PRIMARY_SITE: cecum, ascending, hepatic flexure, transverse, splenic flexure, descending, sigmoid, rectosigmoid, rectum), and count missing, unknown, or both/multiple-primary values. Use the curated side variable as the main grouping, exclude samples without a clear side, and run sensitivity analyses that exclude transverse-colon tumours and, separately, rectal tumours, to show the direction of each gene's effect is stable.

reason: The hypothesis is about mCRC patients; duplicated patients, non-metastatic cases or an imbalance of specimen type by side would bias the 2x2 tables and their p-values.
text: The unit of analysis should be the patient with metastatic CRC, not the sample. Sample IDs include -T01/-T02 suffixes, so some patients may have more than one sequenced tumour; the sample table mixes primary and metastasis specimens and has an MCRC_TYPE column that may include non-metastatic cases. Counting samples double-counts patients and breaks the independence that Fisher's test assumes. Check: count SAMPLE_IDs per PATIENT_ID; tabulate MCRC_TYPE, SAMPLE_TYPE and STAGE_AT_DIAGNOSIS; cross-tabulate SAMPLE_TYPE by side. Keep one sample per patient by a fixed rule (for example the first sample, or the one on the largest panel, or call a patient altered if any of their samples is), restrict to the metastatic-CRC cases, and confirm with a sensitivity analysis within primary-only and metastasis-only specimens.

reason: The data give no ready-made 'oncogenic' flag, so the team must build one; the choice of which variants count is the outcome definition for every gene.
text: The hypothesis says 'oncogenic alterations', but the library's read of data_mutations.txt found no oncogenic/OncoKB annotation column (columns end at Annotation_Status), so counting every nonsynonymous mutation also counts passengers and variants of unknown significance, which are commonest in high-TMB tumours and can distort a right/left comparison. Check: for each of the six genes list the distinct HGVSp_Short values with counts and Variant_Classification, and see what share are known hotspots versus rare scattered missense. Classify with OncoKB-style rules: for the oncogenes count recurrent hotspot/known activating changes (KRAS codons 12/13/59/61/117/146; BRAF V600E and known non-V600 codons such as 469/594/596/601; PIK3CA 542/545/1047 and other recurrent sites; AKT1 E17K); for the tumour suppressors SMAD4 and RNF43 count truncating mutations (nonsense, frameshift, splice site) plus known hotspot missense (SMAD4 R361, P356, D351, G386, D537). Run the test both ways (oncogenic-only and any nonsynonymous) and report whether the conclusion holds in both.

reason: It tells the team that the CNA and SV tables are part of the outcome definition, and how to use them without over-counting shallow copy changes.
text: 'Alterations' covers more than point mutations. OncoKB and the cBioPortal default query also count deep deletions, amplifications and fusions/rearrangements, so a mutation-only analysis can undercount tumour suppressors lost by deletion (SMAD4, RNF43) and miss BRAF fusions. Check: in data_cna.txt read the rows for KRAS, BRAF, PIK3CA, AKT1, RNF43 and SMAD4 and count values of -2 (deep deletion) and 2 (amplification) (MSK-IMPACT files hold mainly -2/0/2, sometimes -1.5); in data_sv.txt count rows where Site1_Hugo_Symbol or Site2_Hugo_Symbol is one of the six genes. Define a gene as altered if it has an oncogenic mutation, or a deep deletion (tumour suppressors), or an amplification (oncogenes), or a structural variant, and report the mutation-only result beside the combined one. Do not count -1/+1 values or seg.mean shifts as alterations.

reason: It gives a concrete data-quality check on the MSS filter and prevents a pooled BRAF or RNF43 definition from hiding or creating a side difference.
text: Two of the six genes have variant classes that behave differently, so the variant definition can change a gene's result. RNF43 G659fs (a homopolymer frameshift) is reported almost only in MSI-H tumours, whereas other (N-terminal) RNF43 truncations are the ones seen in MSS tumours; BRAF V600E and non-V600 BRAF mutations are reported to have different site distributions and should not be assumed to behave alike. Check: within the MSS cohort tabulate RNF43 variants (G659fs versus other truncating versus missense) and BRAF variants (V600E versus non-V600) by side; any RNF43 G659fs in a tumour labelled MSS is a flag for a possibly misclassified MSI case. Report BRAF both as all-oncogenic and as V600E-only, report RNF43 as truncating-only, and re-check the MSI status of G659fs carriers before counting them.

reason: Denominators determine the frequencies being compared; this settles whether per-gene denominators are needed and stops a team from either dropping valid samples or counting unprofiled ones as wild-type.
text: The cohort mixes MSK-IMPACT panel versions (sample IDs end -IM3/-IM5/-IM6; data_gene_panel_matrix.txt gives IMPACT341/410/468). A gene not on a sample's panel is 'not profiled', not wild-type, and a sample with no panel entry must not be treated as wild-type. A published MSK-IMPACT gene table lists all six hypothesis genes (KRAS, BRAF, PIK3CA, AKT1, RNF43, SMAD4) as shared by IMPACT-341, -410 and -468, so no sample should be dropped from any gene's denominator on panel version alone; wrongly excluding IMPACT341 samples for RNF43 would shrink the cohort and lose power for a rare gene. Check: confirm every analysed sample has a non-NA 'mutations' entry in data_gene_panel_matrix.txt, confirm IMPACT341 samples carry RNF43 mutations at a rate similar to IM5/IM6 samples, and cross-tabulate panel version by right/left side. Use all profiled MSS samples as the denominator for all six genes; restrict RNF43 to IM5/IM6 only if the data show zero RNF43 events across all IM3 samples.

reason: It fixes the test, the multiplicity correction and the rule for turning six per-gene results into one label, which is where a multi-gene hypothesis is most easily misjudged.
text: The claim bundles six genes with very different prevalence in CRC (KRAS is common, AKT1 is rare, around 1 percent), so statistical power differs greatly per gene: a rare gene can miss p<0.05 purely for lack of events, and testing six genes without correction can produce a false positive. Treating one non-significant rare gene as contradiction, or one nominal p<0.05 as support, are both errors. Check: for each gene build the 2x2 table (altered/unaltered by right/left) among profiled MSS patients and report the right and left percentages, the odds ratio with 95 percent CI, the two-sided Fisher exact p and the Benjamini-Hochberg q across the six genes; note the direction of each effect and the expected cell counts. Judge the hypothesis on direction plus significance across all six genes together: support needs a right-sided excess in the genes (after correction where counts allow); contradiction needs evidence of no excess or a left-sided excess with CIs that exclude a meaningful right-sided effect; a wide CI on a rare gene is 'underpowered', not 'false'. Use Fisher's exact test rather than chi-square when any expected cell is below 5.

reason: Decides how the label options apply: missing CNA data should not by itself lead to Not verifiable.
text: Meaning of 'altered' when only mutation data exist: the study ships a mutation table and no copy-number or structural-variant table. Two opposite errors are possible. (a) Answering 'Not verifiable' because CNA/SV data are missing: a somatic mutation is a gene alteration, so the relevant variable is present. (b) Presenting the mutation-only frequency as the total alteration rate. Confirm which molecular files exist and that data_gene_panel_matrix.txt marks every sample as profiled for mutations. Then evaluate the hypothesis on mutation frequency, state that it is a lower bound on total alteration frequency (CNA unassessed), and reserve 'Not verifiable' for the case where the genes could not have been observed at all.

reason: Separates a True/False reading from Not verifiable for STAG2, and stops a low count being read wrongly in either direction.
text: Absence of calls is evidence of absence only if the region was assayed. STAG2 is on chromosome X, and some somatic pipelines drop or under-call sex chromosomes; exome kits also differ in gene coverage. Before interpreting a zero or low count: (1) confirm the MAF has mutations on chrX at a plausible rate, including in genes near STAG2, and likewise on chr12 near ESPL1; (2) confirm the gene panel matrix describes every sample as genome-wide (WXS/WGS) rather than a targeted panel. If chrX or the locus is systematically empty, the STAG2 half of the claim is Not verifiable rather than False. If the region is populated, a zero or low count is real evidence against 'frequently altered'. STAG2 is hemizygous in males, so tabulate STAG2-mutated samples by SEX as context.

reason: A symbol mismatch would silently produce a false zero and so a wrong label; the position check is the safeguard.
text: Do not look the genes up by exact current HUGO symbol only. The library's header read indicates this MAF uses outdated symbols (e.g. NALP6, the previous symbol of NLRP6) and has an empty Entrez_Gene_Id column, so an exact match on 'STAG2' or 'ESPL1' could return zero rows for a gene that is present under another name. Search Hugo_Symbol case-insensitively for the approved symbols and their aliases/previous symbols (STAG2: SA2, SA-2, SCC3B, STAG-2; ESPL1: ESP1, KIAA0165, SEPA, separase). Confirm independently by genomic position (GRCh37: STAG2 about chrX:123.09-123.24 Mb; ESPL1 about chr12:53.66-53.69 Mb) and by the RefSeq / Transcript_ID / HGVSc columns. Pool rows under all names for the same locus before counting samples. If a gene is absent under every alias and no rows fall in its coordinates, that is a zero count, not missing data.

reason: The whole verdict rests on a frequency; a wrong denominator or counting rows instead of samples changes it.
text: Numerator and denominator for a gene's frequency. A MAF has one row per mutation, so samples without a mutation in the gene (or with no rows at all) are absent from it. Dividing by the number of samples that appear in the MAF, or by mutation rows, distorts the frequency. Numerator = number of unique Tumor_Sample_Barcode with at least one qualifying mutation in the gene (a sample with several mutations counts once). Denominator = number of samples marked as profiled in data_gene_panel_matrix.txt. Compare that number with the distinct barcodes in the MAF and with the clinical sample table, and confirm every MAF barcode exists in the clinical table. Report n/N explicitly for each gene.

reason: Changes the numerator for both genes if silent or non-coding rows are present.
text: Not every MAF row for a gene is an alteration. The usual definition of an altered sample uses protein-affecting variants only: Frame_Shift_Del/Ins, Splice_Site, Translation_Start_Site, Nonsense_Mutation, Nonstop_Mutation, In_Frame_Del/Ins, Missense_Mutation. Part of this cohort is described as WGS, so the MAF may also hold Silent, Intron, UTR, Flank, IGR or RNA rows that carry a gene symbol. Tabulate Variant_Classification (and Consequence) for the whole file and for STAG2 and ESPL1. Compute the frequency on non-silent coding plus splice-site variants, report how the count changes if silent/non-coding rows are included, and do not let a silent or non-coding row alone make a sample 'altered'.

reason: 'Frequently' is the judgement the label turns on; a pre-set, cohort-relative rule with a proper interval prevents an arbitrary or post-hoc cutoff.
text: Fix the meaning of 'frequently' before looking at the counts. There is no universal threshold: in pan-cancer exome analyses only a few cancer genes exceed 20% of tumours of a type and most genuine cancer genes sit at 2-20%, so a cutoff such as >20% or >50% would reject most real recurrently mutated genes, while accepting any single mutated sample would accept everything. Set a rule in advance that combines (i) n/N with a 95% confidence interval, (ii) the gene's rank or percentile among all genes in this cohort by mutated-sample count, and (iii) comparison with the frequencies of the cohort's top genes. For the interval do not use the Wald (normal-approximation) interval, which behaves badly for small counts in a cohort of about 100; use Wilson, Jeffreys or Clopper-Pearson, e.g. statsmodels.stats.proportion.proportion_confint(n, N, method='wilson'). Under such a rule the claim is supported when each gene is recurrently mutated clearly above the typical gene in the cohort and in the intermediate-or-higher range, and contradicted when a gene has zero or only sporadic (about one sample, within background) mutations. Judge and report the two genes separately: the hypothesis needs both. Say so explicitly if the data are too thin to separate recurrent from sporadic.

reason: Stops the team from applying a driver-significance test to a prevalence claim, while still catching a frequency that is produced by gene length or a few hypermutated samples.
text: 'Frequently altered' is a descriptive prevalence claim, not a claim that the gene is a proven driver. Let the label rest on prevalence (n/N, interval, rank against the cohort's top genes and against background). Do not reject a gene only because its mutations are scattered missense, and do not let a driver-like pattern rescue a gene hit in only one or two samples; with fewer than about 5-10 mutations in a gene, pattern fractions (e.g. >20% truncating for a tumour suppressor) are too unstable to decide anything. Do run these context checks, because raw frequency can mislead: mutation counts scale with coding length, local background rate and tumour mutation burden, so long passenger genes (TTN, MUC16, olfactory receptors) top raw lists and a few hypermutated samples can put mutations into almost any gene. (1) Compute per-sample mutation counts and see whether the samples mutated in STAG2/ESPL1 are mostly the high-burden ones; recompute the frequency without the top-burden outliers. (2) Compare the observed mutated-sample count with a length-scaled expectation (cohort non-silent rate per coding bp x gene coding length x N). (3) Report the truncating fraction and the number of distinct positions per gene. If formal tools (MutSigCV, dNdScv) cannot be run because silent mutations or coverage are missing, say so. Note: the two library facts behind this item pull in different directions (one says the label rests on prevalence, the other says to call a gene frequently mutated only if the excess over background survives); the director's reading is prevalence first, with the background and burden checks reported as a robustness view that should be flagged if it overturns the raw picture.

reason: A numerator inflated by a repeated artefact or germline variant would wrongly support the claim; this sensitivity check can change the count.
text: Check that each gene's hits are independent somatic events. The same indel or SNV at exactly the same position in several tumours is, outside known hotspots, more often a sequencing/alignment artefact (slippage at mononucleotide repeats, low-complexity sequence) or germline leakage than true recurrence. The library's header read saw an identical in-frame 3-bp deletion in one gene in two samples within the first rows of this MAF, and the t_alt_count/t_ref_count columns look empty, so allele-fraction or depth filters cannot be applied. For STAG2 and ESPL1 list every row (sample, position, ref/alt, Variant_Classification, HGVSp_Short, dbSNP_RS, Hotspot) and count distinct variants versus mutated samples. Cohort-wide, tabulate how many (Chromosome, Start_Position, alleles) keys occur in two or more samples and whether they carry dbSNP ids or are indels in repeats. Also check whether mutation calling looks homogeneous across samples (per-sample mutation counts by SAMPLE_TYPE and by assay, since the cohort mixes primary/recurrent tumours and WXS/WGS); if assays differ in yield, give per-assay frequencies. If a gene's count rests mainly on one identical variant repeated across samples, report the frequency with and without it and do not call the gene frequently altered on that variant alone; if the hits are different variants at different positions in different samples, treat them as independent and say so.

reason: Prevents the label being set by recalled published numbers that may refer to a different denominator than the data in hand.
text: Base the verdict strictly on n/N in the deposited tables, not on remembered literature frequencies. Cancer sequencing studies often use a two-stage design (exome/genome discovery set, then a targeted prevalence screen of candidate genes in additional tumours), so published percentages may rest on a larger or different set of samples than the ones deposited, and discovery-set frequencies of selected genes are subject to winner's-curse inflation. Count how many samples the deposited data contain and use that; do not expect the deposited table to reproduce any headline figure you recall, and do not adjust your result toward one.

text: 'Fraction of LOH' is an allele-specific metric. In the MSK facets-suite definition it is (autosomal length of segments whose minor/lesser copy number lcn is 0) divided by (autosomal length of segments with non-missing lcn), chromosomes 1-22. It needs FACETS-style total and minor copy number (tcn/lcn) derived from germline heterozygous-SNP allele ratios, and cannot be computed from total-copy-number log ratios. The library's header read reports: data_cna_hg19.seg has only ID, chrom, loc.start, loc.end, num.mark, seg.mean; data_cna.txt holds gene-level discrete calls (-2..2); no clinical column name contains LOH, PURITY, PLOIDY or FRACTION. Verify by listing the columns of every file, including the '#' description lines. Two tempting reconstructions do not work: (1) read counts in data_mutations.txt (t_ref_count, t_alt_count, n_ref_count, n_alt_count) are at somatic variant sites where the normal is homozygous reference, so they give no B-allele-frequency track; (2) inferring LOH from the TP53 mutation's VAF (e.g. VAF > 0.5) needs purity and locus copy number that are absent, describes only the TP53 locus on 17p rather than the genome-wide fraction, and is undefined for TP53-wild-type tumours so it cannot be compared between groups. Do not build a fraction-LOH variable from somatic read counts or VAFs.

text: Three variables in or derivable from these files are easily mistaken for fraction LOH and are different quantities. (a) Fraction of genome lost (length of segments with negative seg.mean below a threshold): copy-neutral LOH and gain-with-LOH leave total copy number unchanged or raised and are invisible to log ratios (allele-specific reanalysis of TCGA reclassified about 9% of copy-number-neutral and 7% of gain calls as LOH), while in whole-genome-doubled tumours a relative loss (e.g. 3 of 4 copies) gives a negative log ratio without LOH. TP53-mutant tumours are enriched for genome doubling, so the proxy's error differs between the two groups being compared. (b) Fraction Genome Altered (FGA): length of segments with |seg.mean| above a threshold (usually 0.2) over total segmented length; it counts gains and losses alike and says nothing about allelic state. TP53 mutation versus FGA/aneuploidy is a well-known positive association in many cancers, so substituting FGA tends to return 'supports' whatever is true for LOH. (c) The clinical sample table has a column 'LST' (integers 0, 1, 2, ...; 178 of 471 missing; description says only 'LST'). If it is the genomic-scar score it counts large-scale state transitions (breakpoints between adjacent segments of at least 10 Mb), not LOH; in a colorectal table it may mean something else entirely. Read its '#' description and value range. If you compute any of these, write down exactly which segments enter the numerator, the threshold, and that the denominator is summed segment length; name it 'FGA' or 'fraction genome lost', never 'fraction LOH'; report it only as a caveated proxy/sensitivity analysis and do not let it alone decide between the labels.

text: What to count as 'number of copy number alterations'. The number of rows per sample in a .seg file is not a count of alterations: the file lists every segment including copy-neutral ones, so raw segment count mostly reflects noise and segmentation settings. Per sample, on autosomes, compute several metrics and compare them: (a) number of segments with |seg.mean| above a threshold, (b) fraction of genome altered (FGA) = summed length of threshold-crossing segments divided by the summed length of all measured segments of that sample, (c) number of chromosome arms or whole chromosomes whose length-weighted mean is beyond the threshold, (d) amplitude of the largest alterations. Count-based and length-based metrics measure different things and can disagree: a few whole-arm changes give high FGA but few events; a noisy or focally rearranged sample gives many events but low FGA. The hypothesis wording points to an event count, which is also the metric most sensitive to noise. If the metrics rank the lesion types the same way the conclusion is robust; if they disagree, report all of them, say explicitly which one the conclusion rests on (merged/filtered event counts and arm-level events are more defensible for a 'number of CNAs' claim than raw altered-segment counts), and report raw segment count only as a noise indicator.

Counting each threshold-crossing segment as one alteration splits a single whole-arm or whole-chromosome change into several events when it is fragmented, and there is no consensus definition of an arm-level alteration, so state the rule used. Method: assign every autosomal segment to a p or q arm using hg19 centromeres (split segments that span the centromere); per sample and arm compute the fraction of the arm's measured length gained and the fraction lost at the chosen cutoff; call the arm altered if the same-direction altered length exceeds a stated fraction (published rules range from >50% of the arm, the common GISTIC 'broad' setting, to >90%, found best in a clinical validation); count remaining shorter altered runs as focal events after merging adjacent same-state segments. Show the lesion ordering at both 50% and 90% arm fraction. If the ordering differs between the raw altered-segment count and the arm-level plus merged-focal count, report both and rely on the latter. hg19 centromere start-end by chromosome: 1 121535434-124535434; 2 92326171-95326171; 3 90504854-93504854; 4 49660117-52660117; 5 46405641-49405641; 6 58830166-61830166; 7 58054331-61054331; 8 43838887-46838887; 9 47367679-50367679; 10 39254935-42254935; 11 51644205-54644205; 12 34856694-37856694; 13 16000000-19000000; 14 16000000-19000000; 15 17000000-20000000; 16 35335801-38335801; 17 22263006-25263006; 18 15460898-18460898; 19 24681782-27681782; 20 26369569-29369569; 21 11288129-14288129; 22 13000000-16000000. reason: Benign, in-situ and invasive lesions typically differ in purity, which confounds any fixed-threshold comparison between them.
text: Tumour purity. Purity compresses log2 ratios toward zero: observed log2 = log2((p*CN + 2*(1-p))/2) for purity p, so at purity 0.3 a one-copy gain is only about +0.20 and a one-copy loss about -0.23. A fixed seg.mean cutoff therefore under-calls alterations in low-purity or non-clonal lesions, and a low count can mean low purity rather than a quiet genome; a difference in purity between lesions can produce an apparent difference in burden in either direction. Estimate purity per sample from data_mutations.txt as roughly 2 x the median VAF of the higher-VAF somatic mutations (VAF = t_alt_count/(t_alt_count + t_ref_count)), and look at the maximum |seg.mean| of large segments in each sample. If samples differ strongly in purity, use purity-scaled thresholds (or a lenient 0.1 cutoff plus a noise filter) and say explicitly whether any lesion's low or high count could be explained by purity. A lesion with clonal mutations at decent VAF but flat seg.means has a genuinely low count.

reason: A baseline shift in one sample would inflate its alteration count and FGA and could drive the whole comparison.
text: Baseline centring. A mis-centred log2 baseline makes a whole genome look gained or lost when seg.mean is thresholded. For each sample compute the length-weighted median (and main mode) of seg.mean over autosomes. A value more than about 0.05-0.1 away from 0, or an FGA near 100% made of many small same-sign deviations, indicates a baseline shift rather than real alterations. If found, recentre that sample by subtracting its length-weighted median or mode before thresholding, and report results with and without recentring. Median centring is only valid for near-diploid samples; in a highly aneuploid sample the commonest state may not be two copies.

reason: Sex-chromosome and germline/artefact segments add counts that are not somatic alterations and can distort between-lesion differences.
text: Sex chromosomes and recurrent small segments. chrX/Y log2 ratios depend on the sex of the reference, and small segments at the same coordinates in several samples are usually germline CNVs or capture artefacts rather than somatic events. List the chrom values in the seg file (X/Y may be coded X, Y, 23 or 24) and compute burden on autosomes 1-22 only. Look for short threshold-crossing segments with near-identical start/end in unrelated patients or in all lesions of one patient, and exclude or flag them. For matched lesions from one patient, alterations shared by all lesions do not distinguish them, so also report lesion-private alterations.

reason: Determines the comparison design (matched, descriptive) and prevents both pseudoreplicated tests and a label chosen for the wrong reason.
text: Sample size and study design (library report, not checked by the director; confirm against the files). The clinical table is reported to hold only 5 samples from 3 patients, with three of the samples coming from one patient. At these sizes no significance test is informative: rank tests cannot reach p<0.05, and guidance is to do no inferential statistics below about 5 independent observations per group. Treating segments as independent observations (a t-test or chi-square over hundreds of segments) is pseudoreplication and gives meaningless small p-values. Count independent patients per lesion type and identify which samples are matched within one patient. Make the comparison descriptive and per sample, with the matched within-patient comparison (JP against its associated DCIS and IDC in the same patient) as the primary evidence and unmatched samples as supporting. Base the label on the direction and size of the per-sample differences and their robustness to thresholds and metrics, not on a p-value. Small n alone is not the task's criterion for 'Not verifiable'; that label is defined by the absence of relevant variables.

reason: This decides what kind of analysis is possible at all. A team that does not inspect the SV table's columns first may either try to infer chains from data that cannot carry them or overlook what the table does contain.
text: Detecting chained (interdependent) rearrangements requires junction-level structural-variant calls: both breakpoint coordinates and the orientation of every rearrangement, plus matched copy number. Chain-detection methods (ChainFinder, ClusterSV, LINX) cannot run without them. The library's read of data_sv.txt reports 28 rows, all Event_Info = Fusion (ERG / ETV1 / BRAF), with Site1_Hugo_Symbol equal to Site2_Hugo_Symbol and no chromosome, position or partner-locus columns. CHECK this yourself first: read the data_sv.txt header and rows, confirm whether any Site1/Site2 chromosome or position columns or interchromosomal partner information exist, and check whether any other table holds rearrangement junctions. Whatever you find, do not describe an analysis as having modelled or detected chains unless it actually used junction-level data. State explicitly which half of the hypothesis (interdependent genesis of rearrangements vs. dysregulation of cancer genes) each table can or cannot address, and base the label on what the tables hold, not on what you know of the literature.

reason: The seg file is the largest rearrangement-like table and the obvious proxy; the team needs to know the limits of what it can prove in either direction so that neither a positive nor a negative copy-number pattern is over-read.
text: Copy-number tables (data_cna_hg19.seg, data_cna.txt, data_log2_cna.txt) cannot see balanced or reciprocal rearrangements: when both sides of a break are rejoined there is no substantial copy-number change, so translocations and largely copy-neutral closed chains are invisible to read-depth data, and a copy-number breakpoint gives neither its partner locus nor its orientation. CHECK: before using the seg file as a proxy for rearrangements, list what it can show (unbalanced losses and gains and their edges) and verify whether partner-locus information exists anywhere. Treat copy-number breakpoints as evidence about deletions and gains only: absence of copy-number change is not evidence against chained translocations, presence of deletions is not evidence for them, and translocations must not be counted from copy-number data.

reason: The second half of the hypothesis is about how often chained events account for cancer-gene dysregulation. Counting fusions or deletions of known prostate cancer genes is the tempting shortcut, and the team needs to separate 'gene is altered' from 'gene was altered by this mechanism' and know which columns exist to tell them apart.
text: A fusion row or a gene deletion shows that a cancer gene is altered, not how the alteration arose: an oncogenic fusion can come from a simple deletion or a reciprocal event as well as from a chain. The tables contain no expression data, so 'dysregulation' is not measured directly (data_sv.txt has only an RNA_Support flag). The only columns describing what a fusion looks like are, per the library's header read, data_sv.txt Event_Info (only the value 'Fusion') and the clinical columns ERG_FISH_RESULT (levels 'Translocation' and 'Translocation with deletion') and ETS_FUSION_SEQ (fusion partner and reading frame); none of them says whether an event belongs to a chain of interdependent rearrangements. CHECK: list which tables could measure dysregulation and whether any column records the mechanism or event class of each fusion or deletion; cross-tabulate ERG_FISH_RESULT against ETS_FUSION_SEQ and data_sv.txt. For ERG fusions the seg file can at most show whether there is an interstitial loss between TMPRSS2 and ERG on 21q22. Do not read the FISH label 'Translocation' as a chained event, and do not treat a frequency of cancer-gene alterations as a frequency of chain-caused dysregulation.

reason: Any frequency the team reports (the hypothesis says 'frequently') depends on the denominator, and the tables disagree on which samples were profiled. An earlier library fact gave slightly wrong counts (about 81 clinical rows, 56 everywhere); this item carries the corrected numbers so the team does not inherit the error.
text: The tables cover different sample sets, so denominators and 'negatives' are easy to get wrong. Per the library's corrected count (to be verified by you): the clinical tables hold 82 samples / 82 patients; data_gene_panel_matrix.txt, data_cna_hg19.seg and data_mutations.txt each hold 57 sample IDs; data_cna.txt and data_log2_cna.txt hold only 56 sample columns (one WGS sample has segments and mutations but no gene-level CNA column); data_sv.txt has 28 fusion rows (26 ERG, 1 ETV1, 1 BRAF), matching the number of clinical rows with a non-NA ETS_FUSION_SEQ. 29 clinical rows are NA in both ERG_FISH_RESULT and ETS_FUSION_SEQ, and 25 are blank in both (the same number as 82 minus 57). A sample missing from a curated SV table may be unassessed or may simply have no curated fusion; it is not proven rearrangement-free. CHECK: intersect sample IDs across all tables, name the one sample missing from data_cna.txt, and confirm whether the 25 blank rows are exactly the samples without WGS tables. Use 57 as the denominator for fusion- and segment-based statements and 56 for gene-level CNA statements, never all clinical rows; treat blank as not assessed, and treat NA as assessed-negative only if you state that reading as an assumption.

reason: The first half of the hypothesis is a claim about interdependence. If the team builds any within-sample breakpoint statistic, the choice of null model determines whether the result means anything; without this guidance a clustering pattern could be mistaken for evidence of joint origin.
text: 'Interdependent' or simultaneous origin is an inference against a null of independent rearrangements accumulated one after another, and pattern-based shortcuts have high false-positive rates: clustered breakpoints or few copy-number states are suggestive but not conclusive (simulations of purely sequential genomes produce such patterns at a non-trivial rate). Breakpoints that sit close together are also not necessarily mechanistically linked: fragile sites, LINE source regions and recurrently selected driver deletions concentrate independent breaks at the same loci, so a uniform-genome null overstates clustering. CHECK: any statistic offered as evidence of interdependence (clustered breakpoints, deletions on several chromosomes in one sample) must be compared with a simulated or permuted null that keeps each sample's own number of breakpoints and its chromosome/segment lengths, and ideally each locus's breakpoint probability, with multiple-testing correction across samples. Test whether apparently clustered breakpoints recur at the same genomic positions across many samples (fragile site, selection, germline CNV or artifact) or are private to one sample; exclude or model recurrent loci separately. If no adequate null can be built from the available tables, report the pattern as descriptive only and do not call it evidence that the rearrangements arose together.

reason: Cross-sample co-occurrence testing is the most likely substitute analysis when within-sample junction data is thin. The team needs to know both its statistical bias and that it answers a different question from the one the hypothesis asks.
text: Testing whether deletions or fusions co-occur across tumours with Fisher's exact test or correlation is inflated by differences in per-tumour alteration burden: genomically unstable tumours carry more of everything, so unrelated events co-occur by chance. Separately, co-occurrence across tumours says nothing about events arising in one step within a tumour. CHECK: compute each sample's total copy-number-altered fraction or breakpoint count and see whether a co-occurrence signal survives conditioning on it (a null with sample-specific alteration rates, or stratification by burden). With only about 56-57 WGS samples, power is low. Report burden-adjusted results only, and do not equate cross-tumour co-occurrence with interdependent genesis.

reason: The hypothesis names one specific phenomenon. A team that finds highly rearranged samples in the seg file needs criteria to tell which class of event they are looking at before attributing it.
text: Different classes of complex rearrangement are easily conflated. Chromothripsis gives tens to hundreds of breakpoints clustered locally on one or two chromosomes, with copy number oscillating between two (occasionally three) states. Breakage-fusion-bridge gives clustered inverted gains. Chromoplexy-type chains are unclustered, number in the tens, span several chromosomes and cause little copy-number change. Different detection criteria also disagree on a subset of genomes. CHECK: for any sample with many copy-number segments, tabulate breakpoints per chromosome and the number of distinct copy-number states per chromosome, to see whether the complexity is a one-chromosome oscillation rather than a multi-chromosome pattern. Do not count chromothripsis-like samples, or samples that simply have a high copy-number-alteration burden, as support for the specific phenomenon named in the hypothesis.

Method: audit patient/sample/CNA/panel/mutation ID linkage first (one sample per patient? samples profiled for CNA vs mutations, bait versions covering PTEN); then Kaplan-Meier + log-rank and Cox HR, plus Mann-Whitney on PFS_MONTHS. Note there is no PFS status column, so check whether PFS can be treated as all-events or whether censoring is implied by OS/PFS equality; run both ways. Checks: duplicates/multi-sample patients, samples missing from CNA or panel (not profiled != wild-type), BRAF status per sample, agent mix (BRAFi mono vs combo with MEKi), sensitivity to LoF definition, small-n of PTEN group. reason: Every breakpoint- or deletion-based statistic the team might compute starts from the seg file; unfiltered segment counts would feed noise into the null-model and classification checks in the other items.
text: Counting breakpoints or focal deletions straight from a WGS read-depth seg file over-counts: GC and replication-timing 'wave' bias, low-mappability regions, germline CNVs and segments supported by few markers create spurious small segments, and segmentation sensitivity varies with tumour purity and coverage, so segments-per-sample is not comparable across samples. CHECK: look at the distribution of num.mark and segment length; flag segments with few markers or tiny |seg.mean|; flag segments whose boundaries recur at identical coordinates in many samples (germline CNV or artifact). Filter by minimum markers/length and a purity-scaled |seg.mean| threshold, merge adjacent segments with near-equal means before counting breakpoints, and show that any conclusion is stable to those filters.

reason: Decides whether the task is testable at all and which columns are compared; a wrong comparator or a wrong proxy for the study's genetic model changes the label.
text: Which variables represent the two sides of the hypothesis. In DLBCL the 'current established methods' for prognosis are the IPI family (IPI, R-IPI, NCCN-IPI), cell-of-origin (GCB vs ABC), and MYC/BCL2(/BCL6) rearrangement (double-hit) or double-expressor status. The library, reading only the file headers, reports that this dataset has an IPI total plus its five component flags (IPI_ECOG, IPI_ANNARBOR_STAGE, IPI_LDH, IPI_EXTRANODAL_SITES, IPI_AGE), MYC/BCL2/BCL6 FISH status columns (MYC_FISH, BCL2_FISH_STATUS, BCL6_FISH_STATUS), overall survival (OS_MONTHS, OS_STATUS), and the study's own genomic risk label (PROGNOSTIC_MODEL in data_clinical_sample.txt, 'Genomic Risk Model Classification'), but no cell-of-origin or expression column. Confirm all of this yourself. List which comparators are present and how complete each is (FISH columns may be sparsely filled). Suggested design: IPI as the primary comparator, kept at full resolution; FISH/double-hit as a secondary comparator on its own complete subset; state plainly that cell-of-origin could not be compared. The absence of one comparator does not by itself make the claim untestable, and choosing a weak or partial comparator distorts the verdict. Do not use raw mutation counts or TMB as a stand-in for 'the genetic alterations identified' if the study's own genomic risk label is provided.

reason: The hypothesis is a comparative claim; the most likely error is to answer it with a one-sided significance test, which would decide the label on the wrong evidence.
text: What counts as evidence of 'outperforms'. A significant log-rank p or large hazard ratio for the genomic risk groups shows only that they are prognostic, not that they beat an established method; p-values and hazard ratios from classifiers with different group sizes and cut-points are not comparable. Two separately computed Harrell C-indices are also a weak basis: C is insensitive for model comparison, the two C's come from the same patients and are correlated, so comparing separate confidence intervals is not a valid test. Do a head-to-head on the identical patients: (a) Cox models with IPI only, genomic risk only, and both; report the likelihood-ratio chi-square of each term given the other (genomic | IPI and IPI | genomic) and the AIC of the two single-predictor models; (b) a paired bootstrap CI for the difference in C (resample patients, recompute both, take the difference); (c) genomic groups within each IPI stratum and IPI groups within each genomic stratum (stratified log-rank or stratified Cox); (d) absolute spread of 2- and 5-year OS between best and worst group for each system and the share of patients in the extreme groups. 'Genomic adds significantly to IPI' is complementary value, not superiority, unless the reverse test (IPI adds to genomic) and the head-to-head measures also favour the genomic model.

reason: Differential missingness can manufacture or hide a difference between the two models; fixing the analysis set changes every reported number.
text: Compare the models on the same patients. IPI (and its five component columns), the PROGNOSTIC_MODEL label, and OS_MONTHS/OS_STATUS may each be missing for different subsets of the cohort, so per-model 'available case' statistics are not comparable and complete cases may not be a random subset. Count non-missing values for each variable and for their intersection; compare survival and genomic-risk distribution between patients with and without IPI; check whether IPI can be recomputed from the five component flags when the total is blank. Run every head-to-head metric on the identical intersection set, report its n and number of deaths, and add a sensitivity analysis (genomic model on all patients vs on the IPI-complete subset) to show the conclusion does not depend on who has IPI.

reason: A direction or parsing error would flip which model looks better and therefore flip the label.
text: Encoding traps that silently invert the metric. lifelines.utils.concordance_index(event_times, predicted_scores, event_observed) assumes a HIGHER score means LONGER survival, so a risk score (IPI 0-5, or Low<Medium<High) must be negated or the function returns 1-C; scikit-survival's concordance_index_censored assumes higher = higher risk. OS_STATUS is a string of the form '0:LIVING'/'1:DECEASED' and must be parsed into an event indicator (event = 1 for DECEASED). Risk labels are text and sort alphabetically (High<Low<Medium) unless mapped explicitly to an ordered scale. The sample file also has a separate CENSORED column whose description ('True or False') reportedly does not match its values: cross-tabulate it against OS_STATUS before using either. Sanity checks: KM curves should order from lowest-risk group best to highest-risk group worst, and the IPI C-index should be above 0.5 (the library cites roughly 0.63 as a published value for OS in R-CHOP-treated cohorts). A C below 0.5 for either model indicates a coding bug, not a finding.

reason: The result of the head-to-head can depend on an arbitrary coding choice; the team needs to know to test more than one coding.
text: Granularity and ties affect the comparison. Discrimination measures depend on the number of distinct levels of a score: a genomic risk group with a few levels and an IPI coded 0-5 (or as 4 groups: 0-1 low, 2 low-intermediate, 3 high-intermediate, 4-5 high; or R-IPI: 0, 1-2, 3-5) yield very different numbers of tied pairs, and software differs on whether tied scores count 0.5 or are dropped, so the C-index ranking can flip with the coding choice. Tabulate the levels of PROGNOSTIC_MODEL and IPI; compute concordance with a stated tie rule (ties = 0.5) for IPI as 0-5, as 4 groups and as 3 groups against the genomic score; also compare by Cox LR chi-square with each entered as a categorical factor, penalising degrees of freedom with AIC. Report the comparison at matched granularity and at the comparator's native granularity, require a consistent result across codings before calling either model superior, and never weaken the comparator by dichotomising IPI.

label: PLAN
text: PLAN (bd09-team-b): Estimate the per-sample exonic somatic mutation frequency (mutations per Mb of covered exonic bases) in the neuroblastoma cohort and its median. Method: (1) audit sample/patient/panel-matrix/mutation files: unique IDs, duplicates, patient-sample mapping, platform (WXS/WGS/Exome_WGA) batches, samples with zero mutations; (2) median of clinical TOTAL_PER_MB and TMB_NONSYNONYMOUS; (3) independently recompute from data_mutations.txt: count coding mutations per sample / COVERED_BASES, compare with clinical columns; (4) stratify by platform (WGA vs native, WGS vs WXS) and matched/unmatched status; check outlier/hypermutated samples (median robust to them); (5) judge 'high' against standard reference scale for cancers (~1/Mb adult solid-tumour median, >10/Mb high; pediatric tumours typically <1/Mb). Checks: whether cohort is actually high-risk (no risk column -> check MYCN, age, stage), denominators consistent, samples missing from MAF counted as 0 not dropped. Would change method if: clinical per-Mb columns disagree with MAF recomputation, a platform batch drives the median, or duplicates/multi-sample patients exist (then dedupe per patient).

reason: Affects how much weight an apparent advantage of the genetic model deserves, and prevents an overfitted self-built model from being used as evidence.
text: Optimism of a model evaluated on the cohort it was built on. The library judges it very likely (not confirmed) that the study's genomic risk grouping (PROGNOSTIC_MODEL) was fitted on this same cohort using its survival outcome, whereas the IPI was defined externally; scoring both here would then give the genomic model a resubstitution advantage in C-index, KM separation and hazard ratios. Look for any train/validation split flag (none was visible in the headers), quantify the size of the genomic-vs-IPI margin and whether it survives a paired bootstrap CI, state the optimism caveat explicitly, and weigh the size and robustness of the margin rather than resubstitution statistics alone. If you build a genetic predictor yourself from data_mutations.txt / data_log2_cna.txt, the same problem is stronger: many gene indicators fitted and scored on the same patients can separate KM curves from pure noise. In that case put every step (gene selection, weights, cut-points, tuning) inside cross-validation folds, score only out-of-fold predictions, compare that out-of-fold score with IPI on the same patients, and treat the supplied PROGNOSTIC_MODEL column as the primary representation of the study's model. Also: a mutation file lists only mutated calls, so a sample with no row for a gene is wild-type only if it was profiled (check data_gene_panel_matrix.txt and the overlap of sample IDs across the clinical, gene-panel, mutation and CNA files); patients absent from the mutation or CNA tables must not be treated as wild-type.

reason: Adds a second, independent criterion (group size, ordering, accuracy) that can contradict a discrimination-only comparison and so change the conclusion.
text: Check the quality of the risk groups, not just a summary statistic. A risk-group system can show a large hazard ratio or a wide best-vs-worst survival gap while being a poor classification because its extreme groups are tiny, its groups are not monotonically ordered, or its predicted survival is inaccurate. For both the genomic groups and the IPI groups, on the same patients: tabulate group sizes and deaths per group, confirm the KM curves are ordered at 2 and 5 years (with CIs), and compute an overall-accuracy measure for each system (IPCW Brier score at 2 and 5 years or integrated Brier score, expressed relative to the pooled KM) in addition to discrimination. Do not credit a system for separation that comes from a group holding only a few percent of patients or from adjacent groups that do not differ; report disagreement between discrimination and overall accuracy as mixed evidence.
