text: WARNING SIGN: every post-chemo specimen comes from a resistant patient (66/66 resistant vs 38/114 of pre-chemo), and TP53 alterations are concentrated in post-chemo specimens (11/66 vs 5/114). MEANS: the crude TP53-vs-resistance 2x2 (16/16 vs 88/164, Fisher p=1e-4) is partly built in by sampling design, and post-chemo stratum carries zero information; the valid comparison is within pre-chemo specimens. ACTION: changed primary test to pre-chemo-only stratum (5/5 resistant vs 33/109, Fisher p=0.0034) plus CMH stratified by timing (p=0.006); association survives.

label: WARNING SIGN
text: WARNING SIGN: 13 of 16 TP53-altered tumours are mediastinal primaries (13/22 mediastinal vs 3/158 testis/RP), and mediastinal site itself has higher resistance (17/22 vs 87/158); all 16 are NSGCT, 15/16 IGCCCG poor risk. MEANS: TP53 effect could be a proxy for mediastinal site / poor risk. ACTION: stratified by site (within mediastinal 13/13 vs 4/9 resistant, p=0.005; CMH p=0.004) and by risk group (poor: 15/15 vs 36/44, p=0.10 two-sided); association holds within site but is not independent of risk group at this sample size; label unchanged since the hypothesis is about association.

label: WARNING SIGN
text: WARNING SIGN: complete separation - 0 of 16 TP53-altered patients are sensitive, so logistic regression does not converge (coef 22, SE 15000). MEANS: Wald/ML adjusted estimates are unusable; odds ratio is infinite. ACTION: used exact tests (Fisher, CMH, exact stratified permutation) instead of logistic regression.

label: WARNING SIGN
text: WARNING SIGN: the hypothesis is about PitNETs but all 471 samples in /biodsa-data are Colorectal Cancer (ONCOTREE COAD 347, READ 96, COADREAD 13, MACR 10, SRCCR 5) and a regex search of all 7 files for pituitary/PitNET/hypophys/lactotroph etc. terms gives 0 hits. MEANS: there is no PitNET subset to analyse; any TP53-vs-copy-number association measured here is in a different tissue and cannot support or contradict the claim. ACTION: changed the method from 'test the association' to 'verify absence, report a proxy only as a caveated sensitivity analysis'; label decided by data content (Not verifiable), not by the proxy p-value.

label: WARNING SIGN
text: WARNING SIGN: no fraction-LOH variable exists and none can be derived: data_cna_hg19.seg has only ID, chrom, loc.start, loc.end, num.mark, seg.mean (total-copy log ratios); data_cna.txt is discrete -2..2 gene calls; no column name or '#' description in any file matches LOH/purity/ploidy/fraction/lcn/tcn/facets; the clinical 'LST' column (integers 0-14, 178 of 471 missing, description just 'LST') is not an LOH fraction. MEANS: the outcome variable of the hypothesis is absent; fraction genome lost or FGA from seg.mean would be a different quantity (blind to copy-neutral LOH, confounded by genome doubling). ACTION: did not construct a 'fraction LOH'; computed length-weighted autosomal fraction genome lost (seg.mean<=-0.2) and FGA (|seg.mean|>=0.2) only as named proxies and did not let them decide the label.

label: WARNING SIGN
text: WARNING SIGN: data_cna_hg19.seg has 507 exact duplicate rows, all from 8 samples (P-0021563-T01-IM6, P-0002042-T01-IM3, P-0011108-T01-IM5, P-0001295-T01-IM3, P-0013144-T01-IM5, P-0008583-T01-IM5, P-0012653-T02-IM5, P-0002540-T01-IM3) whose every segment is listed twice (autosomal segmented length ~5.4 Gb instead of ~2.7 Gb). MEANS: segment counts and any breakpoint count are doubled for these samples; a length-weighted fraction is unchanged because numerator and denominator double together. ACTION: dropped exact duplicate rows before computing the proxy; the proxy result was identical (median fraction genome lost 0.108 TP53-mutant vs 0.027 wild-type, Mann-Whitney p=5e-8), so only rows changed, not the method.

label: WARNING SIGN
text: WARNING SIGN: in the colorectal proxy analysis the purity proxy (max somatic VAF per sample) correlates strongly with fraction genome lost (Spearman 0.63, p=4e-53), MSI-instable samples are rarely TP53-mutant (22% vs 76% in Stable) with near-zero fraction lost (median 0.004 vs 0.095), and 41 samples flagged USED_IN_GENOMIC_ANALYSIS=No shift the wild-type median from 0.027 (all) to 0.069 (flagged-only kept). MEANS: the pooled proxy effect is partly inflated by MSI and low-purity/excluded samples, though maxVAF differs little between groups (0.43 vs 0.39). ACTION: reported stratified estimates (MSS non-hypermutated: 0.108 vs 0.061, p=8e-4; used-in-analysis: 0.108 vs 0.069, p=3e-3; maxVAF>=0.3: 0.151 vs 0.074, p=5e-7; per panel all same direction); direction is stable but this remains a colorectal fraction-genome-lost proxy and does not change the Not verifiable label.

label: PLAN
text: PLAN (bd39-team-b): Quantity = difference in fraction of genome under LOH between TP53-mutant and TP53-wildtype pituitary neuroendocrine tumours (PitNETs). Method: first confirm the cohort contains PitNET samples and an LOH measure (allele-specific copy number or an LOH column); if both exist, Mann-Whitney test of LOH fraction by TP53 status, restricted to samples profiled for both. Checks: cancer type/oncotree of every sample, sample-ID agreement across clinical/seg/CNA/mutation/panel files, duplicates per patient, whether seg file has allele-specific fields, panel coverage of TP53. Method change triggers: if no PitNET samples or no LOH variable exist, the hypothesis is Not verifiable and any proxy (copy-loss fraction from seg log-ratios in whatever tumour type is present) is reported only as exploratory, not as the answer.

label: WARNING SIGN
text: WARNING SIGN: all 471 samples in /biodsa-data are Colorectal Cancer (oncotree COAD 347, READ 96, COADREAD 13, MACR 10, SRCCR 5; patient histology adenoca/mucinous/signet ring); zero pituitary/PitNET samples. MEANS: the hypothesis population (PitNETs) is absent, so no test on this data can address the claim; the data and hypothesis are mismatched. ACTION: treat as Not verifiable unless a PitNET subset is found; run LOH-proxy vs TP53 in CRC only as an exploratory side check.

label: WARNING SIGN
text: WARNING SIGN: no LOH variable exists in the data: clinical tables have no LOH/FGA column (only LST, missing in 178/471), the seg file has only total log-ratio seg.mean (no allele-specific/minor copy number), data_cna has only -2/0/2 calls. MEANS: fraction of LOH cannot be computed directly; copy-neutral LOH is invisible, only a copy-loss proxy is possible. ACTION: no LOH estimate claimed; a seg-based loss-fraction proxy is labelled exploratory.

label: WARNING SIGN
text: WARNING SIGN: AKT1 oncogenic hotspot mutations occur in only 9 of 923 MSS mCRC patients (7 right, 2 left), and in the metastasis-only subset the AKT1 test is not significant (1 vs 0, p=0.23); SMAD4 loses significance in primary-only (p=0.14) and MSI_STATUS==MSS-only (p=0.075) subsets. MEANS: the AKT1 (and partly SMAD4) result is underpowered in subsets, but direction never reverses; this affects precision, not which method is right. ACTION: kept patient-level Fisher exact (exact test suits sparse counts) on the full cohort; reported the fragility rather than changing method.

label: RESULT
text: RESULT (bd31-team-b): In 923 MSS mCRC patients (241 right, 682 left; MSS = MOLECULAR_SUBTYPE 'MSI Status', early-stage primaries excluded, patient-level), oncogenic alterations are more frequent in right-sided primaries for all six genes: KRAS 65.1% vs 37.8% (OR 3.07), BRAF 15.4% vs 5.3% (OR 3.25), PIK3CA 23.2% vs 13.0% (OR 2.02), AKT1 2.9% vs 0.3% (OR 10.2), RNF43 6.6% vs 1.0% (OR 6.9), SMAD4 24.5% vs 13.6% (OR 2.05); all BH q<=0.002 and robust to 9 sensitivity definitions. Label chosen: True.

label: WARNING SIGN
text: WARNING SIGN: 29 of 99 sample IDs carry suffixes (e.g. B80, B80-0, B80-3, B89-16) that collapse to only 73 base IDs, which looks like multiple samples per patient. MEANS: if they were the same patient, tumours would not be independent and the denominator should be 73 patients, not 99. ACTION: tested it - same-base samples have different sex and ages and share 0-1 mutations (same as unrelated pairs, mean 0.15), so they are distinct patients and the suffix is only a naming scheme; kept denominator 99 and reported the 73-collapse as sensitivity (STAG2 12/73=16.4%, ESPL1 6/73=8.2%), conclusion unchanged.

label: WARNING SIGN
text: WARNING SIGN: ESPL1-mutated tumours have much higher mutation burden (median TMB 8.6 vs 1.9 per Mb; 4 of the 6 are among the 10 most mutated samples; only 2/90 remain after dropping the 9 most mutated), and ESPL1 mutations are 6 missense + 1 nonsense with 2 silent (no truncating enrichment), unlike STAG2 (11/15 truncating). MEANS: ESPL1's 6.1% frequency may be partly passenger mutations in hypermutated tumours, so raw frequency alone overstates the evidence. ACTION: added a per-sample burden x gene-length background test (ESPL1 expected 1.6 tumours, observed 6, p=0.005; p=0.08 if background rate doubled; STAG2 p<1e-5 under all settings) and reported ESPL1 as the weak half of the claim; label stays True because the hypothesis is about frequency of alteration, which is 6% and top 1% of genes.

label: WARNING SIGN
text: WARNING SIGN: the study has only a mutation table (no CNA, SV or expression tables) and data_mutations.txt uses old gene symbols (UTX for KDM6A, MLL for KMT2A, NALP6) and covers only 6,736 genes with 11,223 calls, with no read counts or validation status filled in. MEANS: 'altered' can only be measured as somatic mutation (a lower bound), and gene-symbol aliases could split counts. ACTION: searched aliases and genomic coordinates for STAG2 (chrX:123.09-123.24Mb) and ESPL1 (chr12:53.66-53.69Mb); all calls in those loci are already labelled STAG2 (16 rows) and ESPL1 (9 rows), so no change to counts; noted mutation-only limitation in the answer.

label: RESULT
text: RESULT (bd29-team-b): In the 99-tumour BGI bladder TCC cohort, STAG2 has non-silent somatic mutations in 13/99 tumours (13.1%, mostly truncating, rank ~10 of 5,342 genes) and ESPL1 in 6/99 (6.1%, mostly missense, top 1% of genes, concentrated in high-TMB tumours); 18/99 have either. Label chosen: True, with ESPL1 the weaker half.

label: WARNING SIGN
text: WARNING SIGN: MSI_STATUS is not a usable sole MSS definition: it is NA for 327 of 1134 samples, 7 samples labelled MSS are POLE and 2 are MSI in MOLECULAR_SUBTYPE (MSI score up to 29), and 9 labelled MSI have MOLECULAR_SUBTYPE 'MSI Status' with scores 0-9.4. MEANS: MSS must be defined from MOLECULAR_SUBTYPE (value 'MSI Status' = not MSI, not POLE; MSI score mean 0.83, max 9.4, TMB max 25) rather than the label, otherwise a third of patients are lost or hypermutated tumours stay in. ACTION: main cohort = MOLECULAR_SUBTYPE 'MSI Status', MSI_STATUS not 'MSI', MSI score <10 (918 patients); reran with score<3 & TMB<25 (876 patients), label-only MSS (617), and loose non-MSI (928): all six genes right-enriched in every definition.

label: WARNING SIGN
text: WARNING SIGN: SMAD4 right-vs-left effect is heterogeneous by specimen type: OR 1.21 (p=0.55) in primary specimens vs OR 3.24 (p=8e-6) in metastasis specimens, Breslow-Day p=0.006; it also weakens to OR 1.5 (p=0.09-0.14) in the subset with an explicit MSI_STATUS=MSS label, while the label-NA subset gives OR 2.99. Other five genes are homogeneous (BD p>0.4). MEANS: the pooled SMAD4 estimate depends on the primary/metastasis specimen mix; this changes how confident the SMAD4 component is, not which test is right. ACTION: kept patient-level Fisher as primary, added CMH stratified by specimen type (SMAD4 pooled OR 1.98, CI 1.36-2.89, p=0.0003) and logistic adjustment for specimen type and panel (OR 2.02, p=0.0003); SMAD4 direction is right-sided in every stratum, flagged as the weakest of the six.

label: WARNING SIGN
text: WARNING SIGN: 28+2+1 patients have 2-4 sequenced samples (1134 samples, 1099 patients); 123 samples are 'Early Stage Primary' not mCRC; curated side codes Transverse Colon as 15 Left / 27 Right and one Cecum as Left in the MSS mCRC cohort; one patient (MSI, early stage) has samples on both sides. MEANS: sample-level counting would break independence; side re-derived from site would disagree with the curated side for about 16 patients. ACTION: collapsed to patient (altered if any sample altered; first-sample-only gives the same result), excluded early-stage, used curated side, and reran excluding transverse, excluding rectum/rectosigmoid, and with transverse+cecum forced Right: all six genes stay right-enriched with q<0.05.

label: WARNING SIGN
text: WARNING SIGN: ESPL1's 6 non-silent-mutated samples (6/99 = 6.1%) all sit in the high-burden half of the cohort and 4 of 6 are in the top-10% burden samples (Mann-Whitney p=0.0003 for burden, mutated vs not); excluding top-10% burden samples the frequency falls to 2/89 = 2.2%; 6 of 7 ESPL1 mutations are missense and the gene also carries 2 silent mutations (expected ~0.6). MEANS: part of ESPL1's raw prevalence is passenger load from high-burden tumours, so raw frequency overstates any driver-like recurrence. ACTION: added a per-sample burden-aware, length-scaled expectation (expected 1.7 mutated samples vs 6 observed, ratio 3.5, nominal P about 0.007, not genome-wide significant); kept prevalence as the primary criterion per the pre-registered rule (6.1%, rank 33 of ~19000 genes, 7 distinct variants) but flagged ESPL1 as the weak half of the claim and lowered confidence.

label: WARNING SIGN
text: WARNING SIGN: BRAF right-sided enrichment in MSS mCRC is driven by V600E (27/241 right vs 22/677 left, OR 3.76, p=1e-5); non-V600 oncogenic BRAF is not significantly enriched (8/241 vs 14/677, OR 1.63, p=0.33). AKT1 has only 9 altered patients (7 right, 2 left; min expected cell 2.4; OR 10.1, CI 2.1-49). RNF43 G659fs occurs in 34 samples, all MSI subtype, none in the MSS cohort; without the MSS filter RNF43 would read 12.2% vs 1.6% instead of 7.1% vs 1.2%. MEANS: gene-level claim holds for BRAF as a whole but not for every variant class; AKT1 estimate is imprecise so Fisher exact is required; MSS filter is clean of misclassified MSI. ACTION: used Fisher exact with BH across six genes; reported BRAF both ways; no method change.

label: WARNING SIGN
text: WARNING SIGN: 100 identical variants recur in >=2 samples and 30 in >=3, led by non-hotspot repeats that look like artefacts or germline leakage (ZNF83 p.E293V in 16 samples, ZNF233 frameshift in 13, FGFRL1 2-bp deletion in 8); dbSNP_RS and t_alt/t_ref counts are empty for all 11223 rows so no allele-fraction or dbSNP filter is possible; TTN has only 6 mutated samples against a length-scaled expectation of 22 and MUC16 has none, so the MAF looks curated/filtered. MEANS: gene ranks by raw mutated-sample count include artefact genes, and a uniform length-scaled background is only approximate (it over-predicts very long genes, which makes the excess test conservative for the target genes). ACTION: checked STAG2 (15 non-silent rows, 15 distinct variants, 13 samples) and ESPL1 (7 rows, 7 distinct variants, 6 samples): no repeated variant in either, so their counts are independent events and no rows were dropped; the ranks (STAG2 about 10th, ESPL1 about 33rd) would only improve if artefact genes like ZNF83/ZNF233/FGFRL1 were removed.

label: RESULT
text: RESULT (bd31-team-a): In 918 MSS metastatic CRC patients (241 right, 677 left; curated PRIMARY_TUMOR_LOCATION, MOLECULAR_SUBTYPE-based MSS), oncogenic alterations (hotspot/truncating mutations + amp/deep deletion + SV) right vs left: KRAS 65.1% vs 37.8% (OR 3.07, q=2e-12), BRAF 15.4% vs 5.5% (OR 3.14, q=2e-5), PIK3CA 22.8% vs 13.1% (OR 1.95, q=8e-4), AKT1 2.9% vs 0.3% (OR 10.1, q=2e-3), RNF43 7.1% vs 1.2% (OR 6.35, q=2e-5), SMAD4 22.8% vs 13.1% (OR 1.95, q=8e-4). Label chosen: True.

label: WARNING SIGN
text: WARNING SIGN: 29 sample IDs carry a shared prefix with a numeric suffix (B80-0..B80-13 is 10 samples, B89-* is 8, B59-* is 4), which could mean several samples from one patient although each has its own PATIENT_ID. MEANS: if they were the same patients, samples would not be independent and N=99 would be too large. ACTION: tested it: same-prefix samples differ in sex, age and stage and share essentially no mutations (1 of 88 same-prefix pairs shares a single variant, same rate as unrelated pairs), so they are distinct patients; kept N=99. Worst-case prefix-collapsed frequencies would be STAG2 12/73 (16%) and ESPL1 6/73 (8%), i.e. not lower.

label: RESULT
text: RESULT (bd29-team-a analyst): In the 99 BLCA (=TCC) samples, all profiled WXS/WGS, non-silent somatic mutation frequency is STAG2 13/99 = 13.1% (Wilson 95% 7.8-21.2%; 13/15 mutations truncating, 15 distinct variants, rank about 10 of all genes tied with RB1, 13x the burden-aware length-scaled expectation, 10/89 without top-10% burden samples) and ESPL1 6/99 = 6.1% (Wilson 2.8-12.6%; 6 missense + 1 nonsense, 7 distinct variants, rank 33-51 of ~19000 genes, 3.5x expectation with nominal P about 0.007, but 2/89 without top-10% burden samples). Both genes are found under current symbols and at the expected GRCh37 coordinates; chrX holds 3.8% of non-silent calls so STAG2 was assayable. Label chosen: True, with ESPL1 as the weaker half.

label: WARNING SIGN
text: WARNING SIGN: data_cna_hg19.seg has 507 exactly duplicated rows out of 24908, and 5 of 471 clinical samples have no seg data (4 have no mutation rows). MEANS: any length-weighted copy-number fraction would double-count duplicated segments unless de-duplicated; it affects only which rows are kept, not the method. ACTION: no change to the answer, because the seg-based loss fraction is only an exploratory proxy in colorectal tumours and is not used for the label.

label: RESULT
text: bd39 finding: the dataset is a 471-sample MSK-IMPACT metastatic colorectal cancer cohort with no PitNET samples and no LOH or allele-specific copy-number variable, so the hypothesis 'higher LOH fraction is associated with TP53 mutations in PitNETs' was labelled Not verifiable by team-b; an exploratory copy-loss-fraction proxy in CRC was higher in TP53-mutant tumours (median 0.108 vs 0.027 at seg.mean<-0.2, Mann-Whitney p=5e-8) but this is the wrong tumour type and not LOH.

label: WARNING SIGN
text: WARNING SIGN: the informative (pre-chemo) stratum has only 5 TP53-altered patients; Fisher p=0.0034 becomes 0.039 if one flips to sensitive and 0.33 if two flip; adjusting additionally for IGCCCG poor risk gives exact one-sided p=0.12 (timing x risk) because 15/16 altered patients are poor risk. MEANS: the association is real in direction (16/16 resistant, zero counterexamples) and significant after timing and site stratification, but the data cannot show TP53 is independent of poor-risk status. ACTION: kept exact stratified tests as the method; report label True for association, with independence from risk group flagged as unproven.

label: RESULT
text: bd35 germ cell tumor dataset result (team-b): TP53 mutation or deep deletion found in 16/180 patients, all 16 CHEMO_RESISTANT=Yes versus 88/164 wild-type (Fisher p=1e-4); in pre-chemo specimens only 5/5 vs 33/109 (p=0.0034); within mediastinal primaries 13/13 vs 4/9 (p=0.005); exact test stratified by timing x site p=0.005. Label chosen: True. Data are clean: 180 patients, exactly one sample each, all files' sample IDs match, no duplicates.

label: PLAN
text: PLAN (bd32-team-a analyst): Quantity = per-sample copy-number alteration burden from data_cna_hg19.seg (autosomes), comparing JP (JuP3-JP matched; JuP1, JuP2 unsuffixed judged as JP-only cases, supporting) against JuP3-DCIS and JuP3-IDC. Method = descriptive per-sample: check seg.mean scale and baseline centring; count altered segments, merged same-state events, FGA, and arm-level events (50% and 90% arm fraction) at |log2| cutoffs 0.1/0.2/0.3/0.5, with and without small-segment filter (num.mark<10-50, <1Mb) and recentring; estimate purity from mutation VAFs. Primary evidence = matched within-patient JuP3 comparison; no inferential tests (n=5 samples, 3 patients). Label True only if JP has more CNAs than DCIS and IDC robustly; False if JP consistently has fewer/few. Would change method if: seg.mean is absolute CN not log2, a sample is mis-centred, sample is over-segmented/noisy, purity differs strongly, IDs mismatch or coverage partial.

label: PLAN
text: PLAN (bd32-team-b): Quantity = copy-number alteration burden per sample (number of altered segments and fraction of genome altered at |seg.mean| thresholds 0.1/0.2/0.3, plus arm-level events) from data_cna_hg19.seg, comparing JuP3-JP against its matched JuP3-DCIS and JuP3-IDC (and JP samples JuP1, JuP2 as context). Method: descriptive per-sample comparison (n=1 matched trio, no inferential test possible); weighted by segment length. Checks: seg IDs match clinical sample IDs, duplicates/overlapping segments, per-sample noise level (seg.mean SD, segment count), threshold sensitivity, sex chromosomes excluded. Would change method if: samples missing from seg file, noise/over-segmentation differs strongly between samples (then use length-weighted fraction instead of counts), or result flips across thresholds.

label: PLAN
text: PLAN (bd36-team-a): Quantity: whether the tables contain junction-level rearrangement data (both breakpoints + orientation) that allow modelling interdependent chains (chromoplexy), and if not, what proxies exist. Method: (1) inventory all tables/columns, intersect sample IDs (82 clinical / 57 WGS / 56 CNA), check data_sv.txt and data_mutations.txt for any breakpoint coordinates or partner loci; (2) seg file QC (num.mark, length, recurrent boundaries), filtered+merged deletion calls per sample; (3) descriptive proxy only: per-sample count of chromosomes with focal deletions and clustering of CN breakpoints vs a permutation null keeping per-sample breakpoint counts and locus-specific probabilities, BH-corrected; chromothripsis-like one-chromosome oscillation tabulated separately; (4) cross-tab ERG_FISH_RESULT x ETS_FUSION_SEQ x data_sv, 21q22 TMPRSS2-ERG interstitial loss in seg; cancer-gene deletions (PTEN, NKX3-1, CDKN1B, TP53, RB1, CHD1) frequency. Label rule: True only if junction-level chains can be modelled and chains significantly exceed independent null AND disrupt cancer genes; False if relevant variables exist and contradict; Not verifiable if no junction-level data and CN proxies cannot distinguish chained from independent events. Would change method if SV/other table has coordinates of both breakends.

label: WARNING SIGN
text: WARNING SIGN: Zero cell in the primary 2x2: all 16 TP53-altered patients (15 non-synonymous mutation, 1 deep deletion, 0 SV) are CHEMO_RESISTANT=Yes versus 88/164 wild-type; ML odds ratio is infinite. MEANS: Wald logistic regression and chi-square are not usable; need exact/penalised methods. ACTION: Used two-sided Fisher exact (p=1.0e-4, conditional exact 95% CI lower bound 3.2), 0.5-corrected OR 28.5 and Firth logistic (PLR p=4e-5); method was already planned this way.

label: WARNING SIGN
text: WARNING SIGN: Sample timing is perfectly tied to outcome: all 66 post-chemo specimens are from resistant patients (0 sensitive), and all 76 sensitive patients have pre-chemo specimens; 11 of 16 TP53-altered samples are post-chemo. MEANS: pooled association could reflect acquired/selected TP53 changes or sampling, not a baseline marker. ACTION: Repeated the test in the 113 pre-chemo samples only: 5/5 TP53-altered resistant vs 32/108 wild-type, Fisher p=0.003; association holds, so label unchanged, but stated as association rather than pre-treatment predictor.

label: WARNING SIGN
text: WARNING SIGN: TP53 alterations are concentrated in mediastinal primary NSGCT (13 of 16 altered; 13/22 mediastinal vs 3/157 testis; 0 in 46 seminoma patients; 15/16 are IGCCCG poor risk). MEANS: crude association is confounded with primary site/histology/risk group. ACTION: Stratified: mediastinum 13/13 vs 4/9 resistant (Fisher p=0.005), testis 3/3 vs 84/154 (p=0.25), CMH by site p=0.004, by histology p=0.002, by risk group p=0.09 (poor-risk stratum 15/15 vs 36/44); Firth adjusted for site+histology OR 29, PLR p=0.001; with poor risk+post-chemo+cohort OR 22, p=0.04. Direction never reverses, so crude patient-level result kept as primary.

label: WARNING SIGN
text: WARNING SIGN: Annotation inconsistencies in this germ cell tumour study: gene panel matrix labels all 180 samples WXS although 163 IDs are targeted-panel style (P-...-IM3/IM5) and 17 are DS-test exome-style; Mutation_Status is blank for all panel rows (only DS rows say Somatic); read-count columns for DS rows are inconsistent (t_depth smaller than t_alt_count, n_depth NA), so VAF for the single DS TP53 call (DS-test-007-P p.V173M) cannot be verified. MEANS: wild-type certainty differs by platform and one TP53 call cannot be quality-checked. ACTION: Stratified by cohort/ID scheme (panel: 15/15 vs 81/148, p=4e-4; DS: 1/1 vs 7/16) and recoded the DS call to wild-type (p=1.9e-4); conclusion unchanged. All 15 panel TP53 calls are truncating/splice/DNA-binding-domain missense with 0-3% normal alt reads (max 16/502 in a sample with 78% tumour VAF), none look germline.

label: WARNING SIGN
text: WARNING SIGN: The cohort is enriched for resistant cases (104 of 180 patients CHEMO_RESISTANT=Yes, 58%), and one patient has missing TREATMENT_CHEMOTHERAPY/regimen/cohort but CHEMO_RESISTANT=Yes. MEANS: resistance rates are not population estimates; quote odds ratios; the one untreated-unknown patient is TP53 wild-type. ACTION: Reported ORs; excluding that patient gives n=179, 16/16 vs 87/163, Fisher p=9.6e-5 (unchanged).

label: RESULT
text: RESULT (bd35-team-a analyst): In the germ cell tumour study, 180 patients each have exactly one sample, all profiled for mutations/CNA/SV with exact ID matches; TP53 altered (non-synonymous mutation or deep deletion) in 16 patients, all 16 chemo-resistant vs 88/164 wild-type (Fisher two-sided p=1.0e-4, exact 95% CI lower bound for OR 3.2, 0.5-corrected OR 28.5). Holds for mutation-only (15/15, p=1.9e-4), TP53-or-MDM2-amp (24/26 vs 80/154, OR 11, p=6e-5), pre-chemo samples only (5/5 vs 32/108, p=0.003), within mediastinal primaries (p=0.005) and in Firth models adjusted for site and histology. Label chosen: True.

label: PLAN
text: PLAN (bd36-team-b, chromoplexy hypothesis): Quantity: whether translocations and deletions arise interdependently (chained rearrangements) and hit prostate cancer genes. Audit first: data_sv.txt has only 28 gene-level fusion rows (Site1=Site2 gene, no coordinates, no partner chromosome), so paired rearrangement breakpoints needed for chain modelling may be absent; the only breakpoint-level data are copy-number segments in data_cna_hg19.seg. Method: (1) audit sample ID overlap across clinical/seg/cna/sv/mutations and duplicates; (2) check whether any table carries breakpoint-pair coordinates; if not, the chain model itself cannot be fitted and the core claim is Not verifiable from first principles; (3) proxy tests from seg: per-sample count of focal deletion segments and chromosomes involved, overdispersion vs Poisson, within-sample clustering of deletion breakpoints across chromosomes, deletion breakpoints at TMPRSS2/ERG in fusion-positive samples vs negative (Fisher), focal deletions over PTEN/NKX3-1/TP53/CDKN1B/CHD1/RB1, association of ETS fusion status with deletion burden (Mann-Whitney), purity as confounder of segment counts. Decision rule: label True only if the data can show interdependence of translocations AND deletions (needs linked breakpoints or a strong proxy robust to purity/segmentation noise); label False only if a relevant test contradicts; otherwise Not verifiable. Would change method if a table with SV coordinates is found (then build breakpoint-adjacency chains with permutation null).

text: PLAN (bd38-team-b, NPC ERBB-PI3K hypothesis): Data = 56 NPC patients/samples (1:1), MAF with 1575 rows, mostly nonsynonymous (WES, matched normal). Label False if pathway is recurrently mutated with enrichment/hotspots; True if no or chance-level mutations; Not verifiable only if genes cannot be assessed.

label: PLAN
text: PLAN (bd38-team-a analyst): Quantity = whether the ERBB-PI3K pathway carries more somatic SNV/indel mutations across NPC tumours than a length-aware, per-tumour background predicts. Pre-specified CORE gene list (fixed before any counts): EGFR, ERBB2, ERBB3, ERBB4, PIK3CA, PIK3CB, PIK3CD, PIK3CG, PIK3R1, PIK3R2, PIK3R3, PTEN, AKT1, AKT2, AKT3, MTOR (16 genes). Narrow sensitivity list: ERBB2, ERBB3, ERBB4, EGFR, PIK3CA, PTEN, AKT1. Broad sensitivity list: core + NRG1, EGF, TSC1, TSC2, RICTOR, RPTOR, STK11, INPP4B, PDPK1, RHEB, PIK3C2A, PIK3C2B, PIK3C2G, PIK3C3, PIK3R4, PIK3R5, AKT1S1, MLST8, KRAS, NRAS, HRAS. Primary test (alpha 0.05 nominal, single pre-specified pathway; also report whether it survives Bonferroni x10): self-contained Poisson-binomial test of number of tumours with >=1 nonsilent pathway mutation, with per-tumour probability = 1-exp(-n_i * L_pathway/L_exome), n_i = that tumour's own nonsilent count from the mutation table, gene 'length' approximated from protein length in the file / known CDS lengths; plus a competitive empirical null from random gene sets matched on size/length. Checks: ID mismatch between tables and denominator, Variant_Classification/FILTER tabulation (with/without common_variant and noncoding rows), Entrez=0 so match on Hugo_Symbol with aliases, per-gene breakdown and leave-one-gene-out, hotspot/driver-only tally, load vs cellularity, drop top-load tumours, exact binomial CI and power. Change method if: load is highly heterogeneous (then per-sample conditioning is mandatory, already planned), or silent mutations absent (no dN/dS), or signal carried by one gene or by known hotspots (then weigh recurrence evidence).

text: FINDING: In the cBioPortal discrete copy-number format 0 is defined as diploid / no change (-2 deep loss, -1 single-copy loss, 1 low-level gain, 2 high-level amplification); in a table holding only -2/0/2, 0 therefore means 'no deep deletion or amplification called' and also absorbs hemizygous loss and low-level gain. Non-evaluability is supposed to be recorded differently: the agreed convention is NA for a missing measurement in a discrete CNA file, NA in the 'cna' column of the gene panel matrix for a sample not profiled, and absence from the required _cna case list. BUT the format does not enforce this, and the web did not settle whether a given panel pipeline writes 0 for samples whose copy number could not be evaluated: AACR GENIE staff state that which samples were really profiled for CNA is not reliably recorded (CNA files are optional per centre and the matrix cna column is inferred from presence in the CNA file). A gene panel matrix with only a 'mutations' column, as here, gives no declaration of CNA profiling at all. So 0 cannot be proven to mean 'assessed and intact'; describe it as 'no deep deletion called', and as a sensitivity analysis restrict to samples with evidence that CNA calling worked (e.g. at least one non-zero call in any gene) or check that the result does not depend on samples whose CNA column is all zeros. QUESTION: In -2/0/2 gene-level CNA tables from targeted panels in cBioPortal format, does 0 mean assessed-and-unaltered or can it also cover not-evaluable samples, and how is non-evaluability normally recorded? text: FINDING: There is no consensus single method when proportional hazards fails; the hazard ratio is then a hard-to-interpret average, and guidance is to report model-free summaries alongside the Kaplan-Meier curves: (1) restricted mean survival time (RMST = area under the survival curve to time tau), contrasted as a difference or ratio of RMST, or ratio of restricted mean time lost, which gives an absolute effect with a clear direction even when curves cross; (2) survival proportions at fixed landmark/milestone times (e.g. 6- or 12-month PFS) and the median; (3) weighted log-rank tests (early-emphasis Wilcoxon/Peto, late-emphasis Fleming-Harrington, max-combo) as TESTS only: they give no effect size, a late-emphasis test can favour a group whose curve is below the other early on, and max-combo can reject in both directions on the same data, so they must not be used to state direction. Tau must be fixed before looking at results, with a stated rationale, as a clinically relevant horizon that lies within follow-up of both groups; picking tau to maximise significance exaggerates the effect, and showing RMST over a range of tau is the recommended sensitivity analysis. If no observation is censored (every PFS time an event) the ordinary mean is estimable and RMST at the largest time equals it. The common software default of tau = the smaller of the two groups' largest observed times was NOT confirmed in the pages read. For a directional claim of 'increased PFS', report RMST difference with CI at a pre-set tau plus landmark PFS proportions and say whether the direction is the same at each. QUESTION: When proportional hazards fails with a small group and possibly crossing curves, which summary measures state the direction of a PFS difference, and how is the RMST truncation time chosen? text: FINDING: The cBioPortal file-format documentation lists Mutation_Status as an OPTIONAL MAF column and says only this: 'Somatic' or 'Germline' are supported by the UI in the Mutations tab; 'None', 'LOH' and 'Wildtype' will not be loaded; other values are displayed as text. It does not state in words that a blank is somatic. In practice the only value that marks a row as germline is 'Germline' (the importer ImportExtendedMutationData.java compares with equalsIgnoreCase("Germline") and does not reject a blank status), and cBioPortal maintainers handle blank/NA as non-germline: PR 8692 fixed filters that broke because msk_impact_2017 has NA in MUTATION_STATUS, and the maintainer stated the convention as 'Germline == Germline and have everything else be Somatic'. So a blank Mutation_Status means 'not flagged germline' and is handled as somatic by default by the portal, but it is an absence of a germline flag, not positive evidence that the submitter verified somatic status; corroborate with the clinical SOMATIC_STATUS (Matched) and the study's own germline-read columns. Confidence: high for which value marks germline, medium for the blank default (convention from code and a maintainer comment, not a sentence in the format spec). label: FINDING
text: FINDING: Tumour-derived variant reads in the matched normal are common in myeloid neoplasms and are an accepted, documented phenomenon (tumour-in-normal, TiN, contamination). In the Genomics England review of 771 tumour-normal WGS pairs (Mitchell et al., Nat Commun 2024), 22 of 24 (91%) sorted CD3+ T-cell normals from MPN patients and 43 of 114 (38%) saliva normals from AML patients were contaminated (tumour read fraction in normal >1%), while no cultured-fibroblast normal was; of 108 hotspot driver mutations with tumour VAF >5% in AML and MPN, 51 had VAF >1% in the normal and 27 had VAF >5%, and JAK2 V617F was seen at >10% VAF in the normal of 4 MPN cases. There is no single universal cutoff; the rules in use are: (a) Genomics England flags contamination at >1% tumour read fraction in the normal and then also runs a tumour-only pipeline, removing only variants with population allele frequency >0.01 or in a panel of normals; (b) deTiN (Taylor-Weiner et al., Nat Methods 2018) shows MuTect, Strelka and VarScan lose sensitivity once TiN >0.02 because they reject variants with normal reads, and it rescues variants rejected solely for normal evidence when the normal allele count fits 'tumour DNA mixed into normal at the estimated TiN' better than a germline heterozygous variant (posterior >0.5), treating ExAC frequency >=0.01 as germline, with rescue unreliable at TiN >0.75; (c) Illumina DRAGEN filters alt_allele_in_normal only when normal alt allele frequency exceeds 0.2 plus a contamination tolerance (0 in solid mode, default 0.15 in liquid-tumour mode) and does not call a normal artifact when normal AF < 0.1 x tumour AF. Practical rule: a variant with non-zero normal fraction still counts as somatic when the normal VAF is well below the tumour VAF and far from the ~50%/100% expected of a germline variant, is consistent with the contamination level shown by the same patient's other drivers, and is not a common population polymorphism; requiring zero normal reads is not the accepted standard in blood cancers. Confidence: high for prevalence, medium for the rule (several conventions, no single standard). QUESTION: In matched tumour-normal sequencing of chronic myeloid blood cancers, how commonly does the constitutional (normal) sample contain tumour-derived variant reads, and what thresholds or rules do somatic callers and published studies use to still call a variant somatic when the normal shows variant reads? QUESTION: According to curated functional resources (saturation-mutagenesis phosphatase-activity and protein-abundance screens, ClinVar, OncoKB), which PTEN missense substitutions are classed as loss of function, and specifically how are substitutions at residues R15, P38, V53, G132, G165, Y177 and P204 classified? ANSWER: Partly settled (OncoKB read directly; per-variant screen scores and ClinVar not retrieved). OncoKB: PTEN deletion = Oncogenic / Loss-of-function; truncating mutations = Likely Oncogenic / Likely Loss-of-function; of about 180 curated PTEN alterations 167 are oncogenic, 9 neutral, 4 inconclusive, so a missense variant counts as inactivating only if individually curated or at a recurrence hotspot. Per residue: P38L = Likely Oncogenic, Loss-of-function (hotspot residue, reported in melanoma); P38S = not individually reviewed but hotspot, Likely Oncogenic, Likely Loss-of-function (P38F/H/L are curated). G132D = Likely Oncogenic, Loss-of-function (loss of lipid and protein phosphatase activity, reduced stability, dominant negative); G132S and G132V = Likely Oncogenic, Likely Loss-of-function (read from the gene-page list). G165E = Oncogenic, Loss-of-function; G165R = Likely Oncogenic, Loss-of-function; G165V is curated as oncogenic. Y177C = Likely Oncogenic, Likely Loss-of-function (hotspot; reduced phosphatase activity in the yeast saturation screen); Y177D is curated as likely oncogenic. P204S = statistically significant hotspot, Likely Oncogenic, but no biological effect (loss of function) is stated; the P204L page failed to load. V53: no curated entry; the V53A page says not reviewed, Unknown Oncogenic Effect, so V53 substitutions are variants of unknown significance. R15: R15K and R15S appear in OncoKB's curated PTEN list, but their variant pages failed to load twice and the label is not legible in the gene-page capture, so their class (probably likely oncogenic) is unconfirmed; other R15 substitutions are not curated by name. Screens: the lipid-phosphatase saturation screen scored 7,244 single-amino-acid variants and found 2,273 with reduced activity, 1,789 of them missense (cut-offs quoted in the follow-up paper: wild-type-like fitness score > -1.11, truncation-like < -2.13, hypomorphic in between; this cut-off text came from a search excerpt of a page whose fetched text was truncated). The abundance screen (VAMP-seq) covers about 4,100 missense variants. Scores for the seven residues live in supplementary tables / MaveDB and were not retrieved; ClinVar was not consulted. question: FINDING FROM THE LAB'S LIBRARY, asked for by the director. QUESTION: In discrete gene-level copy-number tables produced from targeted hybrid-capture sequencing panels and distributed in cBioPortal format, where only the values -2, 0 and 2 appear, what does a 0 mean: 'assessed and neither amplified nor deeply deleted', or can it also stand for samples in which copy number was not evaluable (low purity, no matched normal, older panel version)? How is non-evaluability normally recorded? ANSWER: Not fully settled by the web. By the format definition 0 is 'diploid / no change' (-2 deep loss, -1 single-copy loss, 1 low-level gain, 2 high-level amplification), so in a table with only -2/0/2 a 0 formally means 'no deep deletion or amplification called' and also absorbs hemizygous loss and low-level gain. Non-evaluability is meant to be recorded differently: the agreed convention is NA for a missing measurement in a discrete CNA file, NA in the 'cna' column of the gene panel matrix for a sample not profiled, and absence from the required _cna case list. However the format does not enforce this, and no page read states whether a particular panel pipeline writes 0 for samples whose copy number could not be evaluated. AACR GENIE staff say that which samples were really profiled for CNA is not reliably recorded (centre CNA files are optional; the matrix 'cna' column is inferred from presence in the CNA file and 'is not completely accurate'). A gene panel matrix that has only a 'mutations' column declares nothing about CNA profiling. So 0 cannot be shown to mean 'assessed and intact'. Describe it as 'no deep deletion called', and add a restriction sensitivity analysis (for example samples with at least one non-zero CNA call in any gene, or check the result does not hinge on samples whose CNA column is all zeros). The cBioPortal file-format and FAQ pages were fetched but their text was cut off before the copy-number sections; the value definitions were read from the docs text quoted in GitHub issue 4664. HOW SURE: medium for the convention (0 = no change; NA / gene panel matrix / case list for not profiled); low on whether 0 hides non-evaluable samples in any specific panel dataset. SOURCES: https://docs.cbioportal.org/file-formats/, https://github.com/cBioPortal/cbioportal/issues/4664, https://github.com/cBioPortal/cbioportal/issues/1702, https://github.com/cBioPortal/cbioportal/issues/10871, https://www.synapse.org/Synapse:syn7222066/discussion/threadId=11267.

question: FINDING FROM THE LAB'S LIBRARY, asked for by the director. QUESTION: When the proportional-hazards assumption fails in a two-group comparison of progression-free survival with a small group and possibly crossing Kaplan-Meier curves, which summary measures are recommended for stating the direction of the difference (restricted mean survival time, landmark survival proportions, weighted log-rank tests), and how is the truncation time for restricted mean survival time chosen? ANSWER: There is no consensus single method under non-proportional hazards; the hazard ratio becomes a hard-to-interpret average and the log-rank test loses power when curves cross. Guidance is to report model-free summaries with the Kaplan-Meier curves: (1) restricted mean survival time (area under the survival curve up to tau), contrasted as a difference or ratio of RMST or a ratio of restricted mean time lost; it gives an absolute effect with a clear sign even when curves cross. (2) Survival proportions at fixed landmark/milestone times (e.g. 6- or 12-month PFS) and the median. (3) Weighted log-rank tests (early-emphasis Wilcoxon, late-emphasis, max-combo) are tests only: they give no effect size, a late-emphasis test can favour a group whose curve lies below the other, and a max-combo test can reject in both directions on the same data, so they should not be used to state direction. Tau should be fixed before looking at results, with a stated rationale, as a clinically relevant time horizon; choosing tau to maximise significance exaggerates the effect, and showing the RMST difference over a range of tau is the recommended sensitivity analysis. If there is no censoring, the ordinary mean survival time can be used instead of RMST. The widely used software default of tau = the smaller of the two groups' largest observed times was not confirmed in the text read (the survRM2 vignette was cut off before that passage). The remark that a post hoc tau exaggerates significance came from a search excerpt of the JCO commentary, whose fetched text was cut off before that passage. For a claim of 'increased PFS', report the RMST difference with confidence interval at a pre-set tau plus landmark PFS proportions, and say whether the direction agrees across them. HOW SURE: high for the measures and the pre-specification rule for tau; low for the 'minimum of the largest observed times' default, which was not confirmed. SOURCES: https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC7001779/, https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC9081686/, https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC8802494/, https://cran.r-project.org/web/packages/survRM2/vignettes/survRM2-vignette3-2.html.

QUESTION: When the proportional-hazards assumption fails in a two-group comparison of progression-free survival with a small group and possibly crossing Kaplan-Meier curves, which summary measures are recommended for stating the direction of the difference (restricted mean survival time, landmark survival proportions, weighted log-rank tests), and how is the truncation time for restricted mean survival time chosen? ANSWER: There is no consensus single method under non-proportional hazards; the hazard ratio becomes a hard-to-interpret average and the log-rank test loses power when curves cross. Guidance is to report model-free summaries with the Kaplan-Meier curves: (1) restricted mean survival time (area under the survival curve up to tau), contrasted as a difference or ratio of RMST or a ratio of restricted mean time lost; it gives an absolute effect with a clear sign even when curves cross. (2) Survival proportions at fixed landmark/milestone times (e.g. 6- or 12-month PFS) and the median. (3) Weighted log-rank tests (early-emphasis Wilcoxon, late-emphasis, max-combo) are tests only: they give no effect size, a late-emphasis test can favour a group whose curve lies below the other, and a max-combo test can reject in both directions on the same data, so they should not be used to state direction. Tau should be fixed before looking at results, with a stated rationale, as a clinically relevant time horizon; choosing tau to maximise significance exaggerates the effect, and showing the RMST difference over a range of tau is the recommended sensitivity analysis. If there is no censoring, the ordinary mean survival time can be used instead of RMST. The widely used software default of tau = the smaller of the two groups' largest observed times was not confirmed in the text read (the survRM2 vignette was cut off before that passage). The remark that a post hoc tau exaggerates significance came from a search excerpt of the JCO commentary, whose fetched text was cut off before that passage. question: FINDING FROM THE LAB'S LIBRARY, asked for by the director. QUESTION: In the cBioPortal mutation (MAF) file format, how is a row treated when the Mutation_Status field is left blank: is it taken as somatic by default, and which values of that field mark a row as germline? ANSWER: Mutation_Status is an optional column. The format documentation says only: "Somatic" or "Germline" are supported by the UI in the Mutations tab; "None", "LOH" and "Wildtype" will not be loaded; other values are displayed as text. It does not state in words that a blank is somatic, so the format spec alone does not settle the default. What the code and maintainers show: the only value that marks a row as germline is "Germline" (the importer, ImportExtendedMutationData.java, tests equalsIgnoreCase("Germline") and does not reject a row for a blank status), and blank/NA is handled as non-germline. Pull request 8692 fixed study-view filters that broke because a public study (msk_impact_2017) has NA in MUTATION_STATUS, and the maintainer stated the convention as "Germline == Germline and have everything else be Somatic". So in cBioPortal a blank Mutation_Status is handled as somatic by default, and only an explicit "Germline" marks germline. Caveat for the teams: a blank is the absence of a germline flag, not positive evidence that the submitter verified somatic status; it is a valid basis for not excluding rows, but somatic status should be corroborated from other fields (clinical SOMATIC_STATUS = Matched, the study's own tumour and germline read columns). I could not open the frontend source that implements the germline test, so the case-insensitive match is confirmed only in the importer. HOW SURE: medium (high that only 'Germline' marks germline; medium that blank defaults to somatic, since this rests on importer code and a maintainer comment rather than a sentence in the format spec). SOURCES: https://docs.cbioportal.org/file-formats/, https://github.com/cBioPortal/cbioportal/pull/8692, https://github.com/cBioPortal/cbioportal-core/blob/main/src/main/java/org/mskcc/cbio/portal/scripts/ImportExtendedMutationData.java.

question: FINDING FROM THE LAB'S LIBRARY, asked for by the director. QUESTION: In matched tumour-normal sequencing of chronic myeloid blood cancers, how commonly does the constitutional (normal) sample contain tumour-derived variant reads, and what thresholds or rules do somatic callers and published studies use to still call a variant somatic when the normal shows variant reads? ANSWER: It is common and well documented (tumour-in-normal, TiN, contamination). In the Genomics England review of 771 tumour-normal whole-genome pairs (Mitchell et al., Nat Commun 2024), 22 of 24 (91%) sorted CD3+ T-cell normals from myeloproliferative neoplasm patients and 43 of 114 (38%) saliva normals from AML patients were contaminated (tumour read fraction in the normal above 1%); no cultured-fibroblast normal was. Of 108 hotspot driver mutations with tumour VAF above 5% in the AML and MPN cases, 51 had VAF above 1% in the normal and 27 above 5%; JAK2 V617F reached above 10% VAF in the normal in 4 MPN cases. The paper also cites earlier reports of JAK2 V617F in saliva DNA of MPN patients. I did not read a separate contamination rate for CML. There is no single universal threshold; the rules in use are: (a) Genomics England: contamination is flagged at above 1% tumour read fraction in the normal, and such cases are also run tumour-only, removing only variants with population allele frequency above 0.01 or present in a panel of normals. (b) deTiN (Taylor-Weiner et al., Nat Methods 2018): MuTect, Strelka and VarScan lose sensitivity once TiN exceeds 0.02 because they reject variants with reads in the normal, mostly high-allele-fraction clonal drivers; deTiN rescues variants rejected solely for normal evidence when the normal allele count fits 'tumour DNA mixed into the normal at the estimated TiN' better than a germline heterozygous variant or an artifact (posterior above 0.5), treats ExAC frequency of 0.01 or more as germline, and is unreliable when TiN exceeds 0.75. (c) Illumina DRAGEN v3.8: the alt_allele_in_normal filter fires only when the normal alt allele frequency is above 0.2 plus a contamination tolerance (0 in solid-tumour mode, default 0.15 in liquid-tumour mode), and in GATK-acceleration mode no normal artifact is called when normal AF is below 0.1 times tumour AF. Practical consequence: a variant with a non-zero normal fraction still counts as somatic when the normal VAF is well below the tumour VAF and far from the roughly 50% or 100% expected of a germline variant, is in line with the contamination shown by the same patient's other drivers, and is not a common population polymorphism. Requiring zero variant reads in the normal is not the accepted standard in blood cancers. HOW SURE: medium (high that contamination is common in MPN normals; medium on the rule, because several conventions exist and the web does not give one accepted numeric cutoff). SOURCES: https://www.nature.com/articles/s41467-023-44158-2, https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC6528031/, https://support-docs.illumina.com/SW/DRAGEN_v38/Content/SW/DRAGEN/GPipelinePostSomMat_fDG.htm.

text: FINDING: There is no single convention, but in MSK-IMPACT-style clinical cohorts the per-sample tumour purity is normally the pathologist's histological estimate: the MSK-IMPACT methods say an H&E slide is reviewed by a molecular pathology fellow and annotated for tumour purity (used for adequacy, <10% rejected). Copy-number/allele-specific algorithms (ABSOLUTE, ASCAT, FACETS-type) are the standard computational route in research cohorts but fail in copy-number-quiet tumours (thyroid carcinoma is named as the example) and in low-purity flat profiles. VAF-derived purity is a recognised fallback, not the default: TPES computes purity = observed VAF / expected VAF (about 0.5, slightly less for reference-mapping bias) from SNVs that are ASSUMED clonal, heterozygous and in copy-neutral segments, and a Modern Pathology validation used 2 x VAF of KRAS/BRAF at non-amplified diploid loci, 'assumed to involve all tumor cells' (R2 0.79 vs copy-number purity; histology R2 0.01-0.35). Consequence (deduced from the formulas, not quoted from a paper): if purity = 2 x VAF of an anchor driver, the anchor's CCF is 1 by construction and is no evidence of its clonality, and for any other diploid-locus mutation CCF = 2*VAF/purity reduces to VAF_mut/VAF_anchor, so the purity-based CCF and the ratio-to-driver test are the SAME measurement, not two independent lines of evidence; it shows only 'TERT is in as many cells as the anchor', conditional on the anchor being truncal. The subclonal-reconstruction guide adds diagnostics: known early drivers looking subclonal means purity is too high; CCF>1 ('superclonal') means purity underestimated, wrong copy number or germline contamination; SNV-based and CNA-based purity should be compared, especially in tumours with few CNAs. QUESTION: How is a per-sample tumor purity field usually obtained in cBioPortal-style clinical tables (histology, copy-number algorithm, or VAF of a clonal driver), and what do methods papers say about using VAF-derived purity to compute CCF of other mutations? text: FINDING: Two published single-mutation rules are standard, both on CCF computed from VAF, purity and local copy number. (a) McGranahan 2015: clonal if the upper bound of the 95% confidence interval of the CCF is >= 1, subclonal otherwise (chosen deliberately so that subclonal calls are not overestimated). (b) Landau 2013 (ABSOLUTE): clonal if P(CCF > 0.95) > 0.5, subclonal otherwise. A fixed point-estimate cut-off (e.g. CCF >= 0.8) is not one of these. CCF = f/(m*rho) * (rho*N_T + 2*(1-rho)), multiplicity m = max(1, round(f/rho*(rho*N_T + 2*(1-rho)))); choosing m needs allele-specific copy number (total copy number alone cannot bound it), and if m=1 is assumed a clonal mutation on a gained allele gets CCF about equal to its true multiplicity (>1). text: FINDING: The web does not show a systematic, directional VAF bias at the TERT promoter hotspots in hybrid-capture sequencing; no page read reports promoter VAF inflated (or deflated) relative to coding hotspots in the same sample, so the question is NOT settled and an upward assay bias cannot be asserted. What is documented is low depth, not bias: the promoter is >80% GC and one hybrid-capture panel had mean depth 21.6 at the promoter versus 885 elsewhere (12-13 reads at the two hotspots before bait redesign, about 100-125 after), giving dropout and very noisy VAFs (14-75% from 7-47 reads in confirmed-mutant tumours). label: FINDING
text: FINDING: There is no universally agreed threshold for a 'high' mutation rate (a 100,000-genome hypermutation study states there is 'no agreed on definition of hypermutation'), but the paediatric literature uses these conventions: >10 mutations/Mb = hypermutated in both childhood and adult cancers (segmented regression gave 9.91/Mb for childhood, 9.0/Mb for adult), >100/Mb = ultra-hypermutated; the 914-patient paediatric pan-cancer study adds a paediatric-specific tier, 2-10 coding mutations/Mb = 'paediatric highly mutated' ('below this threshold, but markedly above average'), against a typical paediatric range of 0.02-0.49/Mb; the 1,699-case study uses a relative rule, hypermutator = more than 3 s.d. above the histotype mean (5% trimmed). These are per-tumour labels, not labels for a cohort median. Paediatric and embryonal tumours are consistently described as LOW relative to adult cancers: medulloblastoma exomes 'exhibit low mutation rates consistent with other pediatric tumors, with a median of 0.35 non-silent mutations per megabase'; paediatric coding rates are 'overall 14 times lower than in adult cancers' (0.13 vs 1.8/Mb); embryonal rhabdomyosarcoma median 0.27/Mb; rhabdoid tumours 'amongst those with the lowest mutation burden'; childhood genomes are called 'quiet'; adult exome analysis puts paediatric tumours at the lowest end (as low as 0.1/Mb). So on a paediatric-specific reading, 'high' would need roughly >=2/Mb (highly mutated) or >=10/Mb (hypermutated); a median inside 0.02-0.8/Mb is the ordinary paediatric level, which the literature calls low. Caution: targeted-panel burden values run higher than exome values (panel-based median over 2,885 paediatric tumours was 2.5 Mut/Mb) and must not be mixed with exome-based rates. QUESTION: Is there an accepted numeric threshold or conventional verbal description for 'high' vs 'low' somatic coding mutation rate in paediatric solid tumours, and how do genomic studies of paediatric embryonal tumours describe their mutation rates relative to adult cancers? label: FINDING
text: FINDING: cBioPortal defines OS_MONTHS as 'the number of months from a starting point (often time of diagnosis or time of sequencing) to time of death or last follow up', and PFS_MONTHS as the time 'the disease recurred or the patient was last seen'; the *_STATUS column (0: no event, 1: event) is what tells the two apart, and the file-format documentation requires *_STATUS and *_MONTHS in pairs for survival plots. The documentation says nothing about a months column supplied alone and does not define EFS_MONTHS specifically (only the generic PREFIX_STATUS/PREFIX_MONTHS convention). So without a status column a months value is an event time for some patients and a censoring (last follow-up) time for others, and the file cannot say which: a median of OS_MONTHS is a median follow-up/observation time, not a median survival, and is not evidence of poor survival. EFS_MONTHS shorter than OS_MONTHS for a patient is consistent with a non-death event (relapse/progression) before death or last follow-up, but that is an inference from the usual definitions (same start date, same last follow-up), not something the cBioPortal documentation states; EFS equal to OS cannot distinguish 'no event, both censored' from 'death as first event'. QUESTION: In cBioPortal-format clinical patient files, when a survival-months column such as OS_MONTHS or EFS_MONTHS is supplied without a matching status column, does the months value represent time to the event or time to last follow-up? SOURCE: https://docs.cbioportal.org/user-guide/faq/ ; https://docs.cbioportal.org/file-formats/

question: FINDING FROM THE LAB'S LIBRARY, asked for by the director. QUESTION: In clinical tumour sequencing studies distributed in cBioPortal-style clinical sample tables, how is a per-sample 'tumor purity' field usually obtained: pathologist estimate from histology, a copy-number/allele-specific algorithm, or a value computed from variant allele frequencies of called mutations (for example twice the VAF of a presumed clonal heterozygous driver)? If VAF-derived purity is used, what do methods papers say about using it to compute cancer cell fraction for other mutations in the same sample? ANSWER: There is no single convention; the web does not say how any particular study's column was made, so the teams' own check of the column decides that. What the sources establish: (1) In MSK-IMPACT-style clinical cohorts the routine purity value is the pathologist's histological estimate: the MSK-IMPACT methods state that an H&E slide is reviewed by a molecular pathology fellow and annotated for tumour purity (used for sample adequacy; <10% rejected). Histological estimates agree poorly with molecular purity (R2 0.01-0.35 in one validation). (2) Copy-number/allele-specific algorithms (ABSOLUTE, ASCAT and similar) are the standard computational route in research cohorts but fail in copy-number-quiet tumours (thyroid carcinoma is the named example) and in low-purity samples with flat profiles (32% of clinical cases in one series). (3) VAF-derived purity is a recognised fallback, not the default: TPES computes purity = observed VAF / expected VAF (about 0.5, slightly less because of reference-mapping bias) from SNVs that are assumed clonal, heterozygous and in copy-neutral segments, with conservative filtering and several SNVs (concordance reported for >9 SNVs); a Modern Pathology validation used 2 x VAF of KRAS/BRAF at non-amplified diploid loci, with the driver 'assumed to involve all tumor cells' (R2 0.79 against copy-number purity). On using it for CCF: the methods papers treat clonality of the anchor mutation(s) as an assumption of the purity estimate, not as an output. It follows from the formulas (my deduction, not a quoted statement) that if purity = 2 x VAF of an anchor driver, the anchor's CCF is 1 by construction, and for any other mutation at a diploid locus CCF = 2*VAF/purity reduces to VAF_mutation / VAF_anchor. So a purity-based CCF built on VAF-derived purity is the same measurement as the ratio-to-driver test, not a second independent line of evidence; it can show only that the mutation is present in as many cells as the anchor, conditional on the anchor being truncal. The subclonal-reconstruction guide gives diagnostics: known early drivers appearing subclonal means purity is too high; CCF > 1 ('superclonal') means purity underestimated, wrong copy number or germline contamination; SNV-based and CNA-based purity should be compared, especially in tumours with few copy-number changes. HOW SURE: medium. SOURCES: https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC5461196/, https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC6821153/, https://modernpathology.org/article/S0893-3952(22)00261-7/fulltext, https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC7867630/.

question: FINDING FROM THE LAB'S LIBRARY, asked for by the director. QUESTION: When only targeted-panel read counts, purity and segment-level copy number are available (no allele-specific copy number), how do published methods operationally classify a single mutation as clonal versus subclonal: which cancer-cell-fraction rule is standard (for example, upper confidence bound reaching 1, or a posterior probability that CCF exceeds a set value), and how is the ratio of a mutation's VAF to a truncal driver's VAF validated as a substitute, including the need to correct both loci for copy number? ANSWER: CCF rule (settled): two published rules are standard, both applied to CCF computed from VAF, purity and local copy number. (a) McGranahan et al. 2015: clonal if the upper bound of the 95% confidence interval of the CCF is >= 1, subclonal otherwise; chosen deliberately so that subclonal mutations are not overestimated. (b) Landau et al. 2013 (ABSOLUTE): clonal if P(CCF > 0.95) > 0.5, subclonal otherwise. A fixed point-estimate cut-off is not one of the standard rules. CCF = f/(m*rho) * (rho*N_T + 2*(1-rho)), with multiplicity m = max(1, round(f/rho * (rho*N_T + 2*(1-rho)))). Choosing m properly needs allele-specific copy number (total copy number cannot bound it, e.g. copy-neutral LOH); if m = 1 is assumed, a clonal mutation on a gained allele gets a CCF about equal to its true multiplicity (>1). At low depth CCF is coarse (20 reads at 50% purity: one read moves CCF by 0.2), which is why interval rules are used, and the guide warns that small targeted panels rarely support real subclonal reconstruction. Ratio to a truncal driver (not settled): the search found no methods paper that validates the VAF ratio or a cut-off for it; it is not a standardised test. What is published is the principle that two VAFs are directly comparable, and proportional to the fraction of tumour cells, only when both loci have the same copy-number state and normal admixture; otherwise copy number shifts VAF and mimics or hides subclonality. The admissible form is therefore a ratio of copy-number-corrected quantities, [f_T*(rho*N_T + 2(1-rho))/m_T] / [f_D*(rho*N_D + 2(1-rho))/m_D]; purity cancels only when both loci are diploid, so the driver locus must be adjusted as well as the TERT locus. A reasonable pre-fixed rule, by analogy with rule (a) and stated as my extension rather than a published standard: call a mutation subclonal only when the upper 95% bound of its CCF (or of the corrected ratio, carrying binomial uncertainty from both loci) is below 1, and report rule (b) as a sensitivity analysis. One ddPCR study judged clonality by agreement of mutant allele fractions with expected values to within about 10 percentage points. Confidence by part: high for the two CCF rules and the formula; low for the ratio-to-driver test, which the web does not settle. HOW SURE: medium. SOURCES: https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC4636056/, https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC3575604/, https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC7867630/, https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC5538405/, https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC8973808/.

QUESTION: Is there an accepted numeric threshold, or a conventional verbal description, for a 'high' versus 'low' somatic coding mutation rate in paediatric solid tumours specifically (for example the definitions of hypermutation used in paediatric cancer studies), and how do genomic studies of paediatric embryonal tumours describe their mutation rates relative to adult cancers? ANSWER: No single accepted threshold exists; a large hypermutation study says 'there is no agreed on definition of hypermutation'. The conventions in use are: (1) >10 mutations/Mb = hypermutated, applied to childhood and adult cancers alike (segmented regression gave 9.91/Mb for childhood and 9.0/Mb for adult tumours; 'for consistency, we use 10 Mut/Mb'), and >100/Mb = ultra-hypermutated. (2) The 914-patient paediatric pan-cancer study adds a paediatric-specific tier: >10/Mb 'hypermutators', and 2-10 coding mutations/Mb 'paediatric highly mutated' ('below this threshold, but markedly above average'), against cancer-type rates of 0.02-0.49/Mb. This is the only paediatric-specific numeric definition of 'high' I found. (3) The 1,699-case study uses a relative rule: hypermutators are more than three standard deviations above the mean of their histotype (5% trimmed). All three label individual tumours, not a cohort median. Verbal convention: paediatric and embryonal tumours are described as low relative to adult cancers. Medulloblastoma exomes 'exhibit low mutation rates consistent with other pediatric tumors, with a median of 0.35 non-silent mutations per megabase'; paediatric coding rates are 'overall 14 times lower than in adult cancers' (0.13 vs 1.8/Mb); embryonal rhabdomyosarcoma median 0.27/Mb; rhabdoid tumours are 'amongst those with the lowest mutation burden'; childhood genomes are 'typically thought of as quiet'; the adult 27-type analysis places paediatric tumours at the lowest end (as low as 0.1/Mb); a review states adult cancers 'on average exhibit substantially higher mutational burdens compared with the vast majority of childhood tumors'. So on a paediatric-specific reading, 'high' would mean roughly >=2/Mb (highly mutated) or >=10/Mb (hypermutated); a rate within about 0.02-0.8/Mb is the ordinary paediatric level, which the field calls low. Caution: targeted-panel burden runs higher than exome-based values (the panel-based median over 2,885 paediatric tumours was 2.5 Mut/Mb), so panel figures should not be used as the scale for exome rates. I deliberately did not open disease-specific studies of the tumour type in the task. HOW SURE: high that the 10/Mb and 2-10/Mb conventions exist and that embryonal/paediatric tumours are described as low; medium that these per-tumour labels are the right yardstick for a cohort median, since no source defines 'high' for a median. (2) The 914-patient paediatric pan-cancer study adds a paediatric-specific tier: >10/Mb 'hypermutators', and 2-10 coding mutations/Mb 'paediatric highly mutated' ('below this threshold, but markedly above average'), against cancer-type rates of 0.02-0.49/Mb. This is the only paediatric-specific numeric definition of 'high' I found. (3) The 1,699-case study uses a relative rule: hypermutators are more than three standard deviations above the mean of their histotype (5% trimmed). All three label individual tumours, not a cohort median. Verbal convention: paediatric and embryonal tumours are described as low relative to adult cancers. Medulloblastoma exomes 'exhibit low mutation rates consistent with other pediatric tumors, with a median of 0.35 non-silent mutations per megabase'; paediatric coding rates are 'overall 14 times lower than in adult cancers' (0.13 vs 1.8/Mb); embryonal rhabdomyosarcoma median 0.27/Mb; rhabdoid tumours are 'amongst those with the lowest mutation burden'; childhood genomes are 'typically thought of as quiet'; the adult 27-type analysis places paediatric tumours at the lowest end (as low as 0.1/Mb); a review states adult cancers 'on average exhibit substantially higher mutational burdens compared with the vast majority of childhood tumors'. So on a paediatric-specific reading, 'high' would mean roughly >=2/Mb (highly mutated) or >=10/Mb (hypermutated); a rate within about 0.02-0.8/Mb is the ordinary paediatric level, which the field calls low. Caution: targeted-panel burden runs higher than exome-based values (the panel-based median over 2,885 paediatric tumours was 2.5 Mut/Mb), so panel figures should not be used as the scale for exome rates. I deliberately did not open disease-specific studies of the tumour type in the task. HOW SURE: high that the 10/Mb and 2-10/Mb conventions exist and that embryonal/paediatric tumours are described as low; medium that these per-tumour labels are the right yardstick for a cohort median, since no source defines 'high' for a median. text: FINDING FROM THE LAB'S LIBRARY, asked for by the director. QUESTION: In hybrid-capture targeted sequencing, do the two recurrent TERT promoter hotspot substitutions (the C>T changes at -124 and -146 from the start codon) show systematically biased variant allele frequencies relative to coding hotspots in the same sample, for instance from GC-rich low-coverage capture, reference-allele dropout, or allele-specific amplification, and in which direction? ANSWER: Not settled by the web. No page read reports a systematic directional bias (inflated or deflated) of TERT promoter VAF relative to coding hotspots in the same sample, so an upward assay bias cannot be asserted, and neither can its absence be proven from these sources. What is documented is low depth rather than bias: the promoter is >80% GC and is captured poorly; in one hybrid-capture panel mean depth at the promoter was 21.6 versus 885 for other genes (12-13 reads at the two hotspots before bait redesign, about 100-125 after), causing dropout and very noisy allele fractions (14-75% from 7-47 reads in Sanger-confirmed mutant tumours). The only generic directional effect named in the methods papers is reference-mapping bias, which pulls the alternate-allele fraction slightly below its true value for all SNVs; that would understate, not overstate, clonality. A ddPCR study (orthogonal to capture) found TERT promoter mutant allele fractions matching the values expected from clonal 1p/19q or chromosome 10 loss to within 0.5-6.2 points in most tumours, i.e. the mutation behaves as an ordinary clonal heterozygous marker when measured without capture. TERT allele fractions above the driver's and CCF > 1 are therefore better attributed to causes that can be checked in the data: binomial noise at low promoter depth combined with the caller's minimum alt-read floor, which keeps upward-fluctuating calls (my inference, not from a paper); copy number at either locus (gain of the mutant TERT allele on 5p, or extra wild-type copies at the driver locus); or purity set too low. Suggested check: compare depth at the TERT call with depth at the driver call in each sample and see whether ratios above 1 sit in the low-depth TERT calls; use intervals, not point ratios. HOW SURE: low. SOURCES: https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC8756133/, https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC8973808/, https://www.jmdjournal.org/article/S1525-1578(18)30076-X/fulltext, https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC6821153/, https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC6778654/.

question: FINDING FROM THE LAB'S LIBRARY, asked for by the director. QUESTION: In cBioPortal-format clinical patient files, when a survival-months column such as OS_MONTHS or EFS_MONTHS is supplied without a matching status column, what does the months value represent: time to the event, or time to last follow-up for patients without an event? ANSWER: Either, depending on the patient, and without the status column the file does not say which. The cBioPortal FAQ defines OS_MONTHS as 'the number of months from a starting point (often time of diagnosis or time of sequencing) to time of death or last follow up', and PFS_MONTHS as the time 'the disease recurred or the patient was last seen'. The *_STATUS column ('0:' = no event, '1:' = event) is what separates event times from censoring times, and the file-format documentation requires *_STATUS and *_MONTHS as a pair for survival plots. The documentation does not cover a months column supplied alone, and it does not define EFS_MONTHS specifically (only OS and DFS are listed, plus the generic PREFIX_STATUS / PREFIX_MONTHS pairing), so the web does not settle the lone-column case beyond this general definition. Consequences: a median of OS_MONTHS without status is a median observation time mixing deaths and censored patients; it is not a median survival and is not evidence of poor survival. EFS_MONTHS shorter than OS_MONTHS is consistent with a non-death event (relapse or progression) before death or last follow-up, but that is my inference from the standard definitions, assuming both are measured from the same start and to the same last contact; cBioPortal's documentation does not state it. EFS equal to OS cannot distinguish 'no event, both censored' from 'death as the first event'. HOW SURE: high for the documented definition (event or last follow-up); medium for the EFS-shorter-than-OS inference, which no source states. SOURCES: https://docs.cbioportal.org/user-guide/faq/, https://docs.cbioportal.org/file-formats/.

label: FINDING
text: FINDING: Standard software defines the two-sided exact/permutation log-rank p-value by ordering relabellings on the absolute standardised statistic, not by doubling a tail: R coin uses P(|c(T)| >= |c(t)|) with the permutation mean and variance (fixed across relabellings, so this is ordering by |O-E|, equivalent to a chi-square ordering only if the variance is not recomputed per relabelling), counting ties as 'at least as extreme' (>=). Doubling, 2*min(upper, lower), is a second convention found in teaching notes, so a p-value must state which was used. coin::logrank_test defaults: type 'logrank', ties.method 'mid-ranks' (subjects with tied event times share one risk set and one score; 'average-scores' is the StatXact alternative); exact() exists for univariate two-sample problems only (shift or split-up algorithm); approximate() draws nresample = 10000 relabellings. The plain label-permutation log-rank test is valid at any sample size only when both groups have the same censoring distribution; with unequal follow-up, small samples or heavy censoring it is not reliable (Heinze 2003 gives exact tests that condition on realised follow-up). With a one-patient group the full enumeration has only N equally likely outcomes, so p moves in steps of 1/N and a correct Monte-Carlo run must converge to the enumeration value under the same definition; a disagreement across 0.05 therefore comes from the definition (doubling vs |Z| ordering, > vs >= at ties, recomputed chi-square, add-one correction), not from sampling (this last sentence is the library's reasoning, not a quoted source). QUESTION: How is the two-sided p-value defined for an exact or permutation log-rank test with a single-subject group, how are ties handled, is the test valid under unequal censoring, and what does R coin do by default?
