text: FINDING: Firth-penalised Cox regression (R coxphf) always returns a finite hazard ratio under monotone likelihood, and by default (pl = TRUE, alpha = 0.05) reports profile penalised likelihood confidence limits and penalised likelihood-ratio p-values rather than Wald ones; Heinze and Schemper (2001) say these are preferable to Wald inference, and the manual advises maxstep = 0.1 and maxit = 500 if the profile limits fail to converge. Monotone likelihood for a one-patient group arises only when that patient's death is the first event while everyone else is at risk (the failing subject has the highest covariate value in every risk set); if wild-type deaths precede it, the ordinary Cox estimate is finite and Firth only shrinks it slightly. The sources give no numbers for the one-subject case and no explicit rule for reading a significant result that rests on one subject, so the web does not settle that part; what they do say is that fewer than about 10 events per variable signals unreliable Cox inference and that p-values should not be over-read. Penalisation repairs the estimate, it does not add information: the penalised likelihood-ratio p-value still relies on a chi-square approximation, whereas the exact permutation p for a one-patient group cannot be smaller than 1/N, so a Firth fit should be reported as a sensitivity analysis beside the exact test and not as the deciding result (this last sentence is the library's reasoning, not a quoted source). QUESTION: What does Firth's penalised partial likelihood report for a Cox model with monotone likelihood caused by a single-subject group, and how should a nominally significant result resting on one subject be interpreted? SOURCE: https://georgheinze.r-universe.dev/coxphf/doc/manual.html ; https://doi.org/10.1111/j.0006-341x.2001.00114.x ; https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC4375289/

label: FINDING
text: FINDING: In-silico missense predictors are not considered reliable on their own for calling BRCA1/2 missense variants damaging. Ernst et al. 2018 tested SIFT, PolyPhen-2, Align-GVGD and MutationTaster2 on 236 expert-classified BRCA1/2 missense variants: PolyPhen-2 had sensitivity 0.67 and specificity 0.67, SIFT had sensitivity 1.00 but poor specificity, all tools gave an unacceptable share of false positives, and the authors conclude the tools are not suitable to predict pathogenicity of BRCA1/2 variants of uncertain significance (SIFT is usable at most to predict benignity). The AMP/ASCO/CAP 2017 somatic guideline says missense prediction tools have moderate specificity (about 60 to 80 percent) and tend to over-predict deleterious impact; under ACMG/AMP, concordant in-silico tools count only as supporting evidence (likelihood ratio about 2). In cBioPortal-curated BRCA2 alterations 83.6 percent of driver mutations are truncating while missense variants make up 96.7 percent of variants of unknown significance. No source was found on MutationAssessor for BRCA1/2 specifically, and the web did not show one agreed convention for 'mutated' in tumour-sequencing survival studies: cBioPortal's default gene query counts every stored (non-synonymous) mutation and offers truncating-only or driver-only as explicit restrictions. So a SIFT/PolyPhen 'predicted damaging' grouping is a labelled sensitivity analysis at most, not a better primary definition than any-nonsynonymous; truncating-only is the better-founded alternative. QUESTION: Are SIFT, PolyPhen-2 and MutationAssessor predictions reliable for classifying somatic missense variants in BRCA1/2 as damaging according to ACMG/AMP and ENIGMA guidance, and what conventions define a gene as 'mutated' in tumour-sequencing survival studies? label: FINDING
text: FINDING: TMB_NONSYNONYMOUS is not supplied by the study's authors; cBioPortal's own datahub curators add it with their TMB script (datahub-study-curation-tools/tmb), computed from the study's MAF. It was added to all 71 targeted-panel studies in August 2021 after a coding-sequence (CDS) length was added to each of 52 gene panels; it counts nonsynonymous variants only (cBioPortal's lead states that silent variants are excluded and that exome studies divide by 30 Mb), the panel studies use the gene panel's CDS length as denominator (stated purpose of the CDS field; the script README itself could not be opened, so the exact Variant_Classification list and any minimum panel size are unconfirmed), and non-protein-coding panel genes are excluded from the calculation. MUTATION_RATE is not defined on any cBioPortal page read: the curation guide names only the TMB column as script-generated, so MUTATION_RATE is by elimination a column delivered by the data provider, and its counted variant classes and denominator are NOT settled by the web. Consequence: a mismatch between a recomputed value and one of these columns can come from definitional differences (variant classes, excluded non-coding genes, per-sample panel version, a MAF revised after the column was computed); no page read says either column draws on a second assay such as exome sequencing, but for MUTATION_RATE this is unproven rather than excluded. QUESTION: How are MUTATION_RATE and TMB_NONSYNONYMOUS defined for targeted-panel samples in cBioPortal study files, and who computes each? label: FINDING
text: FINDING: The methodological literature read accepts two designs as evidence on panel-versus-exome TMB correlation, and both need an exome-derived value for the same tumours: (a) in-silico restriction, where exome calls (usually TCGA) are restricted to the panel's genes and compared with the full-exome TMB (the Friends of Cancer Research phase I design, which the authors themselves call 'theoretical' variability), and (b) empirical paired sequencing of the same tumours on the panel and on exome, which is the stronger design; exome TMB is treated as the gold or reference standard in both. No source read treats a panel-only analysis (for example correlating disjoint gene subsets of one panel) as evidence about panel-versus-exome correlation; such an analysis measures only the panel's internal consistency and sampling noise, and panel-size modelling gives a model-based precision estimate, not an observed correlation with exome. This rests on a limited set of reviews and consortium papers, not an exhaustive search, so 'no panel-only design is accepted' is absence of evidence in what was read. QUESTION: Which study designs count as evidence about panel-versus-exome TMB correlation, and is any panel-only analysis regarded as informative? SOURCE: https://jitc.bmj.com/content/8/1/e000147 ; https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC6631597/ ; https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC6249625/ ; earlier department reads: https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC7574938/ ; https://www.annalsofoncology.org/article/S0923-7534(19)45993-0/fulltext

label: FINDING
text: FINDING: The web does not document any convention in which a Matched_Norm_Sample_Barcode of 'NORMAL' with blank Center and Score marks a different assay. What is documented: the vcf2maf converter (MSKCC) hard-codes the defaults tumor_id 'TUMOR' and normal_id 'NORMAL' and a default centre of '.', so the literal 'NORMAL' is the placeholder written when no normal sample ID is passed to the tool (its README says to omit --normal-id when there was no matched normal); and in cBioPortal's MAF format Center and Matched_Norm_Sample_Barcode are optional free-text columns. Such rows therefore went through a different conversion or annotation path from the rest of the file (different processing provenance), which fits rows added or re-annotated separately, but it neither shows nor excludes a second sequencing source; the placeholder alone is not evidence of exome or another assay. To decide, look at assay-bearing fields in those rows (Sequencer, Sequence_Source, Validation_Method, read depths, whether the genes lie inside the panel). QUESTION: What does a small block of MAF rows with Matched_Norm_Sample_Barcode 'NORMAL' and blank Center and Score mean when all other rows have the barcode blank and centre filled? label: FINDING
text: FINDING: Exome data of the 2009-2013 era do not give usable genotypes at the TERT promoter hotspots (hg19 chr5:1295228 C228T, chr5:1295250 C250T), so a sample with exome sequencing and no promoter call is 'not assayed / unknown', not wild-type. Evidence read: (a) Agilent's 2021 announcement of SureSelect Human All Exon V8 advertises that V8 'covers the TERT promoter and hard-to-capture exons that are omitted by other exomes on the market', i.e. earlier designs did not target it (no V1-V4/50Mb bait BED file was inspected, so the literal bait statement is inferred, not checked). (b) The TCGA glioblastoma 2013 paper used Agilent SureSelect Human All Exon 50 Mb for its 291 exomes but genotyped the TERT promoter only from whole-genome sequencing: of 42 WGS cases just 25 had adequate promoter coverage (>10 reads), 21 of 25 mutant (15 C228T, 6 C250T). (c) The TCGA pan-glioma 2016 paper took TERT promoter calls from targeted sequencing (n=287) plus WGS (n=42), not exomes, and lists promoter status as unknown for 434 of 520 IDH-wild-type cases. (d) The promoter is >80% GC; even a targeted panel with baits on it missed all 17 Sanger-confirmed mutations in 25 glioblastomas at auto-filter settings (mean depth about 21). (e) Independently of coverage, TCGA open-access somatic MAF policy excludes unvalidated calls classed 5'Flank/UTR/Intron/IGR, so exome-derived public call sets of that period do not report promoter calls. Confidence: high for the practical conclusion, medium for the bait-design detail. QUESTION: Do whole-exome capture designs in common use around 2009-2013 (e.g. Agilent SureSelect All Exon) include bait coverage of the TERT core promoter hotspots C228T/C250T, and do exome-derived somatic call sets from that period usually report calls there? SOURCE: https://www.agilent.com/about/newsroom/presrel/2021/02jun-ca21013.html ; https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC3910500/ ; https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC4754110/ ; https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC8756133/ ; https://docs.gdc.cancer.gov/Encyclopedia/pages/Mutation_Annotation_Format_TCGAv2/

label: FINDING
text: FINDING: In MutSig output MAFs (final_analysis_set.maf style) is_coding, is_flank and categ are helper columns MutSig adds itself; they are labels derived from Variant_Classification, not a record of a filter. MutSig2CV source (add_helper_is_fields.m): is_coding is TRUE when the mutation type matches indel|read-through|de novo|start|stop|missense|nonsense|silent|splice|synon|frame|shift|nonstop and is forced FALSE when it matches IGR|flank|UTR|intron|promoter|unknown|non-coding|mismatch|^RNA; is_flank is defined simply as NOT is_coding (so it means 'any non-coding call', and a promoter/5'Flank row would be is_coding=0, is_flank=1). categ is the index of the mutation-context category used in the background model: in MutSigCV 1.x 1=CpG transitions, 2=CpG transversions, 3=C:G transitions, 4=C:G transversions, 5=A:T transitions, 6=A:T transversions, 7=null+indel; in MutSig2CV the categories are discovered per run (default k=5) and defined in mutcategs.txt, so the numbering is run-specific. MutSig itself does NOT strip non-coding calls inside gene footprints (it keeps them as effect 'ncd' for background-rate estimation and drops only intergenic/unknown-gene rows, rows outside target intervals, duplicate patients, blacklisted sites and poorly covered genes); it uses each patient's fraction of is_flank rows to infer the coverage model: 0 = 'coding only' (fracflank < 0.03), 1 = exome + 100 bp flanks, 2 = all capture, 3 = WGS. Therefore a table in which every row has is_coding=1 and is_flank=0 means the MAF fed to MutSig was already coding-only ('TCGA coding only' scheme): non-coding calls, promoters included, were removed or never called upstream. That matches TCGA open-access policy (GDC TCGA MAF v2 spec): a .somatic.maf may contain unvalidated somatic calls only from coding regions and splice sites, and Variant_Classification 3'UTR, 3'Flank, 5'UTR, 5'Flank, IGR, Intron is not allowed unless validated. So the columns are valid in-data evidence that the table is coding-only by construction and that absence of TERT promoter rows is uninformative; confirm directly by tabulating Variant_Classification (no 5'Flank/UTR/Intron/IGR rows). They cannot tell whether a promoter call was made and then filtered or never made. The column categ_ignoring_null_categ was not found documented. Confidence: high on definitions, medium-high on the interpretation. QUESTION: In MAF files from the Broad MutSig/Oncotator pipeline, what do is_coding, is_flank and categ mean, and does a file where every row has is_coding=1 and is_flank=0 indicate that calls outside coding territory (including promoters) were filtered out before release? SOURCE: https://github.com/getzlab/MutSig2CV/blob/master/src/add_helper_is_fields.m ; https://github.com/getzlab/MutSig2CV/blob/master/src/impute_callschemes.m ; https://github.com/getzlab/MutSig2CV/blob/master/src/MutSig_2CV_v3_11_core.m ; https://github.com/getzlab/MutSig2CV ; https://www.genepattern.org/modules/docs/MutSigCV/1/ ; https://docs.gdc.cancer.gov/Encyclopedia/pages/Mutation_Annotation_Format_TCGAv2/

label: FINDING
text: FINDING: No recorded variable (IDH-wild-type, non-G-CIMP, ATRX retained) is an accurate stand-in for TERT promoter (TERTp) status in glioblastoma; none of the papers read reports a formal sensitivity/specificity for these proxies, but their counts give the error rates. Fraction of IDH-wild-type GBM that is TERTp-wild-type: 14.7% (16/109, panel sequencing); 16.9% of all GBM are TERTp-wt/IDH-wt (44/260), 'about 20%'; TCGA pan-glioma assayed cases 19 wt vs 67 mutant among IDH-wt (22% wt); editorial summary 'up to 80%' of IDH-wt GBM mutant. So calling every IDH-wt/non-G-CIMP sample 'mutant' is wrong for roughly 15-22% of them. In the other direction IDH-mutant non-codeleted astrocytic tumours are TERTp-mutant in only about 5% (8/154), and all 4 TERTp-wt cases among 25 WGS-genotyped TCGA GBMs carried ATRX+IDH1+TP53 mutations and were G-CIMP-enriched, so IDH-mutant/G-CIMP is a fairly clean 'wild-type' label, but it is a tiny group in GBM (about 5-10%) and it misses most true wild-types: in one cohort 16 of about 27-28 TERTp-wt grade IV tumours were IDH-wt (derived specificity of 'IDH-wt => mutant' only about 40%, sensitivity near 100%, PPV about 85%). ATRX: loss of ATRX is specific for TERTp-wt (0/80 TERTp-mutant IDH-wt GBMs had ATRX loss by IHC; ATRX mutation 6/93 mutant vs 6/16 wt) but insensitive: only 22-31% of TERTp-wt/IDH-wt GBMs show ATRX loss (8/37; 4/13), i.e. 70-78% of them retain ATRX. G-CIMP has no separate published figures in the pages read; it tracks IDH mutation. The TERTp-wt/IDH-wt group is also not a low-TERT control: 50% (19/38) carry rearrangements upstream of TERT with raised TERT mRNA and 38.5% are ALT-positive. A proxy comparison therefore tests IDH/G-CIMP/ATRX status against TERT expression, not promoter mutation, and can serve only as a clearly labelled sensitivity analysis. The TCGA pan-glioma paper reports TERT RNA-seq expression as a 91% sensitive / 95% specific surrogate for TERTp mutation, but using expression to define the mutation group is circular for a mutation-vs-expression hypothesis. Confidence: medium (counts are from single cohorts; sensitivity/specificity values are derived, not quoted). QUESTION: In adult diffuse high-grade gliomas, how accurately do IDH-wild-type status, absence of G-CIMP, or retained ATRX expression predict a TERT promoter mutation (sensitivity, specificity, fraction of IDH-wild-type tumours that are promoter-wild-type)? question:
FINDING FROM THE LAB'S LIBRARY, asked for by the director. QUESTION: For an exact (full-enumeration) or permutation log-rank test in which one of the two groups contains a single subject, how is the two-sided p-value conventionally defined (ordering by the chi-square statistic versus doubling a one-sided tail), how are tied event times handled, and is the permutation log-rank test valid when the censoring (follow-up) distributions differ between the groups? What do standard implementations (for example R coin::logrank_test with distribution = 'exact' or 'approximate') do by default? ANSWER: Two-sided definition. R coin defines the two-sided p-value as P(|c(T)| >= |c(t)|): relabellings are ordered by the absolute standardised statistic, with ties counted as at least as extreme (>=). It does not double a tail. The standardisation uses the permutation mean and variance, which are the same for every relabelling, so this is an ordering by |O - E|. It matches a chi-square ordering only if the variance is not recomputed for each relabelling. Doubling, 2*min(upper tail, lower tail), is a second convention that appears in teaching notes (seen only as a search excerpt). Neither is wrong, but they differ when the permutation distribution is skewed, so each p-value must say which was used.

Ties. coin::logrank_test defaults to type = 'logrank' and ties.method = 'mid-ranks': subjects with the same event time share one risk set and get the same score. The alternatives are 'Hothorn-Lausen' and 'average-scores' (the StatXact method, which averages the scores of arbitrarily broken ties).

Reference distribution. exact() is available for univariate two-sample problems only (shift or split-up algorithm). approximate() draws nresample = 10000 relabellings by default. I did not see on the pages read that the default for logrank_test is the asymptotic distribution, or whether coin's Monte-Carlo p-value adds one to numerator and denominator; I believe the default is asymptotic and no add-one is applied, but that is from memory. An arXiv paper (search excerpt only) argues Monte-Carlo permutation p-values should use (b+1)/(m+1).

Validity under unequal censoring. Wang, Lagakos and Gray (2010) state that standard permutation methods are valid at any sample size when the two censoring distributions are equal, and do not work well when they differ, in small samples or with heavy censoring. Heinze, Gnant and Schemper (2003) state that the exact complete-permutation test requires equal follow-up, that the asymptotic test does not keep its size when group sizes differ substantially, and propose exact tests that condition on realised follow-up.

What this means for a one-patient group (my reasoning, not a quoted source). The full enumeration has only N equally likely outcomes, one per patient taking the lone mutant label, so p moves in steps of 1/N and cannot be below 1/N (2/N if doubled). Log-rank scores are right-skewed, so the opposite tail often holds nothing as extreme and the |Z|-ordered two-sided p equals the one-sided p, while doubling gives twice that. A correct Monte-Carlo run converges to the enumeration value under the same definition. A disagreement across 0.05 therefore points to a definitional difference: doubling versus |Z| ordering, > versus >= at tied statistics (including floating-point near-ties), ordering by a chi-square whose variance is recomputed per relabelling, or an add-one correction. The teams should recompute both under one stated definition; the coin-style |O - E| ordering with >= is the software default. Either way the test's validity still depends on comparable follow-up in the two groups. HOW SURE: medium. SOURCES: https://search.r-project.org/CRAN/refmans/coin/html/SurvivalTests.html, https://search.r-project.org/CRAN/refmans/coin/html/NullDistribution.html, https://cran.r-project.org/web/packages/coin/vignettes/coin.pdf, https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC2950789/, https://doi.org/10.1111/j.0006-341x.2003.00132.x, https://www.math.wustl.edu/~sawyer/handouts/survrank.pdf, https://arxiv.org/abs/1603.05766v1.

question:
FINDING FROM THE LAB'S LIBRARY, asked for by the director. QUESTION: When a Cox model has monotone likelihood because one covariate group consists of a single subject who has an early event, what does Firth's penalised partial likelihood (for example R coxphf) report as the hazard ratio, profile-likelihood confidence interval and p-value, and how do methodological sources recommend interpreting a nominally significant result that rests on a single subject? ANSWER: What the method reports. Firth's penalised partial likelihood always gives a finite hazard ratio where the ordinary estimate diverges and its Wald interval covers the whole real line. coxphf by default (pl = TRUE, alpha = 0.05) reports profile penalised likelihood confidence limits and penalised likelihood-ratio p-values; Wald versions are available but Heinze and Schemper (2001) and the coxphf manual say the profile and likelihood-ratio versions are preferable. The manual warns the profile limits and p-values can fail to converge and suggests maxstep = 0.1 and maxit = 500 in that case.

When it applies. By the definition in the manual and the paper, monotone likelihood occurs when at every event time the subject who fails has the highest (or always the lowest) covariate value in the risk set. For a one-patient group that holds only if that patient's death is the first event. If any wild-type death comes earlier, the ordinary Cox estimate is finite and Firth only shrinks it slightly.

Numbers and interpretation: not settled by the web. The sources I read give no numerical result for a one-subject group and no explicit recommendation on reading a nominally significant result that rests on one subject. The nearest guidance is a general note (Yoneoka and Saito 2015) that fewer than about 10 events per variable marks unreliable Cox inference and that p-values should not be over-relied on.

My reasoning, not a quoted source. Penalisation repairs the estimate but adds no information. If the lone mutant has the first of N at-risk events, the unpenalised likelihood-ratio statistic is 2*ln(N) (about 8.7 for N = 76, chi-square p about 0.003), and the penalised version will be somewhat smaller, so a Firth fit would probably look nominally significant. That p-value rests on a chi-square approximation with one informative subject, whereas the exact permutation p cannot be below 1/N. A Firth fit would therefore give a large finite hazard ratio with a very wide, asymmetric interval and would not change how the subgroup should be treated: report it as a sensitivity analysis beside the exact test, and describe the result as resting on one patient. HOW SURE: medium for how the method behaves; low for the interpretation, which the web did not settle. SOURCES: https://georgheinze.r-universe.dev/coxphf/doc/manual.html, https://doi.org/10.1111/j.0006-341x.2001.00114.x, https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC4375289/.

question:
FINDING FROM THE LAB'S LIBRARY, asked for by the director. QUESTION: Are in-silico missense predictions (SIFT, PolyPhen-2, MutationAssessor functional impact score) considered reliable for classifying somatic missense variants in large DNA-repair tumour-suppressor genes such as BRCA1/2 as functionally damaging, according to variant-interpretation guidance (ACMG/AMP, ENIGMA), and what conventions do tumour-sequencing survival studies use when defining a gene as 'mutated' (all nonsynonymous, truncating only, or predicted-deleterious only)? ANSWER: Reliability: no, not on their own. Ernst et al. (2018, read) tested SIFT, PolyPhen-2, Align-GVGD and MutationTaster2 on 236 expert-classified BRCA1/2 missense variants. PolyPhen-2 had sensitivity 0.67 and specificity 0.67; SIFT had sensitivity 1.00 but poor specificity; all tools produced an unacceptable share of false positives, and combining them did not fix this. The authors conclude the tools are not suitable to predict pathogenicity of BRCA1/2 variants of uncertain significance and that SIFT and MutationTaster2 are usable at most to predict benignity.

Guidance. The AMP/ASCO/CAP 2017 somatic guideline says missense prediction tools have moderate specificity (about 60 to 80 percent) and tend to over-predict deleterious impact. Under ACMG/AMP, concordant in-silico tools count only as supporting evidence, a likelihood ratio of about 2. Both statements were seen as search excerpts; the guideline page returned only front matter when opened. The ENIGMA BRCA1/2 expert-panel paper also returned only front matter, so I cannot quote its computational-evidence rules. I found nothing on MutationAssessor for BRCA1/2 specifically.

Conventions for 'mutated'. The web did not show one agreed convention. cBioPortal's default gene query counts every stored mutation (it stores non-synonymous calls) and offers truncating-only or driver-only as explicit restrictions (search excerpt). In cBioPortal-curated BRCA2 alterations, 83.6 percent of driver mutations are truncating, while missense variants make up 96.7 percent of variants of unknown significance (search excerpt).

What this means for the teams. A SIFT/PolyPhen 'predicted damaging' grouping is not a validated definition of a functionally damaging BRCA2 mutation and deserves little weight against the any-nonsynonymous definition, which matches the hypothesis wording and the cBioPortal default. It can be run as a labelled sensitivity analysis. Truncating-only is the better-founded alternative definition. HOW SURE: medium. SOURCES: https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC5870501/, https://ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pmc/articles/PMC5707196/, https://doi.org/10.1038/s41436-021-01265-z, https://www.cell.com/ajhg/fulltext/S0002-9297(24)00257-X, https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC8161351/, https://docs.cbioportal.org/user-guide/oql/.

QUESTION: Do the whole-exome capture designs in common use around 2009-2013 (for example Agilent SureSelect All Exon versions) include bait coverage of the TERT core promoter hotspot positions (the C228T and C250T sites, about 124 and 146 bp upstream of the start codon), and do exome-derived somatic call sets from that period usually report calls there? question: FINDING FROM THE LAB'S LIBRARY, asked for by the director. QUESTION: In MAF files produced by the Broad Institute MutSig / Oncotator pipeline, what do the columns is_coding, is_flank and categ mean, and does a file in which every row has is_coding = 1 and is_flank = 0 indicate that calls outside coding territory (including promoters) were filtered out before the file was released? ANSWER: In MutSig output MAFs (final_analysis_set.maf style) is_coding, is_flank and categ are helper columns MutSig adds itself; they are labels derived from Variant_Classification, not a record of a filter. MutSig2CV source (add_helper_is_fields.m): is_coding is TRUE when the mutation type matches indel|read-through|de novo|start|stop|missense|nonsense|silent|splice|synon|frame|shift|nonstop and is forced FALSE when it matches IGR|flank|UTR|intron|promoter|unknown|non-coding|mismatch|^RNA; is_flank is defined simply as NOT is_coding (so it means 'any non-coding call', and a promoter/5'Flank row would be is_coding=0, is_flank=1). categ is the index of the mutation-context category used in the background model: in MutSigCV 1.x 1=CpG transitions, 2=CpG transversions, 3=C:G transitions, 4=C:G transversions, 5=A:T transitions, 6=A:T transversions, 7=null+indel; in MutSig2CV the categories are discovered per run (default k=5) and defined in mutcategs.txt, so the numbering is run-specific. MutSig itself does NOT strip non-coding calls inside gene footprints (it keeps them as effect 'ncd' for background-rate estimation and drops only intergenic/unknown-gene rows, rows outside target intervals, duplicate patients, blacklisted sites and poorly covered genes); it uses each patient's fraction of is_flank rows to infer the coverage model: 0 = 'coding only' (fracflank < 0.03), 1 = exome + 100 bp flanks, 2 = all capture, 3 = WGS. So the columns are valid in-data evidence that the table is coding-only by construction and that absence of TERT promoter rows is uninformative; confirm directly by tabulating Variant_Classification (no 5'Flank/UTR/Intron/IGR rows). They cannot tell whether a promoter call was made and then filtered or never made. The column categ_ignoring_null_categ was not found documented. HOW SURE: high. SOURCES: https://github.com/getzlab/MutSig2CV/blob/master/src/add_helper_is_fields.m, https://github.com/getzlab/MutSig2CV/blob/master/src/impute_callschemes.m, https://github.com/getzlab/MutSig2CV/blob/master/src/MutSig_2CV_v3_11_core.m, https://github.com/getzlab/MutSig2CV, https://www.genepattern.org/modules/docs/MutSigCV/1/, https://docs.gdc.cancer.gov/Encyclopedia/pages/Mutation_Annotation_Format_TCGAv2/.

text: FINDING FROM THE LAB'S LIBRARY, asked for by the director. QUESTION: In MAF files produced by the Broad Institute MutSig / Oncotator pipeline, what do the columns is_coding, is_flank and categ mean, and does a file in which every row has is_coding = 1 and is_flank = 0 indicate that calls outside coding territory (including promoters) were filtered out before the file was released? ANSWER: In MutSig output MAFs (final_analysis_set.maf style) is_coding, is_flank and categ are helper columns MutSig adds itself; they are labels derived from Variant_Classification, not a record of a filter. MutSig2CV source (add_helper_is_fields.m): is_coding is TRUE when the mutation type matches indel|read-through|de novo|start|stop|missense|nonsense|silent|splice|synon|frame|shift|nonstop and is forced FALSE when it matches IGR|flank|UTR|intron|promoter|unknown|non-coding|mismatch|^RNA; is_flank is defined simply as NOT is_coding (so it means 'any non-coding call', and a promoter/5'Flank row would be is_coding=0, is_flank=1). categ is the index of the mutation-context category used in the background model: in MutSigCV 1.x 1=CpG transitions, 2=CpG transversions, 3=C:G transitions, 4=C:G transversions, 5=A:T transitions, 6=A:T transversions, 7=null+indel; in MutSig2CV the categories are discovered per run (default k=5) and defined in mutcategs.txt, so the numbering is run-specific. MutSig itself does NOT strip non-coding calls inside gene footprints (it keeps them as effect 'ncd' for background-rate estimation and drops only intergenic/unknown-gene rows, rows outside target intervals, duplicate patients, blacklisted sites and poorly covered genes); it uses each patient's fraction of is_flank rows to infer the coverage model: 0 = 'coding only' (fracflank < 0.03), 1 = exome + 100 bp flanks, 2 = all capture, 3 = WGS. Therefore a table in which every row has is_coding=1 and is_flank=0 means the MAF fed to MutSig was already coding-only ('TCGA coding only' scheme): non-coding calls, promoters included, were removed or never called upstream. That matches TCGA open-access policy (GDC TCGA MAF v2 spec): a .somatic.maf may contain unvalidated somatic calls only from coding regions and splice sites, and Variant_Classification 3'UTR, 3'Flank, 5'UTR, 5'Flank, IGR, Intron is not allowed unless validated. So the columns are valid in-data evidence that the table is coding-only by construction and that absence of TERT promoter rows is uninformative; confirm directly by tabulating Variant_Classification (no 5'Flank/UTR/Intron/IGR rows). They cannot tell whether a promoter call was made and then filtered or never made. The column categ_ignoring_null_categ was not found documented. HOW SURE: high. SOURCES: https://github.com/getzlab/MutSig2CV/blob/master/src/add_helper_is_fields.m, https://github.com/getzlab/MutSig2CV/blob/master/src/impute_callschemes.m, https://github.com/getzlab/MutSig2CV/blob/master/src/MutSig_2CV_v3_11_core.m, https://github.com/getzlab/MutSig2CV, https://www.genepattern.org/modules/docs/MutSigCV/1/, https://docs.gdc.cancer.gov/Encyclopedia/pages/Mutation_Annotation_Format_TCGAv2/.

question: FINDING FROM THE LAB'S LIBRARY, asked for by the director. QUESTION: In adult diffuse high-grade gliomas, how accurately do IDH-wild-type status, absence of the G-CIMP methylation phenotype, or retained ATRX expression predict the presence of a TERT promoter mutation (reported sensitivity, specificity and the fraction of IDH-wild-type tumours that are promoter-wild-type)? ANSWER: No recorded variable (IDH-wild-type, non-G-CIMP, ATRX retained) is an accurate stand-in for TERT promoter (TERTp) status in glioblastoma; none of the papers read reports a formal sensitivity/specificity for these proxies, but their counts give the error rates. Fraction of IDH-wild-type GBM that is TERTp-wild-type: 14.7% (16/109, panel sequencing); 16.9% of all GBM are TERTp-wt/IDH-wt (44/260), 'about 20%'; TCGA pan-glioma assayed cases 19 wt vs 67 mutant among IDH-wt (22% wt); editorial summary 'up to 80%' of IDH-wt GBM mutant. So calling every IDH-wt/non-G-CIMP sample 'mutant' is wrong for roughly 15-22% of them. In the other direction IDH-mutant non-codeleted astrocytic tumours are TERTp-mutant in only about 5% (8/154), and all 4 TERTp-wt cases among 25 WGS-genotyped TCGA GBMs carried ATRX+IDH1+TP53 mutations and were G-CIMP-enriched, so IDH-mutant/G-CIMP is a fairly clean 'wild-type' label, but it is a tiny group in GBM (about 5-10%) and it misses most true wild-types: in one cohort 16 of about 27-28 TERTp-wt grade IV tumours were IDH-wt (derived specificity of 'IDH-wt => mutant' only about 40%, sensitivity near 100%, PPV about 85%). G-CIMP has no separate published figures in the pages read; it tracks IDH mutation. The TERTp-wt/IDH-wt group is also not a low-TERT control: 50% (19/38) carry rearrangements upstream of TERT with raised TERT mRNA and 38.5% are ALT-positive. A proxy comparison therefore tests IDH/G-CIMP/ATRX status against TERT expression, not promoter mutation, and can serve only as a clearly labelled sensitivity analysis. question: FINDING FROM THE LAB'S LIBRARY, asked for by the director. QUESTION: In MAF-format mutation files exported from a clinical targeted-sequencing pipeline, what does it mean when a small block of rows has a generic Matched_Norm_Sample_Barcode value such as 'NORMAL' and blank Center and Score fields while all other rows have the barcode blank and the centre and assay name filled: is this a known sign of rows merged from a different pipeline version or annotation pass, or of a different assay? ANSWER: Not settled by the web: no page documents this pattern as a marker of a different assay. What is documented: the vcf2maf converter (MSKCC) hard-codes the defaults tumor_id 'TUMOR', normal_id 'NORMAL' and centre '.', so the literal 'NORMAL' is the placeholder written when no normal sample ID is passed to the tool (its README says to omit --normal-id when there was no matched normal). In cBioPortal's MAF format, Center and Matched_Norm_Sample_Barcode are optional free-text columns. My reading: those rows went through a different conversion or annotation path from the rest of the file. That fits rows added or re-annotated separately, but it neither shows nor excludes a second sequencing source, and the placeholder alone is not evidence of exome or another assay. The assay-bearing fields of those rows (Sequencer, Sequence_Source, Validation_Method, read depths, whether the genes lie inside the panel) are what would decide it. Note that vcf2maf's default centre is '.', not blank, so the blank Center and Score are not explained by that default. HOW SURE: low for the interpretation (high only for the fact that 'NORMAL' is vcf2maf's default placeholder). SOURCES: https://github.com/mskcc/vcf2maf/blob/main/vcf2maf.pl, https://github.com/mskcc/vcf2maf, https://docs.bcbi.brown.edu/codiac-for-health/ursa-ri/datasets/cbioportal-for-cancer-genomics/data-dictionary.

text: FINDING: Both cBioPortal and OncoKB keep 'mutations' and deletions as separate alteration categories while treating both as inactivating. cBioPortal OQL has distinct data types: Mutations (MUT; subtypes MISSENSE, NONSENSE, NONSTART, NONSTOP, FRAMESHIFT, INFRAME, SPLICE, TRUNC), Fusions (FUSION) and Copy Number Alterations (AMP, HOMDEL = 'Deep Deletions', GAIN, HETLOSS = 'Shallow Deletions'); a default gene query is 'MUT FUSION AMP HOMDEL', so the default 'altered' frequency includes deep deletions and fusions/SVs but shallow deletions are excluded, and TRUNC is a mutation subtype that never includes HOMDEL. OncoKB lists 'Deletion' (defined as copy number loss resulting in partial or whole deletion of the gene) as an entry separate from 'Truncating Mutations' for TP53 and RB1, and annotates both Likely Oncogenic / Likely Loss-of-function. So the tools' nomenclature is: umbrella word = 'alterations'; 'mutations' = sequence variants (SNV/indel); deep deletions and SVs are loss-of-function ALTERATIONS but not 'mutations'. The web did not yield a formal rule for the free-text phrase 'loss-of-function mutations': published prose is mixed (some papers write 'loss-of-function mutations or deletions' or 'alterations (truncating mutations, fusions, homozygous deletion)', others loosely call a gene 'mutant' when lost by copy number) - these usage examples were seen in search snippets only. Recommended reading: strict/primary = sequence variants in the mutation file; union with deep deletion (-2) and disruptive SVs reported alongside as 'LoF alterations', and the label should be checked under both. text: FINDING: There is no universally accepted frequency cut-off for calling a gene alteration common/frequent versus uncommon/rare within a tumour type; two reviews say so explicitly ('a universally accepted frequency threshold for defining rarity is lacking'; 'no unified definition'). The cut-offs that do have published use are: 'rare' = 5% or less of cases of a specific cancer type (precision-oncology/lung-cancer usage; alterations above 5% are said to 'exceed the frequency threshold for rare'), and the Lawrence et al. 2014 pan-cancer bands: 'high' frequency = more than 20% of tumours of a type, 'intermediate' = 2-20%, lower = below 2%. Under these, a gene altered in over 20% of cases is not 'uncommon' by any published usage; 5% or less is 'rare'; values between 5% and 20% are 'intermediate frequency' - neither rare nor high - so a 10% cut-off has no external support and such values cannot be called uncommon or common on convention alone. 'Recurrent' is not a frequency band (it denotes repeated/statistically significant occurrence and is applied even to low-frequency long-tail genes; this last point is from search snippets and background knowledge, not a page read). Confidence: medium-high that no convention exists, medium for the bands. QUESTION: Is there an accepted frequency convention for calling a gene alteration common/frequent/recurrent versus uncommon/rare within a tumour type, and how do landmark cohort papers use the words? question: FINDING FROM THE LAB'S LIBRARY, asked for by the director. QUESTION: Is there an accepted frequency convention in tumour-genomics reporting for calling a gene alteration 'common', 'frequent' or 'recurrent' versus 'uncommon' or 'rare' within a tumour type (for example cut-offs such as 1%, 5%, 10% or 20% of cases), and how do landmark sequencing-cohort papers typically apply these words? ANSWER: No. There is no universally accepted cut-off, and two reviews say so explicitly ('a universally accepted frequency threshold for defining rarity is lacking'; 'no unified definition'). The cut-offs with published use are these. 'Rare' means 5% or less of cases of a specific cancer type in precision-oncology and lung-cancer usage; alterations above 5% are described as exceeding the threshold for rare. The Lawrence et al. 2014 pan-cancer analysis of 4,742 tumours describes genes mutated in more than 20% of tumours of a type as 'high' frequency, 2-20% as 'intermediate' frequency, and the rest as lower. Under these, a gene altered in more than 20% of cases is not 'uncommon' by any published usage, and 5% or less is 'rare'. Values between 5% and 20% are 'intermediate': neither rare nor high. A 10% cut-off has no external support that I found, so frequencies between the teams' 10% and 20% cut-offs cannot be called uncommon or common on convention alone. 'Recurrent' is not a frequency band: it denotes repeated or statistically significant occurrence and is applied even to low-frequency long-tail genes; that point rests on search snippets and background knowledge, not a page I read. I did not find or read a landmark paper that defines 'uncommon' numerically. HOW SURE: medium. text: FINDING: Direction of a common association: the exact conditional test of the common odds ratio (the exact counterpart of Cochran-Mantel-Haenszel, conditioning on every stratum's margins). SAS: PROC FREQ, EXACT COMOR. Homogeneity of the stratum odds ratios: Zelen's exact test. R: NSM3::zelen.test(z) with z an array of K 2x2 tables ('small data sets only'); SAS: PROC FREQ, EXACT EQOR. Base R does not test homogeneity (mantelhaen.test note: 'Currently, no inference on homogeneity of the odds ratios is performed') and its asymptotic CMH is valid only without three-way interaction. Python: statsmodels StratifiedTable offers only asymptotic tests, test_null_odds (Mantel-Haenszel chi-square) and test_equal_odds (Breslow-Day, optional Tarone adjustment), plus shift_zeros, which adds 0.5 to every cell of a table containing a zero; its documentation lists no exact option, and I found no documented Python function for either exact test. The MSK FACETS QC code (facets-preview facets_fit_qc, 'valid purity filter') marks a fit with purity NA or the 0.3 placeholder as failing QC, i.e. such fits are treated as unevaluable, not as confirmed diploid tumours. So a fraction-altered of exactly 0 means 'no usable copy-number signal': either a genuinely quiet genome or too little tumour, and the second case is where mutation calls can be missed (MSK clinical reports carry the comment 'Low tumor content (approximately 20% or less). Negative results should be interpreted with caution'). I found no published, recommended procedure for using FGA=0 as a purity flag; the web does not settle that part. The only guidance read is the author's: with no copy-number change, estimate purity from the mutations, since the allele fraction of high-confidence calls is about 0.5 x purity. A defensible sensitivity analysis built on that: flag samples with FGA exactly 0 (or missing); split them by whether they have called mutations at a reasonable allele fraction (tumour demonstrably present, quiet genome) or have no mutations / only very low allele fractions (probable low purity); compare the share of flagged samples across the groups; repeat the frequency comparison without the probable-low-purity samples, leaving the primary denominator unchanged. HOW SURE: medium for the interpretation; low for a recommended flagging procedure (none found). QUESTION: For a rare binary event compared between groups within a small number of strata, some of which have zero events in a cell, which exact methods are recommended for testing the direction of a common association and the homogeneity of stratum-specific odds ratios (for example the exact conditional test of the common odds ratio and Zelen's exact test), and which Python or R functions implement them? ANSWER: Direction of a common association: the exact conditional test of the common odds ratio (the exact counterpart of Cochran-Mantel-Haenszel, conditioning on every stratum's margins). R: mantelhaen.test(x, exact=TRUE, alternative='less' or 'greater') on a 2x2xK array; it returns the exact p-value, the conditional maximum-likelihood common odds ratio and an exact confidence interval. SAS: PROC FREQ, EXACT COMOR. Homogeneity of the stratum odds ratios: Zelen's exact test. R: NSM3::zelen.test(z) with z an array of K 2x2 tables ('small data sets only'); SAS: PROC FREQ, EXACT EQOR. Base R does not test homogeneity (mantelhaen.test note: 'Currently, no inference on homogeneity of the odds ratios is performed') and its asymptotic CMH is valid only without three-way interaction. Python: statsmodels StratifiedTable offers only asymptotic tests, test_null_odds (Mantel-Haenszel chi-square) and test_equal_odds (Breslow-Day, optional Tarone adjustment), plus shift_zeros, which adds 0.5 to every cell of a table containing a zero; its documentation lists no exact option, and I found no documented Python function for either exact test. In Python they must be coded from the definitions (my derivation, not a documented routine): for the common-odds-ratio test, the null distribution of the total event count in the group of interest is the convolution of the per-stratum hypergeometric distributions (scipy.stats.hypergeom), and the one-sided p-value is the tail at the observed total; for Zelen, enumerate all sets of tables with the same margins and the same total, and sum the probabilities of those no more probable than the observed set. A stratum with no events at all has a one-point distribution and adds nothing. Check any hand-coded version against R if R is available. Cautions from the sources: a simulation study (Reis, Hirji, Afifi 1999; abstract read) recommends exact tests, Zelen among them, for sparse tables because asymptotic ones do not hold their size, but finds that all homogeneity tests 'had low power for small strata sizes, even with moderate to large heterogeneity', so a non-significant Zelen test with a handful of events does not show the odds ratios are equal and cannot confirm a reversal either; SAS warns that CMH-type tests have low power when strata point in opposite directions. With very few events, report the per-stratum counts and say the stratum pattern is not distinguishable from noise unless the exact homogeneity test rejects. HOW SURE: high for the R and SAS functions and the statsmodels limits; medium for the hand-coded Python route. SOURCES: https://search.r-project.org/R/refmans/stats/html/mantelhaen.test.html, https://go.documentation.sas.com/api/docsets/statug/v_023/content/statug_freq_details92.htm, https://search.r-project.org/CRAN/refmans/NSM3/html/zelen.test.html, https://www.statsmodels.org/stable/generated/statsmodels.stats.contingency_tables.StratifiedTable.html, https://www.statsmodels.org/stable/generated/statsmodels.stats.contingency_tables.StratifiedTable.test_equal_odds.html, https://onlinelibrary.wiley.com/doi/10.1002/(SICI)1097-0258(19990430)18:8%3C893::AID-SIM84%3E3.0.CO;2-5.

text: FINDING: In the Broad Spectrum Mill route used for consortium TMT acetylomes, the site table has one row per variable-modification (VM) site, PSMs are merged into one row for all non-conflicting observations of that site (missed-cleavage forms, charge states, confident and ambiguous localisations), and PTM site reports use the 'unexpand subgroups' protein grouping, so a peptide shared by paralogues is meant to be reported once under one representative accession, not once per paralogue; separate rows still arise for (a) different acetyl-site combinations of the same tail peptide (each mono/di/tri-acetyl form is its own row, chemically overlapping and correlated) and (b) paralogue-specific peptide sequences (H2B variants differ at a few N-terminal residues, so rows under different HIST*H2B* symbols can be different peptides but the same histone family). Other pipelines (PDC CDAP: MS-GF+ plus PhosphoRS plus parsimony gene roll-up) and later re-annotation of sites to chosen isoforms can relabel gene and position, so the web does NOT settle whether this particular table duplicates one peptide under several symbols: check empirically (rows with correlation about 1 and identical NA pattern are one measurement; collapse them and count histone-family peptides, not rows). Site-level values are log2 ratios to the common reference with sample-level normalisation only; none of the pipeline descriptions normalises to parent-protein abundance, and PTM reviews say protein abundance must be assessed separately, so protein adjustment is still needed and is not double-correction. The Spectrum Mill wording was read in search excerpts of methods sections; the opened pages were cut off before Methods. QUESTION: How are acetylated peptides mapping to several histone paralogues assigned gene symbol and site label in TMT acetyl pipelines, can one peptide appear as several rows, and are site log ratios protein-normalised? text: FINDING: Permutation tests are valid only if observations are exchangeable under the null; when data come in blocks (batches, sessions, families) the permutation literature (Winkler et al. 2014, 2015) says to restrict shuffling to rearrangements that respect the block structure, i.e. permute labels WITHIN block (or shuffle whole blocks), and to handle nuisance variables by permuting residuals (Freedman-Lane type). For multi-plex TMT this means sample labels should be permuted within plex (plex = exchangeability block) or plex should enter as a nuisance/blocking term; an unrestricted permutation is only valid if plex has no effect on values or missingness, which is false for sites missing in whole plexes. TMT methods papers do not use sample permutation at all: MSstatsTMT fits linear mixed models with mixture (plex) as a random effect and tolerates missing values, and msTrawler models between-batch differences in number and quality of observations 'without relying on unverifiable imputations or discarding reliable measurements'. So for sites missing in whole plexes: do not impute, test on observed plexes only, permute within plex (which keeps each permuted data set's missingness and per-group n identical to the observed one), and require a minimum number of informative plexes (plexes holding both Wnt groups). No TMT-specific paper on permutation exchangeability was found; this is the general principle applied to plexes. QUESTION: For multi-plex TMT with a common reference and plex-structured missingness, are samples exchangeable across plexes in a sample-label permutation test or should labels be permuted within plex, and how to treat sites missing in whole plexes? SOURCE: https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC4010955/ ; https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC4644991/ ; https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC8015007/ ; https://www.nature.com/articles/s41592-023-02120-6

text: FINDING: Beta-catenin N-terminal degron phosphorylation (CK1alpha primes S45, then GSK3beta phosphorylates T41, S37, S33, creating the beta-TrCP docking site) marks the protein for ubiquitylation and degradation, so phospho-S33/S37/T41/S45 is an OFF/destruction mark, not an activity mark; Wnt activation shows as loss of this phosphorylation and accumulation of beta-catenin. S552 (AKT) and S675 (PKA) are alternative phosphorylations that 'may enhance' beta-catenin activity but are driven by PI3K/AKT and cAMP/PKA, so they are not specific readouts of canonical Wnt. The pages read did not cover GSK3B S9 or bulk-tissue total beta-catenin; background knowledge (not web-verified here) is that GSK3B S9 is an AKT/insulin-pathway inhibitory site not required for Wnt signalling, and that total beta-catenin in bulk tissue is dominated by the junctional E-cadherin-bound pool, so both are weak Wnt readouts; target-gene expression (AXIN2, NKD1, RNF43, ZNRF3, LGR5 ...) remains the accepted readout. Standard database searches identify only peptides present in the reference protein database; single-amino-acid-variant peptides are 'usually not present in the database and therefore not identified' unless a customised variant database is used. Because all exon-3 hotspot codons (32-45) lie on one tryptic peptide (about residues 20-49, AAVSHWQQQSYLDSGIHSGATTTAPSLSGK; sequence from background knowledge), in a degron-mutant tumour the degron phosphosite rows from a reference search report only the wild-type allele (plus non-tumour cells), not the stabilised mutant protein, and several hotspot mutations remove the phospho-acceptor itself; degron phosphosite values are therefore biased/uninterpretable as Wnt activity in mutant tumours and must not be used as an independent Wnt readout there. QUESTION: Which beta-catenin protein and phosphosite measurements are accepted readouts of canonical Wnt activity in bulk tumour proteomics, and are degron phosphopeptides from a mutant allele quantified by standard reference-database searches? text: FINDING: The uppercase values START_CODON_SNP, START_CODON_INS, DE_NOVO_START_IN_FRAME and DE_NOVO_START_OUT_FRAME are GATK Funcotator class names; Funcotator's MAF writer translates only some classes to MAF style (MISSENSE->Missense_Mutation, SPLICE_SITE->Splice_Site, START_CODON_DEL->Translation_Start_Site, etc.) and leaves these four untranslated, so a MAF mixing 'Splice_Site' with 'START_CODON_SNP' was annotated by Funcotator (Oncotator writes Start_Codon_SNP / De_novo_Start_OutOfFrame instead). Funcotator calls SPLICE_SITE any variant overlapping a window of --splice-site-window-size bases (default 2) on EITHER side of an exon/intron boundary, i.e. by default the 2 intronic bases AND the first/last 2 exonic bases of each internal exon edge (the transcript's outermost exon ends are not checked); in the code the splice check comes before the start-codon and missense/nonsense/silent classification, so it overrides them. For an exonic splice-window variant Funcotator still fills codon and protein change and stores the coding consequence (MISSENSE, SILENT, NONSENSE...) in secondaryVariantClassification; for an intronic one the secondary class is INTRON, the codon change is a 'c.e<exon>+/-N' string and no protein change is set. So a Splice_Site row carrying a synonymous or missense protein change is an exonic variant within 2 bases of the exon edge, flagged by position only, with no evidence about splicing; only Splice_Site rows without a protein change are at the intronic +/-1,2 essential positions. Counting all Splice_Site rows as truncating overstates truncating calls; narrow to intronic ones (plus exonic ones whose own consequence is nonsense). Confidence high (read in Funcotator source and docs). QUESTION: Which annotation tool emits START_CODON_SNP/DE_NOVO_START_* and how does it define Splice_Site (bases either side, exonic bases, meaning of a Splice_Site row with a protein change)? label: FINDING
text: FINDING: There is no accepted numeric convention for 'frequently mutated'; the pages read show no field-wide threshold. In practice 'frequently/recurrently mutated' is a descriptive prevalence statement (percent of tumours with a non-silent mutation) and 'significantly mutated' is reserved for excess over a background model (MutSigCV or dNdScv q<0.1, InVEx q<=0.2); thresholds for 'frequent' are set per study (one oral-SCC exome study required both q<0.1 and >=5% of tumours, and separately listed genes that were 'frequently mutated' but 'showed no significant enrichment': TTN 28.3%, PCLO 16.7%, CSMD3 14.2%, MUC16 12.5%). In UV-driven tumours raw prevalence is explicitly treated as uninformative: in 121 melanoma exomes 515 genes were non-silently mutated in >10% of tumours and 78 in >20%, about 85% of those mutations were UV-type, and the authors concluded many high-frequency gene mutations are UV passenger events; a uniform-background test called 544 genes 'significant', tracking silent rate and low expression. Genes that such studies do claim as affected often have modest prevalence (PPP6C 9%, ARID2 loss-of-function 7%, p16INK4a loss-of-function 12% in that melanoma cohort) and are worded as 'n tumours (x%) harboured mutations', justified by a per-gene background test (intron/UTR or synonymous control), loss-of-function burden, clustering/hotspots or pathway role, not by prevalence. So 'frequently' can honestly mean prevalence or excess, and a verdict must state which; fix the criterion in advance and report both. Confidence medium (consistent practice across papers read, but no formal standard exists). QUESTION: Is there an accepted convention for 'frequently mutated' versus 'significantly mutated' in high-burden UV-driven tumours, and how are modest-prevalence genes worded and justified? text: FINDING: The web pages read give no published figure for the neutral nonsense share under a UV signature or for its gene-to-gene range; that part is unsettled. From the genetic code alone (library's own arithmetic, not a sourced number): 23 of 549 possible single-base changes in sense codons are nonsense (4.2%); restricting to C>T at dipyrimidines with uniform codon usage gives about 5% nonsense, 34% silent, 61% missense (about 7-8% of non-silent substitutions), consistent with the 2:1 nonsynonymous:synonymous ratio reported for melanoma exomes. UV-type single-base changes can create a stop only at Gln (CAA, CAG), Arg CGA and Trp TGG codons (CC>TT also turns TGG into TAA), so a gene's neutral nonsense expectation scales with its Gln, Trp and CGA content and local context and can differ severalfold between genes; glutamine-rich proteins have a higher expectation. dNdScv handles this per gene: a 192-rate trinucleotide model (strand-aware) is fitted on all genes, and each gene has its own L matrix counting sites of each of the 192 classes that would be synonymous, missense, nonsense or essential-splice, so expected nonsense and splice counts are gene-specific; the gene's rate comes from its synonymous count plus a negative-binomial regression on covariates across genes, which dominates in small cohorts where genes have 0 or few synonymous hits. By default it tests truncating as nonsense plus essential-splice with one shared ratio (constrain_wnon_wspl=TRUE, likelihood-ratio test), drops samples with >3000 coding mutations, keeps at most 3 mutations per gene per sample, warns about adjacent substitutions, and handles dinucleotide/complex changes and indels outside dN/dS in a separate negative-binomial model. The authors report that in melanoma the trinucleotide model is biased (UV context extends beyond +/-1 base; a pentanucleotide model removes the bias) and that a uniform-rate model on neutral melanoma data gave 368 false-positive genes. A binomial test of a gene's truncating share against one cohort-wide fraction controls the gene's mutation rate but not its composition, so with a handful of truncating calls its p-values are approximate, not reliable to within a factor of about 2 in expectation. Confidence: high for dNdScv mechanics, low for the numeric shares. QUESTION: Under a UV signature what share of coding substitutions is nonsense under neutrality, how much does it vary by gene, and how does dNdScv account for it in cohorts under 100 tumours? text: FINDING: In the cBioPortal structural-variant format, DNA_support and RNA_support are optional yes/no flags supplied by the data provider: DNA_support = 'Fusion detected from DNA sequence data', RNA_support = 'Fusion detected from RNA sequence data' (the newer SV table repeats the word DNA for RNA_Support, a documentation typo; the legacy fusion format says RNA). text: FINDING: RIN1 (Ras and Rab interactor 1) is a RAS effector that binds GTP-loaded RAS with affinity similar to RAF1 (Kd about 22 nM) and competes directly with RAF1 for RAS; unlike other effectors it INHIBITS transformation by activated RAS (about twofold fewer soft-agar colonies; stronger when membrane-targeted) and is restrained by 14-3-3 binding at Ser351 (phosphorylated by PKD). Search summaries (not opened) add that it is a RAB5 exchange factor promoting EGFR endocytosis/degradation and an ABL kinase activator. So RIN1 is a negative modulator of the RAS-RAF branch, not a MAPK activator; no page read describes RIN1 fusions as a known MAPK-activating event, and inferring that a RIN1 fusion raises RAF signalling would be speculation. On immunoglobulin partners: the web only partly settles it. Read sources establish the general artefact class: very high expression of one partner produces non-specific chimeras by reverse-transcriptase template switching during cDNA preparation, and fusions recurring at improbable frequency or with promiscuous partners are filtered as false positives (Stransky 2014); a myeloma fusion study pooled IGLL5 into the IGL locus, removed 18 highly recurrent IGL fusions for low whole-genome support, and states that transcript overexpression makes false-positive chimeric transcripts more likely (Foltz 2020). No page read states specifically that IGLL5/IGLJ chimeras in solid tumours come from plasma-cell infiltration or read-through; that mechanism is plausible but unconfirmed here (Arriba documentation could not be retrieved). Practical reading: a gene--IGLL5/IGLJ call with RNA support only, no DNA support, recurring across samples with the same Ig partner, should be treated as probable artefact or at most unknown, neither as a pathway alteration nor as proof of none. Confidence: high for RIN1 function, medium for the Ig artefact answer. QUESTION: What is RIN1's role in RAS signalling, and are chimeric transcripts joining an expressed gene to immunoglobulin lambda segments (IGLL5, IGLJ) a recognised RNA-seq fusion-caller artefact? question: FINDING FROM THE LAB'S LIBRARY, asked for by the director. QUESTION: In isobaric-tag (TMT) acetyl-lysine enrichment proteomics as processed by common large-consortium pipelines, how is an acetylated peptide that maps to several histone paralogues (for example the H2B N-terminal tail) assigned a gene symbol and site label: can one peptide quantification appear as separate rows under different paralog names or different lysine positions, and are the reported site-level log ratios normalised to parent-protein abundance or not? ANSWER: Partly settled. (1) Row construction: in the Broad Spectrum Mill route used for consortium TMT acetylomes, the site table has one row per variable-modification (VM) site; PSMs are merged into a single row for all non-conflicting observations of that site (different missed-cleavage forms, precursor charges, confident and ambiguous localisations), and the PTM site reports use the 'unexpand subgroups' protein grouping (the proteome uses 'expand subgroups, top uses shared'). By design, then, a peptide shared by paralogues is reported once under one representative accession of its protein group, not once per paralogue. Separate rows still legitimately arise for (a) different acetyl-site combinations of the same tail peptide (each mono/di/tri-acetyl form is its own row; these overlap chemically and are strongly correlated) and (b) paralogue-specific peptide sequences (H2B variants differ at a few N-terminal residues, so rows under different H2B gene symbols can be different peptides from the same histone family; this sequence point is background knowledge, not read on the web). (2) Other pipelines differ: the PDC common data analysis pipeline uses MS-GF+, PhosphoRS and a 'generalized parsimony' gene roll-up, and downstream resources re-annotate sites to chosen isoforms and recompute positions, so gene symbol and lysine number can be relabelled. The web therefore does NOT settle whether the teams' table duplicates one peptide quantification under several paralog symbols; that has to be checked in the table itself (rows with correlation near 1 and identical missing-value pattern are one measurement and should be collapsed; count independent peptides, not rows, and treat paralog symbols as histone-family labels). (3) Normalisation: site values are log2 ratios to the common reference with sample-level normalisation only. No pipeline description read includes normalisation to parent-protein abundance, and PTM methods reviews state that protein abundance must be assessed separately, so protein adjustment by the analyst is still needed and is not a double correction. Caveat: the Spectrum Mill wording was read in search excerpts of methods sections; the pages opened with the contents tool were cut off before their Methods sections. HOW SURE: medium. SOURCES: https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12326532/, https://proteomics.broadinstitute.org/millhtml/SM_slides/SpectrumMillOverview.pdf, https://proteomic.datacommons.cancer.gov/pdc-docs/data-analysis-guides, https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC10530292/, https://ddd.uab.cat/pub/tesis/2026/hdl_10803_697478/kji1de1.pdf, https://doi.org/10.1093/bioinformatics/btaf046.

question: FINDING FROM THE LAB'S LIBRARY, asked for by the director. QUESTION: For multi-plex TMT experiments with a common reference channel and plex-structured missing values, what do methods papers recommend for permutation or resampling tests of a sample-level variable: are samples exchangeable across plexes, or should labels be permuted within plex (restricted permutation / blocking), and how should sites missing in whole plexes be handled? ANSWER: No TMT-specific methods paper on permutation exchangeability was found, so this is the general permutation principle applied to plexes. Permutation tests are valid only if observations are exchangeable under the null. Where data have a block structure, the permutation literature (Winkler et al. 2014 and 2015) says to use only rearrangements that respect it: permute within block (within-block exchangeability) or shuffle whole blocks, and deal with nuisance variables by permuting residuals. For multi-plex TMT, the plex is the natural exchangeability block: samples in a plex share the same peptide selection, reference-channel denominator and missingness. Labels should therefore be permuted within plex, or plex should enter the model as a nuisance or blocking term. Unrestricted permutation across plexes is valid only if plex affects neither the values nor the missingness, which is false for sites missing in whole plexes. TMT statistics papers do not use sample permutation: MSstatsTMT fits linear mixed-effects models with mixture (plex) as a random effect and tolerates missing values; msTrawler models between-batch differences in the number and quality of observations 'without relying on unverifiable imputations or discarding reliable measurements'. For sites missing in whole plexes: do not impute; test on the observed plexes only; permute within plex, which keeps the missingness pattern and per-group sample counts of every permuted data set equal to the observed one; and require a minimum number of informative plexes (plexes that contain both groups). The teams' unrestricted permutation p-values should be re-run with within-plex permutation before being relied on. HOW SURE: medium. SOURCES: https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC4010955/, https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC4644991/, https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC8015007/, https://www.nature.com/articles/s41592-023-02120-6.

question: FINDING FROM THE LAB'S LIBRARY, asked for by the director. QUESTION: Which protein-level and phosphosite-level measurements are accepted readouts of canonical Wnt/beta-catenin pathway activity in bulk tumour proteomics (total beta-catenin abundance, phosphorylation at S33/S37/T41/S45, S552, S675, GSK3B S9), and when a tumour carries a missense mutation inside the beta-catenin degron, are the degron phosphopeptides from the mutant allele still identified and quantified by standard reference-database searches or only those from the wild-type allele? ANSWER: Readouts: phosphorylation of the beta-catenin N-terminal degron (CK1alpha primes S45, then GSK3beta phosphorylates T41, S37 and S33, creating the beta-TrCP docking site) marks the protein for ubiquitylation and proteasomal degradation. Phospho-S33/S37/T41/S45 is therefore a destruction (pathway-off) mark; Wnt activation appears as loss of this phosphorylation with accumulation and nuclear translocation of beta-catenin. S552 (AKT) and S675 (PKA) are alternative phosphorylations that 'may enhance' beta-catenin activity, but they are driven by PI3K/AKT and cAMP/PKA signalling and are not specific to canonical Wnt. The pages read did not address GSK3B S9 or how well total beta-catenin in bulk tissue tracks Wnt activity, so the web did not settle those two. Background knowledge, not verified here: GSK3B S9 is an AKT-type inhibitory site that is not required for Wnt signalling, and total beta-catenin in bulk tissue is dominated by the junctional, cadherin-bound pool; both are weak readouts, and target-gene expression remains the accepted one. Mutant allele: standard database searches identify only peptides present in the reference protein database; single-amino-acid-variant peptides are 'usually not present in the database and therefore not identified' unless a customised variant database is searched. All exon 3 hotspot codons (32 to 45) lie on one tryptic peptide (about residues 20 to 49; sequence from background knowledge). In a degron-mutant tumour, degron phosphosite rows from a reference search therefore report only the wild-type allele (plus non-tumour cells), not the stabilised mutant protein, and several hotspot mutations remove the phospho-acceptor residue itself. Degron phosphosite values are thus systematically biased in mutant tumours and should not be used there as a Wnt readout independent of the mutation call. Total beta-catenin protein is quantified from peptides outside the degron, so it includes both alleles. HOW SURE: medium. SOURCES: https://doi.org/10.1146/annurev-biochem-040320-103615, https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12900645/, https://digitalcommons.providence.org/cgi/viewcontent.cgi?article=4099&context=publications, https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC10825656/, https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC4392723/.

QUESTION: Which protein-level and phosphosite-level measurements are accepted readouts of canonical Wnt/beta-catenin pathway activity in bulk tumour proteomics (total beta-catenin abundance, phosphorylation at S33/S37/T41/S45, S552, S675, GSK3B S9), and when a tumour carries a missense mutation inside the beta-catenin degron, are the degron phosphopeptides from the mutant allele still identified and quantified by standard reference-database searches or only those from the wild-type allele? ANSWER: Readouts: phosphorylation of the beta-catenin N-terminal degron (CK1alpha primes S45, then GSK3beta phosphorylates T41, S37 and S33, creating the beta-TrCP docking site) marks the protein for ubiquitylation and proteasomal degradation. Phospho-S33/S37/T41/S45 is therefore a destruction (pathway-off) mark; Wnt activation appears as loss of this phosphorylation with accumulation and nuclear translocation of beta-catenin. S552 (AKT) and S675 (PKA) are alternative phosphorylations that 'may enhance' beta-catenin activity, but they are driven by PI3K/AKT and cAMP/PKA signalling and are not specific to canonical Wnt. The pages read did not address GSK3B S9 or how well total beta-catenin in bulk tissue tracks Wnt activity, so the web did not settle those two. Background knowledge, not verified here: GSK3B S9 is an AKT-type inhibitory site that is not required for Wnt signalling, and total beta-catenin in bulk tissue is dominated by the junctional, cadherin-bound pool; both are weak readouts, and target-gene expression remains the accepted one. Mutant allele: standard database searches identify only peptides present in the reference protein database; single-amino-acid-variant peptides are 'usually not present in the database and therefore not identified' unless a customised variant database is searched. All exon 3 hotspot codons (32 to 45) lie on one tryptic peptide (about residues 20 to 49; sequence from background knowledge). In a degron-mutant tumour, degron phosphosite rows from a reference search therefore report only the wild-type allele (plus non-tumour cells), not the stabilised mutant protein, and several hotspot mutations remove the phospho-acceptor residue itself. Degron phosphosite values are thus systematically biased in mutant tumours and should not be used there as a Wnt readout independent of the mutation call. Total beta-catenin protein is quantified from peptides outside the degron, so it includes both alleles. HOW SURE: medium. SOURCES: https://doi.org/10.1146/annurev-biochem-040320-103615, https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12900645/, https://digitalcommons.providence.org/cgi/viewcontent.cgi?article=4099&context=publications, https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC10825656/, https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC4392723/.

question: FINDING FROM THE LAB'S LIBRARY, asked for by the director. QUESTION: Which variant annotation tool emits the Variant_Classification values START_CODON_SNP, START_CODON_INS, DE_NOVO_START_IN_FRAME and DE_NOVO_START_OUT_FRAME, and how does that tool define Splice_Site: how many bases either side of an exon boundary are included, are exonic bases included, and does a Splice_Site row that also reports a protein change (synonymous or missense) indicate an exonic variant whose effect on splicing is not established? ANSWER: Tool: GATK Funcotator. These four uppercase names are Funcotator's internal class names, and its MAF writer (MafOutputRendererConstants) translates only some classes to MAF style (MISSENSE->Missense_Mutation, NONSENSE->Nonsense_Mutation, SPLICE_SITE->Splice_Site, START_CODON_DEL->Translation_Start_Site, INTRON->Intron, ...) while leaving START_CODON_SNP, START_CODON_INS, DE_NOVO_START_IN_FRAME and DE_NOVO_START_OUT_FRAME untranslated. A MAF that mixes 'Splice_Site'/'Intron' with those uppercase values is therefore Funcotator output (Oncotator writes Start_Codon_SNP, De_novo_Start_OutOfFrame instead). Splice_Site definition: any variant overlapping a window of --splice-site-window-size bases on either side of a splice site; the default is 2 (FuncotatorUtils.DEFAULT_SPLICE_SITE_WINDOW_SIZE = 2). In the source the window is [exonStart-2, exonStart+1] and [exonEnd-1, exonEnd+2], so yes, exonic bases are included: by default the first/last 2 exonic bases as well as the 2 intronic bases at each exon edge (the 5' end of the first exon and 3' end of the last exon are not checked). The splice check runs before start-codon and missense/nonsense/silent classification, so it overrides them (only NONSTOP is tested earlier). Protein change: for an exonic variant in the window Funcotator still sets codon change and protein change and records the coding consequence (MISSENSE, SILENT, NONSENSE, ...) in secondaryVariantClassification; for an intronic variant in the window the secondary class is INTRON, the codon change is a 'c.e<exon>+/-N' string, and no protein change is set. So yes: a Splice_Site row that reports a synonymous or missense protein change is an exonic variant within 2 bases of the exon edge, labelled by position alone; the tool makes no prediction of a splicing effect. Only Splice_Site rows without a protein change sit at the intronic +/-1,2 essential positions. Counting every Splice_Site row as truncating overstates truncating calls; the defensible narrow definition is intronic Splice_Site rows plus exonic ones whose own consequence is nonsense. Caveat: whether the dataset's depositor used the default window of 2 cannot be known from the web; the teams can check it from each row's distance to the exon edge. HOW SURE: high. SOURCES: https://github.com/broadinstitute/gatk/blob/master/src/main/java/org/broadinstitute/hellbender/tools/funcotator/dataSources/gencode/GencodeFuncotationFactory.java, https://github.com/broadinstitute/gatk/blob/master/src/main/java/org/broadinstitute/hellbender/tools/funcotator/mafOutput/MafOutputRendererConstants.java, https://github.com/broadinstitute/gatk/blob/master/src/main/java/org/broadinstitute/hellbender/tools/funcotator/FuncotatorUtils.java, https://gatk.broadinstitute.org/hc/en-us/articles/360035531732-Funcotator-Annotation-Specifications.

question: FINDING FROM THE LAB'S LIBRARY, asked for by the director. QUESTION: In cancer genome sequencing studies of high-mutation-burden, UV-driven tumours, is there an accepted convention for calling a gene 'frequently mutated' as distinct from 'significantly mutated' (for example a minimum share of tumours, or a requirement of excess over a background model such as dN/dS or MutSig-style tests), and how do such studies typically word and justify claims that a gene is frequently affected when its prevalence is modest relative to the many passenger genes mutated in a similar share of tumours? ANSWER: No accepted numeric convention exists. None of the papers read applies a field-wide threshold for 'frequently mutated'. Usage is: 'frequently/recurrently mutated' = descriptive prevalence (share of tumours with a non-silent mutation); 'significantly mutated' = statistical excess over a background model (MutSigCV or dNdScv q<0.1; InVEx q<=0.2 in melanoma). Any prevalence cut-off is set per study: one oral-SCC exome study defined 'significantly and frequently mutated' as q<0.1 AND >=5% of tumours, and listed separately genes that were 'frequently mutated' but 'showed no significant enrichment' (TTN 28.3%, PCLO 16.7%, CSMD3 14.2%, MUC16 12.5%), attributing them to very large genes. In UV-driven tumours raw prevalence is explicitly treated as uninformative. In 121 melanoma exomes (Hodis 2012), 515 genes carried non-silent mutations in >10% of tumours and 78 in >20%; about 85% of those mutations were UV-type and the authors concluded that many high-frequency gene mutations are UV passenger events. A uniform-background test there called 544 genes 'significantly' mutated, tracking silent mutation rate and low expression. Lawrence 2013 makes the same point across cancers (olfactory receptors, titin on 'significant' lists) and defines the goal as genes mutated 'more frequently than expected by random chance'. Wording and justification for modest-prevalence genes: studies state counts and percentages plainly ('11 melanomas (9%) harbored nonsynonymous PPP6C mutations'; ARID2 loss-of-function in 7%; p16INK4a loss-of-function in 12%) and rest the claim that the gene is a real target on a per-gene background test (intron/UTR or synonymous control), loss-of-function burden, clustering at hotspots, or pathway-level aggregation (13% of samples with a loss-of-function hit in any SWI/SNF component), not on prevalence. For the teams this means the label depends on which reading is chosen, and the literature supports both readings existing; a verdict should fix the criterion in advance, report prevalence with interval and the background-aware result side by side, and say which one it rests on. HOW SURE: medium. SOURCES: https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC3600117/, https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC3919509/, https://www.thno.org/v07p1088.htm, https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC5720395/.
