question: FINDING FROM THE LAB'S LIBRARY, asked for by the director. QUESTION: Under a UV-type mutational signature (C>T and CC>TT at dipyrimidines), what share of coding single- and double-base substitutions is expected to be nonsense under neutrality, how much does this expected share vary from gene to gene with codon composition, and how do dN/dS-based methods such as dNdScv account for this when testing a single gene for an excess of truncating mutations in a cohort of fewer than 100 tumours? ANSWER: Expected nonsense share: the web did not settle this. No page read gives a published figure for the neutral nonsense fraction under a UV signature, nor a gene-to-gene range. What follows on the numbers is my own genetic-code arithmetic, not a sourced value: 23 of the 549 possible single-base changes in sense codons are nonsense (4.2%); restricted to C>T at dipyrimidines with uniform codon usage and uniform flanks, about 5% are nonsense, 34% silent and 61% missense, i.e. roughly 7-8% of non-silent substitutions. That silent share matches the 2:1 nonsynonymous:synonymous ratio reported for melanoma exomes, which is some reassurance. Real codon usage and the uneven trinucleotide rates of UV will shift it. Gene-to-gene variation: UV-type single-base changes can create a stop only at Gln (CAA, CAG), Arg CGA and Trp TGG codons; CC>TT additionally turns TGG into TAA and can hit Gln/Arg codons across a codon boundary. A gene's neutral nonsense expectation therefore scales with its Gln, Trp and CGA content and flanking context, and can plausibly differ severalfold between genes; glutamine-rich proteins sit at the high end (from background knowledge, not read here, p300/EP300 has a glutamine-rich C-terminal region, so it deserves a specific check). No source quantified the spread. How dNdScv handles it (read in the paper's methods and the R source): a 192-rate trinucleotide substitution model, strand-aware, is fitted across all genes; each gene has its own L matrix giving the number of sites in each of the 192 classes whose mutation would be synonymous, missense, nonsense or essential-splice, so expected nonsense and splice counts are gene-specific by construction ('correcting for ... sequence composition (L)'). The gene's mutation rate combines its own synonymous count with a negative-binomial regression on epigenomic covariates across genes; in small datasets, where most genes have zero or few synonymous mutations, the across-gene (Gamma) term dominates. The default gene test treats truncating = nonsense + essential splice with one shared ratio (constrain_wnon_wspl=TRUE, 2-df likelihood-ratio test) for power. Defaults also drop samples with more than 3000 coding mutations and keep at most 3 mutations per gene per sample. Dinucleotide and complex substitutions are not part of dN/dS: rows with multi-base ref/alt are labelled MNV and go with indels into a separate negative-binomial model with CDS length as offset; if CC>TT is supplied as two adjacent single-base rows the function warns and counts them as two independent substitutions. The authors report that in melanoma the trinucleotide model is biased because the UV context extends beyond the +/-1 base (a pentanucleotide model removes the bias), and that a uniform-rate model run on neutralised melanoma genomes produced 368 false-positive genes while the per-gene models were calibrated. Nothing in these pages addresses small-count behaviour of the likelihood-ratio p-value specifically. Implication for the teams' test: a binomial test of a gene's truncating share against one cohort-wide fraction conditions on the gene's own mutation count, so it controls rate, but not composition. With a handful of truncating calls per gene, an expectation that is off by a factor of about 2 changes the p-value materially, so those per-gene p-values are approximate; a gene-specific expectation (dNdScv, or site counts from the gene's CDS under the cohort's trinucleotide spectrum) is needed before relying on them. HOW SURE: low. SOURCES: https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC5720395/, https://github.com/im3sanger/dndscv/blob/master/R/dndscv.R, https://github.com/im3sanger/dndscv/blob/master/vignettes/dNdScv.Rmd, https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC3600117/.

question: FINDING FROM THE LAB'S LIBRARY, asked for by the director. QUESTION: In the cBioPortal structural-variant file format, what do the DNA_support and RNA_support fields mean, and when the gene panel matrix marks a sample as profiled for structural variants but the sample has no rows in the SV file, does the convention treat it as 'profiled with no event found' or can it mean the sample was not assayed by the RNA-based method? ANSWER: DNA_support and RNA_support are optional yes/no flags supplied by the data provider. DNA_support = 'Fusion detected from DNA sequence data'; RNA_support = 'Fusion detected from RNA sequence data' (the current SV column table repeats the word DNA in the RNA_Support row, a documentation typo; the legacy fusion-format section says RNA). They describe the evidence type for a row that exists and say nothing about samples without rows. The gene panel matrix exists because, in the documentation's words, the MAF and structural variant formats 'are unable to include samples which are sequenced but contain no called mutations'; a panel name in a sample's structural_variants cell means profiled, NA means not profiled. So the portal convention is 'profiled, no event reported'. However, the matrix holds one panel name per sample per profile and cannot record which assay (DNA exome or RNA-seq) was run on which sample. If the SV rows are RNA-supported only while the panel named is a DNA assay such as WXS, the files cannot show that the samples without rows had RNA sequenced. In that situation a missing fusion row is an unverified negative for RNA-detected fusions, not an observed negative. The documentation does not address mixed DNA/RNA assays directly, so this last step is a reading of the format's limits, not a stated rule. Confidence split: high for the field definitions and the matrix convention, medium for whether a sample without rows was RNA-assayed. HOW SURE: medium. SOURCES: https://docs.cbioportal.org/file-formats/.

question: FINDING FROM THE LAB'S LIBRARY, asked for by the director. QUESTION: What is the role of the RIN1 protein in RAS signalling, and are chimeric transcripts joining an expressed gene to immunoglobulin lambda segments (IGLL5, IGLJ) a recognised artefact of RNA-seq fusion callers, for example from plasma-cell infiltration or read-through mapping? ANSWER: RIN1: a RAS effector that binds GTP-loaded RAS with affinity similar to RAF1 (Kd about 22 nM) and competes directly with RAF1 for RAS. Unlike other effectors it inhibits transformation by activated RAS (about twofold fewer soft-agar colonies, more when membrane-targeted) and is restrained by 14-3-3 binding at Ser351, a PKD site. Search summaries that I did not open add that it is a RAB5 exchange factor promoting EGFR endocytosis and an ABL kinase activator. RIN1 is thus a negative modulator of the RAS-RAF branch, not a MAPK activator. No page I read describes RIN1 fusions as a known MAPK-activating event; arguing that a RIN1 fusion raises RAF signalling would be speculation. Immunoglobulin partners: the web only partly settles this. The general artefact class is established: very high expression of one partner produces non-specific chimeras through reverse-transcriptase template switching during cDNA preparation, and fusions recurring at improbable frequency are filtered as false positives (Stransky 2014). A myeloma fusion study pooled IGLL5 into the IGL locus, removed 18 highly recurrent IGL fusions for low whole-genome support, filtered promiscuous partners, and states that transcript overexpression makes false-positive chimeric transcripts more likely (Foltz 2020). Not settled: no page I read says specifically that IGLL5/IGLJ chimeras in solid tumours arise from plasma-cell infiltration or read-through mapping; that mechanism is plausible but unconfirmed here, and the Arriba documentation could not be retrieved. Practical reading: a gene-IGLL5/IGLJ call with RNA support only, no DNA support, and the same Ig partner recurring across samples is a probable artefact or at best an unknown. It should not be counted as a pathway alteration, and it does not by itself confirm 'no other pathway alteration' either. Confidence split: high for RIN1 function, medium for the immunoglobulin artefact question. HOW SURE: medium. SOURCES: https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC133556/, https://doi.org/10.1038/ncomms5846, https://www.nature.com/articles/s41467-020-16434-y.

label: FINDING
text: FINDING: PDX passage numbering is NOT uniform across groups, so the label alone does not fix the meaning. Zero-based convention (NCI PDMR, Jackson Laboratory, Tentler et al. 2012 review): P0/F0/G0 = the first tumour grown in a mouse implanted directly with patient material; P1 = first mouse-to-mouse transplant; JAX calls P2 the 'tertiary passage'. One-based convention (Lai et al. 2017 review, Fig. 1): P0 = the patient's tumour itself, P1 = first mouse engrafted from the patient, P2 = secondary recipients. Practical rule: if a dataset has xenograft-class samples labelled X0 alongside separately labelled patient tumours (T), the zero-based reading is the only consistent one, so X0 = patient-to-mouse step only and X1 = engraftment plus one serial transfer; under that reading only tumour-vs-X0 pairs isolate initial engraftment and tumour-vs-X1 pairs include one extra passage. Confidence: high that conventions differ, medium for which one a given study uses without its own methods text. QUESTION: In PDX studies what do passage labels X0, X1, X2 (P0/P1, F0/F1) denote - is passage 0 the first mouse tumour and passage 1 the first mouse-to-mouse transplant, or is the first mouse tumour numbered 1, and do conventions differ? SOURCE: https://dctd.cancer.gov/drug-discovery-development/reagents-materials/pdmr/models ; https://tumor.informatics.jax.org/mtbwi/live/www/html/SOCHelp.html ; https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC3928688/ ; https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC5427553/

label: FINDING
text: FINDING: Published methods define clonal selection/clonal dynamics quantitatively, as a shift in the cellular prevalence of mutation clusters between samples, and that quantity needs allele counts: PyClone takes deeply sequenced mutations (coverage >1000x) plus allele-specific copy number per locus and tumour content, and its authors describe 'sets of mutations whose cellular prevalences shift together' across samples as the route to identifying clones changing under selection; the subclonal-reconstruction practical guide says VAF must be converted to cellular prevalence/cancer cell fraction using allele-specific copy number and purity. Presence/absence of variant calls plus copy-number profiles therefore cannot measure clone proportions; at most they can show the coarse, extreme outcome (a block of tumour mutations or a copy-number state missing from the xenograft, i.e. a bottleneck to a subset of clones), and no source read states that presence/absence alone is an accepted demonstration. Control for spatial sampling in the one design read (TRACERx lung PDX): multi-region sequencing of the patient tumour and several independent PDX models from different regions; it found engraftment is a genomic bottleneck with models often representing a single tumour subclone, and that later evolution in the mouse added only modestly to tumour-PDX distance; mouse-read removal is a required control. Detection-noise controls (deep targeted resequencing of all sites in all samples) are implied by PyClone's deep-sequencing input but were not read in a methods section here. Confidence: medium. QUESTION: How is clonal selection at engraftment operationally defined and demonstrated in bulk tumour-vs-xenograft comparisons - is presence/absence of variant calls plus copy-number differences accepted, or are allele counts and clonal prevalences required, and what controls separate it from spatial sampling and detection noise? SOURCE: https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC4864026/ ; https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC7867630/ ; https://www.nature.com/articles/s41467-024-47547-3

text: FINDING: SOMATIC_STATUS is a curation label, not pipeline output, and the web does not settle whether 'Unmatched' means the calls were made without a normal. The cBioPortal datahub curation guide tells curators to 'always include matched normal status for all samples with column SOMATIC_STATUS added' and to normalise its values to Matched/Unmatched; it is typed in by the datahub curator when building data_clinical_sample.txt, and in a public example file its description line is just 'Somatic Status' with no further definition. No documentation read links it to the MAF Matched_Norm_Sample_Barcode column or says which takes precedence when they disagree, and nothing read says the importer or any caller uses it. So it is intended to record whether a sample had a matched normal, but it cannot be taken as proof that tumour and xenograft calls came from different pipelines, nor as proof that they did not; a value perfectly aligned with sample class is equally consistent with a per-class curation rule. Treat the calling regime as unknown and test for it in the data (e.g. germline-like, cross-patient recurrent one-sided calls) rather than inferring it from this field. Confidence: medium on who assigns it, low on what Unmatched implies for the calls. QUESTION: In cBioPortal-format studies what does sample-level SOMATIC_STATUS (Matched/Unmatched) mean, who assigns it, and does Unmatched imply somatic and copy-number calls were made without a matched normal even when the MAF lists a matched-normal barcode for every row? label: FINDING
text: FINDING: In Broad D-ToxoG (oxoG filter) output carried in Oncotator/Firehose MAFs, oxoGCut is the filter decision and isArtifactMode is only an eligibility flag. The GDC code that consumes D-ToxoG MAFs treats a record as 'Failed dToxoG' if and only if oxoGCut == '1' and never consults isArtifactMode; the filter (Costello 2013) targets only C>A/G>T substitutions (strongest in CCG>CAG), scoring each by FoxoG (fraction of alt reads in the artefact read orientation) against MuTect tumor_lod, and passes all other substitution types. So a row with isArtifactMode = 1 and oxoGCut = 0 is a C>A/G>T call that was tested and RETAINED: keep it as a passing somatic call; only oxoGCut = 1 rows are suspected artefacts to drop. Exact definitions of qox, pox and pox_cutoff were NOT found on any page read (by name: per-call artefact p-value, its FDR q-value, and the per-sample p cutoff; unverified), so do not build a custom filter on them. QUESTION: What do isArtifactMode, oxoGCut, qox, pox, pox_cutoff mean in Broad Oncotator/Firehose MAFs, and is isArtifactMode = 1 with oxoGCut = 0 a retained call or a suspected artefact? SOURCE: https://github.com/NCI-GDC/variant-filtration-tool/blob/main/gdc_filtration_tools/tools/dtoxog_maf_to_vcf.py and https://doi.org/10.1093/nar/gks1443 and https://github.com/NCI-GDC/variant-filtration-tool.

label: FINDING
text: FINDING: There is no single standard list of activating KIT mutations in melanoma; two conventions exist. Narrow (Dumaz 2014): four driver hotspots holding about 70 percent of melanoma KIT mutations: L576 (exon 11), K642 (exon 13), W557 to V560 (exon 11), D816 to A829 (exon 17 into the first codon of exon 18). Broad (clinical trials and reviews): any mutation in the screened exons 9, 11, 13, 17 and 18, with exons 11, 13 and 17 dominant (exon 11 about 50 to 60 percent incl. L576P about 30 percent, V559A/D, W557R, D579H; exon 13 K642E 10 to 15 percent, V654A, S628N; exon 17 D816, D820Y, N822I/K/Y 5 to 10 percent; exon 18 A829P, P838L, V852I); exon 9 mutations are rare in melanoma. Exon 11 in-frame deletions/insertions/duplications (e.g. deletions affecting W557/K558, Y570_L576del) ARE counted as activating alongside missense substitutions, though they are rare in melanoma (mutations are almost all missense, unlike GIST), so In_Frame_Del/In_Frame_Ins rows in exon 11 must be included in a hotspot count; frameshift and nonsense KIT calls are not activating. QUESTION: Which KIT exons and codons form the conventional hotspot-restricted activating set in melanoma, and are exon 11 in-frame indels counted with missense substitutions? question: FINDING FROM THE LAB'S LIBRARY, asked for by the director. QUESTION: In patient-derived xenograft studies, what do passage labels such as X0, X1, X2 (or P0/P1, F0/F1) conventionally denote? Specifically, is passage 0 the first tumour grown in a mouse directly from patient tissue and passage 1 the first mouse-to-mouse transplant, or is the first mouse tumour usually numbered 1? Do conventions differ between groups? ANSWER: Conventions differ between groups, so the label alone does not fix the meaning. Zero-based convention: NCI PDMR states that 'PDX model nomenclature begins with passage 0 (P0) which represents tumor material obtained from a mouse that was implanted with Originator material'; the Jackson Laboratory protocol speaks of P0 tumours when a graft establishes, then P1, and calls P2 'the tertiary passage'; the Tentler et al. 2012 review says 'the generation harbouring the patient-derived material is termed F0, with subsequent generations numbered consecutively (F1, F2, F3)', some groups writing G0, G1. Under this convention passage 0 is the first mouse tumour and passage 1 is the first mouse-to-mouse transplant. One-based convention: the Lai et al. 2017 review (Fig. 1) labels the patient's tumour P0, the first engrafted mice P1 and the secondary recipients P2, so there the first mouse tumour is numbered 1. Practical rule for a given dataset: if xenograft-class samples carry the label X0 alongside separately labelled patient tumours, only the zero-based reading is consistent, so X0 measures the patient-to-mouse step alone and X1 measures engraftment plus one serial transfer. A fifth source (Mattar et al. 2018, MSK) appeared to give the zero-based definition in its search snippet, but the fetched text did not include that passage, so it is not relied on. HOW SURE: high that conventions differ and that zero-based numbering is used by the large repositories; medium for which convention a particular study uses without its own methods text. question: FINDING FROM THE LAB'S LIBRARY, asked for by the director. QUESTION: In bulk-sequencing comparisons of a patient tumour with its xenograft, how is 'clonal selection at engraftment' operationally defined and demonstrated? Is a change in presence/absence of somatic variant calls plus copy-number state differences accepted as evidence, or do published methods require allele counts and inferred clonal prevalences (mutation-cluster cellular frequencies) to show that clone proportions shifted? What controls are used to separate it from spatial sampling of the tumour and from detection noise? ANSWER: The methods read define it quantitatively, as a shift between samples in the cellular prevalence of clusters of mutations, and that quantity requires allele counts. The PyClone paper takes as input deeply sequenced mutations (coverage >1000x) plus allele-specific copy number at each locus, corrects for normal-cell contamination, and describes 'sets of mutations whose cellular prevalences shift together' across samples as 'a route to precisely identifying clones whose prevalences are changing under selective pressures'. The practical guide to subclonal reconstruction says variant allele frequency must be converted to cellular prevalence or cancer cell fraction using allele-specific copy number and purity. Presence/absence of calls plus copy-number profiles therefore cannot measure clone proportions. At most they can show the coarse outcome: a block of tumour mutations or a copy-number state missing from the xenograft, i.e. a bottleneck to a subset of clones. No source read states that presence/absence alone is, or is not, an accepted demonstration, so the web does not settle that boundary. Spatial-sampling control, from the one design read (TRACERx lung PDX): multi-region sequencing of the patient tumour and several independent PDX models from different regions of the same tumour. That study found engraftment is a genomic bottleneck with models often representing a single tumour subclone, that different subclones were captured by independent models, and that later evolution in the mouse added only modestly to tumour-PDX distance; it also treats removal of mouse reads as a required step. Detection-noise control: deep targeted resequencing is implied by PyClone's input requirement, but no methods section describing it was read here, so that part is weaker. HOW SURE: medium. SOURCES: https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC4864026/, https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC7867630/, https://www.nature.com/articles/s41467-024-47547-3.

QUESTION: In cBioPortal-format studies, what does the sample-level SOMATIC_STATUS field (Matched / Unmatched) mean, who assigns it, and does 'Unmatched' imply that somatic mutation and copy-number calls for that sample were made without a matched normal even when the mutation file lists a matched-normal barcode for every row? ANSWER: It is a curation label added by the cBioPortal datahub curator, not an output of the calling pipeline, and the web does not settle what 'Unmatched' implies for the calls. The datahub curation guide instructs curators to 'always include matched normal status for all samples with column SOMATIC_STATUS added' and to normalise its values to Matched or Unmatched. In a public example data_clinical_sample.txt the description line for the column is just 'Somatic Status', with no further definition. Nothing read links the field to the MAF Matched_Norm_Sample_Barcode column, says which takes precedence when they disagree, or says the importer uses it. So the field is meant to record whether a sample had a matched normal, but it is neither proof that the two sample classes were called by different pipelines nor proof that they were not; a value that tracks sample class exactly is equally consistent with a per-class curation rule. The calling regime should be treated as unknown and tested for in the data. The excerpt of the File-Formats page returned by the gateway stopped before the mutation-format section, so the MAF column definitions were not read. HOW SURE: medium on who assigns it and what it is meant to record; low on whether Unmatched means the calls lacked a matched normal. text: FINDING: The accepted correction for prevalent (already-treated) subjects is a delayed-entry Cox model on the time-since-treatment-start scale with each subject entering the risk set at their sampling time; this needs the duration before entry, and when that duration is unknown 'the delayed entry estimator is not a viable option and biases in the parameter estimate can occur' (Azzato 2009, citing Brookmeyer). With duration unknown the recommended analysis is restriction to incident subjects (here: biopsied before/off treatment) as the unbiased estimate, plus a comparison of incident versus prevalent strata (stratum-specific HRs and a biomarker-by-flag interaction test) and a check of whether the hazard changes with time (non-proportional hazards); pharmacoepidemiology guidance (ENCePP ch.6; Ray 2003) says prevalence bias is a selection bias that cannot be removed at the analysis stage when the selecting factor (time on drug) is unmeasured, and that even recording prior duration does not fix it because early failures were never enrolled. A yes/no 'already on treatment' flag (covariate or stratum) only lets the baseline hazard differ; it leaves three biases: (1) survivor selection/depletion of susceptibles - on-treatment patients are those not yet resistant, fast-progressing carriers were never sampled, so within that stratum a harmful biomarker's HR is pulled toward 1 (direction inferred from the mechanism, not quoted as a formula); (2) mixed unknown durations - if the HR varies with time since treatment start, the estimate is a different weighted average than in incident cases (Azzato found incident-vs-all differences came from non-proportional hazards, not survival bias, once left truncation was handled); (3) the biomarker itself may have been changed by the treatment before sampling (Ray: covariates at entry 'plausibly affected by the drug'), which for a treatment-acquired alteration biases away from 1. So the stratified estimate is acceptable only if the off-treatment-only HR agrees with it; if they differ, trust the off-treatment subset. QUESTION: With clock starting at biopsy and some patients already on treatment for unknown time (left truncation, unknown entry), what analyses are recommended for a biomarker vs time-to-resistance and what are the biases of adjusting/stratifying on a binary on-treatment flag? text: FINDING: Convention: a patient without a documented progression-type event is censored at the date of the last adequate disease assessment that showed no progression, NOT at the last vital-status follow-up (FDA 2018 endpoint guidance: assign progression to the earliest time it is observed and censor 'at the date when the last radiological assessment determined a lack of progression'); extending the censoring time to last follow-up would count unassessed time as event-free. Censoring assumes censored patients have the same future risk as those still followed; stopping assessment for clinical reasons (or death before the event, which FDA calls informative censoring in time-to-progression analyses) can violate this. Recommended sensitivity analyses: (a) bracket the truth - rerun treating the early-censored patients as events at their censoring time (worst case) and as ordinary right-censored (and/or event-free to last follow-up, best case), including worst case applied to one group only (tipping-point style); (b) compare adequacy/length of assessment follow-up and the censoring pattern between the groups being compared, and count deaths among patients no longer assessed; (c) inverse-probability-of-censoring weights: model the hazard of being censored on baseline covariates (Cox model for censoring), weight each person-interval by 1/P(still uncensored), use stabilized or truncated weights, and get CIs by bootstrap because the naive variance has poor coverage - IPCW only corrects censoring that depends on measured covariates. One trial's median PFS moved from 32 to 43 months in one arm purely from a change of censoring rule, so the result should be shown under more than one rule. QUESTION: When progression is known only up to the last clinical assessment (earlier than last vital-status follow-up), what is the standard censoring time and which sensitivity analyses address informative censoring? text: FINDING: MSK-IMPACT-type tumour-normal hybrid-capture panels call gene-level copy number from tumour coverage relative to a pool of unmatched diploid normal controls (FFPE and blood; the best-fitting normal is chosen by lowest sum-squared log-ratio and 'may not always be the matched normal'), GC-normalised and segmented by CBS; a whole-gene event is called only if fold change > 2.0 (gain) or < -2.0 (loss, i.e. tumour:normal ratio below 0.5) with FDR-corrected P < 0.05, germline CNVs seen in the matched normal are subtracted, and calls are manually reviewed. The rule is applied to the observed ratio with NO tumour-purity or ploidy correction, and the output has only -2 / 0 / 2 (no shallow -1/+1), so 0 means 'no high-level event called', which includes low-level gains, single-copy losses and missed events. Purity dependence (arithmetic derived from the threshold, not quoted): on an autosome a 2-fold ratio needs about 2+2/purity copies (4 at 100%, 6 at 50%, 12 at 20% purity), and a homozygous deletion gives ratio 1-purity so it cannot pass the 0.5 threshold unless purity exceeds ~50%; deep deletions (e.g. TP53) are therefore systematically under-called in impure samples and amplifications need higher copy number. The assay accepts samples down to 10% purity. X-chromosome handling in males is NOT stated in the MSK-IMPACT methods papers read - the web did not settle it; general practice (CNVkit docs) is that a male sample against a diploid-X (female) reference sits at log2 about -1 on X unless coverage is doubled or a haploid-X reference is used. Check in the data: if chrX segment means in data_cna_hg19.seg centre near 0 in these male patients, X was normalised to a male/haploid baseline and AR (chrX ~66.8-66.95 Mb, hg19) gain calls are on a 1-copy baseline; if they centre near -1, AR amplification is under-called. In cBioPortal discrete CNA files 0 is defined as 'diploid' (-2 deep loss possibly homozygous deletion, 2 high-level amplification); whether a gene was assayed is conveyed by the gene panel matrix / gene_panel property (NA = not profiled), not by the CNA value, and the format page does not define NA inside the discrete CNA matrix, so 0 by itself does not prove the gene was on the panel - confirm with data_gene_panel_matrix.txt and the panel gene list. QUESTION: How are amplifications/deep deletions called in discrete gene-level CNA tables from tumour-normal targeted panels in cBioPortal format (thresholds, purity), how are X genes handled in males, and does 0 distinguish no alteration from not on panel? SOURCE: https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC5808190/ ; https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC5461196/ ; https://docs.cbioportal.org/file-formats/ ; https://cnvkit.readthedocs.io/en/stable/sex.html

question: FINDING FROM THE LAB'S LIBRARY, asked for by the director. QUESTION: In mutation annotation files produced by the Broad Institute's Oncotator / Firehose pipeline, what do the columns isArtifactMode, oxoGCut, qox, pox and pox_cutoff mean, and is a row with isArtifactMode = 1 but oxoGCut = 0 considered a retained (passing) somatic call or a suspected artefact that analysts are advised to exclude? ANSWER: These columns are the output of the Broad D-ToxoG / oxoG filter for 8-oxoguanine oxidation artefacts. What the pages I read establish: (1) Costello et al. 2013 define the filter: the artefact is a C>A / G>T transversion at low allele fraction, strongest in CCG>CAG context, seen as G>T only on read 1 and C>A only on read 2. Each call is scored by FoxoG (fraction of alt-supporting reads in the artefact read orientation) against MuTect tumor_lod (pass threshold tumor_lod > -10 + (100/3)*FoxoG); all non-C>A/G>T substitutions pass regardless. The authors estimate the filter removes only about 1.4% of true C>A mutations and leaves about 0.1% artefacts among passed calls. (2) The NCI GDC code that consumes the D-ToxoG output MAF (dtoxog_maf_to_vcf.py, 'extract the sites that failed') marks a record as 'Failed dToxoG' if and only if oxoGCut == '1'; it never consults isArtifactMode. So oxoGCut is the filter decision (1 = cut as a suspected oxoG artefact, 0 = passed), and isArtifactMode = 1 only says the substitution is of the artefact-mode type (C>A/G>T) and was therefore eligible for the test. A row with isArtifactMode = 1 and oxoGCut = 0 is a tested-and-retained passing somatic call and should be kept; only oxoGCut = 1 rows are the ones to exclude. The isArtifactMode reading is an inference from the column name plus the two sources, not a sentence I read in documentation. NOT settled by the web: no page I opened defines qox, pox or pox_cutoff. By name they are probably the per-call artefact p-value, its FDR-adjusted q-value and the per-sample p-value cutoff used to set oxoGCut, but that is unverified, so teams should not build their own filter on those three columns. A search snippet I did not open (RTCGA data summaries) showed oxoGCut with a single distinct value in released Firehose MAFs, consistent with cut rows already having been removed. HOW SURE: medium (high that oxoGCut = 1 is the failing flag and oxoGCut = 0 rows are retained; low for the exact definitions of qox, pox and pox_cutoff, which the web did not settle). SOURCES: https://github.com/NCI-GDC/variant-filtration-tool/blob/main/gdc_filtration_tools/tools/dtoxog_maf_to_vcf.py, https://doi.org/10.1093/nar/gks1443, https://github.com/NCI-GDC/variant-filtration-tool.

question: FINDING FROM THE LAB'S LIBRARY, asked for by the director. QUESTION: When a hotspot-restricted definition of activating KIT mutations is used in melanoma, which exons and codons are conventionally included (for example exon 9, 11, 13, 17 and 18 positions), and are in-frame insertions and deletions in exon 11 counted alongside missense substitutions? ANSWER: There is no single standard list; the literature uses two conventions. Narrow (Dumaz et al. 2014, abstract): 70% of melanoma KIT mutations lie in four hotspots shown to be oncogenic drivers: L576 (exon 11), K642 (exon 13), W557-V560 (exon 11) and D816-A829 (exon 17, ending at the first codon of exon 18); the authors say testing should concentrate on these. Broad (clinical trials and reviews): any mutation in the screened exons 9, 11, 13, 17 and 18. Exons 11, 13 and 17 dominate: exon 11 is about 50-60% of cases (L576P alone about 30%; also V559A/D, W557R, D579H and deletions affecting W557/K558); exon 13 carries K642E (10-15%), plus V654A and S628N; exon 17 carries D816, D820Y and N822I/K/Y (about 5-10%); exon 18 entries in the reviews' catalogue are A829P, P838L and V852I. Exon 9 mutations are rare in melanoma (absent in the early Bastian series, 0-9% in trial cohorts). L576P and K642E together are over half of all melanoma KIT mutations and are the prototypical hotspots; outside them is a long tail of rare variants. Exon 11 in-frame indels: yes, they are counted as activating alongside missense substitutions. The 2025 review lists deletions affecting W557/K558 with the exon 11 substitutions as disrupting the juxtamembrane auto-inhibitory segment; Beadling et al. reported an exon 11 in-frame deletion and an exon 11 insertion/duplication in melanoma, Torres-Cabala two exon 11 insertions, and the pooled catalogue includes Y570_L576del (exon 11), Y503delinsFAH (exon 9) and R815_D816delinsS (exon 17). They are uncommon in melanoma, where KIT mutations are almost all missense (unlike GIST, where exon 11 in-frame deletions predominate). So In_Frame_Del / In_Frame_Ins rows in exon 11 belong in a hotspot count; frameshift and nonsense KIT calls are not activating. HOW SURE: medium (high for the exons, codons and inclusion of exon 11 in-frame indels; the web shows no single agreed 'standard' list, and for Dumaz et al. only the abstract was readable). SOURCES: https://doi.org/10.1097/cmr.0000000000000116, https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12650433/, https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC7329741/, https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC3935736/.

question: FINDING FROM THE LAB'S LIBRARY, asked for by the director. QUESTION: In somatic MAF files, what do the Variant_Classification values 'Targeted_Region' and 'Frame_Shift' (without _Ins or _Del) denote, and are they conventionally treated as protein-altering when counting non-silent mutations per gene? ANSWER: Targeted_Region is a legal value in the TCGA MAF v2.4.1 specification and is allowed in open-access somatic MAFs, but the spec gives it no precise definition (the nearest text is 'indels that overlap ... the targeted region of a genetic element of interest'). In vcf2maf it is the catch-all: 'Annotate everything else simply as a targeted region' (TFBS or regulatory-region ablation/amplification, feature elongation/truncation). Before a 2016 fix, complex in-frame delins that VEP labels protein_altering_variant also fell into it, so a Targeted_Region row can be a real coding change. Tools disagree on counting it: cBioPortal's default import filter removes only Silent, Intron, IGR, 3'UTR, 5'UTR, 3'Flank and 5'Flank, so Targeted_Region is kept and shown as a mutation; maftools' default non-silent list (Frame_Shift_Del, Frame_Shift_Ins, Splice_Site, Translation_Start_Site, Nonsense_Mutation, Nonstop_Mutation, In_Frame_Del, In_Frame_Ins, Missense_Mutation) excludes it and treats everything else as silent. So it is not conventionally in the protein-altering set, but it is not safely silent either; judge each row by its protein change and Variant_Type and report counts with and without it. Bare 'Frame_Shift' is not in the TCGA spec's enumerated values nor in cBioPortal's allowed list, and no page I read defines it: the web does not settle this one. By name it is a frameshift indel whose _Ins/_Del suffix is missing, which is biologically protein-altering (truncating), but any exact-match filter built from the standard list (maftools default included) would silently drop it. Recommended handling: count it as protein-altering for any-non-silent counts, never as an activating hotspot. HOW SURE: medium for Targeted_Region (definitions and tool defaults read directly); low for bare Frame_Shift (non-standard value, not defined on any page read; interpretation is by name only). SOURCES: https://docs.gdc.cancer.gov/Encyclopedia/pages/Mutation_Annotation_Format_TCGAv2/, https://github.com/mskcc/vcf2maf/issues/33, https://github.com/cBioPortal/cbioportal/blob/master/docs/File-Formats.md, https://rdrr.io/bioc/maftools/src/R/read_maf_dt.R.

text: FINDING: OncoKB (public API, data v7.7) annotates amplification of all four oncogenes as driver events: BRAF Amplification = Oncogenic (gain-of-function); PIK3CA Amplification, AKT1 Amplification and KRAS Amplification = Likely Oncogenic (likely gain-of-function). SMAD4 Deletion = Likely Oncogenic (loss-of-function, a curated variant); RNF43 Deletion is not a separately curated variant but is returned as Likely Oncogenic by OncoKB's rule that a deletion is a truncating alteration in a tumour suppressor. cBioPortal's default query is 'MUT FUSION AMP HOMDEL', so by default it counts every amplification (+2) and deep deletion (-2) of a queried gene as altered regardless of driver status; the OQL DRIVER modifier restricts to OncoKB/CancerHotspots drivers. So under both conventions, amplification (value 2 in data_cna.txt) of KRAS, BRAF, PIK3CA and AKT1 all belong in 'oncogenic alteration', not KRAS alone, and deep deletion (-2) of SMAD4 and RNF43 belongs too; gains (+1) and shallow deletions (-1) do not. Caveat: these are current OncoKB annotations and the version used when a study was published may differ, so report mutation-only and mutation+CNA results side by side. QUESTION: In OncoKB's curation rules and the cBioPortal default 'altered' definition, are amplifications of BRAF, PIK3CA and AKT1 (as opposed to KRAS) annotated oncogenic/likely oncogenic, and are homozygous deletions of SMAD4 and RNF43 annotated oncogenic? SOURCE: https://public.api.oncokb.org/api/v1/annotate/copyNumberAlterations?hugoSymbol=BRAF&copyNameAlterationType=AMPLIFICATION (same endpoint for PIK3CA, AKT1, KRAS AMPLIFICATION and SMAD4, RNF43 DELETION) ; https://www.oncokb.org/gene/BRAF/Amplification ; https://www.oncokb.org/gene/SMAD4/Deletion ; https://docs.cbioportal.org/user-guide/oql/

question: FINDING FROM THE LAB'S LIBRARY, asked for by the director. QUESTION: In a time-to-event analysis where the clock starts at tumour biopsy and some patients had already been on the treatment of interest for an unknown duration before the biopsy (left truncation with unknown entry time), what analyses are recommended to test whether a biomarker is associated with time to treatment resistance, and what are the known biases of adjusting or stratifying only on a yes/no 'already on treatment' flag? ANSWER: Accepted approach when the delay is KNOWN: a delayed-entry (left-truncated) Cox model on the time-since-treatment-start scale, with each patient entering the risk set at the sampling time; it gives an unbiased HR if entry is independent of outcome given covariates and hazards are proportional, and a 'prevalent' covariate is then unnecessary (Azzato 2009). When the delay is UNKNOWN, the same paper states that 'the delayed entry estimator is not a viable option and biases in the parameter estimate can occur'. The remedy the guidance gives is restriction: ENCePP ch. 6 says selection biases 'cannot be removed at the analysis stage if the factors responsible for the selection are not known or not measured' and that prevalence bias 'may be removed by restricting the analysis to incident drug users', at the cost of precision; Ray 2003 adds that even recording prior duration does not resolve it, because the survivors exclude people who failed before follow-up began, and recommends a comparative analysis of new versus prevalent users and a check of whether the hazard varies with time before pooling them. So the recommended set is: (1) off-treatment-at-biopsy patients only, as the unbiased estimate; (2) stratum-specific HRs for on- and off-treatment patients with a biomarker-by-flag interaction test; (3) a proportional-hazards / time-varying-HR check; (4) the pooled stratified estimate reported only as secondary. Biases left by a binary flag (it only lets the baseline hazard differ): (a) survivor selection / depletion of susceptibles - on-treatment patients are those not yet resistant and fast progressors were never sampled, so a harmful biomarker's HR in that stratum is pulled toward 1 (this direction is my inference from the stated mechanism, 'underascertainment of events that occur early in therapy'; no source gives it as a formula for a biomarker); (b) patients in the 'yes' stratum have mixed unknown durations, so if the HR changes with time on treatment the estimate is a different weighted average than in incident patients (Azzato found incident-vs-all differences were due to non-proportional hazards); (c) characteristics measured at entry may already have been changed by the treatment (Ray 2003), which for a treatment-acquired alteration biases away from 1. The net direction is therefore not fixed; the stratified estimate is sufficient only if it agrees with the off-treatment-only estimate. No source read gives a method that recovers an unbiased estimate from a binary flag alone. HOW SURE: medium. SOURCES: https://www.nature.com/articles/6605062, https://doi.org/10.1093/aje/kwg231, https://encepp.europa.eu/encepp-toolkit/methodological-guide/chapter-6-methods-address-bias-and-confounding_en, https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11588434/.

question: FINDING FROM THE LAB'S LIBRARY, asked for by the director. QUESTION: When an event such as disease progression is only known up to the last clinical assessment, which can be much earlier than the last vital-status follow-up, what is the standard convention for the censoring time and what sensitivity analyses are recommended for possibly informative censoring (for example best-case/worst-case imputation or inverse-probability-of-censoring weights)? ANSWER: Convention: censor at the last adequate disease assessment that showed no event, not at the last vital-status contact. FDA's 2018 oncology endpoint guidance recommends 'assigning the progression date to the earliest time when any progression is observed without prior missing assessments and censoring at the date when the last radiological assessment determined a lack of progression'. Extending the censoring time to last follow-up would count unassessed time as event-free. The same guidance notes that censoring 'assumes that the patients with censored observations have the same risk' as those still followed, and calls censoring deaths in a time-to-progression analysis informative censoring. Recommended sensitivity analyses: (1) bracketing - the Clinical Cancer Research PFS overview says 'the most practical suggestion is to perform sensitivity analyses, making assumptions which likely bracket the truth (treating the times as progressions, then as right censored observations)'; applying the worst case to one group only gives a tipping-point version (tipping-point analysis appeared only in a search result I did not open). (2) FDA: pre-specify a primary and one or more sensitivity analyses, compare adequacy of follow-up between groups, and count deaths among patients lost to assessment, since an imbalance overestimates event-free time in the group with less follow-up. (3) Inverse-probability-of-censoring weights (tutorial, PMC13748472): fit a model (e.g. Cox) for being censored given covariates, weight by 1/P(remaining uncensored), use stabilized or truncated weights for extreme values, and bootstrap the confidence interval because the naive variance has poor coverage; the tutorial's worked cases assume censoring is independent of the event given the measured covariates, so IPCW does not correct dependence on unmeasured factors. A commentary in European Journal of Cancer shows the size of the issue: changing only the censoring rule moved one arm's median PFS from 32 to 43 months. Progression is also interval-censored between assessments; assigning it to the assessment date is the usual convention. HOW SURE: high. SOURCES: https://www.fda.gov/media/71195/download, https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC3654394/, https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC13748472/, https://www.ejcancer.com/article/S0959-8049(24)00678-6/fulltext.

question: FINDING FROM THE LAB'S LIBRARY, asked for by the director. QUESTION: In discrete gene-level copy-number tables produced from tumour-normal targeted hybrid-capture sequencing panels and distributed in cBioPortal format, how are amplifications and deep deletions called (fold-change thresholds, dependence on tumour purity), how are X-chromosome genes handled in male patients, and does a value of 0 distinguish 'no alteration' from 'gene not on the panel'? ANSWER: Calling (MSK-IMPACT validation paper, Cheng 2015): tumour coverage of target regions is compared with a set of unmatched normal FFPE and blood controls (the best comparator is the one with the lowest sum-squared log-ratio and 'may not always be the matched normal'), GC-normalised and segmented by circular binary segmentation; a whole-gene event is called when 'fold change >2.0 (gain) or <-2.0 (loss), P < 0.05 (false discovery rate-corrected)'. Copy-number events found in the matched normal are subtracted as germline. Zehir 2017 describes only 'an in-house developed algorithm' with manual review of every call. Purity: the rule is applied to the observed tumour:normal ratio with no purity or ploidy correction (the 2015 paper lists purity estimation as future work). By arithmetic from the threshold (my derivation, not a quoted statement) an autosomal gene needs about 2 + 2/purity copies to reach 2-fold: 4 copies at 100% purity, 6 at 50%, 12 at 20%. A homozygous deletion gives a ratio of 1 - purity, so it cannot pass the 0.5 threshold unless purity is above about 50%. Deep deletions are therefore under-called in impure samples and amplifications need higher copy number. Samples are accepted down to 10% purity; in the 10,000-patient cohort samples with no alterations were excluded if purity was under 20% 'due to the risk of false negatives'. Only -2, 0 and 2 are produced, so 0 also covers low-level gains and single-copy losses. X-linked genes in males: not settled. Neither MSK-IMPACT paper says how chromosome X is treated in male patients. General practice (CNVkit documentation) is that a male sample against a diploid-X reference sits at log2 about -1 on X unless its X coverage is doubled or a haploid-X ('male') reference is used. The teams can check this in the segment file: X-chromosome segment means centred near 0 in these male patients mean a one-copy baseline was used; centred near -1 means X-linked amplifications are under-called. Value 0: the cBioPortal format defines 0 as 'diploid', -2 as 'a deep loss, possibly a homozygous deletion' and 2 as 'a high-level amplification'. Whether a gene was assayed is recorded in the gene panel matrix file or the gene_panel meta property (NA = sample not profiled), not in the CNA value; the format page does not define NA inside the discrete copy-number matrix. So 0 alone does not distinguish 'not altered' from 'not on the panel'; that needs the gene panel matrix and the panel's gene list. HOW SURE: medium. SOURCES: https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC5808190/, https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC5461196/, https://docs.cbioportal.org/file-formats/, https://cnvkit.readthedocs.io/en/stable/sex.html.

text: FINDING: SAMPLE_CLASS is an optional, free-text cBioPortal sample attribute meaning only 'the type of sample'; it is not required, not validated against origin, and a cBioPortal developer stated it is not used in page logic. The public datahub curation rule normalises it to exactly three values, 'Tumor', 'Cell Line', 'Xenograft' - there is NO 'Organoid' value - and cBioPortal says clinical data are free-form with no ontology, organised as the study authors chose. So curated studies can and do mark cell lines and xenografts, but an organoid/tumoroid has no dedicated class and nothing forces any model-derived sample to be flagged. The web did not yield an audit of how often the field is left as 'Tumor' for model-derived samples, so that frequency is unsettled; what is settled is that a uniform SAMPLE_CLASS='Tumor' is weak evidence and cannot by itself show that no organoid/xenograft-derived sample is present. Establish origin from other columns (derivation/sample-type descriptions, ID conventions defined in the '#' rows) or state it is undetermined. QUESTION: In cBioPortal clinical sample files, is SAMPLE_CLASS reliably set to a distinct value for organoid-, cell-line- or xenograft-derived samples, or commonly left at 'Tumor'? text: FINDING: The web gives no accepted, validated rule for classifying a sample as culture/model-derived from panel VAFs and log-ratio amplitudes alone, and none for telling an independent later biopsy from a later passage of one culture; treat both as unsettled and any such call as suggestive only. What sources do support: (1) tumour purity is the cancer-cell fraction and is what VAF reflects, so a stroma-free culture should show clonal VAFs and copy-number log-ratio amplitudes near their full-purity values - but a high-purity patient tumour looks the same, so this is necessary, not sufficient. (2) A xenograft is NOT pure: human stroma is quickly replaced by mouse stroma, PDX purity mimics patient tumours of that cancer type and stays stable across passages; mouse reads must be separated from human reads. (3) Organoid genomes keep the parent tumour's point mutations and CNAs, but sampling bias and clonal selection reshape subclonal composition at establishment and during passaging. (4) In 1,451 PDX/patient samples (509 models) CNAs were strongly conserved from patient tumour to late passage, and patient-vs-PDX CNA differences were comparable to multiregion differences within a patient - so the SIZE of genomic divergence between two serial samples cannot discriminate 'new biopsy' from 'later passage'. Serial-sample comparison can show shared truncal alterations (same patient/lineage) but not which undefined ID code means passage, biopsy or mouse engraftment; that needs metadata. QUESTION: From targeted-panel VAFs and copy-number log-ratio segments alone, what are accepted signs of a purified culture/model-derived sample versus bulk tumour, and how to tell an independent later biopsy from a later passage of the same culture? text: FINDING: In rectal cancer TNT = total neoadjuvant therapy (a full course of systemic chemotherapy added before surgery to SCRT or CRT, as induction or consolidation), CRT = chemoradiotherapy/chemoradiation (long-course radiotherapy with concurrent fluoropyrimidine), SCRT = short-course radiotherapy (5 x 5 Gy = 25 Gy, radiation without concurrent chemotherapy). These are treatment regimens, not response codes. Clinical response after them is a recognised categorical observation that does not need a numeric grade: complete clinical response (cCR) is defined as absence of clinical evidence of residual tumour, and the MSK/OPRA three-tier schema calls visible tumour on endoscopy or a palpable tumour nodule an incomplete clinical response (ICR), with near-complete (NCR) between. So clinically evident residual tumour after TNT/CRT/SCRT does correspond to a recognised 'not complete response' category. But the category is assigned by a structured assessment (digital rectal exam, endoscopy, MRI, about 8 +/- 4 weeks after TNT in OPRA) and recorded as such; a record that a specimen was derived after a named regimen is not that assessment. From it one can infer at most 'viable tumour existed somewhere at that time', which does not separate near-complete from incomplete response, does not say the sampled lesion was the irradiated rectal primary, and reflects combined chemo-plus-radiation (radiation only for SCRT), not chemotherapy sensitivity alone. QUESTION: What do TNT, CRT and SCRT stand for in rectal cancer records, and is sampleable residual tumour after neoadjuvant treatment itself a recognised clinical response observation or is a formal graded measure always required? text: FINDING: SMAD4 is less concordant between primary and matched metastasis than KRAS/BRAF/PIK3CA, but it is NOT reported as more frequent in the metastasis than in the primary of the same metastatic patients. Numbers read: KRAS/BRAF/PIK3CA median concordance 93.7% / 99.4% / 93% (meta-analysis of 61 studies) and >90% in an MSK paired series; in 95 primary-metastasis pairs on a 170-gene panel SMAD4 was mutated in 15% of primaries vs 14% of metastases, yet SMAD4 variant concordance was the lowest of the top six genes at 61% (average 85%), i.e. discordance goes both ways; in a 19-pair series SMAD4 was discordant in 1 pair. SMAD4 alteration is enriched by stage rather than by specimen: mutation in 7% of invasive primaries without distant metastasis vs 35% of primaries with distant metastasis vs 31% of distant metastases (Miyaki 1999), and Smad4 protein loss was seen in 37% of primaries and their corresponding metastases. No source read gave paired concordance for SMAD4 homozygous deletion specifically, so that part is not settled. Use: in an all-metastatic cohort the literature does not predict a large primary-vs-metastasis difference in SMAD4 frequency, so a sharp difference by specimen type is not an expected biological pattern to model; do not drop either specimen type, but run the right/left test stratified by specimen type (e.g. Mantel-Haenszel or separate primary-only and metastasis-only tables) next to the pooled test, and check whether the SMAD4 difference sits in the deep-deletion calls (purity-sensitive) rather than in mutations. QUESTION: In colorectal cancer, how concordant are SMAD4 alterations between primary and matched metastases, and is SMAD4 loss more frequent in metastases than primaries, in contrast to KRAS, BRAF, PIK3CA? ANSWER: SAMPLE_CLASS is an optional, free-text sample attribute that a cBioPortal developer defined only as 'the type of sample' and said is not used in page logic. cBioPortal states that clinical data are free-form, follow no ontology (cancer type excepted) and are organised as the study authors chose, so nothing validates the field against a sample's real origin. What is settled is that a uniform SAMPLE_CLASS of 'Tumor' is weak evidence and cannot by itself show that no organoid- or xenograft-derived sample is present; origin has to be established from other columns or declared undetermined. Limits of the reading: the file-formats page was only partly retrievable, so the statement that only PATIENT_ID and SAMPLE_ID are required columns rests on a search excerpt of that page, not a full read. question: FINDING FROM THE LAB'S LIBRARY, asked for by the director. QUESTION: From targeted-panel sequencing output alone (variant allele fractions from tumour read counts, and copy-number log-ratio segment amplitudes), what are the accepted signs that a sample is a purified culture or model-derived specimen (organoid, cell line, xenograft) rather than bulk patient tumour tissue, and what are the accepted ways to tell an independent later biopsy of a patient from a later passage of the same culture? ANSWER: The web does not settle this. No accepted, validated criterion was found for calling a sample culture- or model-derived from panel VAFs and log-ratio amplitudes alone, and none for separating an independent later biopsy from a later passage of one culture. Any such call is suggestive only. What the sources read do support: (1) Tumour purity is the cancer-cell fraction and is what VAF reflects, so a stroma-free culture is expected to show clonal VAFs and log-ratio amplitudes near their full-purity values. A high-purity patient tumour looks the same, so high purity is necessary but not sufficient. That expectation is an inference from the definition of purity, not a published classification rule. (2) A xenograft is not a pure sample: human stroma is quickly replaced by mouse stroma, PDX purity mimics patient tumours of the same cancer type and stays stable across passages, and mouse reads have to be separated from human reads. (3) Organoids keep the parent tumour's point mutations and copy-number alterations, but sampling bias and clonal selection reshape subclonal composition at establishment and during passaging. (4) In 1,451 PDX and matched patient samples from 509 models, copy-number alterations were strongly conserved from patient tumour through late passage, and patient-versus-PDX differences were comparable to multiregion differences within one patient. The size of genomic divergence between two serial samples therefore cannot discriminate a new biopsy from a later passage. Comparing serial samples can show shared truncal alterations (same patient and lineage), but not what an undefined sample code denotes; that needs metadata. Limits of the reading: only abstracts and introductions were retrievable for most of these papers, and the claim that subclonal change is largest at induction and early passages rests on a search excerpt. HOW SURE: low (medium that no accepted criterion exists and that divergence size cannot separate biopsy from passage; low on any specific sign). SOURCES: https://aacrjournals.org/cancerrescommun/article/2/5/353/696472/Tumor-Purity-in-Preclinical-Mouse-Tumor, https://www.nature.com/articles/s41588-020-00750-6, https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC6604205/, https://www.j-organoid.org/journal/view.php?number=95, https://www.nature.com/articles/s41467-018-05190-9.

question: FINDING FROM THE LAB'S LIBRARY, asked for by the director. QUESTION: In rectal cancer treatment records, what do the abbreviations TNT, CRT and SCRT conventionally stand for, and is the presence of sampleable residual tumour after such neoadjuvant treatment itself a recognised clinical response observation (for example incomplete response versus complete response), or is a formal graded measure always required? ANSWER: TNT is total neoadjuvant therapy: a full course of systemic chemotherapy given before surgery in addition to SCRT or CRT, as induction or consolidation. CRT is chemoradiotherapy (chemoradiation): long-course radiotherapy with concurrent fluoropyrimidine. SCRT is short-course radiotherapy, 5 x 5 Gy (25 Gy), which is radiation without concurrent chemotherapy. All three name treatment regimens, not responses. A numeric grade is not always required: clinical response is a recognised categorical observation. Complete clinical response is defined as the absence of clinical evidence of residual tumour, and the three-tier MSK/OPRA schema classes visible tumour on endoscopy or a palpable tumour nodule as incomplete clinical response, with near-complete response between the two. Clinically evident residual tumour after TNT, CRT or SCRT therefore does correspond to a recognised 'not complete response' category. However, that category is assigned by a structured assessment (digital rectal examination, endoscopy and MRI, at about 8 +/- 4 weeks after TNT in OPRA) and recorded as such. A record that a specimen was derived after a named regimen is not that assessment. It supports at most the inference that viable tumour existed somewhere at that time; it does not separate near-complete from incomplete response, does not show the sampled lesion was the treated rectal primary, and reflects combined chemotherapy plus radiation (radiation only for SCRT), not chemotherapy sensitivity alone. Whether that inference counts as a per-patient clinical observation in the task's sense is a judgement for the director; the sources do not decide it. Limits of the reading: the 25 Gy in five fractions figure and the concurrent-fluoropyrimidine detail for CRT come partly from search excerpts of the ESMO guideline and a Thieme review that were not opened; pathological tumour regression grading was not read in this session. HOW SURE: high for the abbreviations; medium for the response-category part. SOURCES: https://www.ctro.science/article/S2405-6308(26)00149-7/pdf, https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC10705332/, https://www.mskcc.org/clinical-updates/rectal-cancer-response-to-total-neoadjuvant-therapy-predicts-organ-preservation-and-survival-outcomes, https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC9851947/.

ANSWER: Yes to all. OncoKB (public API, data version v7.7) returns: BRAF Amplification = Oncogenic (gain-of-function); PIK3CA Amplification = Likely Oncogenic; AKT1 Amplification = Likely Oncogenic; KRAS Amplification = Likely Oncogenic; SMAD4 Deletion = Likely Oncogenic (loss-of-function, a curated variant). RNF43 Deletion is not a separately curated variant (variantExist=false) but is still returned as Likely Oncogenic through OncoKB's rule that a deletion is a truncating alteration in a tumour suppressor. cBioPortal's default query is 'MUT FUSION AMP HOMDEL', so it counts every amplification and deep deletion of a queried gene as altered whether or not it is a driver; the optional OQL DRIVER modifier restricts to OncoKB/CancerHotspots drivers. Consequence for the teams: amplification (2 in data_cna.txt) of all four oncogenes, not KRAS alone, and deep deletion (-2) of SMAD4 and RNF43 belong in 'oncogenic alteration'; gains (+1) and shallow deletions (-1) do not. Caveats: these are OncoKB's current annotations and the version in use when a given study was done may differ; I could not read the SOP's copy-number rule text itself (the page fetch returned only the table of contents), so the rule is taken from the per-gene API output and the two OncoKB variant pages. HOW SURE: high. SOURCES: https://public.api.oncokb.org/api/v1/annotate/copyNumberAlterations?hugoSymbol=BRAF&copyNameAlterationType=AMPLIFICATION, https://public.api.oncokb.org/api/v1/annotate/copyNumberAlterations?hugoSymbol=PIK3CA&copyNameAlterationType=AMPLIFICATION, https://public.api.oncokb.org/api/v1/annotate/copyNumberAlterations?hugoSymbol=AKT1&copyNameAlterationType=AMPLIFICATION, https://public.api.oncokb.org/api/v1/annotate/copyNumberAlterations?hugoSymbol=KRAS&copyNameAlterationType=AMPLIFICATION, https://public.api.oncokb.org/api/v1/annotate/copyNumberAlterations?hugoSymbol=SMAD4&copyNameAlterationType=DELETION, https://public.api.oncokb.org/api/v1/annotate/copyNumberAlterations?hugoSymbol=RNF43&copyNameAlterationType=DELETION, https://www.oncokb.org/gene/BRAF/Amplification, https://www.oncokb.org/gene/SMAD4/Deletion, https://docs.cbioportal.org/user-guide/oql/.

question: FINDING FROM THE LAB'S LIBRARY, asked for by the director. QUESTION: In colorectal cancer, how concordant are SMAD4 alterations (mutations and homozygous deletions) between a patient's primary tumour and matched metastases, and is SMAD4 loss reported to be more frequent in metastatic lesions than in primaries (acquired or selected during progression) in contrast to KRAS, BRAF and PIK3CA? ANSWER: Partly settled. SMAD4 is less concordant than KRAS/BRAF/PIK3CA, but it is not reported as more frequent in the metastasis than in the primary of the same metastatic patients. KRAS, BRAF and PIK3CA: median concordance 93.7%, 99.4% and 93% in a meta-analysis of 61 studies, and >90% in an MSK paired series. SMAD4: in 95 primary-metastasis pairs on a 170-gene panel it was mutated in 15% of primaries vs 14% of metastases, yet SMAD4 variant concordance was the lowest of the six most-mutated genes at 61% (average 85%), so discordance runs in both directions; in a 19-pair series SMAD4 was discordant in one pair. The enrichment is by stage, not by specimen: SMAD4 mutation was found in 7% of invasive primaries without distant metastasis, 35% of primaries with distant metastasis and 31% of distant metastases (Miyaki 1999, with the same mutation in primary and metastasis in four paired cases), and Smad4 protein loss was seen in 37% of primaries and their corresponding metastases (Losi 2007). Not settled: no source I read reported paired concordance for SMAD4 homozygous deletions specifically. Consequence for the teams: in a cohort where every patient is metastatic, the literature does not predict a large primary-vs-metastasis difference in SMAD4 frequency, so a sharp specimen-type difference is not an established biological pattern; keep both specimen types, run the right/left test stratified by specimen type alongside the pooled test, and check whether the difference sits in deep-deletion calls rather than mutations (that last suggestion is my inference, not from a source). HOW SURE: medium. SOURCES: https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC8197329/, https://www.nature.com/articles/1202642, https://doi.org/10.3892/or.17.5.1095, https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC4431733/, https://www.thelancet.com/article/S2352-3964(19)30057-X/fulltext, https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC3417049/, https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC2360736/.

question: FINDING FROM THE LAB'S LIBRARY, asked for by the director. QUESTION: In comparisons of mutation frequency between clinical groups using tumour-normal targeted panel sequencing, what is the standard way to guard against false wild-type calls from low tumour purity (for example a minimum tumour-content or variant-allele-fraction-based purity threshold), and are post-treatment rectal primaries or small biopsies known to have systematically lower tumour content? ANSWER: Not fully settled: the web gives no single universal cut-off, but 20% and 30% tumour purity are the defensible thresholds for a sensitivity analysis. What I read: MSK-IMPACT's validated detection limit is about 2% variant allele fraction for hotspot and 5% for non-hotspot mutations (so a clonal heterozygous non-hotspot mutation needs roughly 10% purity; that conversion is my arithmetic, VAF = purity/2). In a paired colorectal study on a 425-gene panel, below 30% purity 86% of the missed mutations were high-frequency (VAF>10%) ones, against 8% above 30%. With an older KRAS assay, detection fell from 41% (>50% tumour cells) to 27% (20-50%) to 0% (<20%). A Delphi consensus requires a 'false negative cannot be excluded' warning on wild-type results from samples below the assay's neoplastic-cell threshold, and one clinical-sequencing paper recommends judging purity from the mutant allele fraction and copy-number changes in the specimen itself. A further colorectal paper has a figure titled 'Threshold of tumour purity for mutation calling' but the fetch cut off before the value. Suggested test for the teams (my recommendation from these sources, not a quoted standard): estimate purity per sample as about twice the highest or truncal (APC/TP53/KRAS) VAF from the read counts, compare its distribution between right and left, and rerun the gene tests excluding samples below 20% and below 30%. Second part: the web did not establish that post-treatment rectal primaries have systematically lower tumour content. One 17-patient pre/post chemoradiation exome study found treatment did not change the distribution of established mutations; it cites 9-20% complete pathological response, which makes lower residual tumour plausible but gives no purity figures. Biopsies were not shown to be worse: paired biopsy-vs-resection sequencing found all but 3.7% of resection mutations in the biopsy, and biopsy vs surgical material did not change KRAS detection. So the purity imbalance has to be tested in the data, not assumed. Confidence is medium for the thresholds and low for the post-treatment rectal and biopsy part. HOW SURE: medium. SOURCES: https://www.jmdjournal.org/article/S1525-1578(15)00045-8/fulltext, https://ascopubs.org/doi/pdfdirect/10.1200/JCO.2022.40.16_suppl.e15557, https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC10154864/, https://doi.org/10.1200/jco.2010.28.15_suppl.3571, https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC6851675/, https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC6887630/, https://europepmc.org/article/MED/30741375, https://aacrjournals.org/clincancerres/article/25/18/5561/264501/Integrative-Molecular-Characterization-of.

text: FINDING FROM THE LAB'S LIBRARY, asked for by the director. QUESTION: In comparisons of mutation frequency between clinical groups using tumour-normal targeted panel sequencing, what is the standard way to guard against false wild-type calls from low tumour purity (for example a minimum tumour-content or variant-allele-fraction-based purity threshold), and are post-treatment rectal primaries or small biopsies known to have systematically lower tumour content? ANSWER: Not fully settled: the web gives no single universal cut-off, but 20% and 30% tumour purity are the defensible thresholds for a sensitivity analysis. What I read: MSK-IMPACT's validated detection limit is about 2% variant allele fraction for hotspot and 5% for non-hotspot mutations (so a clonal heterozygous non-hotspot mutation needs roughly 10% purity; that conversion is my arithmetic, VAF = purity/2). In a paired colorectal study on a 425-gene panel, below 30% purity 86% of the missed mutations were high-frequency (VAF>10%) ones, against 8% above 30%. With an older KRAS assay, detection fell from 41% (>50% tumour cells) to 27% (20-50%) to 0% (<20%). A Delphi consensus requires a 'false negative cannot be excluded' warning on wild-type results from samples below the assay's neoplastic-cell threshold, and one clinical-sequencing paper recommends judging purity from the mutant allele fraction and copy-number changes in the specimen itself. A further colorectal paper has a figure titled 'Threshold of tumour purity for mutation calling' but the fetch cut off before the value. Suggested test for the teams (my recommendation from these sources, not a quoted standard): estimate purity per sample as about twice the highest or truncal (APC/TP53/KRAS) VAF from the read counts, compare its distribution between right and left, and rerun the gene tests excluding samples below 20% and below 30%. Second part: the web did not establish that post-treatment rectal primaries have systematically lower tumour content. One 17-patient pre/post chemoradiation exome study found treatment did not change the distribution of established mutations; it cites 9-20% complete pathological response, which makes lower residual tumour plausible but gives no purity figures. Biopsies were not shown to be worse: paired biopsy-vs-resection sequencing found all but 3.7% of resection mutations in the biopsy, and biopsy vs surgical material did not change KRAS detection. So the purity imbalance has to be tested in the data, not assumed. Confidence is medium for the thresholds and low for the post-treatment rectal and biopsy part. HOW SURE: medium. label: FINDING
text: FINDING: The web does not settle what the 'LST' column in this clinical table means; no page read defines an integer per-patient clinical quantity abbreviated LST. Two readings exist. (a) Genomic scar: Large-scale State Transitions = chromosomal breaks between adjacent segments >10 Mb after filtering alterations <3 Mb (Popova 2012), a breakpoint COUNT used for HRD; it is not an LOH measure, and in TCGA the number of LSTs and telomeric-AI events rises with the number of whole-genome doublings while the number of LOH events falls, so LST and LOH move in opposite directions with WGD. (b) Clinical: in colorectal literature LST = laterally spreading tumour, an endoscopic lesion type (non-polypoid lesion >10 mm), which is a category, not a count. An LST-like count CAN be computed without allele-specific data: shallowHRD counts 'Large-scale Genomic Alterations (LGAs), evaluated in a similar way to LSTs but independent of the ploidy, with no reference to an absolute copy number' from read-depth ratio segments, but it is built and validated for genome-wide shallow WGS (>0.3x, 20-60 kb windows), not for targeted-panel segments; no source read validates it on panel seg files. Either way LST must not be used as fraction LOH. Teams can discriminate the readings by the column's range (genomic LST in chromosomally unstable tumours usually runs to tens; values confined to 0-3 point away from a scar count) and by whether it tracks seg-file breakpoint counts. QUESTION: What can 'LST' denote as a small non-negative integer per patient in a metastatic solid-tumour clinical table, and can large-scale state transitions be computed from targeted-panel total-copy-number segments without allele-specific data?
