label: FINDING
text: FINDING: In the cBioPortal file format, allele-specific copy number (ASCN) lives in exactly two documented places. (1) data_mutations.txt, as namespace columns that only load if the mutation meta file has 'namespaces: ascn': ASCN.ASCN_METHOD (e.g. FACETS), ASCN.CCF_EXPECTED_COPIES, ASCN.CCF_EXPECTED_COPIES_UPPER, ASCN.EXPECTED_ALT_COPIES, ASCN.CLONAL, ASCN.TOTAL_COPY_NUMBER, ASCN.MINOR_COPY_NUMBER, ASCN.ASCN_INTEGER_COPY_NUMBER (all eight required once the namespace is declared). These are per-mutation, so they give allelic state only at mutated loci. (2) data_clinical_sample.txt, attribute ASCN_WGD with values 'WGD' / 'no WGD'. The format defines NO standard slot for genome-wide allele-specific segments or for fraction LOH, purity or ploidy: the SEG file is fixed at ID, chrom, loc.start, loc.end, num.mark, seg.mean; discrete CNA is gene-level -2..2; arm-level CNA is a Generic Assay with only Loss/Gain/Unchanged; FRACTION_GENOME_ALTERED and MUTATION_COUNT are auto-computed by the portal and must not be in the files; MAF Mutation_Status='LOH' rows are not loaded. Fraction LOH, purity, ploidy, FACETS tcn/lcn would therefore appear only as study-specific custom clinical columns or extra seg columns with non-standard names. Systematic absence check: (i) no MAF column starts with 'ASCN.'; (ii) no ASCN_WGD in the sample table; (iii) seg file has exactly the six standard columns (no tcn, lcn, tcn.em, lcn.em, cf); (iv) case-insensitive header scan of both clinical tables for LOH, PURITY, PLOIDY, WGD, DOUBL, FACETS, TCN, LCN, MCN, MINOR, ALLEL, CCF, CLONAL, HRD, TAI; (v) no generic-assay file among the supplied files. QUESTION: Which cBioPortal study files and columns conventionally carry allele-specific copy-number results, and what are their standard names? SOURCE: https://github.com/cBioPortal/cbioportal/blob/master/docs/File-Formats.md ; https://github.com/mskcc/facets-suite

label: FINDING
text: FINDING: No validated method was found for estimating genome-wide fraction LOH from total-copy-number log-ratio segments alone, and no source read reports a concordance figure between a losses-only fraction and allele-specific fraction LOH; the web does not supply a number that would license the substitution. What the sources do establish argues against it. FACETS paper: copy-neutral LOH is 'not detectable by analyzing total copy number alone' and segmenting total read count 'will inevitably miss' it. TCGA allele-specific reanalysis (4,950 tumours): 9% of apparent copy-number wild-type calls and 7% of gain calls are actually LOH. MSK-IMPACT whole-genome-doubling study (9,692 patients, FACETS): WGD in 28.2% of advanced cancers and 36% of colorectal cancers (exclusively microsatellite-stable), median ploidy 3.3 vs 2.1; about 70% of arm/chromosome-length single-copy losses in WGD tumours arose AFTER doubling (total 3, major 2, minor 1), i.e. they are losses relative to ploidy that retain heterozygosity and are not LOH, while true LOH segments (total 2, major 2) can look only mildly lost or near-neutral. WGD is associated with TP53 mutation, so the proxy's error differs between the TP53-mutant and wild-type groups. Conclusion: a copy-loss fraction is a different variable from fraction LOH and should stay out of the label. QUESTION: Is there a validated method for estimating genome-wide fraction LOH from total-copy-number log-ratio segments alone, and how well does a losses-only fraction agree with allele-specific fraction LOH in tumours with frequent whole-genome doubling? SOURCE: https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC5027494/ ; https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC6072608/ ; https://www.cell.com/cell-systems/fulltext/S2405-4712(21)00383-5 ; https://doi.org/10.1200/po.22.00555

label: FINDING
text: FINDING: Ensembl VEP defines upstream_gene_variant as 'a sequence variant located 5' of a gene' (SO:0001631, IMPACT MODIFIER) and assigns it per transcript when the variant lies outside that transcript but within --distance bp of it on its 5' side; the default is 5000 bp, measured to the transcript's 5' end (the annotated transcription start, not the CDS start), and vcf2maf.pl does not change --distance. So an upstream_gene_variant entry for a second transcript proves only 'within 5 kb upstream of that transcript's annotated start', not 'in the promoter'; the DISTANCE column in the MAF is for the picked effect only and all_effects carries no distance, so the offset to the second transcript's start must be computed from coordinates. vcf2maf does NOT report the most severe effect across transcripts of a gene: it sorts all effects by biotype priority, then severity, then transcript length, takes the gene of the top-ranked effect, and then reports the effect on that gene's --custom-enst isoform if one is listed, otherwise on its VEP CANONICAL=YES isoform (falling back to the worst effect only if neither exists). Hence a variant that is missense in the canonical/override transcript and upstream of a shorter transcript is written as Missense_Mutation with the upstream entry visible only in all_effects; it becomes 5'Flank only when the canonical/override transcript itself starts downstream of the variant (even if a non-canonical transcript makes it missense). The label therefore reflects which isoform is flagged canonical, not biology. QUESTION: In Ensembl VEP how is upstream_gene_variant defined and what is the default distance, and how does vcf2maf choose the single effect that sets Variant_Classification (5'Flank versus Missense_Mutation) when a variant is coding in one transcript and upstream of another of the same gene? SOURCE: https://www.ensembl.org/info/genome/variation/prediction/predicted_data.html ; https://www.ensembl.org/info/docs/tools/vep/script/vep_options.html ; https://www.ensembl.org/info/docs/tools/vep/vep_formats.html ; https://raw.githubusercontent.com/mskcc/vcf2maf/main/vcf2maf.pl

label: FINDING
text: FINDING: In vcf2maf.pl, when the VCF has no usable normal genotype the code sets Match_Norm_Seq_Allele1 and Match_Norm_Seq_Allele2 both to the reference allele (source comment: 'If normal genotype is unavailable, then we'll assume it's ref/ref homozygous'), and when tumour genotype is missing it sets Tumor_Seq_Allele1 = reference and Tumor_Seq_Allele2 = variant ('assume it's ref/var heterozygous'). t_depth, t_ref_count, t_alt_count, n_depth, n_ref_count and n_alt_count are initialised as empty strings and filled only if FORMAT DP / AD exist for that sample, so without them they stay blank. Normal alleles equal to the reference together with blank depth/count columns are therefore tool defaults and are not evidence that a call is somatic; somatic status must rest on other grounds (study design/matched-normal information in the clinical table, Mutation_Status if populated, population allele frequency columns). This describes vcf2maf's current main branch; a study file produced by another converter may differ. QUESTION: When vcf2maf converts a VCF lacking per-sample genotype and read-depth fields, what does it write by default into Match_Norm_Seq_Allele1/2, t_depth, n_depth, t_ref_count and t_alt_count? SOURCE: https://raw.githubusercontent.com/mskcc/vcf2maf/main/vcf2maf.pl

label: FINDING
text: FINDING: There is no single promoter window, but published cancer non-coding screens anchor it on annotated transcription start sites (TSS) of ALL transcripts, not just the canonical one: PCAWG drivers (Rheinbay et al.) used 200 bp either side of every protein-coding transcript's TSS (GENCODE v19), collapsed per gene, with the global set of CDS and splice-site bases SUBTRACTED, and 5'UTR as a separate element (5'UTR minus CDS); Weinhold et al. 2014 used 2000 bp upstream to 200 bp downstream of all TSSs with ORFs (plus 5 bp) removed and 5'UTR tested separately; Fredriksson et al. 2017 (melanoma promoter hotspots) used +/-500 bp of the nearest annotated TSS with no CDS exclusion stated; a 2024 preprint used -1000 to +500 bp of canonical-transcript TSSs and called that more inclusive than earlier work. So 5'UTR bases a few hundred bp downstream of a TSS are routinely inside 'promoter' windows (PCAWG reports 'promoter and/or 5'UTR' hits), but the two large systematic screens explicitly exclude any base that is coding in any annotated transcript, so a variant inside a longer isoform's annotated CDS is classed as coding there even if it is within 200 bp of a shorter isoform's TSS; under a purely positional window (e.g. +/-500 bp) the same variant counts as promoter. The web does not give one convention for the alternative-isoform case: calling such variants promoter mutations is defensible only if the shorter isoform's start is the supported one. Annotation sets flag the supported start this way: GENCODE tags upstream_ATG ('an upstream ATG exists when a downstream ATG is better supported'), downstream_ATG ('an upstream ATG is used where a downstream ATG seems more evolutionary conserved'), cds_start_NF, non_ATG_start, RP_supported_TIS (ribosome-profiling support), CAGE_supported_TSS, CCDS, appris_principal, basic, MANE_Select and Ensembl_canonical; MANE Select / RefSeq Select / Ensembl canonical are chosen from PhyloCSF conservation of the CDS, RNA-seq and CAGE expression at the TSS, APPRIS principal and UniProt/Swiss-Prot canonical concordance and length (Ensembl disqualifies transcripts whose CDS is 75% or less of the longest). MANE is defined on GRCh38, so on a GRCh37 file check the transcript's status in current MANE/RefSeq Select rather than trusting the old CANONICAL flag. QUESTION: How is a gene's promoter delimited relative to the TSS in cancer studies of recurrent non-coding mutations, are variants in a 5'UTR or in a longer isoform's CDS just upstream of a shorter isoform's start conventionally called promoter mutations, and how do annotation sets mark the supported translation start? SOURCE: https://www.biorxiv.org/content/10.1101/237313v1.full ; https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC4217527/ ; https://journals.plos.org/plosgenetics/article?id=10.1371%2Fjournal.pgen.1006773 ; https://www.biorxiv.org/content/10.1101/2024.06.03.597231v1.full ; https://www.gencodegenes.org/pages/tags.html ; https://www.ensembl.org/info/genome/genebuild/canonical.html ; https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/refseq/MANE/ ; https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/refseq/refseq_select/

label: FINDING
text: FINDING: No conventional prevalence floor was found: none of the sources read defines 'frequently mutated/altered' by a percentage of tumours, and the web does not settle a numeric cutoff. Large cohort papers tie gene-level claims to statistical excess over background, and report prevalence only as a description. Lawrence et al. 2014 (4,742 tumours, 21 types) define candidate cancer genes as genes with somatic point mutations 'at a statistically significant rate or pattern' (MutSig, FDR q<=0.1) and state that 'the mere presence of somatic mutations is insufficient to implicate a gene', because 93% of all genes carried mutations in at least five samples. The same paper uses prevalence bands descriptively: >20% of tumours is 'a high proportion', 2-20% is 'intermediate frequency', and most cancer genes are in the 2-20% band or lower; half of its significant gene-by-tumour-type pairs involved <=6.1% of patients and a quarter <=3.1%. So single-digit-percent genes are routinely reported as significantly/recurrently mutated, but only when the excess over background is significant; prevalence alone is not the criterion. Conversely, Lawrence et al. 2013 show that 'mutated at a significant frequency' under a naive background gave 450 genes in 178 lung squamous tumours, many implausible (olfactory receptors, TTN, MUC16), and the FLAGS paper uses 'frequently mutated genes' purely descriptively for genes that often carry variants because they are long. Two practical points from the same sources: (a) power is low in small cohorts - Lawrence 2014 found sample sizes of that study inadequate to detect genes mutated at 5% above background in 17 of 21 tumour types under an exome-wide threshold (p<=0.1/20,000), so non-significance in about 100 tumours is not evidence of no excess; (b) both Lawrence 2014 and Martincorena 2017 use restricted hypothesis testing on a pre-specified gene list to regain power, so testing only the two named genes without exome-wide correction is an accepted practice. (confidence: medium). QUESTION: In cancer-genomics literature, when a gene is described as 'frequently altered' or 'frequently mutated' in a tumour type, is there a conventional prevalence floor (a percentage of tumours), or is the term normally tied to statistical significance above background mutation rate (for example MutSigCV or dNdScv q-values)? How do large cohort papers use the phrase for genes mutated in a single-digit percentage of tumours. SOURCE: https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC4048962/ ; https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC3919509/ ; https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC5720395/ ; https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC4267152/.

label: FINDING
text: FINDING: Definition: dN/dS for somatic data is the ratio of non-synonymous to synonymous mutations normalised by what is expected neutrally given the gene's sequence composition and the mutation spectrum (Martincorena 2017 use a 192-rate trinucleotide, strand-aware Poisson model and separate ratios for missense, nonsense and essential-splice mutations); synonymous mutations are assumed neutral and serve as the background, dN/dS=1 is neutrality, and a gene dN/dS of 10 means about 90% of its non-synonymous mutations are drivers. Simpler versions test observed non-silent counts with a binomial against (silent rate x neutral NS:S ratio x length) (Krauthammer-group paper, PMC3989533). Neutral expectation: about 3 non-silent to 1 silent. Greenman 2006 estimate the null silent fraction as 0.246 ('silent:nonsilent ratio in the absence of selection will typically be 1:3') and warn that spectrum or composition can change it substantially; Lawrence 2014 use 'the 3:1 typical ratio of non-silent to silent mutations' in their power model, and their exome-wide counts (540,831 missense + 46,264 nonsense + 33,637 splice vs 207,144 synonymous) give 3.0:1 (missense:silent 2.6:1). The ratio is spectrum-dependent: UV C>T at dipyrimidines gives a mean per-gene NS:S of 1.67 and 1.93 overall in sun-exposed melanoma, so the cohort's own exome-wide non-silent:silent ratio (ideally excluding known drivers) should be used as the neutral value rather than a fixed 3. Genome-wide dN/dS in cancer is close to 1, and Tokheim 2016 note the non-silent:silent ratio varies far less across tumours than mutation rate does. Power: a gene-only (local) test is weak. Martincorena 2017 say the per-gene-rate model (dNdSloc) 'lacks statistical power to detect positively selected genes in smaller datasets'; the dNdScv vignette says it is 'typically only powered in very large datasets' (in 196 simulated breast exomes it detected only ARID1A); Lawrence 2013 say silent substitutions alone are too sparse to correct rates gene-by-gene. No source read gives a minimum count; by the library's own arithmetic (one-sided binomial against a 25% silent fraction, not from a source) a gene needs at least 11 mutations with 0 silent, 18 with 1 silent, 23 with 2 silent to reach p<0.05, so a gene with a handful of mutations cannot be tested this way and the result should be reported as uninformative, not as evidence of neutrality. dNdScv input: a 5-column table (sampleID, chr, pos, ref, alt) of independent somatic events, substitutions and indels, which must include the synonymous mutations because the background is fitted on them; it needs no coverage, depth or allele counts for exome/genome data (the only coverage argument, dc, is for duplex sequencing). Reference annotation and covariates for GRCh37/hg19 ship with the R package (refdb='hg19' default). Defaults: samples with more than 3,000 coding mutations are dropped and at most 3 mutations per gene per sample are kept (set to Inf to disable); the vignette warns that theta<1 signals a poorly fitting dataset. So it can run on a MAF-derived table without coverage or allele counts provided the R package is installed locally; whether the package is available offline in the teams' environment was not checked. (confidence: high). QUESTION: How is a gene-level non-silent to silent (dN/dS-type) comparison defined for somatic mutation data, what non-silent:silent ratio is expected under neutrality in an exome given typical mutation spectra, and how many mutations per gene are needed for such a test to have useful power? What does dNdScv require as input and can it run on a mutation table without coverage or allele counts. SOURCE: https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC5720395/ ; https://github.com/im3sanger/dndscv/blob/master/vignettes/dNdScv.Rmd ; https://github.com/im3sanger/dndscv/blob/master/man/dndscv.Rd ; https://github.com/im3sanger/dndscv ; https://doi.org/10.1534/genetics.105.044677 ; https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC4048962/ ; https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC3989533/ ; https://www.pnas.org/doi/full/10.1073/pnas.1616440113.

label: FINDING
text: FINDING: Recommended practice in the sources read: (1) estimate the background per gene AND per patient - MutSigCV uses patient-specific mutation frequency and spectrum plus gene-specific rates from expression level and replication time, estimating a background 'for each gene-patient-category combination' from silent and flanking non-coding mutations and pooling genes with similar covariates because per-gene silent counts are too sparse; (2) model the remaining gene-to-gene rate variation as overdispersion - dNdScv fits a negative-binomial (Gamma-Poisson) regression of synonymous counts on 20 covariates and combines it with the gene's own synonymous count; (3) limit or separate hypermutators - dNdScv by default removes samples with more than 3,000 coding mutations and caps mutations per gene per sample at 3, and Martincorena 2017 restrict driver-number analyses to tumours with fewer than 500 coding mutations because 'even very small inaccuracies in these models can lead to considerable biases in samples with large numbers of mutations'; they find dN/dS very close to 1 in APOBEC, tobacco and mismatch-repair hypermutators, i.e. the great majority of coding mutations in such tumours are passengers; (4) use ratiometric evidence (non-silent:silent ratio, inactivating fraction, clustering), which Tokheim 2016 show is far less sensitive to unexplained rate variability than rate-based tests. The term 'Poisson-binomial' does not appear in the sources read; the nearest documented form is Lawrence 2014's per-patient probability of at least one non-silent hit, p0 = 1-(1-mu*f_g)^(L*3/4), tested binomially across patients, which becomes a Poisson-binomial when mu is made patient-specific (library's inference). Failure modes of a uniform per-base rate x coding length: the direction is the opposite of the example in the question. Lawrence 2013 show a uniform rate UNDER-predicts background for long, low-expressed, late-replicating genes (olfactory receptors, TTN, MUC16, RYR2/3, CSMD3), producing false positives even though length was already accounted for; mutation rate differs about 2.9-fold between extreme expression percentiles and about 2.9-fold between latest and earliest replication percentiles, and the gene-specific rate factor at the 90th percentile is 3.9x the median (Lawrence 2014). It correspondingly OVER-predicts for highly expressed, early-replicating genes (known cancer genes trend this way), giving false negatives ('false-negative results if the baseline frequency is overestimated'). The problem grows with sample size and with tumour mutation rate; in a neutral melanoma simulation the uniform dN/dS model called 368 genes significant at q<0.05 versus none for the local or covariate models; Tokheim 2016 show unexplained rate variability of CV 0.05-0.2 sharply raises false positives at high background rates, and that MutSigCV p-values are conservative in the P<=0.05 range. Pooling burden across patients is also unsafe: Lawrence 2013 state patient heterogeneity can produce both false positives and false negatives. Implication for trust: an excess-over-background result from a burden x length null is at best order-of-magnitude (a factor of roughly 3-4 either way from unmodelled gene-level rate variation alone); for a gene whose hits sit mainly in high-burden tumours, check whether the excess survives after dropping those tumours or giving each tumour its own rate, and whether the gene's own non-silent:silent ratio and truncating fraction depart from the cohort-wide values; if not, the mutations are consistent with passengers. (confidence: medium). QUESTION: In whole-exome somatic mutation studies, what approaches are recommended for judging whether a gene's mutations in high-mutation-burden tumours are passengers (per-sample burden-aware null models such as Poisson-binomial, covariate-adjusted background rates, exclusion of hypermutated samples), and what are the known failure modes of a uniform per-base rate scaled by coding length (for example over-prediction for very long or late-replicating genes). SOURCE: https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC3919509/ ; https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC4048962/ ; https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC5720395/ ; https://github.com/im3sanger/dndscv/blob/master/man/dndscv.Rd ; https://www.pnas.org/doi/full/10.1073/pnas.1616440113.

label: FINDING
text: FINDING: In FFPE lymphoma tissue, capture-based DNA sequencing misses a large share of FISH-positive rearrangements: in 233 FFPE DLBCLs a 481-gene capture panel had sensitivity versus break-apart FISH of 50 percent for MYC, 80 percent for BCL2 and 69 percent for BCL6 (misses were breakpoints outside the probe-covered region, mostly intergenic); in 34 FFPE high-grade B-cell lymphomas DNA sequencing found 6 of 12 MYC, 10 of 10 BCL2 and 13 of 18 BCL6 rearrangements and missed 5 of 12 FISH-defined MYC/BCL2 double-hit cases; a breakpoint-targeted capture design reached 94 percent concordance. FFPE processing fragments DNA, which is stated to compromise sequencing-based rearrangement analysis, and breakpoints flanked by non-unique sequence (common at IG loci) are also missed. The web pages read gave NO head-to-head FFPE-versus-frozen sensitivity figure and did NOT document how often research cohorts supplement FFPE sequencing calls with FISH; the sources say only that FISH remains the gold standard, that sequencing should not replace it, and that the two are complementary. Exome capture (coding exons only) should be no better than these dedicated panels (inference, not sourced). Consequence: SV-negative means not detected, the under-calling is not equal across tissue types, so SV frequencies and double-hit flags should be compared within one tissue type or cohort (or stratified), not pooled across subsets with different FFPE/frozen mix; this corrects the earlier note that the bias is roughly equal across subsets. QUESTION: How sensitive is exome or targeted-capture sequencing for IGH-BCL2, MYC and BCL6 rearrangements in FFPE lymphoma tissue compared with frozen tissue and FISH, and is it usual to supplement sequencing calls with FISH in the FFPE part of a cohort? text: FINDING: Guidance on time-to-event data says the follow-up end (censoring) date must be defined separately for each endpoint: OS is censored at the date last known alive, PFS at the last date the patient was known progression-free (last disease assessment); the two dates legitimately differ, and normally censored PFS is shorter than or equal to censored OS (using last-known-alive as the PFS censor date is named as a common mistake that inflates PFS). A censored PFS time LONGER than a censored OS time is therefore not explained by the usual rule and, under one time origin, is logically inconsistent (progression-free at t implies alive at t); it points to the two times coming from different date sources, data locks or time origins in that cohort. The pages read do not discuss this exact pattern and no lymphoma-specific source was found, so the cause is an inference, not a sourced fact. Accepted handling per the guidance: analyse each endpoint on its own time and status (do not drop or silently edit the records), check whether the pattern is confined to one cohort because differential censoring between groups can bias Kaplan-Meier and Cox results, and run sensitivity analyses with alternative censoring dates (for example cap PFS at the OS time, or extend OS to the PFS time since the patient was then alive, or stratify by or exclude that cohort) and report whether the log-rank result changes; because these patients are censored on both endpoints the changes alter time at risk, not event counts. QUESTION: What explains recorded PFS time longer than OS time in patients censored on both endpoints in lymphoma cohort data, and how should such records be handled in Kaplan-Meier and Cox analyses? text: FINDING: OncoKB grades specific alterations, not any nonsilent mutation in a gene, and its actionable-genes list (read 2026-11-15) has NO therapeutic level (1 to 4, R1, R2) for EZH2, CREBBP, BCL2, STAT3 or SGK1 in DLBCL or any other B-cell lymphoma; tazemetostat and venetoclax do not appear on the page, and SGK1 and linker histone H1 genes are not listed at all. EZH2 and CREBBP 'Oncogenic Mutations' in DLBCL NOS and follicular lymphoma and the IGH::BCL2 fusion appear only in the diagnostic tiers (by row position Dx3 for EZH2/CREBBP and IGH::BCL2 in DLBCL, Dx2 for IGH::BCL2 in follicular lymphoma; the tier is inferred from row order). STAT3 is listed only for T-cell large granular lymphocytic leukemia (diagnostic). BRAF therapeutic entries are allele-specific (V600E or V600: hairy cell leukemia with vemurafenib, histiocytoses, solid tumours) with none for DLBCL or follicular lymphoma. For EZH2 OncoKB curates Y646C/F/H/N/S, A682G, A692V and a few other SET-domain variants as oncogenic and other missense variants (R207Q, R213H, R502Q, K515R, P577L) as inconclusive. BCL2 mutations are reported as venetoclax RESISTANCE markers, not sensitivity markers; CREBBP has only low-level evidence (HAT-domain mutations, CIViC). H1 mutations are loss-of-function tumour-suppressor drivers with no drug attached. In DLBCL the genetic subtypes are described as suggesting therapeutic vulnerabilities for future drug development, not established targets. text: FINDING: CORRECTION to fact sl-biodsa-test-da9df46295e5 (one clause was wrong; its conclusion is unchanged). In a whole-genome-doubled tumour of ploidy about 3.3, a segment with total copy 2 / major 2 / minor 0 is true LOH and reads as a CLEAR relative loss (log2(2/3.3) is about -0.7 at full purity), not as near-neutral. FINDING: The web does not settle how a one-row-per-gene phospho value in a portal-format file was computed, and nothing read says it is protein-normalised. The portal's documented convention for mass-spec phospho data is one row per SITE (named GENE|GENE_

, multi-site peptides chained with underscores), and its CPTAC import script only cleans rows, renames, and averages duplicate rows; it has no step that subtracts or divides by protein abundance. A row per gene listing many sites is therefore a non-standard collapse whose rule (mean, median, sum, best site) is undocumented in what could be opened; a phosphoproteomics review says many tools 'simply collapse' sites into one protein phosphorylation value (median site log-ratio is the rule quoted for one multi-omics analysis, seen only as a search excerpt) and warns this mixes sites with different function. TMT phospho reports are sample-median-centred by default, not protein-corrected. Working assumption: the gene-level value is a mean or median over whichever sites were quantified and is NOT protein-normalised, so 'phospho minus protein' is a legitimate but coarse 'average net phosphorylation per molecule across measured sites', not CDK4/6-site occupancy; the set of sites feeding the average may differ between TMT plexes. Teams can test the normalisation question in the data: a strong positive correlation of the phospho row with the protein row across samples means it is not protein-normalised; near-zero or negative would suggest it already is. Confidence: medium for 'not protein-normalised', low for the exact collapse statistic. QUESTION: In portal-format phosphoproteomic tables with one row per gene concatenating many phosphosites, how is the gene-level value computed from site log-ratios and is it already normalised to parent protein abundance? text: FINDING: Non-malignant stromal, endothelial and immune cells in tumour tissue do carry RB1 (pathology studies use them as the internal positive control when tumour cells are RB-negative, and exclude cases lacking it), so a tumour whose cancer cells have lost RB1 never reads zero in bulk: admixture RAISES its measured RB1 toward the stromal level, and low purity therefore hides RB loss. How much RB protein quiescent stroma holds relative to proliferating RB-intact carcinoma cells is NOT settled by the sources read (a review says only that RB levels 'fluctuate as a function of cellular proliferation'); if stroma holds less, low purity LOWERS bulk RB1 in an RB-intact tumour. So purity compresses both kinds of tumour toward the stromal level rather than biasing in one direction: an RB1-low value in a low-purity sample cannot be produced by admixture if the cancer cells lost RB (admixture works against it, so the call is conservative), but it could be produced by dilution of an RB-intact tumour if stroma is RB-poor. Decide empirically: among RB1-wild-type tumours regress RB1 protein on purity (positive slope means dilution lowers RB1 and a low-purity RB1-low call is suspect; flat or negative slope means purity cannot explain it); check whether the low-purity RB1-low sample sits below what its purity predicts; and look for the RB-loss signature that stroma cannot mimic (high CDKN2A/p16 RNA or protein, high E2F targets, RB1 truncating mutation). Do not drop the sample on purity alone. Confidence: medium (stromal RB expression well supported; direction for RB-intact tumours is reasoning, not a sourced measurement). QUESTION: How does RB1 protein in stromal and immune cells compare with proliferating carcinoma cells, and which way does low purity bias bulk RB1 protein in RB1-intact versus RB1-lost tumours? question: FINDING FROM THE LAB'S LIBRARY, asked for by the director. QUESTION: In cancer-genomics literature, when a gene is described as 'frequently altered' or 'frequently mutated' in a tumour type, is there a conventional prevalence floor (a percentage of tumours), or is the term normally tied to statistical significance above background mutation rate (for example MutSigCV or dNdScv q-values)? How do large cohort papers use the phrase for genes mutated in a single-digit percentage of tumours? ANSWER: No conventional prevalence floor was found: none of the sources read defines 'frequently mutated/altered' by a percentage of tumours, and the web does not settle a numeric cutoff. Large cohort papers tie gene-level claims to statistical excess over background, and report prevalence only as a description. Lawrence et al. 2014 (4,742 tumours, 21 types) define candidate cancer genes as genes with somatic point mutations 'at a statistically significant rate or pattern' (MutSig, FDR q<=0.1) and state that 'the mere presence of somatic mutations is insufficient to implicate a gene', because 93% of all genes carried mutations in at least five samples. The same paper uses prevalence bands descriptively: >20% of tumours is 'a high proportion', 2-20% is 'intermediate frequency', and most cancer genes are in the 2-20% band or lower; half of its significant gene-by-tumour-type pairs involved <=6.1% of patients and a quarter <=3.1%. So single-digit-percent genes are routinely reported as significantly/recurrently mutated, but only when the excess over background is significant; prevalence alone is not the criterion. Conversely, Lawrence et al. 2013 show that 'mutated at a significant frequency' under a naive background gave 450 genes in 178 lung squamous tumours, many implausible (olfactory receptors, TTN, MUC16), and the FLAGS paper uses 'frequently mutated genes' purely descriptively for genes that often carry variants because they are long. Two practical points from the same sources: (a) power is low in small cohorts - Lawrence 2014 found sample sizes of that study inadequate to detect genes mutated at 5% above background in 17 of 21 tumour types under an exome-wide threshold (p<=0.1/20,000), so non-significance in about 100 tumours is not evidence of no excess; (b) both Lawrence 2014 and Martincorena 2017 use restricted hypothesis testing on a pre-specified gene list to regain power, so testing only the two named genes without exome-wide correction is an accepted practice. HOW SURE: medium. SOURCES: https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC4048962/, https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC3919509/, https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC5720395/, https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC4267152/.

question: FINDING FROM THE LAB'S LIBRARY, asked for by the director. QUESTION: How is a gene-level non-silent to silent (dN/dS-type) comparison defined for somatic mutation data, what non-silent:silent ratio is expected under neutrality in an exome given typical mutation spectra, and how many mutations per gene are needed for such a test to have useful power? What does dNdScv require as input and can it run on a mutation table without coverage or allele counts? ANSWER: Definition: dN/dS for somatic data is the ratio of non-synonymous to synonymous mutations normalised by what is expected neutrally given the gene's sequence composition and the mutation spectrum (Martincorena 2017 use a 192-rate trinucleotide, strand-aware Poisson model and separate ratios for missense, nonsense and essential-splice mutations); synonymous mutations are assumed neutral and serve as the background, dN/dS=1 is neutrality, and a gene dN/dS of 10 means about 90% of its non-synonymous mutations are drivers. Simpler versions test observed non-silent counts with a binomial against (silent rate x neutral NS:S ratio x length) (Krauthammer-group paper, PMC3989533). Neutral expectation: about 3 non-silent to 1 silent. Greenman 2006 estimate the null silent fraction as 0.246 ('silent:nonsilent ratio in the absence of selection will typically be 1:3') and warn that spectrum or composition can change it substantially; Lawrence 2014 use 'the 3:1 typical ratio of non-silent to silent mutations' in their power model, and their exome-wide counts (540,831 missense + 46,264 nonsense + 33,637 splice vs 207,144 synonymous) give 3.0:1 (missense:silent 2.6:1). The ratio is spectrum-dependent: UV C>T at dipyrimidines gives a mean per-gene NS:S of 1.67 and 1.93 overall in sun-exposed melanoma, so the cohort's own exome-wide non-silent:silent ratio (ideally excluding known drivers) should be used as the neutral value rather than a fixed 3. Genome-wide dN/dS in cancer is close to 1, and Tokheim 2016 note the non-silent:silent ratio varies far less across tumours than mutation rate does. Power: a gene-only (local) test is weak. Martincorena 2017 say the per-gene-rate model (dNdSloc) 'lacks statistical power to detect positively selected genes in smaller datasets'; the dNdScv vignette says it is 'typically only powered in very large datasets' (in 196 simulated breast exomes it detected only ARID1A); Lawrence 2013 say silent substitutions alone are too sparse to correct rates gene-by-gene. No source read gives a minimum count; by the library's own arithmetic (one-sided binomial against a 25% silent fraction, not from a source) a gene needs at least 11 mutations with 0 silent, 18 with 1 silent, 23 with 2 silent to reach p<0.05, so a gene with a handful of mutations cannot be tested this way and the result should be reported as uninformative, not as evidence of neutrality. dNdScv input: a 5-column table (sampleID, chr, pos, ref, alt) of independent somatic events, substitutions and indels, which must include the synonymous mutations because the background is fitted on them; it needs no coverage, depth or allele counts for exome/genome data (the only coverage argument, dc, is for duplex sequencing). Reference annotation and covariates for GRCh37/hg19 ship with the R package (refdb='hg19' default). Defaults: samples with more than 3,000 coding mutations are dropped and at most 3 mutations per gene per sample are kept (set to Inf to disable); the vignette warns that theta<1 signals a poorly fitting dataset. So it can run on a MAF-derived table without coverage or allele counts provided the R package is installed locally; whether the package is available offline in the teams' environment was not checked. HOW SURE: high. SOURCES: https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC5720395/, https://github.com/im3sanger/dndscv/blob/master/vignettes/dNdScv.Rmd, https://github.com/im3sanger/dndscv/blob/master/man/dndscv.Rd, https://github.com/im3sanger/dndscv, https://doi.org/10.1534/genetics.105.044677, https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC4048962/, https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC3989533/, https://www.pnas.org/doi/full/10.1073/pnas.1616440113.

question: FINDING FROM THE LAB'S LIBRARY, asked for by the director. QUESTION: In whole-exome somatic mutation studies, what approaches are recommended for judging whether a gene's mutations in high-mutation-burden tumours are passengers (per-sample burden-aware null models such as Poisson-binomial, covariate-adjusted background rates, exclusion of hypermutated samples), and what are the known failure modes of a uniform per-base rate scaled by coding length (for example over-prediction for very long or late-replicating genes)? ANSWER: Recommended practice in the sources read: (1) estimate the background per gene AND per patient - MutSigCV uses patient-specific mutation frequency and spectrum plus gene-specific rates from expression level and replication time, estimating a background 'for each gene-patient-category combination' from silent and flanking non-coding mutations and pooling genes with similar covariates because per-gene silent counts are too sparse; (2) model the remaining gene-to-gene rate variation as overdispersion - dNdScv fits a negative-binomial (Gamma-Poisson) regression of synonymous counts on 20 covariates and combines it with the gene's own synonymous count; (3) limit or separate hypermutators - dNdScv by default removes samples with more than 3,000 coding mutations and caps mutations per gene per sample at 3, and Martincorena 2017 restrict driver-number analyses to tumours with fewer than 500 coding mutations because 'even very small inaccuracies in these models can lead to considerable biases in samples with large numbers of mutations'; they find dN/dS very close to 1 in APOBEC, tobacco and mismatch-repair hypermutators, i.e. the great majority of coding mutations in such tumours are passengers; (4) use ratiometric evidence (non-silent:silent ratio, inactivating fraction, clustering), which Tokheim 2016 show is far less sensitive to unexplained rate variability than rate-based tests. The term 'Poisson-binomial' does not appear in the sources read; the nearest documented form is Lawrence 2014's per-patient probability of at least one non-silent hit, p0 = 1-(1-mu*f_g)^(L*3/4), tested binomially across patients, which becomes a Poisson-binomial when mu is made patient-specific (library's inference). Failure modes of a uniform per-base rate x coding length: the direction is the opposite of the example in the question. Lawrence 2013 show a uniform rate UNDER-predicts background for long, low-expressed, late-replicating genes (olfactory receptors, TTN, MUC16, RYR2/3, CSMD3), producing false positives even though length was already accounted for; mutation rate differs about 2.9-fold between extreme expression percentiles and about 2.9-fold between latest and earliest replication percentiles, and the gene-specific rate factor at the 90th percentile is 3.9x the median (Lawrence 2014). It correspondingly OVER-predicts for highly expressed, early-replicating genes (known cancer genes trend this way), giving false negatives ('false-negative results if the baseline frequency is overestimated'). The problem grows with sample size and with tumour mutation rate; in a neutral melanoma simulation the uniform dN/dS model called 368 genes significant at q<0.05 versus none for the local or covariate models; Tokheim 2016 show unexplained rate variability of CV 0.05-0.2 sharply raises false positives at high background rates, and that MutSigCV p-values are conservative in the P<=0.05 range. Pooling burden across patients is also unsafe: Lawrence 2013 state patient heterogeneity can produce both false positives and false negatives. Implication for trust: an excess-over-background result from a burden x length null is at best order-of-magnitude (a factor of roughly 3-4 either way from unmodelled gene-level rate variation alone); for a gene whose hits sit mainly in high-burden tumours, check whether the excess survives after dropping those tumours or giving each tumour its own rate, and whether the gene's own non-silent:silent ratio and truncating fraction depart from the cohort-wide values; if not, the mutations are consistent with passengers. SOURCES: https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC3919509/, https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC4048962/, https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC5720395/, https://github.com/im3sanger/dndscv/blob/master/man/dndscv.Rd, https://www.pnas.org/doi/full/10.1073/pnas.1616440113.

question: FINDING FROM THE LAB'S LIBRARY, asked for by the director. QUESTION: In Ensembl VEP, how is the consequence 'upstream_gene_variant' defined (what distance from which transcript feature, and what is the default distance), and when a variant is coding in one transcript and upstream of another transcript of the same gene, how does vcf2maf choose the single effect that sets Variant_Classification (when does a row become 5'Flank rather than Missense_Mutation)? ANSWER: VEP: upstream_gene_variant is the Sequence Ontology term SO:0001631, 'a sequence variant located 5' of a gene', IMPACT MODIFIER. It is assigned per transcript. The --distance option is documented as the distance 'between a variant and a transcript for which Ensembl VEP will assign the upstream_gene_variant or downstream_gene_variant consequences', 'Default: 5000'; the consequences page says VEP by default includes upstream and downstream annotations for variants within 5 kb of a feature. So the entry means: the variant lies outside that transcript and within 5,000 bp on the 5' side of the transcript's annotated start (the transcript 5' end, not the CDS start). The output field DISTANCE is the 'shortest distance from variant to transcript'. The vcf2maf.pl VEP command line does not set --distance, so the 5 kb default applies. vcf2maf: it does not report the most severe effect across a gene's transcripts. It (1) sorts every transcript effect by transcript biotype priority, then consequence severity (missense_variant ranks 6, upstream_gene_variant 16), then transcript length; (2) takes the gene symbol of the top-ranked effect; (3) reports that gene's effect on a user-supplied --custom-enst isoform if one is listed, otherwise on the isoform VEP flags CANONICAL=YES; (4) falls back to the worst effect only if the gene has neither. Variant_Classification is then mapped from that one effect: missense_variant -> Missense_Mutation, upstream_gene_variant -> 5'Flank, 5_prime_UTR_variant -> 5'UTR. So a variant that is missense in the canonical (or override) transcript and upstream of a shorter transcript is written as Missense_Mutation, with the upstream entry appearing only in all_effects. The row becomes 5'Flank only when the canonical/override transcript itself begins downstream of the variant, even if a non-canonical transcript makes it missense. What the entry can prove: only that the variant is within 5 kb upstream of the second transcript's annotated start. It does not show promoter location by itself. The MAF's DISTANCE column belongs to the picked effect, and all_effects carries gene, consequence, protein change, transcript and RefSeq IDs but no distance, so the offset to the second transcript's start has to be computed from coordinates. The Missense label reflects which isoform is flagged canonical, not which start site is biologically used. Caveat: this describes vcf2maf's current main branch; the study file may have been produced by a different version or annotator. HOW SURE: high. SOURCES: https://www.ensembl.org/info/genome/variation/prediction/predicted_data.html, https://www.ensembl.org/info/docs/tools/vep/script/vep_options.html, https://www.ensembl.org/info/docs/tools/vep/vep_formats.html, https://raw.githubusercontent.com/mskcc/vcf2maf/main/vcf2maf.pl.

question: FINDING FROM THE LAB'S LIBRARY, asked for by the director. QUESTION: When vcf2maf converts a VCF that lacks per-sample genotype and read-depth fields, what does it write by default into Match_Norm_Seq_Allele1, Match_Norm_Seq_Allele2, t_depth, n_depth, t_ref_count and t_alt_count? ANSWER: Match_Norm_Seq_Allele1 and Match_Norm_Seq_Allele2 are both set to the reference allele; the source comment reads 'If normal genotype is unavailable, then we'll assume it's ref/ref homozygous', and they are overwritten only if the normal sample has a usable GT. Likewise Tumor_Seq_Allele1 = reference and Tumor_Seq_Allele2 = variant ('assume it's ref/var heterozygous'). All MAF fields start as empty strings; t_depth and n_depth are filled only from a per-sample DP, and t_ref_count/t_alt_count (and n_ref_count/n_alt_count) only from per-sample AD, so without those fields they stay blank. Consequence: normal alleles equal to the reference, alongside blank depth and count columns, are tool defaults and are not evidence that calls are somatic. The somatic-status check needs another basis, such as the study's matched-normal design in the clinical table, Mutation_Status if populated, or population allele-frequency columns. Caveat: read from vcf2maf's current main branch; a file made by another converter or version may fill missing values differently. HOW SURE: high. SOURCES: https://raw.githubusercontent.com/mskcc/vcf2maf/main/vcf2maf.pl.

question: FINDING FROM THE LAB'S LIBRARY, asked for by the director. QUESTION: In cancer-genomics studies of recurrent non-coding mutations, how is a gene's 'promoter' usually delimited relative to the transcription start site (typical window sizes upstream and downstream), and are variants that fall in a 5'UTR or inside the annotated coding sequence of a longer isoform, but just upstream of a shorter isoform's start, conventionally reported as promoter mutations? How do reference annotation sets indicate which of two alternative translation start sites is the supported one? ANSWER: Windows: there is no single standard. Those read: PCAWG driver analysis (Rheinbay et al., preprint methods) used 200 bp either side of every protein-coding transcript's TSS (GENCODE v19), collapsed per gene, with the global set of CDS and splice-site bases subtracted, and 5'UTR as a separate element (5'UTR minus CDS). Weinhold et al. 2014 used 2,000 bp upstream to 200 bp downstream of all TSSs, removed ORFs (extended 5 bp), and tested Ensembl-defined 5'UTRs separately. Fredriksson et al. 2017 (melanoma promoter hotspots) used +/-500 bp of the nearest annotated TSS (GENCODE 17) and states no CDS exclusion. A 2024 preprint used 1,000 bp upstream to 500 bp downstream of canonical-transcript TSSs and described that as more inclusive than earlier studies. Windows are usually anchored on the TSS of all annotated transcripts, not only the canonical one. 5'UTR: bases a few hundred bp downstream of a TSS fall inside these windows, so 5'UTR variants near the TSS are routinely counted as promoter mutations; PCAWG reports 'promoter and/or 5'UTR' hits. Coding sequence of a longer isoform: the web does not settle this with one convention. The two large systematic screens (PCAWG, Weinhold) explicitly remove any base that is coding in any annotated transcript from promoter elements, so by their rules a variant inside the longer isoform's annotated CDS is a coding variant even if it lies within 200 bp of a shorter isoform's TSS. Under a purely positional window (Fredriksson's +/-500 bp) the same variant counts as a promoter-region mutation. I did not find a source stating a rule for this alternative-isoform case specifically. Calling such variants promoter mutations is therefore defensible only if the shorter isoform's start is the supported one; otherwise the systematic-screen convention classes them as coding. Which start is supported: GENCODE transcript tags include upstream_ATG ('an upstream ATG exists when a downstream ATG is better supported'), downstream_ATG ('an upstream ATG is used where a downstream ATG seems more evolutionary conserved'), cds_start_NF ('the coding region start could not be confirmed'), non_ATG_start, RP_supported_TIS (translation initiation site supported by ribosome profiling), CAGE_supported_TSS, CCDS, appris_principal, basic, MANE_Select and Ensembl_canonical. MANE Select is one transcript per locus, identical in 5'UTR, CDS and splicing between RefSeq and Ensembl, with the TSS set from FANTOM CAGE data and start codons revised when evidence warrants (the page gives FNDC5 as an example). Ensembl canonical is scored on PhyloCSF conservation of the CDS, RNA-seq intron and CAGE expression, agreement with APPRIS principal and UniProt canonical isoforms, and CDS length, disqualifying transcripts whose CDS is 75% or less of the longest. RefSeq Select uses curator picks, prior clinical use, CDS conservation, expression, Swiss-Prot match, CAGE and protein length. MANE is defined on GRCh38, with mappings to GRCh37. Not verified from a page I read: older GRCh37 VEP caches may assign CANONICAL by an earlier, more length-based rule, so the CANONICAL flag in an older GRCh37 MAF may not reflect the currently supported start; checking the transcript's present MANE Select / RefSeq Select status would be the safer test. HOW SURE: medium. SOURCES: https://www.biorxiv.org/content/10.1101/237313v1.full, https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC4217527/, https://journals.plos.org/plosgenetics/article?id=10.1371%2Fjournal.pgen.1006773, https://www.biorxiv.org/content/10.1101/2024.06.03.597231v1.full, https://www.nature.com/articles/s41586-020-1965-x, https://www.gencodegenes.org/pages/tags.html, https://www.ensembl.org/info/genome/genebuild/canonical.html, https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/refseq/MANE/, https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/refseq/refseq_select/.

question: FINDING FROM THE LAB'S LIBRARY, asked for by the director. QUESTION: In clinical annotation tables of solid-tumour sequencing cohorts with metastatic disease, what can the abbreviation 'LST' denote when it is a small non-negative integer per patient: the genomic-scar count 'large-scale state transitions', or a clinical quantity? No page I read defines an integer per-patient clinical quantity abbreviated LST. Two readings exist. (a) Genomic scar: Large-scale State Transitions, a count of chromosomal breaks between adjacent segments >10 Mb after filtering alterations <3 Mb (Popova 2012), used for HRD scoring. It is a breakpoint count, not an LOH measure: in TCGA the number of LSTs and telomeric-allelic-imbalance events rises with the number of whole-genome doublings while the number of LOH events falls. question: FINDING FROM THE LAB'S LIBRARY, asked for by the director. QUESTION: In the cBioPortal study file format, which files and columns conventionally carry allele-specific copy-number results (for example FACETS-derived total and minor copy number, mutation-level ASCN annotation columns, or sample-level attributes for fraction LOH, purity, ploidy and genome doubling), and what are their standard names? ANSWER: The cBioPortal file-format specification documents allele-specific copy number (ASCN) in exactly two places. (1) data_mutations.txt, as namespace columns that are imported only when the mutation meta file declares 'namespaces: ascn': ASCN.ASCN_METHOD (e.g. 'FACETS'), ASCN.CCF_EXPECTED_COPIES, ASCN.CCF_EXPECTED_COPIES_UPPER, ASCN.EXPECTED_ALT_COPIES, ASCN.CLONAL, ASCN.TOTAL_COPY_NUMBER, ASCN.MINOR_COPY_NUMBER, ASCN.ASCN_INTEGER_COPY_NUMBER; all eight are required once the namespace is declared. They are per-mutation, so they describe allelic state only at mutated loci. (2) data_clinical_sample.txt, attribute ASCN_WGD with values 'WGD' or 'no WGD'. The specification defines no standard slot for genome-wide allele-specific segments and no standard attribute name for fraction LOH, purity or ploidy. The SEG file is fixed at ID, chrom, loc.start, loc.end, num.mark, seg.mean. Discrete CNA is gene-level -2..2. Arm-level CNA is a Generic Assay with only Loss/Gain/Unchanged. FRACTION_GENOME_ALTERED and MUTATION_COUNT are computed by the portal and should not be in the files. MAF rows with Mutation_Status 'LOH' are not loaded. Fraction LOH, purity, ploidy or FACETS tcn/lcn would therefore appear only as study-specific custom clinical columns or extra seg columns with non-standard names. Systematic absence check: (i) no MAF column begins 'ASCN.'; (ii) no ASCN_WGD in the sample table; (iii) the seg file has exactly the six standard columns (no tcn, lcn, tcn.em, lcn.em, cf); (iv) case-insensitive header scan of both clinical tables for LOH, PURITY, PLOIDY, WGD, DOUBL, FACETS, TCN, LCN, MCN, MINOR, ALLEL, CCF, CLONAL, HRD, TAI; (v) no generic-assay file among the supplied files. HOW SURE: high for the documented ASCN columns, ASCN_WGD and the fixed seg format (read in full); medium for the statement that no standard name exists for fraction LOH, purity or ploidy (it rests on their absence from the specification; individual studies use their own custom names, which I did not survey). SOURCES: https://github.com/cBioPortal/cbioportal/blob/master/docs/File-Formats.md, https://github.com/mskcc/facets-suite.

question: FINDING FROM THE LAB'S LIBRARY, asked for by the director. QUESTION: How sensitive is exome or targeted-capture sequencing for detecting IGH-BCL2, MYC and BCL6 rearrangements in formalin-fixed paraffin-embedded lymphoma tissue compared with fresh-frozen tissue and with FISH, and is it usual for a study to supplement sequencing-based rearrangement calls with FISH or another assay in the FFPE part of a cohort? ANSWER: Partly settled. Versus FISH in FFPE tissue, capture sequencing misses many rearrangements: in 233 FFPE DLBCLs a 481-gene capture panel had sensitivity against break-apart FISH of 50% for MYC, 80% for BCL2 and 69% for BCL6 (17 of 17 re-examined misses had breakpoints outside the probe-covered region, 16 intergenic); in 34 FFPE high-grade B-cell lymphomas DNA sequencing found 6/12 MYC, 10/10 BCL2 and 13/18 BCL6 rearrangements and missed 5 of 12 FISH-defined MYC/BCL2 double-hit cases; a capture design aimed at known breakpoints reached 94.2% concordance. Stated reasons for misses: breakpoints outside captured regions, non-unique sequence flanking breakpoints (common at IG loci), and FFPE-induced DNA fragmentation, which one source says 'compromises sequencing-based analyses of chromosomal rearrangements'. NOT settled: none of the pages read gives a head-to-head FFPE-versus-frozen sensitivity figure for these rearrangements, and none documents how often research cohorts supplement FFPE sequencing calls with FISH. The sources say only that FISH remains the gold standard, that sequencing 'should not replace FISH', and that the two methods are complementary. That exome capture (coding exons only) does no better than these dedicated panels is my inference, not a sourced statement. Practical reading: SV-negative means 'not detected'; under-calling is plausibly worse in FFPE and is not equal across tissue types, so SV frequencies and double-hit flags should be compared within one tissue type/cohort or stratified by it, not pooled across subsets with different FFPE/frozen mix. This corrects the earlier department note that the bias is roughly equal across subsets. HOW SURE: medium (high for under-detection versus FISH in FFPE, especially MYC and BCL6; low for the FFPE-versus-frozen size of the effect and for how usual FISH supplementation is, which the web did not settle). SOURCES: https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11251499/, https://doi.org/10.4149/neo_2024_240527n236, https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC8184748/, https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s12308-019-00360-0.

question: FINDING FROM THE LAB'S LIBRARY, asked for by the director. QUESTION: Is there any validated method for estimating the genome-wide fraction of LOH from total-copy-number log-ratio segments alone (no B-allele frequencies, no purity or ploidy estimate), and how well does a losses-only fraction agree with allele-specific fraction LOH in tumours with frequent whole-genome doubling? ANSWER: I found no validated method, and no source reporting a concordance figure between a losses-only fraction and allele-specific fraction LOH; the web does not supply a number that would support the substitution. This is absence of evidence within a 10-call search, but the sources read argue against the substitution in principle. The FACETS paper states copy-neutral LOH is 'not detectable by analyzing total copy number alone' and that segmenting total read count 'will inevitably miss' it. An allele-specific reanalysis of 4,950 TCGA tumours reclassified as LOH 9% of apparent copy-number wild-type calls and 7% of gain calls. In the MSK-IMPACT genome-doubling study (9,692 patients, FACETS), WGD occurred in 28.2% of advanced cancers and 36% of colorectal cancers (only microsatellite-stable ones), with median ploidy 3.3 versus 2.1; about 70% of arm- or chromosome-length single-copy losses in WGD tumours arose after doubling (total 3, major 2, minor 1), so they are losses relative to ploidy that keep heterozygosity and are not LOH. Conversely copy-neutral LOH that is later doubled (total 4, minor 0) reads as neutral or gain. WGD is associated with TP53 mutation in the same study, so the proxy's error differs between the two groups being compared. A copy-loss fraction is therefore a different variable from fraction LOH, and keeping it out of the label has published support. HOW SURE: medium: high that total copy number alone cannot detect copy-neutral LOH and that post-WGD losses are mostly not LOH; the claim that no validated total-copy-number-only method exists is a negative result from a limited search, and no quantitative agreement figure was found. SOURCES: https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC5027494/, https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC6072608/, https://www.cell.com/cell-systems/fulltext/S2405-4712(21)00383-5, https://doi.org/10.1200/po.22.00555.

text: FINDING FROM THE LAB'S LIBRARY, asked for by the director. QUESTION: Is there any validated method for estimating the genome-wide fraction of LOH from total-copy-number log-ratio segments alone (no B-allele frequencies, no purity or ploidy estimate), and how well does a losses-only fraction agree with allele-specific fraction LOH in tumours with frequent whole-genome doubling? ANSWER: I found no validated method, and no source reporting a concordance figure between a losses-only fraction and allele-specific fraction LOH; the web does not supply a number that would support the substitution. This is absence of evidence within a 10-call search, but the sources read argue against the substitution in principle. The FACETS paper states copy-neutral LOH is 'not detectable by analyzing total copy number alone' and that segmenting total read count 'will inevitably miss' it. An allele-specific reanalysis of 4,950 TCGA tumours reclassified as LOH 9% of apparent copy-number wild-type calls and 7% of gain calls. In the MSK-IMPACT genome-doubling study (9,692 patients, FACETS), WGD occurred in 28.2% of advanced cancers and 36% of colorectal cancers (only microsatellite-stable ones), with median ploidy 3.3 versus 2.1; about 70% of arm- or chromosome-length single-copy losses in WGD tumours arose after doubling (total 3, major 2, minor 1), so they are losses relative to ploidy that keep heterozygosity and are not LOH. Conversely copy-neutral LOH that is later doubled (total 4, minor 0) reads as neutral or gain. WGD is associated with TP53 mutation in the same study, so the proxy's error differs between the two groups being compared. A copy-loss fraction is therefore a different variable from fraction LOH, and keeping it out of the label has published support. question: FINDING FROM THE LAB'S LIBRARY, asked for by the director. QUESTION: In lymphoma cohort or registry data, what explains a recorded progression-free survival time that is longer than the recorded overall survival time for patients censored on both endpoints (for example different last-contact dates for disease status and vital status, or different time origins), and what is the accepted way to handle such records in Kaplan-Meier and Cox analyses? ANSWER: Not fully settled. What the guidance says: the follow-up end (censoring) date is defined separately for each endpoint. OS is censored at the date last known alive, PFS at the last date the patient was known progression-free (last disease assessment), so the two censoring times legitimately differ. Under that rule censored PFS should be shorter than or equal to censored OS; using 'last known alive' as the PFS censor date is named as a common mistake that inflates PFS. A censored PFS longer than censored OS is therefore the reverse of the expected pattern and, under one time origin, logically inconsistent (progression-free at time t implies alive at t). It indicates that the two times in that cohort come from different date sources, data locks or time origins (for example disease status updated later than vital status, or different time zero). That explanation is my inference: the pages read do not discuss this exact pattern and I found no lymphoma-specific source. Handling consistent with the guidance: do not drop or silently edit the records; analyse each endpoint on its own time and status; check whether the pattern is confined to one cohort, because censoring that differs systematically between groups can bias Kaplan-Meier and Cox results; run sensitivity analyses with alternative censoring dates (cap PFS at the OS time; or extend OS to the PFS time; or stratify by or exclude the affected cohort) and report whether the log-rank result changes. Because these patients are censored on both endpoints, such changes alter time at risk, not event counts. HOW SURE: medium for the per-endpoint censoring rule and the sensitivity-analysis approach; low for the specific cause of PFS longer than OS, which is inferred. SOURCES: https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC13687036/, https://aacrjournals.org/clincancerres/article/19/10/2613/77658/Missing-Data-and-Measurement-Variability-in, https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC2698020/.

question: FINDING FROM THE LAB'S LIBRARY, asked for by the director. QUESTION: In B-cell lymphoma, which specific alterations of EZH2, BRAF, STAT3, SGK1, CREBBP and BCL2 are graded as therapeutically actionable (and at what evidence level) by frameworks such as OncoKB: any nonsilent mutation in the gene or only particular hotspot or domain variants? Are mutations in linker histone H1 genes regarded as a therapeutic target? ANSWER: OncoKB grades specific alterations ('Oncogenic Mutations' or named variants), never any nonsilent mutation. Its actionable-genes page as read on 2026-11-15 has no therapeutic level (1-4, R1, R2) for EZH2, CREBBP, BCL2, STAT3 or SGK1 in DLBCL or any other B-cell lymphoma; tazemetostat and venetoclax do not appear on the page; SGK1 and the H1 genes are not listed at all. EZH2 and CREBBP 'Oncogenic Mutations' in DLBCL NOS and follicular lymphoma, and the IGH::BCL2 fusion, appear only in the diagnostic tiers (Dx3 for EZH2, CREBBP and IGH::BCL2 in DLBCL; Dx2 for IGH::BCL2 in follicular lymphoma; the tier is inferred from row order in the flattened page text, so treat it as approximate). STAT3 is listed only for T-cell large granular lymphocytic leukemia (diagnostic). BRAF therapeutic entries are allele-specific (V600E/V600: hairy cell leukemia with vemurafenib, histiocytoses, solid tumours); there is none for DLBCL or follicular lymphoma. For EZH2, OncoKB curates Y646C/F/H/N/S, A682G, A692V and a few other SET-domain variants as oncogenic, and R207Q, R213H, R502Q, K515R, P577L as inconclusive. Outside OncoKB: the FDA gave accelerated approval (June 2020) to tazemetostat for relapsed/refractory follicular lymphoma, not DLBCL, with an EZH2 mutation found by an approved test (response 69% in mutant versus 34% in wild type); CIViC ties tazemetostat to EZH2 Y646 variants, A682G and A692V. I could not establish from the pages read why tazemetostat is absent from the current OncoKB list. BCL2 mutations are reported as markers of venetoclax resistance, not sensitivity. CREBBP has only low-level evidence (HAT-domain mutations and mTOR inhibition, CIViC, follicular lymphoma). H1 mutations are loss-of-function tumour-suppressor driver events; no drug is attached in the abstract read (full text paywalled) and they are not in OncoKB, so they are not regarded as a therapeutic target. A consensus review describes DLBCL genetic subtypes as suggesting therapeutic vulnerabilities 'for future drug development', i.e. inferred, not established, targets. So counting any nonsilent mutation overstates targetability: restrict to EZH2 Y646/A682/A692, BRAF V600E and comparable hotspot or domain variants, and call the rest candidate targets. HOW SURE: medium (high that OncoKB is alteration-specific and lists no therapeutic level for these genes in DLBCL; medium for the exact diagnostic tiers; medium for H1, based on an abstract and absence from OncoKB). FINDING FROM THE LAB'S LIBRARY, asked for by the director. QUESTION: In mass-spectrometry phosphoproteomic datasets distributed in cancer-genomics portal format, when a table gives one row per gene whose name concatenates many phosphosite identifiers, how is that gene-level value conventionally computed from the site-level log-ratios (mean, median, sum, most-variable or best-covered site), and is it already normalised to the parent protein's abundance? ANSWER: Not settled by the web within the call limit. What the pages I opened do show: (1) The portal's own convention for mass-spec phospho data is one row per SITE, not per gene. Its CPTAC import script (ms2cbioportal.py) names rows GENE|GENE_

, chaining multi-site peptides with underscores (this docstring came from a search excerpt of the file; the part I opened shows the processing order: clean rows, format gene names, select sample columns, remove infinities, average duplicate rows, optional proteomic ruler). There is no step in that sequence that subtracts or divides by protein abundance. (2) A one-row-per-gene table listing many sites is therefore a non-standard collapse, and I found no document stating its rule. A phosphoproteomics review (Mantini et al. 2020) says many tools 'simply collapse quantitative information from multiple phosphosites into a single protein phosphorylation value' and warns that this loses site-specific behaviour (activating versus inhibiting sites). The only explicit rule I saw was a median of the log-ratios of all sites from the protein, in a search excerpt of that review, not in the text I could open. (3) The FragPipe TMT tutorial says TMT-Integrator writes gene-, protein-, peptide- and site-level reports with median centring as the default normalisation; no protein-abundance correction is mentioned in the part read. Working assumption for the teams: the value is a mean or median over whichever sites were quantified and is NOT protein-normalised. Under that assumption 'phospho minus protein' is a legitimate but coarse measure (average net phosphorylation per molecule across measured sites, not CDK4/6-site occupancy), and the sites feeding the average may differ between TMT plexes. The normalisation question can be checked in the data: a strong positive correlation between the gene-level phospho row and the protein row means it is not protein-normalised; near zero or negative would suggest it already is. I could not reach the 'Protein level Data' section of the portal file-format page (the tool returned only the top of the page). HOW SURE: low for the collapse statistic (web does not settle it); medium that the value is not protein-normalised. SOURCES: https://github.com/cBioPortal/CPTAC-proteomics-pipeline/blob/master/ms2cbioportal.py, https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC6731080/, https://doi.org/10.1002/pmic.201900312, https://fragpipe.nesvilab.org/docs/tutorial_tmt.html, https://github.com/cbioportal/cbioportal/blob/master/docs/File-Formats.md.

question: FINDING FROM THE LAB'S LIBRARY, asked for by the director. QUESTION: In bulk tumour tissue proteomics, how does RB1 protein abundance in non-malignant stromal and immune cells compare with that in proliferating carcinoma cells, and in which direction does low tumour purity bias the measured bulk RB1 protein level in a tumour whose cancer cells have intact RB1 versus one whose cancer cells have lost RB1? ANSWER: Partly settled. Non-malignant cells in tumour tissue do carry RB1: pathology studies use them as the internal positive control when tumour cells are RB-negative ('Stromal cells served as the positive internal control. Cases lacking adequate internal control were excluded' in a small-cell lung cancer series; 'RB1-positive endothelial cells served as an internal positive control' in a glioblastoma series; endothelial staining likewise in a prostate series). Those three sentences are search excerpts of the pages; the tool returned only the top of each page when opened, where the one directly relevant passage was the glioblastoma paper's statement that RB1 FISH signal persists in 'intratumoral non-neoplastic elements such as endothelial cells' when tumour cells have homozygous deletion. So for a tumour whose cancer cells have lost RB1, admixture RAISES bulk RB1 toward the stromal level and low purity hides the loss, as the briefing said. The quantitative comparison of stroma with proliferating RB1-intact carcinoma cells is NOT settled: the only statement found is that 'RB levels fluctuate as a function of cellular proliferation' (review, search excerpt), with no direction or magnitude, and no source gave a measured stroma-to-carcinoma ratio or a purity effect on RB1 in bulk proteomics. The direction for an RB1-intact tumour is therefore reasoning, not a sourced fact: if quiescent stroma holds less RB than cycling cancer cells, low purity LOWERS bulk RB1 in an intact tumour. Taken together, purity compresses both kinds of tumour toward the stromal level rather than biasing one way. An RB1-low value in a low-purity sample cannot be created by admixture if the cancer cells truly lost RB (admixture works against it, so that call is conservative), but it could come from dilution of an RB1-intact tumour if stroma is RB-poor. Neither team's rule is safe on its own; the data can decide: among RB1-wild-type tumours regress RB1 protein on purity (positive slope means dilution lowers RB1 and a low-purity RB1-low call is suspect; flat or negative means purity cannot explain it), check whether the sample sits below what its purity predicts, and look for RB-loss features stroma cannot mimic (high p16/CDKN2A RNA or protein, high E2F targets, RB1 truncating mutation). HOW SURE: medium: high that stromal and endothelial cells express RB1 and that admixture masks loss in RB1-lost tumours; low on the stroma-versus-carcinoma level and hence on the direction for RB1-intact tumours. SOURCES: https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC9623236/, https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC3246124/, https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC2914856/, https://aacrjournals.org/clincancerres/article/28/2/255/675586/Relevance-of-pRB-Loss-in-Human, https://aacrjournals.org/clincancerres/article/20/4/890/78787/Rb-Loss-Is-Characteristic-of-Prostatic-Small-Cell.

QUESTION: How is cisplatin (platinum) resistance or platinum-refractory disease conventionally defined in clinical studies of germ cell tumours - does it include incomplete marker response, viable non-teratomatous tumour at post-chemotherapy surgery, or relapse after a complete response, and can a patient be classed as resistant without documented disease progression or salvage chemotherapy? ANSWER: There is no single definition; two conventions coexist, and a review says the definition varies by study. (a) Narrow trial terms require documented progression: 'cisplatin-refractory' = response or stabilisation on treatment but progression within 4 weeks of the last cisplatin-based cycle; 'absolutely refractory' = progression during cisplatin-based therapy (German Testicular Cancer Study Group trial and a 2006 review). (b) The broader 'resistant' label means failure to achieve a durable (continuous) complete response to platinum chemotherapy. A Memorial Sloan Kettering salvage trial defines clinical platinum resistance exactly that way and counts failure of marker normalisation as an incomplete response; in that trial, viable tumour that was completely resected counted as a complete response to chemotherapy plus surgery. Independent genomic resistant-versus-sensitive studies are broader still: one defines resistance as progressive disease (relapse or incomplete response) after one or more complete platinum regimens, or viable non-teratomatous disease in a post-chemotherapy surgical sample; another adds persistent or rising markers four weeks after chemotherapy. Two others use progression or relapse (or rising markers) only, and class necrosis/teratoma-only resections without later relapse as sensitive. So: incomplete marker response, viable non-teratoma at post-chemotherapy surgery and relapse after a complete response are all included in the broad convention used by some genomic studies, but not by every study, and none of them alone meets the narrow 'refractory' definition. Under the broad convention a patient can be resistant with no recorded progression and no salvage chemotherapy (for example, viable tumour found and resected at post-chemotherapy surgery, or a marker-positive incomplete response); under the narrow one they cannot. The few such labels are therefore plausible rather than evident errors: keep the study's flag for the primary test and re-run with those patients excluded or recoded as a sensitivity analysis, after checking them against the post-chemotherapy surgery pathology columns. The web does not settle what this dataset's own flag encodes: the searches surfaced what appears to be the dataset's source study, and I did not open it or base the answer on it. HOW SURE: high that the convention is heterogeneous and that the broad definition can label a patient resistant without progression or salvage therapy; low on what this particular dataset's flag encodes. QUESTION: In cBioPortal-format discrete copy-number tables produced by targeted-panel pipelines that contain only the values -2, 0 and 2, are single-copy (hemizygous) losses simply not reported, and what log2-ratio thresholds on the accompanying segment file are conventionally used to call single-copy loss versus deep deletion? ANSWER: Yes: in a -2/0/2 table single-copy losses are not reported, so 0 means 'no event called', not 'two copies'. cBioPortal's format defines -2 = deep loss (possibly homozygous deletion), -1 = single-copy loss, 0 = diploid, 1 = low-level gain, 2 = high-level amplification, and its FAQ says only deep deletions and amplifications are treated as biologically relevant by default. The MSK-IMPACT panel pipeline reports a whole-gene event only when the tumour/normal coverage fold change is >2.0 (gain) or <-2.0 (loss) with FDR-corrected P<0.05, i.e. a log2 ratio of roughly >= +1 or <= -1, so it never emits -1 or +1. (A cBioPortal datahub thread documents another -2/0/2 table built the same way from binary amplification/deletion calls, with 'no event' written as 0.) For the segment file there is no universal cutoff, because the expected log2 ratio depends on tumour purity and ploidy. In a pure diploid tumour a clonal single-copy loss is log2(1/2) = -1.0; at 50% tumour fraction it is about -0.415 and a homozygous deletion is about -1.0 (the purity figures are my arithmetic from the standard mixing formula, consistent with CNVkit's documentation). The most commonly used fixed cutoffs are CNVkit's defaults: seg.mean < -1.1 = 0 copies (deep deletion); -1.1 to -0.25 = 1 copy (single-copy loss); -0.25 to +0.2 = neutral; +0.2 to +0.7 = 3 copies; above +0.7 = 4 or more. CNVkit states the inner cutoffs detect single-copy changes down to about 30% purity and the outer ones assume 100% purity. GISTIC uses a fixed low-level noise threshold of 0.1 or 0.3 for shallow events and sample-specific high-level thresholds. To verify the counted deep deletion, read the seg.mean of the segment overlapping the gene in that sample: at or below about -1 supports the call; between about -0.25 and -1 points to single-copy loss. Because the panel's loss threshold (ratio 0.5) equals a clonal single-copy loss in a pure diploid sample, a -2 with seg.mean near -1 in a high-purity tumour may not be a true homozygous deletion (my inference from the thresholds, not stated in a source). Single-copy loss read from the segment file should be a labelled sensitivity analysis, not part of the primary alteration definition. HOW SURE: high for the meaning of the discrete values and the panel pipeline's fold-change criteria; medium for the segment-file cutoffs, which are tool defaults rather than a universal standard and shift with purity and ploidy. SOURCES: https://github.com/cBioPortal/cbioportal/blob/master/docs/File-Formats.md, https://docs.cbioportal.org/user-guide/faq/, https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC5808190/, https://github.com/cBioPortal/cbioportal/issues/4664, https://github.com/cBioPortal/datahub/issues/2269, https://cnvkit.readthedocs.io/en/stable/pipeline.html, https://cnvkit.readthedocs.io/en/stable/calling.html.
