question: FINDING FROM THE LAB'S LIBRARY, asked for by the director. QUESTION: In clinical hybrid-capture targeted sequencing panels of the MSK-IMPACT type, how is a gene-level amplification call made (fold-change and significance thresholds, any manual review), how are the discrete copy-number values 2 / 0 / -2 in a cBioPortal discrete CNA file derived from those calls, and can a gene be reported as amplified when its sample-level log2 ratio is below 1? ANSWER: Call rule: coverage of the gene's target regions in the tumour (normalised for total coverage, square-root transformed, GC-Loess corrected) is compared with a pool of diploid normal FFPE/blood controls. A whole-gene gain or loss is significant when fold change > 2.0 (gain) or < -2.0 (loss) with P < 0.05 after false-discovery-rate correction. Fold change is a linear tumour:normal ratio, so the gain cut-off corresponds to a gene-level log2 ratio of about 1. Germline copy-number calls from the matched normal are subtracted. cBioPortal coding: cBioPortal does not compute or re-threshold discrete CNA values; it loads the integer matrix the submitter provides. In an MSK-IMPACT study 2 is the lab's amplification call, -2 its deep-deletion call and 0 'no call' (not 'diploid'); there is no GISTIC step and no -1/+1 level. Amplified below log2 1: by the published rule, no - the gene's own fold change must exceed 2. The web did not settle whether clinical sign-out review reports amplification below that cut-off; I found no page describing manual review of copy-number calls (the manual-review text I saw concerns mutations). An earlier department note records a 'borderline' fold-change 1.5-2 category from the ERBB2 validation paper; I did not re-read that passage this time. An amplified call beside a log2 value below 1 in a .seg segment mean or a curated sample-level column is not in itself a contradiction, because those are different quantities from the gene-level exon fold change (a segment mean averages neighbouring probes). That last point is my inference, not a sourced statement. Implication for using other genes as background: calls are threshold-dependent, so a gene near fold change 2 flips with a modest purity change while a high-level amplicon does not; stratify any background 'call loss' rate by baseline log-ratio. Evidence quality: the threshold sentence is from the primary validation paper and is repeated in a later paper from the same lab, but I saw it only as search excerpts - the full-text fetches were cut off before the methods section. The cBioPortal statement is likewise from a search excerpt of a cBioPortal forum answer. HOW SURE: high for the fold change > 2 / FDR P < 0.05 rule; medium for the cBioPortal 2/0/-2 coding; low for whether amplification is ever reported below log2 ratio 1 (not settled by the web). SOURCES: https://doi.org/10.1016/j.jmoldx.2014.12.006, https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC5808190/, https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC6825534/, https://www.jmdjournal.org/article/S1525-1578(16)30233-1/fulltext, https://groups.google.com/g/cbioportal/c/qP_OaeRdbDo.

question: FINDING FROM THE LAB'S LIBRARY, asked for by the director. QUESTION: In institutional clinical sequencing sample identifiers of the form P-#######-T01-IM3, does the T-number (T01, T02, T03) reflect the order in which specimens were collected from the patient or the order in which they were accessioned for sequencing, so that an archival pre-treatment specimen can carry a higher T-number than a later biopsy? ANSWER: The web does not settle this with an explicit rule. Nothing I found says the T-number encodes collection order, and the evidence points to a per-patient counter assigned when a specimen is accessioned for sequencing. (1) The AACR GENIE / Sage staff answer defines T01 only as 'a string used as a unique sample identifier' for that patient, and the IM suffix as a further differentiator (IM3 rows carry panel IMPACT341). (2) The MSK-IMPACT cohort paper says specimens are accessioned by the molecular diagnostics lab when received for testing (search excerpt only). (3) In a public MSK sample table, patient P-0000114 has T01 = lymph-node metastasis with age at sequencing report 58 and T02 = primary tumour with age at sequencing report 59: the T-number follows sequencing-report order, and the primary carries the higher number. (4) MSK-CHORD timeline files hold a sample-acquisition date separately from the sequencing date (P-0002880-T02-IM6: acquired day 622, sequenced day 746). So an archival pre-treatment specimen submitted after a later biopsy can plausibly carry a higher T-number. A higher T-number on a sample labelled pre-treatment therefore does not contradict the curated pre/post label, but the T-number cannot confirm the ordering either. Suggested handling: keep the curated pre/post label as primary and report pairs with inverted T-numbers as a sensitivity stratum. HOW SURE: low to medium: inferred from a non-chronological official definition and a few examples; no explicit statement of the convention was found. SOURCES: https://www.synapse.org/Synapse:syn7222066/discussion/threadId=9817, https://drive.google.com/file/d/1Txdaa7JKOVMS3TZ8g9tkQUzZPkNc2m24/view, https://groups.google.com/g/cbioportal/c/y_fd7cu-N0M, https://mskcc-epi-bio.github.io/gnomeR/articles/qa-impact-data.html, https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC5461196/.

question: FINDING FROM THE LAB'S LIBRARY, asked for by the director. QUESTION: In paired biopsies of the same gastro-oesophageal adenocarcinoma taken at different times or sites without an intervening therapy targeted at the gene in question, how concordant are focal oncogene amplification calls (for example MYC, CCNE1, EGFR, KRAS, CDK6, MET) on targeted sequencing panels, and is a negative-control-gene comparison an accepted way to judge whether loss of a drug-targeted amplification exceeds assay and sampling background? ANSWER: Concordance: discordance is common. The multi-cohort study of paired primary and synchronous metastatic gastro-oesophageal adenocarcinoma (Pectasides et al., Cancer Discovery 2018) reported 'oncogene amplification profiles commonly discordant' within the primary tumour and between primary and disseminated disease. The same group later summarised it as discordance in 42% of single-nucleotide variants/indels and 63% of gene amplifications. Divergent primary/metastasis profiling changed treatment assignment in 32% (9/28) of patients, and a review puts discordant oncogene amplification at about one third of patients (these two figures from search excerpts). Limits: these numbers count any difference in either direction, across sites, on exome or targeted assays with their own thresholds. I did not find per-gene rates for MYC, CCNE1, EGFR, KRAS, CDK6 or MET, nor a rate for serial biopsies on one assay, so there is no clean literature figure for spontaneous loss of an amplification call in the later sample. The background is clearly not negligible and is well above the 7-12% HER2 IHC/FISH primary-versus-metastasis discordance already in department memory. Negative-control genes: I found no source that validates this comparison for amplification loss, and I ran no successful search for the methodological literature. It is the general negative-control-outcome idea from epidemiology applied to this setting - reasonable, but not an established standard in this field. Conditions for it to be valid (my reasoning, not sourced): control genes must share the assay, purity and sampling effects but not be selected by the therapy; exclude genes on the ERBB2 amplicon (17q12 neighbours such as CDK12); match or stratify on baseline log-ratio because near-threshold calls flip more easily; analyse within pair because a purity collapse removes every call in that pair at once; and note that concurrent chemotherapy, and RTK/RAS amplifications that are themselves resistance mechanisms, can move the control genes too. The most informative pattern is at pair level: the ERBB2 call lost while other amplifications in the same pair are retained. HOW SURE: medium that amplification discordance between paired samples is common; low for any specific background rate; low that a negative-control-gene comparison is an accepted standard (not settled by the web). SOURCES: https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/28978556, https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC6891164/, https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC7232941/, https://doi.org/10.1158/2159-8290.c.6547418.

text: FINDING: A seg segment that spans a gene the panel does not target is not a measurement of that gene: seg.mean is the mean log-ratio of the markers inside the segment, all of which sit on panel exons or backbone/tiling SNPs elsewhere, so the off-panel locus is interpolated ('no change-point detected between the flanking markers') and any gain or loss smaller than the gap between the nearest flanking markers is invisible; only broad, arm-scale events are genuinely supported. MSK's own facets-suite gene-level caller reflects this: it keeps a gene only if SNP loci fall inside the gene's boundaries (inner merge of gene-segment with gene-SNP tables) and suppresses AMP/HOMDEL calls on segments longer than 10 Mb. A check that uses only the seg file: for the segment spanning each locus compute length divided by num.mark (local marker spacing) and the distance from the locus to the segment's ends; if spacing is in the Mb range the locus is inferred, not assayed. Either way DNA copy number at a TF locus is not its expression. question: FINDING FROM THE LAB'S LIBRARY, asked for by the director. QUESTION: In a segmented copy-number (.seg) file produced from a hybrid-capture targeted gene-panel sequencing assay, what does the num.mark column count, and when a segment spans a gene that the panel does not target, is that gene's copy number considered measured (for example by genome-wide tiling or SNP backbone probes) or inferred from distant flanking probes? How densely are such backbone probes typically spaced? ANSWER: (1) num.mark is the number of markers, i.e. the data points given to the segmentation algorithm, that fall inside the segment. The DNAcopy manual defines it as 'the number of markers in the segment', with loc.start and loc.end being the map locations where the segment starts and ends; CNVkit's format page calls it the 'number of probes or bins covered by the segment'. It is not a count of genes or bases. What one marker is depends on the pipeline: a capture target or exon interval, a backbone SNP, an off-target bin, or (in FACETS) a SNP or pseudo-SNP locus placed along the target intervals. Samples whose marker counts are several times higher than the rest were therefore most likely segmented with a different marker definition or a different assay; the web does not say which pipeline made any particular file, so that part is not settled. (2) A segment spanning an off-panel gene is an inference, not a measurement of that gene. seg.mean is the average log-ratio of the markers inside the segment, and those markers sit on panel exons or backbone SNPs elsewhere; the off-panel locus is interpolated on the assumption that no change-point lies between the nearest flanking markers. Broad, arm-scale gains and losses are genuinely supported, but any event smaller than the gap between flanking markers is invisible. This is the library's reading of the format definitions rather than a quoted statement; it is consistent with MSK's facets-suite gene-level caller, which keeps a gene only if SNP loci fall inside the gene's boundaries and suppresses amplification or homozygous-deletion calls on segments longer than 10 Mb. A backbone SNP that happens to lie inside or beside a gene would be a direct marker there, so the teams can check local density from the seg file itself: segment length divided by num.mark for the spanning segment, and the distance from the locus to the segment ends. (3) Backbone density ranges from tens of kb to several Mb by design. MSK-IMPACT papers state the assay captures '>1,000 intergenic and intronic single-nucleotide polymorphisms (tiling probes), interspersed homogenously across the genome' to aid genome-wide copy number, with probes covering about 1.2 Mb in total; spread over a roughly 3,100 Mb genome that averages about one tiling SNP per 3 Mb (library arithmetic, not a published figure). For comparison, IDT's xGen CNV Backbone panel has over 9,000 probes about every 0.34 Mb, and Twist exome backbones come at 25, 50 or 100 kb intervals. Caveat on sourcing: the MSK-IMPACT tiling-probe sentence was seen only as search excerpts, quoted identically from several MSK papers; when those pages were opened the gateway returned only the abstract and introduction, so the Methods text was not read in full. The DNAcopy, CNVkit, FACETS, facets-suite, IDT and Twist statements were read on the opened pages. Bottom line for the director: the seg file is a real DNA copy-number variable, but at the three off-panel regulator loci it carries interpolated, Mb-scale copy number at best, and copy number is in any case not the expression measure that defines the subtypes. HOW SURE: high for what num.mark counts; medium for 'inferred, not measured' (derived from the format definitions and facets-suite code, not a direct quoted statement); medium for backbone spacing (MSK-IMPACT figure from search excerpts only, per-3-Mb average is library arithmetic). SOURCES: https://rdrr.io/bioc/DNAcopy/man/DNAcopy.html, https://cnvkit.readthedocs.io/en/stable/fileformats.html, https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC5027494/, https://github.com/mskcc/facets-suite/blob/master/R/gene-level-changes.R, https://raw.githubusercontent.com/mskcc/facets/master/vignettes/FACETS.pdf, https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC9633455/, https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC5397722/, https://www.idtdna.com/pages/products/next-generation-sequencing/workflow/xgen-ngs-hybridization-capture/pre-designed-hyb-cap-panels/human-cnv-backbone-hyb-panel, https://doi.org/10.1101/2024.05.19.594885.

text: FINDING: DEFINITIONS. Level 1 = FDA-recognized biomarker predictive of response to an FDA-approved drug in this indication (tumour type). Level 2 = standard-care biomarker recommended by the NCCN or other expert panels, predictive of response to an FDA-approved drug in this indication (called 2A before Dec 2019). Level 3A = compelling clinical evidence supports the biomarker as predictive of response to a drug in this indication (not yet standard care). Level 3B = standard-care or investigational biomarker predictive of response to an FDA-approved or investigational drug in ANOTHER indication (since Dec 2019 this merges the old 2B and 3B). Level 4 = compelling biological (laboratory) evidence only. R1 = standard-care biomarker predictive of resistance to an FDA-approved drug in this indication (e.g. EGFR T790M, RAS in colorectal). R2 = compelling clinical evidence of resistance (investigational). OncoKB groups 1 and 2 as 'standard care', 3A/3B as 'clinical evidence' and 4 as 'biological evidence'. Exact current wording for 1, 3A, 4, R1, R2 could not be read from the OncoKB levels page (it is an image); those definitions are from the 2017 OncoKB paper and the page's short labels, while the wording for 2 and 3B is verbatim from the OncoKB annotator README. CONVENTION. There is no single convention; the web does not settle one tier. What published studies did: (a) levels 1-2 only ('standard care' / 'clinically actionable' in the MSK clinical update: 'harboring an OncoKB Level 1 or Level 2 predictive biomarker'): 7.5% of samples in the 2017 OncoKB paper, 8.9% (2017 knowledge base) rising to 31.6% (2022 knowledge base) of 47,271 tumours in the 2023 OncoKB paper; (b) levels 1-3A ('at least one clinically actionable genomic alteration (OncoKB levels 1-3A)' in the 2023 OncoKB paper, which calls 3B, 4 and no-level 'limited to no clinical actionability'): 18.1% (2017) to 35.9% (2022); (c) levels 1-3B (the usual headline in 2017-2022 cohort papers): 36.7% of patients in the MSK-IMPACT 10,000-patient paper, 41% in the 2017 OncoKB paper, 44% in a 1,671-patient biliary cfDNA study (which separately called levels 1 and 3A in that tumour 'clinically significant'), 48% in an ASCO 2022 abstract ('OncoKB Levels 1/2/3'); (d) levels 1-4 called 'potentially actionable' in a 2019 liquid-biopsy abstract. Level 4 is usually left out of the headline and R1/R2 are resistance levels that are not counted as actionable-for-response. Studies level only alterations that OncoKB calls oncogenic or likely oncogenic. So the teams should report 1-2, 1-3A and 1-3B separately; a claim worded 'clinically actionable' in a 2017-2022 sequencing paper most often means 1-3B, and one worded 'standard care' or 'FDA-recognized/guideline' means 1-2. CROSS-TUMOUR RULE. A level 1, 2 or 3A biomarker does NOT keep its level in another tumour type: it is assigned Level 3B there (Level 2B in the pre-Dec-2019 scheme). Propagation is solid-to-solid or heme-to-heme only; R1/R2 and Level 4 never propagate, and some lineage-specific and all germline associations do not propagate. Exceptions are tumour-agnostic approvals (e.g. MSI-H, NTRK fusions, TMB-H, RET fusions, BRAF V600E since 2022), which are Level 1 in all solid tumours. A sample takes the single highest level among all its alterations; the annotator's order is R1 > 1 > 2 > 3A > 3B > 4 > R2 (HIGHEST_LEVEL) and 1 > 2 > 3A > 3B > 4 for the sensitive-only column (HIGHEST_SENSITIVE_LEVEL), which is the one to use for an actionability share. NOTE: one search hit looked like the study behind the task's dataset; it was not opened and nothing here comes from it. KRAS G12C colorectal: 3A Nov 2021, Level 2 by 2024, Level 1 by Jan 2025; pancreatic Level 2 May 2023. MET exon 14 skipping, NSCLC: Level 2A already in 2017 (crizotinib, NCCN); Level 1 May 2020 (capmatinib), tepotinib Mar 2021. MET amplification NSCLC is Level 2 today. RET fusions, NSCLC: Level 2 before 2020 (cabozantinib/vandetanib; selpercatinib and pralsetinib added at Level 2 Nov-Dec 2018); Level 1 May 2020 (selpercatinib), pralsetinib Sep 2020; thyroid Level 1 2020; all solid tumours Level 1 Oct 2022. PIK3CA, breast: Level 3A in 2017; Level 1 June 2019 (alpelisib). By Oct 2022 Level 1 is limited to C420R, E542K, E545A/D/G/K, Q546E/R, H1047L/R/Y and other oncogenic PIK3CA mutations are Level 2; capivasertib Level 1 Dec 2023. FGFR3, bladder: Level 3 in 2017; Level 1 May 2019 (erdafitinib; R248C, S249C, G370C, Y373C and FGFR3 fusions); other oncogenic FGFR3 mutations in bladder are Level 2 today. IDH1 (R132C/G/H/L/S), cholangiocarcinoma: 2B to 3A Dec 2019; Level 1 Aug 2021 (ivosidenib). IDH1/IDH2 in AML were Level 1 from 2017-2018. FGFR2 fusions, cholangiocarcinoma: Level 3 in 2017; Level 1 May 2020 (pemigatinib). BRAF V600E outside melanoma (melanoma Level 1 since 2011): NSCLC Level 2A in early 2017 then Level 1 in 2017; anaplastic thyroid Level 1 2018; Erdheim-Chester/histiocytosis Level 1 2017-2018; colorectal Level 1 Apr 2020 (encorafenib + cetuximab); glioma Level 2 May 2020; biliary Level 2 June 2022; all solid tumours except colorectal Level 1 Sep 2022. ERBB2 amplification: breast Level 1 (1998), oesophagogastric Level 1 (2010); colorectal Level 2 Apr 2020 and Level 1 today (the date of the step up was not read; the FDA approval was in 2023); biliary, salivary, uterine serous and small bowel Level 2 in 2024; other solid tumours 3A since May 2024. ERBB2 mutations: NSCLC Level 2A Dec 2019 (ado-trastuzumab emtansine), Level 1 Sep 2022 (trastuzumab deruxtecan); breast was 3A in 2017 and is Level 2 today (the date was not read); elsewhere 3B. Other Level 1 pairs and the year the biomarker was first FDA-recognized: EGFR L858R/exon 19 deletion NSCLC (2013 label), EGFR T790M (2015), EGFR S768I/L861Q/G719X (2018), EGFR exon 20 insertions (2021), ALK fusions NSCLC (2011), ROS1 fusions NSCLC (2016), KIT in GIST (2002), PDGFRA exon 18 GIST (2020), BRCA1/2 ovarian (2014; somatic 2018), HRR genes in prostate (2020), MSI-H all solid tumours (2017), NTRK fusions all solid tumours (2018), TMB-H all solid tumours (2020). text: FINDING: TUMOUR TYPES (somatic 'Oncogenic Mutations', current OncoKB). BRCA1 and BRCA2: Level 1 in ovarian/fallopian tube/peritoneal cancer (olaparib, niraparib, rucaparib, olaparib + bevacizumab) and in prostate cancer (olaparib, rucaparib, and PARP inhibitor combinations); Level 2 in pancreatic adenocarcinoma/acinar cell carcinoma (rucaparib, since Mar 2022) and BRCA2 in uterine sarcoma (Mar 2022). Somatic BRCA1/2 in breast cancer is Level 3A, not 1 or 2: it was Level 2 from Dec 2018 and was demoted to 3A in Nov 2021 because the FDA labels are germline-only; somatic BRCA1/2 with olaparib in pancreatic cancer is also 3A. ATM, CHEK2, PALB2 (and BARD1, BRIP1, CDK12, CHEK1, FANCL, RAD51B, RAD51C, RAD51D, RAD54L): Level 1 in prostate cancer only (olaparib, since June 2020; talazoparib + enzalutamide added 2023). PALB2 is also Level 2 in pancreatic cancer (rucaparib, Mar 2022). In every other solid tumour type these genes reach only Level 3B by propagation. Before June 2020 ATM was Level 4 and the non-BRCA HRR genes had no Level 1-2 anywhere. The CHEK2 page was read and shows prostate only; the ATM gene page failed to load, so ATM rests on the actionable-genes table and news log. ONCOGENIC REQUIREMENT. Yes. The level attaches to 'Oncogenic Mutations', defined by OncoKB as point mutations, rearrangements/fusions or gene deletions 'considered oncogenic, likely oncogenic or resistance'; variants of unknown significance get no level. The variant need not be truncating, but for tumour suppressors OncoKB curates all truncating mutations (nonsense, frameshift, splice-site) as likely oncogenic, so in practice: truncating variants and deep deletions count; missense or in-frame variants count only if individually curated as oncogenic or likely oncogenic; amplification does not count. A biliary cfDNA study applying this rule found about 90% of BRCA1/2 cfDNA variants unclassified. A team that counts every HRR-gene mutation, or counts them outside ovarian, prostate and pancreatic cancer, will overstate the Level 1-2 tier. MET EXON 14. OncoKB's levelled group in NSCLC is 'D1010, Exon 14 Deletion, Exon 14 in-frame deletions (963_1010del), Exon 14 splice mutations (963_1010splice)': Level 1 capmatinib and tepotinib, Level 2 crizotinib. Individually listed variants include X963_splice (acceptor end of exon 14), X1006_splice to X1010_splice (donor end), D1010 and D1010H/N/Y; all are likely oncogenic. Y1003 substitutions (CBL binding site) are Level 3A, not 1 or 2. Some files use the alternative isoform numbering 981_1028 for the same exon. OncoKB matches on gene, protein change and consequence, not on genomic coordinates. Its SOP defines a splice mutation as a change in the 2-base region at either end of an intron and leaves variant-type assignment to the sequencing assay. The annotator maps the mutation-file class Splice_Site to splice_region_variant and has no mapping for Intron or Splice_Region. So a deeper intronic variant (polypyrimidine tract or branch point) is annotated as exon 14 skipping only if the mutation file already labels it as a splice variant at codons 963-1010 (e.g. X963_splice, X1010_splice) or as an exon 14 in-frame deletion. The web did not settle an explicit list of intronic genomic positions: no source read gives one. QUESTION: For somatic (not germline) mutations in homologous-recombination repair genes such as BRCA1, BRCA2, ATM, CHEK2 and PALB2, in which tumour types does OncoKB assign level 1 or 2, does it require the variant to be truncating or otherwise known oncogenic, and which MET splice-site or intronic positions are annotated as exon 14 skipping? MET exon 14 skipping, NSCLC: Level 2A already in 2017 (crizotinib, NCCN); Level 1 May 2020 (capmatinib), tepotinib Mar 2021. MET amplification NSCLC is Level 2 today. RET fusions, NSCLC: Level 2 before 2020 (cabozantinib/vandetanib; selpercatinib and pralsetinib added at Level 2 Nov-Dec 2018); Level 1 May 2020 (selpercatinib), pralsetinib Sep 2020; thyroid Level 1 2020; all solid tumours Level 1 Oct 2022. IDH1 (R132C/G/H/L/S), cholangiocarcinoma: 2B to 3A Dec 2019; Level 1 Aug 2021 (ivosidenib). IDH1/IDH2 in AML were Level 1 from 2017-2018. FGFR2 fusions, cholangiocarcinoma: Level 3 in 2017; Level 1 May 2020 (pemigatinib). BRAF V600E outside melanoma (melanoma Level 1 since 2011): NSCLC Level 2A in early 2017 then Level 1 in 2017; anaplastic thyroid Level 1 2018; Erdheim-Chester/histiocytosis Level 1 2017-2018; colorectal Level 1 Apr 2020 (encorafenib + cetuximab); glioma Level 2 May 2020; biliary Level 2 June 2022; all solid tumours except colorectal Level 1 Sep 2022. question: FINDING FROM THE LAB'S LIBRARY, asked for by the director. QUESTION: For somatic (not germline) mutations in homologous-recombination repair genes such as BRCA1, BRCA2, ATM, CHEK2 and PALB2, in which tumour types does OncoKB assign level 1 or 2, does it require the variant to be truncating or otherwise known oncogenic, and which MET splice-site or intronic positions are annotated as exon 14 skipping? ANSWER: TUMOUR TYPES (somatic 'Oncogenic Mutations', current OncoKB). BRCA1 and BRCA2: Level 1 in ovarian/fallopian tube/peritoneal cancer (olaparib, niraparib, rucaparib, olaparib + bevacizumab) and in prostate cancer (olaparib, rucaparib, and PARP inhibitor combinations); Level 2 in pancreatic adenocarcinoma/acinar cell carcinoma (rucaparib, since Mar 2022) and BRCA2 in uterine sarcoma (Mar 2022). Somatic BRCA1/2 in breast cancer is Level 3A, not 1 or 2: it was Level 2 from Dec 2018 and was demoted to 3A in Nov 2021 because the FDA labels are germline-only; somatic BRCA1/2 with olaparib in pancreatic cancer is also 3A. ATM, CHEK2, PALB2 (and BARD1, BRIP1, CDK12, CHEK1, FANCL, RAD51B, RAD51C, RAD51D, RAD54L): Level 1 in prostate cancer only (olaparib, since June 2020; talazoparib + enzalutamide added 2023). PALB2 is also Level 2 in pancreatic cancer (rucaparib, Mar 2022). In every other solid tumour type these genes reach only Level 3B by propagation. Before June 2020 ATM was Level 4 and the non-BRCA HRR genes had no Level 1-2 anywhere. The CHEK2 page was read and shows prostate only; the ATM gene page failed to load, so ATM rests on the actionable-genes table and news log. ONCOGENIC REQUIREMENT. Yes. The level attaches to 'Oncogenic Mutations', defined by OncoKB as point mutations, rearrangements/fusions or gene deletions 'considered oncogenic, likely oncogenic or resistance'; variants of unknown significance get no level. The variant need not be truncating, but for tumour suppressors OncoKB curates all truncating mutations (nonsense, frameshift, splice-site) as likely oncogenic, so in practice: truncating variants and deep deletions count; missense or in-frame variants count only if individually curated as oncogenic or likely oncogenic; amplification does not count. A biliary cfDNA study applying this rule found about 90% of BRCA1/2 cfDNA variants unclassified. A team that counts every HRR-gene mutation, or counts them outside ovarian, prostate and pancreatic cancer, will overstate the Level 1-2 tier. MET EXON 14. OncoKB's levelled group in NSCLC is 'D1010, Exon 14 Deletion, Exon 14 in-frame deletions (963_1010del), Exon 14 splice mutations (963_1010splice)': Level 1 capmatinib and tepotinib, Level 2 crizotinib. Individually listed variants include X963_splice (acceptor end of exon 14), X1006_splice to X1010_splice (donor end), D1010 and D1010H/N/Y; all are likely oncogenic. Y1003 substitutions (CBL binding site) are Level 3A, not 1 or 2. Some files use the alternative isoform numbering 981_1028 for the same exon. OncoKB matches on gene, protein change and consequence, not on genomic coordinates. Its SOP defines a splice mutation as a change in the 2-base region at either end of an intron and leaves variant-type assignment to the sequencing assay. The annotator maps the mutation-file class Splice_Site to splice_region_variant and has no mapping for Intron or Splice_Region. So a deeper intronic variant (polypyrimidine tract or branch point) is annotated as exon 14 skipping only if the mutation file already labels it as a splice variant at codons 963-1010 (e.g. X963_splice, X1010_splice) or as an exon 14 in-frame deletion. The web did not settle an explicit list of intronic genomic positions: no source read gives one. CONFIDENCE DETAIL: high for tumour types and the oncogenic requirement; low for intronic positions, which the web did not settle beyond the protein-level splice variants. HOW SURE: medium. SOURCES: https://www.oncokb.org/actionable-genes, https://www.oncokb.org/gene/BRCA2/Oncogenic%20Mutations, https://www.oncokb.org/gene/BRCA2/Truncating%20Mutations, https://www.oncokb.org/gene/CHEK2/Oncogenic%20Mutations, https://www.oncokb.org/gene/MET, https://www.oncokb.org/gene/MET/X1010_splice, https://www.oncokb.org/gene/MET/Exon%2014%20Deletion, https://www.oncokb.org/gene/MET/Exon%2014%20splice%20mutations, https://sop.oncokb.org/static/sop/OncoKB_Curation_Standard_Operating_Procedure_v6_4.pdf, https://faq.oncokb.org/data-curation, https://raw.githubusercontent.com/oncokb/oncokb-annotator/master/AnnotatorCore.py, https://www.oncokb.org/news, https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S0923753422041412.

text: FINDING: MSK-IMPACT discrete copy-number calls are whole-gene calls from tumour-versus-normal coverage: GC-normalised target coverage is divided by a best-fit unmatched normal, log-ratios are segmented by circular binary segmentation, and a gene is called gained if fold change > 2.0 or lost if fold change < -2.0 with FDR-corrected P < 0.05 against a null built from the segment cluster nearest log-ratio 0 (Cheng 2015); Hyman 2015 states the same rule as 'at least a twofold gain or loss relative to the normalised baseline', adds that narrow amplicons are weighted over broad gains, and that calls are manually reviewed. No purity or ploidy correction is described: Cheng 2015 lists purity/ploidy estimation as future work and the FACETS paper presents purity- and ploidy-adjusted integer copy number as a separate analysis. So a call depends on purity and a purity change alone can create or remove one. No low-level (+1/-1) or arm-level category exists in the rule; single-copy and broad changes below twofold are not reported as discrete calls and show only in the .seg file. To reproduce a call, the segment threshold is roughly log2 ratio >= +1 (amplification) or <= -1 (deletion); this log2 conversion, and the consequence that with a diploid baseline a homozygous deletion reaches -1 only at purity >= 50% and an n-copy amplification reaches +1 only when purity*(n-2) >= 2, are the library's arithmetic, not statements in the sources. Not settled: whether the thresholds were changed for the 468/505-era pipeline (Cheng 2015 says threshold tuning was ongoing), and manual review can override the rule. Confidence medium-high. QUESTION: How are the -2/0/2 discrete copy-number calls in cBioPortal-format MSK-IMPACT data made, are they purity-corrected, and are arm-level or low-level changes reported? SOURCE: https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC5808190/ ; https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC4940024/ ; https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC5027494/

text: FINDING: There is no single convention for 'newly acquired alteration' in paired targeted-panel studies; the papers read report two tiers side by side. A 108-patient MSK-IMPACT longitudinal study of translocation-associated sarcomas (including alveolar RMS) counted every reported alteration absent from the first test as acquired (122 events in 53% of patients), then split them by OncoKB into oncogenic/likely oncogenic (27%) versus VUS (73%) and based its per-histotype comparisons and its 'recurrent acquired' list (TP53 first) on the oncogenic tier; in ARMS 35% of cases acquired VUS only and amplifications were mostly present at baseline. A paired cholangiocarcinoma MSK-IMPACT study filtered to OncoKB oncogenic variants for its main concordance figures but also showed shared/private fractions for oncogenic plus VUS together. A 2013 NSCLC paired study split 311 alterations into known recurrent versus likely passenger and found concordance 94% versus 63%, so the passenger/VUS tier is where most apparent private or 'acquired' calls sit. Practical reading: an all-calls count is a legitimate, published quantity but must be named as such; VUS are not dropped but reported as a separate stratum; a driver-only count needs OncoKB (or similar) annotation, which the task tables lack, so teams should state the limitation and test sensitivity with a proxy (for example known hotspots, truncating mutations in tumour suppressors, focal amplifications/deep deletions of known drivers). Confidence medium: three papers, not a formal standard. QUESTION: In paired earlier/later tumour panel studies, is a newly acquired alteration defined over all calls or only oncogenic/likely oncogenic ones, and how are VUS treated? SOURCE: https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC13347250/ ; https://doi.org/10.1200/po.23.00534 ; https://ascopubs.org/doi/10.1200/JCO.2012.47.7737

text: FINDING: In the curated pan-cancer oncogenic pathway templates (Sanchez-Vega 2018, as shipped in maftools oncogenic_sig_patwhays.tsv) KRAS, NRAS, HRAS and all four ERBB receptors (EGFR, ERBB2, ERBB3, ERBB4) belong to the separate RTK-RAS pathway (85 genes), not to PI3K; the PI3K template (29 genes) is AKT1/2/3, AKT1S1, DEPDC5, DEPTOR, EIF4EBP1, INPP4B, MAPKAP1, MLST8, MTOR, NPRL2, NPRL3, PDK1, PIK3CA, PIK3CB, PIK3R1, PIK3R2, PIK3R3, PPP2R1A, PTEN, RHEB, RICTOR, RPTOR, RPS6, RPS6KB1, STK11, TSC1, TSC2 - so MTOR is PI3K, RAS and ERBB are not. KEGG draws it differently: the KEGG ErbB signalling map hsa04012 (87 genes in MSigDB) contains EGFR, ERBB2/3/4, their ligands, PIK3CA/CB/CD/CG, PIK3R1/2/3/5, AKT1/2/3, MTOR and also KRAS, NRAS, HRAS, RAF, MEK, ERK, but not PTEN, TSC1, TSC2; the KEGG PI3K-Akt map hsa04151 (several hundred genes) contains KRAS, NRAS, HRAS, MTOR, EGFR, ERBB2/3/4, PIK3CA and AKT1 (checked by Entrez ID; the list I got was cut off before PTEN). 'ERBB-PI3K signalling pathway' is not a named gene set in either resource, so there is no single conventional membership: a template-style list (ERBB receptors + PI3K/AKT/MTOR/PTEN core) excludes RAS, a KEGG-ErbB-style list includes RAS and MTOR; both are defensible, so report both and say if the label depends on the choice. The phrase itself was deliberately not searched (it would lead to the task source). QUESTION: Which pathway are KRAS/NRAS/HRAS, MTOR and ERBB receptor genes assigned to in curated templates and KEGG, and which genes does 'ERBB-PI3K signalling pathway' conventionally cover? text: FINDING: vcf2maf sets FILTER=common_variant from population allele counts only, not from dbSNP membership. Release v1.6.11 (Nov 2016) defined it as: allele count in at least one ExAC subpopulation (AFR, AMR, EAS, FIN, NFE, OTH, SAS) > 16 and ClinVar not pathogenic, configurable with --max-filter-ac; release v1.6.12 (Dec 2016) tightened it to AC > 10, dropped the ClinVar exception and instead removed a whitelist of known somatic events from the ExAC VCF. Before v1.6.11 the tag used ExAC allele frequencies (MSKCC ngs-filters describes ExAC AF > 0.0004), and the current main branch has default max_subpop_af = 0.0004 instead of an allele count. The tag only labels rows, it removes nothing. Consequence: a variant with an rsID and a low non-zero population frequency passes unflagged whenever no single ExAC subpopulation has more than 10 alleles (16 in v1.6.11), or when it is absent from ExAC but present in 1000 Genomes/ESP/dbSNP, or sits at a whitelisted somatic site; because the cut is an absolute count per subpopulation, small subpopulations tolerate much higher frequencies than large ones. So absence of the flag does not exclude rare germline variants: unflagged pathway calls that carry dbSNP IDs or any ExAC/1000G frequency should be listed and the test rerun without them. Which vcf2maf version annotated a given file is not recorded in the file, so the 10-vs-16-vs-AF rule cannot be pinned down from the web. QUESTION: What exact rule sets FILTER=common_variant in vcf2maf, and would a variant with a dbSNP ID and low non-zero population frequency pass unflagged? SOURCE: https://zenodo.org/records/164894 ; https://github.com/mskcc/vcf2maf/releases/tag/v1.6.12 ; https://raw.githubusercontent.com/mskcc/vcf2maf/main/vcf2maf.pl ; https://github.com/vanallenlab/common_variant_filter ; https://github.com/mskcc/ngs-filters/

text: FINDING: A uniform (length-scaled, no covariate) background null is known to be badly anti-conservative at gene level but the web gives no single inflation factor for a pathway-level test, and no methods paper read here prescribes a correction for non-silent-only data. Evidence read: Lawrence 2013 - an average-rate method on 178 lung squamous exomes called 450 genes at q<0.1, 101 of them olfactory receptors, with very long genes over-represented although length was already accounted for; their Supplementary Fig. S1 simulation (20,000 genes, 200 patients, no drivers, mean 10 mutations/Mb) gives about 1 false positive under a truly uniform rate but 59 when gene rates are 4, 8 and 20 per Mb (25/50/25 percent) and the same threshold is used, and the same heterogeneity makes the test conservative for low-rate genes (a driver needs 10-fold rather than 4-fold excess). Tokheim 2016 - p-values of several driver methods are not uniform under the null and most methods yield many false positives, worst in high-mutation-rate cancers; they recommend checking observed against theoretical p-values. NIMBus 2020 - assuming a constant rate gives overdispersed counts and numerous false positives; the fix is a gamma-Poisson (negative binomial) model. Practical reading (library inference, not a quoted recommendation): the bias for one pathway can go either way depending on whether its genes have above- or below-average background rates, so treat p-values between 0.005 and 0.08 as not robust; calibrate with an empirical null from random gene sets matched on gene number and total coding length drawn from the same table, and/or replace Poisson/binomial with a negative binomial whose dispersion is estimated from the across-gene spread of non-silent counts per bp, and report whether the call survives. QUESTION: How anti-conservative is a uniform length-scaled background null for pathway mutation-burden tests, and what calibration or overdispersion correction is recommended when only non-silent calls exist? SOURCE: https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC3919509/ ; https://media.springernature.com/original/springer-static/esm/art%3A10.1038%2Fnature12213/MediaObjects/41586_2013_BFnature12213_MOESM255_ESM.pdf ; https://www.pnas.org/doi/full/10.1073/pnas.1616440113 ; https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC7580035/

The versions are nested (410 inside 468 inside 505), so an alteration in any gene outside these two lists was assayable in the earlier sample whatever its panel. How this was obtained: the 505-vs-468 list is a direct set difference of the cBioPortal API definitions of IMPACT505 (505 symbols) and IMPACT468. The 468-vs-410 list is from a paper's supplementary table that splits the 468 genes into 341-panel genes, 69 genes added at 410 and 58 added at 468; its 468 total matches the cBioPortal IMPACT468 list once renamed symbols are reconciled. Caveats: (1) cBioPortal's IMPACT468 holds 469 symbols; the extra one is GTF2I, which is in neither the supplementary 468 list nor IMPACT505. (2) cBioPortal uses current HGNC symbols (CCNQ, WHR1, NSD2, NSD3, H3C*/H3-3A histone names, KMT2A/C/D, ELOC, AMER1 and others) where older tables use the previous names, so match on both. (3) FOXO1 was added at the 410 version and is on all three; PAX3 and PAX7 are not on any version as genes. (4) No independent IMPACT410 gene list was read, and gene membership says nothing about which introns are tiled for rearrangement detection. HOW SURE: high for 505 vs 468; medium to high for 468 vs 410 (single supplementary table, total cross-checked). SOURCES: https://www.cbioportal.org/api/gene-panels/IMPACT505, https://www.cbioportal.org/api/gene-panels/IMPACT468, https://www.thelancet.com/cms/10.1016/S2589-7500(21)00104-7/attachment/93631f3d-043d-42b8-b9b4-c0df6cc9a5cb/mmc1.pdf.

question: FINDING FROM THE LAB'S LIBRARY, asked for by the director. QUESTION: In cBioPortal-format data from a targeted hybrid-capture panel where the discrete copy-number table contains only the values -2, 0 and 2, how are those calls made (fold-change and significance thresholds), are they corrected for tumour purity, and are arm-level or low-level gains and losses reported at all? ANSWER: Calling rule (MSK-IMPACT validation paper, Cheng 2015): GC-normalised coverage of target regions in the tumour is divided by that of the best-fitting normal from a pool of control normals (not necessarily the matched normal), log-transformed, and segmented by circular binary segmentation; segments are clustered and the cluster nearest log-ratio 0 defines a null distribution. A whole-gene event is called when fold change > 2.0 (gain) or < -2.0 (loss) with P < 0.05 after false-discovery-rate correction; germline copy-number calls from the matched normal are subtracted. Hyman 2015 states the same rule as 'at least a twofold gain or loss relative to the matched normalised baseline', adds that narrow amplicons are considered more likely significant than broad gains, and that every call is manually reviewed. Cheng 2015 names purity/ploidy estimation as future work, and the FACETS paper presents purity-, ploidy-adjusted integer copy number as a separate analysis needed to interpret panel calls. Sub-threshold and broad changes are visible only in the segment file. Threshold to reproduce a call from segments: about log2 ratio >= +1 for an amplification and <= -1 for a deletion. This conversion is my arithmetic, not a statement in the sources, as is the consequence that with a diploid baseline a homozygous deletion reaches -1 only at purity >= 50%, and an n-copy amplification reaches +1 only when purity x (n - 2) >= 2. question: FINDING FROM THE LAB'S LIBRARY, asked for by the director. QUESTION: In studies that sequence paired earlier and later (relapse or metastasis) tumour samples from the same patient with a targeted panel, how is a 'newly acquired alteration' conventionally defined: are all called variants and copy-number calls counted, or only oncogenic or likely oncogenic alterations (for example OncoKB-annotated), and how are variants of unknown significance treated? ANSWER: The web does not show one fixed convention. The three papers read report two tiers side by side: all reported alterations, and the oncogenic or likely oncogenic subset, with the interpretation resting mainly on the second. (1) A 108-patient longitudinal MSK-IMPACT study of translocation-associated sarcomas, including alveolar rhabdomyosarcoma, counted every reported alteration absent from the first test as acquired (122 events in 53% of patients, mean 2.1 per case), then split them by OncoKB: 27% oncogenic/likely oncogenic, 73% VUS. Its per-histotype comparison and its list of recurrent acquired events (TP53 first, 10% of patients) use the oncogenic tier. In ARMS, 35% of cases acquired VUS only, and the amplifications were mostly present at baseline. (2) A paired cholangiocarcinoma MSK-IMPACT study filtered alterations to OncoKB oncogenic variants for its main results, and defined concordance as shared over (shared + private to either sample), reported both as overall (oncogenic mutations, CNAs and rearrangements) and mutation-only; it also showed one figure with oncogenic and VUS together (849 alterations, 38% oncogenic). (3) A 2013 paired NSCLC panel study split 311 alterations into known recurrent versus likely passenger; concordance was 94% versus 63%, so most apparently private calls sat in the passenger tier (abstract only read). What this means for the teams: counting every call is a published quantity, but it is the broader of two and should be named 'all alterations private to the later sample'. VUS are not discarded in these papers; they are reported as their own stratum. A driver-only count needs OncoKB-style annotation, which the task tables do not hold, so the group comparison should be stated as an all-calls result and, if possible, re-run on a proxy driver subset to see whether the direction holds. HOW SURE: medium. SOURCES: https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC13347250/, https://doi.org/10.1200/po.23.00534, https://ascopubs.org/doi/10.1200/JCO.2012.47.7737.

label: FINDING
text: FINDING: The sources read (array CGH, SNP array, shallow WGS and whole-genome-amplification papers; none exome-specific) define GC waves as deviations of log ratio from the 2-copy baseline whose size and direction follow regional GC content, seen on every platform. After a genome-wide GC regression the four most GC-rich chromosomes (19, 22, 17, 16) sat consistently ABOVE baseline and the five most AT-rich (4, 13, 5, 6, 3) BELOW; an uncorrected wave on 19p produced a false duplication call, and wave-driven false positives were 2-20 Mb. Direction is not fixed: peaks and troughs sit at the same positions in all samples, but amplitude varies sample to sample and in a few samples the wave is reversed (a 'slight dip in chromosome 19' recurred in tumour and normal profiles in another dataset). Amplitude grows with low DNA quantity and poor quality (FFPE noise is reproducible in size and shape and is not removed by deeper sequencing); no source gives a universal amplitude, but waves were large enough to hide or fragment simulated arm-level changes of +/-0.25 log2 and they add spurious breakpoints. Recurrent artefacts also cluster at (peri)centromeric and (sub)telomeric regions. No source gives 'location in a GC-rich region' as a sufficient criterion. Criteria the sources do support, usable without per-target GC: (1) coordination, the same sample shows same-sign small shifts across the GC-rich set 16/17/19/22 with opposite-sign shifts on AT-rich 3/4/5/6/13; (2) recurrence, the same segments at the same coordinates appear in unrelated samples or in normals, whereas true CNAs are uncorrelated with the wave; (3) amplitude tracks sample quality/noise and the sample has excess segments; (4) orthogonal confirmation (FISH in the source; allelic imbalance is my inference). Apply any exclusion identically to every sample, because 1q, 16p, 17q, 19q and 20 are also genuine recurrent gains in breast lesions. Exome-specific amplitude and a validated rule for separating waves from subclonal gains were NOT found. QUESTION: In tumour-vs-normal exome log2 profiles, what do GC-wave artefacts look like after segmentation (regions, direction, amplitude) and what criteria separate them from true low-level or subclonal gains when per-target GC is unavailable? SOURCE: https://www.jmdjournal.org/article/S1525-1578(12)00174-2/fulltext ; https://doi.org/10.1093/nar/gkn556 ; https://doi.org/10.1093/bioinformatics/btp132 ; https://d-nb.info/1098924398/34 ; https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC4248318/ ; https://ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pmc/articles/PMC2490749/

label: FINDING
text: FINDING: For a clonal one-copy change in a diploid genome at lesional-cell fraction p, expected log2 ratio is log2(1 + p/2) for a gain and log2(1 - p/2) for a loss (for a subclonal event replace p by p x cancer-cell fraction). Values gain/loss: p=1.0 +0.585/-1.00; 0.8 +0.49/-0.74; 0.6 +0.38/-0.51; 0.5 +0.32/-0.415; 0.4 +0.26/-0.32; 0.3 +0.20/-0.23; 0.2 +0.14/-0.15; 0.1 +0.07/-0.07. CNVkit docs state the pure values and the 50% loss value (-0.415) and suggest thresholds of 0.1-0.2 with downstream filtering or 0.3 without. Solving the formula, a one-copy gain crosses |log2| 0.3 only at p>=0.46 (loss p>=0.38), crosses 0.2 at p>=0.30 (loss p>=0.26) and crosses 0.1 at p>=0.14 (loss p>=0.13). A clinical CNVkit panel validation (in silico and wet dilution) confirmed observed log2 tracks this formula and lost a heterozygous deletion at about 50% purity with a -0.4 cutoff, while a high-level amplification stayed detectable down to 20%. A clonal heterozygous SNV has VAF about p/2, so at p=0.1-0.2 mutations at 5-10% VAF are still callable at exome depth while a one-copy arm change is only 0.07-0.15 log2, inside FFPE noise/wave range; a flat profile is then uninformative, not quiet. Working rule (my derivation, not a published cutoff): estimate p as 2 x VAF of the shared truncal mutations; p below about 0.25-0.3 means flat = uninformative at a 0.2 cutoff; p at or above about 0.4-0.5 means flat = no clonal arm-level events. The pages read did NOT give a minimum purity for FACETS or Sequenza specifically; CopyDetective's paper says the detectable cell fraction is sample-specific (set by coverage and event length) and should be computed per sample. QUESTION: What log2 ratio is expected for a clonal single-copy gain or loss as a function of lesional-cell fraction, and below what fraction do exome callers stop detecting arm-level events while point mutations are still called? SOURCE: https://cnvkit.readthedocs.io/en/stable/calling.html ; https://cnvkit.readthedocs.io/en/stable/heterogeneity.html ; https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC9302205/ ; https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC7604644/ ; https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC5027494/

label: FINDING
text: FINDING: There is no single convention; published precursor-vs-synchronous-carcinoma breast studies use both counts and genome fractions, and thresholds range from about 0.08 to 0.3 log2. (a) Kim et al. 2015 (pure DCIS vs synchronous DCIS and IDC, 180K aCGH plus exome) report 'the numbers of CNAs' as a COUNT of gained/lost segments with log2 > 0.3 or < -0.3, no minimum size stated (medians 28, 71 and 56 per lesion; group difference not significant). (b) Liao et al. 2012 (FFPE BAC aCGH, autosomes only) compare 'average fractional gain/loss/total fractional CNAs', i.e. FRACTION of the genome called altered, with data-derived cutoffs of -0.125/+0.1325 (noise mode +/-1.96 SD), yet word the result as 'a larger number of CNAs', so 'number' is used loosely for fraction. (c) Hernandez et al. 2012 (BAC aCGH, microdissected to >70% tumour cells) classify each clone as amplification >0.45, gain >0.08 to 0.45, loss <-0.08 and compare per-locus frequencies, not a per-sample total. (d) Pareja et al. 2020 (exome, FACETS) compare the frequency of gains/losses and amplifications/homozygous deletions and count CNA events on phylogeny branches; cutoffs were not in the text retrieved. (e) Johnson et al. 2012 report percent of genome shared. Minimum segment sizes were not stated in these studies; a clinical panel pipeline required more than four contiguous bins. So a literal 'number of CNAs' is most often a count of threshold-crossing gained/lost segments at about +/-0.3 (which excludes small low-level segments), while low cutoffs near 0.1 come from high-purity microdissected array data with platform-specific noise estimates; report both the segment/event count and fraction of genome altered and state the cutoff. QUESTION: When studies compare the 'number of copy number alterations' between a precursor or benign lesion and a synchronous carcinoma from segmented log2 data, how is the number defined and what thresholds and minimum sizes are standard? SOURCE: https://www.oncotarget.com/article/3162/text/ ; https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC3465468/ ; https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC4975517/ ; https://aacrjournals.org/clincancerres/article/26/14/3682/9977/Whole-Exome-Sequencing-Analysis-of-the-Progression ; https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC3327281/ ; https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC9302205/

The malformed 'TC'/'C' suffixes are of unknown meaning (16 of the 18 such rows in the file are CALR) so I did not count them as orthogonal validation. t_alt_count/n_alt_count are empty; variant reads were derived as reads x percentage: tumour variant reads range 1-16 (median 6), germline depth behind the 0% calls is 2,2,3,4,4,5,6,7,9,11,15,16,17,17,18,23,23,26,37. question: FINDING FROM THE LAB'S LIBRARY, asked for by the director. QUESTION: In curated oncogenic signalling pathway templates (for example the pan-cancer curated pathway templates and the KEGG ErbB and PI3K-Akt maps), which pathway are KRAS/NRAS/HRAS, MTOR and the ERBB receptor genes assigned to: are RAS genes part of the PI3K pathway or of a separate RTK-RAS pathway, and when a paper speaks of an 'ERBB-PI3K signalling pathway' which genes does that phrase conventionally cover? ANSWER: Curated pan-cancer templates (Sanchez-Vega 2018 gene lists, read as the table shipped with maftools): KRAS, NRAS, HRAS and all four ERBB receptors (EGFR, ERBB2, ERBB3, ERBB4) are in a separate RTK-RAS pathway (85 genes); they are NOT in the PI3K template. The PI3K template has 29 genes: AKT1, AKT2, AKT3, AKT1S1, DEPDC5, DEPTOR, EIF4EBP1, INPP4B, MAPKAP1, MLST8, MTOR, NPRL2, NPRL3, PDK1, PIK3CA, PIK3CB, PIK3R1, PIK3R2, PIK3R3, PPP2R1A, PTEN, RHEB, RICTOR, RPTOR, RPS6, RPS6KB1, STK11, TSC1, TSC2. So MTOR is PI3K; RAS and ERBB are RTK-RAS. KEGG draws the boundary differently. The KEGG ErbB signalling map hsa04012 (87 genes in the MSigDB copy) contains EGFR, ERBB2/3/4 and their ligands, PIK3CA/CB/CD/CG, PIK3R1/2/3/5, AKT1/2/3, MTOR, and also KRAS, NRAS, HRAS with the RAF-MEK-ERK arm; it does not contain PTEN, TSC1 or TSC2. The KEGG PI3K-Akt map hsa04151 contains KRAS, NRAS, HRAS, MTOR, EGFR, ERBB2/3/4, PIK3CA and AKT1 (confirmed by Entrez ID, mapped to symbols from my own knowledge; the list returned was cut off after 258 entries, before PTEN, so PTEN membership was not confirmed there). The phrase 'ERBB-PI3K signalling pathway' is not a named gene set in either resource, and the web as consulted does not settle a single conventional membership. I did not search the phrase itself because that would lead to the task's source. Two readings are defensible: a template-style list (ERBB receptors plus the PI3K/AKT/MTOR/PTEN core) excludes RAS; a KEGG-ErbB-style list includes RAS and MTOR. Neither team's list can be called the primary one on convention alone; the result should be reported for both, and the label should be flagged as definition-dependent if they disagree. HOW SURE: high for template and KEGG membership; low for any single conventional meaning of the phrase (not settled). SOURCES: https://raw.githubusercontent.com/PoisonAlien/maftools/master/inst/extdata/oncogenic_sig_patwhays.tsv, https://www.gsea-msigdb.org/gsea/msigdb/human/download_geneset.jsp?geneSetName=KEGG_ERBB_SIGNALING_PATHWAY&fileType=json, https://rest.kegg.jp/link/hsa/hsa04151, https://www.genome.jp/entry/pathway+hsa04012, https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC6070353/.

question: FINDING FROM THE LAB'S LIBRARY, asked for by the director. QUESTION: When a mutation table carries the FILTER value 'common_variant' as assigned by the standard MAF annotation pipeline used for public cancer-genomics portals (vcf2maf), what exact rule sets it: which population database and sub-populations, what allele-frequency or allele-count threshold, and would a variant with a dbSNP ID and a low but non-zero population frequency pass unflagged? ANSWER: The rule is based on population allele counts in ExAC, not on dbSNP membership. vcf2maf v1.6.11 release notes (Nov 2016): common_variant is set 'if allele count across at least one ExAC subpopulation (AFR AMR EAS FIN NFE OTH SAS) is >16, and ClinVar doesn't say it's pathogenic', configurable with --max-filter-ac. v1.6.12 (Dec 2016): cutoff tightened from AC>16 to AC>10, ClinVar exception dropped, and a whitelist of known somatic events is removed from the ExAC VCF instead. Before v1.6.11 the tag used ExAC allele frequencies (the MSKCC ngs-filters README gives ExAC AF > 0.0004). The current main branch sets a default max_subpop_af of 0.0004 in place of an allele count; I read that default in the script header but not the body, so the database it is applied to in current versions (I believe gnomAD subpopulations) is not confirmed. The ExAC file used by default in the allele-count era appears to be the non-TCGA ExAC r0.3.1 sites VCF, but I saw that only in a search snippet of a fork. Yes, a variant with a dbSNP ID and a low non-zero frequency passes unflagged: an rsID alone never triggers the tag; a variant is unflagged if no single ExAC subpopulation carries more than 10 alleles (16 in v1.6.11), if it is absent from ExAC but present in 1000 Genomes, ESP or dbSNP, or if it is at a whitelisted somatic site. Because the cut is an absolute count per subpopulation, it corresponds to a much higher frequency in small subpopulations than in large ones. The tag only labels rows and removes nothing. So the absence of the flag does not rule out rare germline variants. Unflagged calls in the pathway genes that carry an rsID or any population-frequency entry still need to be listed and the test rerun without them. Which vcf2maf version annotated the teams' file is not something the web can tell, so whether the 10, 16 or frequency rule applied is unsettled. HOW SURE: high for the ExAC subpopulation allele-count rule and that low-frequency dbSNP variants pass; medium for which version and threshold applies to this file. SOURCES: https://zenodo.org/records/164894, https://github.com/mskcc/vcf2maf/releases/tag/v1.6.12, https://raw.githubusercontent.com/mskcc/vcf2maf/main/vcf2maf.pl, https://github.com/vanallenlab/common_variant_filter, https://github.com/mskcc/ngs-filters/.

question: FINDING FROM THE LAB'S LIBRARY, asked for by the director. QUESTION: For self-contained pathway or gene-set mutation-burden tests on exome data that use a uniform, coding-length-scaled background rate without gene-specific covariates (expression, replication timing) or a silent-mutation background, how anti-conservative is the null known to be, and what simple calibration or overdispersion correction do methods papers recommend when only non-silent calls are available? ANSWER: Partly settled. At gene level the uniform null is known to be badly anti-conservative, but none of the papers read gives an inflation factor for a single pathway-level test, and none prescribes a correction specifically for non-silent-only data. What the sources say: Lawrence 2013 applied an average-rate method to 178 lung squamous exomes and got 450 genes at q<0.1, 101 of them olfactory receptors, with very long genes over-represented even though the test already scaled for length. Their Supplementary Fig. S1 simulation (20,000 genes of 1,500 bp, 200 patients, no drivers, mean 10 mutations/Mb) yields about 1 false positive when the rate really is uniform and 59 when gene rates are 4, 8 and 20 per Mb (25/50/25%) under the same threshold. The same figure shows the bias runs both ways: for low-rate genes the uniform null is conservative (a driver needs a 10-fold rather than 4-fold excess to be detected). Tokheim 2016 found the p-values of several driver methods inconsistent with the uniform distribution expected under the null, with many false positives especially in high-mutation-rate cancers, and made comparison of observed against theoretical p-values part of their evaluation framework. NIMBus 2020 states that assuming a constant rate gives overdispersed counts and numerous false positives, and corrects it with a gamma-Poisson (negative binomial) model. My reading, not a quoted recommendation: for one pathway the direction of the bias depends on whether its genes have above- or below-average background rates, so p-values between about 0.005 and 0.08 under this null should be treated as not robust. The two simple checks consistent with these papers are (a) an empirical null from random gene sets matched on number of genes and total coding length, drawn from the same mutation table, and (b) replacing the Poisson/binomial with a negative binomial whose dispersion is estimated from the across-gene spread of non-silent counts per bp. The label should rest on whether the call survives both. HOW SURE: medium: high that the uniform null is miscalibrated at gene level and that negative-binomial overdispersion is the standard remedy; low on the size of the effect for one pathway and on any prescribed fix for non-silent-only data (not settled by the web). SOURCES: https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC3919509/, https://media.springernature.com/original/springer-static/esm/art%3A10.1038%2Fnature12213/MediaObjects/41586_2013_BFnature12213_MOESM255_ESM.pdf, https://www.pnas.org/doi/full/10.1073/pnas.1616440113, https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC7580035/.

question: FINDING FROM THE LAB'S LIBRARY, asked for by the director. QUESTION: In tumour-versus-normal log2 ratio profiles derived from whole-exome sequencing (especially of archival or low-input tissue), what do GC-content 'wave' artefacts look like after segmentation: which genomic regions are typically affected (for example gene-dense, GC-rich subtelomeric regions and chromosomes 16, 17, 19, 22), in which direction and at what amplitude, and what criteria are recommended to tell them apart from true low-level or subclonal copy-number gains when GC content per target is not available? ANSWER: Partly settled. The pages read are array-CGH, SNP-array, shallow-WGS and whole-genome-amplification papers; none is exome-specific, so exome amplitude figures and a validated rule for separating waves from subclonal gains were not found. What they establish: GC waves are deviations of the log ratio from the two-copy baseline whose size and direction follow regional GC content, on every platform. Regions and direction: after a genome-wide GC regression the four most GC-rich chromosomes (19, 22, 17, 16) sat consistently above baseline and the five most AT-rich (4, 13, 5, 6, 3) below; an uncorrected wave on 19p produced a false duplication call, and wave-driven false positives were 2-20 Mb. The direction is not fixed: peaks and troughs fall at the same positions in all samples, but amplitude differs between samples and in a few samples the wave is reversed (another dataset had a recurrent slight dip on chromosome 19 in tumour and normal profiles). Recurrent artefacts also cluster at (peri)centromeric and (sub)telomeric regions; in amplified DNA, over-represented regions are GC-rich and artefacts are reproducible. Amplitude: no universal figure. It grows with low DNA quantity and poor quality; FFPE-related noise is reproducible in size and shape and is not removed by deeper sequencing. Waves were large enough to hide or fragment simulated arm-level changes of +/-0.25 log2, and they add spurious breakpoints. Criteria: no source treats location in a GC-rich region as sufficient. Supported criteria that work without per-target GC are (1) coordination: the same sample shows same-sign small shifts across 16/17/19/22 with opposite-sign shifts on 3/4/5/6/13; (2) recurrence: the same segments at the same coordinates appear in unrelated samples or in normals, whereas true alterations are uncorrelated with the wave; (3) amplitude tracks the sample's noise and the sample has excess segments; (4) orthogonal confirmation (FISH in the source; using allelic imbalance is my inference, not from a page read). Any exclusion should be applied identically to every sample, because 1q, 16p, 17q, 19q and 20 are also genuine recurrent gains in breast lesions. HOW SURE: medium. SOURCES: https://www.jmdjournal.org/article/S1525-1578(12)00174-2/fulltext, https://doi.org/10.1093/nar/gkn556, https://doi.org/10.1093/bioinformatics/btp132, https://d-nb.info/1098924398/34, https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC4248318/, https://ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pmc/articles/PMC2490749/.

Waves were large enough to hide or fragment simulated arm-level changes of +/-0.25 log2, and they add spurious breakpoints. Criteria: no source treats location in a GC-rich region as sufficient. Supported criteria that work without per-target GC are (1) coordination: the same sample shows same-sign small shifts across 16/17/19/22 with opposite-sign shifts on 3/4/5/6/13; (2) recurrence: the same segments at the same coordinates appear in unrelated samples or in normals, whereas true alterations are uncorrelated with the wave; (3) amplitude tracks the sample's noise and the sample has excess segments; (4) orthogonal confirmation (FISH in the source; using allelic imbalance is my inference, not from a page read). question: FINDING FROM THE LAB'S LIBRARY, asked for by the director. QUESTION: For exome-based copy-number segmentation, what log2 ratio is expected for a clonal single-copy gain or loss as a function of the fraction of lesional cells in the sample, and below what lesional-cell fraction do standard callers (for example FACETS, CNVkit, Sequenza) stop detecting arm-level events while somatic point mutations may still be called? ANSWER: Formula settled; tool-specific cut-offs not settled. For a clonal one-copy change in a diploid genome at lesional-cell fraction p, expected log2 ratio = log2(1 + p/2) for a gain and log2(1 - p/2) for a loss (for a subclonal event, replace p by p x cancer-cell fraction). Gain/loss: p=1.0 +0.585/-1.00; 0.8 +0.49/-0.74; 0.6 +0.38/-0.51; 0.5 +0.32/-0.415; 0.4 +0.26/-0.32; 0.3 +0.20/-0.23; 0.2 +0.14/-0.15; 0.1 +0.07/-0.07. CNVkit's documentation gives the pure values and the 50% loss value and suggests cut-offs of 0.1-0.2 with downstream filtering or 0.3 without. Solving the formula, a one-copy gain crosses |log2| 0.3 only at p >= 0.46 (loss p >= 0.38), 0.2 at p >= 0.30 (loss p >= 0.26) and 0.1 at p >= 0.14 (loss p >= 0.13). A clinical CNVkit panel validation confirmed that observed log2 follows this formula under dilution and lost a heterozygous deletion at about 50% purity with a -0.4 cut-off, while a high-level amplification remained detectable down to 20%. A clonal heterozygous point mutation has VAF about p/2, so at p = 0.1-0.2 mutations at 5-10% VAF are still callable at exome depth while a one-copy arm change is only 0.07-0.15 log2; a flat profile is then uninformative rather than quiet. Working rule (my derivation from the formula, not a published cut-off): estimate p as 2 x VAF of the shared truncal mutations; below about 0.25-0.3 a flat profile is uninformative at a 0.2 cut-off; at or above about 0.4-0.5 a flat profile means no clonal arm-level events. Not found: a stated minimum purity for FACETS or Sequenza (the FACETS paper text retrieved gave none; no Sequenza page was read). The CopyDetective paper says the detectable cell fraction is sample-specific, set by coverage and event length, and should be computed per sample. HOW SURE: medium. SOURCES: https://cnvkit.readthedocs.io/en/stable/calling.html, https://cnvkit.readthedocs.io/en/stable/heterogeneity.html, https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC9302205/, https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC7604644/, https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC5027494/.

question: FINDING FROM THE LAB'S LIBRARY, asked for by the director. QUESTION: When published studies compare the 'number of copy number alterations' between a precursor or benign lesion and a synchronous carcinoma from segmented log2 data, how is that number conventionally defined: count of gained/lost segments, count of merged events or altered chromosome arms, or fraction of genome altered; and what log2 thresholds and minimum segment sizes are standard for such counts? ANSWER: No single convention; counts and genome fractions are both used, with cut-offs from about 0.08 to 0.3 log2. Kim et al. 2015 (pure DCIS vs synchronous DCIS and IDC; 180K aCGH plus exome) report 'the numbers of CNAs' as a count of gained/lost segments with log2 > 0.3 or < -0.3, with no minimum size stated (medians 28, 71 and 56 per lesion; group difference not significant). Liao et al. 2012 (FFPE BAC aCGH, autosomes only) compare average fractional gain, loss and total fractional CNAs, i.e. fraction of the genome called altered, with data-derived cut-offs of -0.125/+0.1325 (noise mode +/- 1.96 SD), yet describe the result as 'a larger number of CNAs'. Hernandez et al. 2012 (BAC aCGH, microdissected to >70% tumour cells) classify each clone as amplification > 0.45, gain > 0.08 to 0.45, loss < -0.08 and compare per-locus frequencies, not a per-sample total. Pareja et al. 2020 (exome, FACETS) compare the frequency of gains/losses and amplifications/homozygous deletions and count CNA events on phylogeny branches; their cut-offs were not in the text retrieved. Johnson et al. 2012 report percentage of genome shared. Minimum segment sizes were not stated in these studies; a clinical panel pipeline required more than four contiguous bins. No study read counted altered chromosome arms as its 'number'. So a literal 'number of CNAs' is most often a count of threshold-crossing gained/lost segments at about +/-0.3, which excludes small low-level segments; cut-offs near 0.1 come from high-purity microdissected array data with platform-specific noise estimates. The wording 'number' is also used for genome fraction, so reporting both, with the cut-off stated, matches practice. HOW SURE: medium. SOURCES: https://www.oncotarget.com/article/3162/text/, https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC3465468/, https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC4975517/, https://aacrjournals.org/clincancerres/article/26/14/3682/9977/Whole-Exome-Sequencing-Analysis-of-the-Progression, https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC3327281/, https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC9302205/.

text: REPLY to director Q1 (CNA all-zero samples, bd08-team-b): 25 of 66 samples have 0 for every one of the 59 genes in data_cna.txt (bait_v3 7/10, bait_v4 3/11, bait_v5 15/45; v3 vs rest Fisher p=0.03); there are no NA values and the panel matrix has only a 'mutations' column, so PTEN=0 means 'no deep deletion called', not proven intact. Mean -2 calls per sample are 1.3 (v3), 0.36 (v4), 0.98 (v5), Kruskal p=0.46; PTEN -2 calls are 1/10, 0/11, 7/45. The sample with PTEN=-2 plus a PTEN missense is DS-vem-16-MT1 (patient VT016m1, V53E, bait_v3, PFS 1.9 mo): it has the most -2 calls (9), five of them on chromosome 10 (PTEN, FAS, FGFR2, TET1, MAP3K8), so the 'deep deletion' is probably a single-copy chromosome-10 loss over-called, and -2 calls cannot be read as strict homozygous loss. With the 21 all-zero samples removed from the reference group, PTEN LoF vs others is HR 1.79 (95% CI 0.91-3.51, p=0.09; median PFS 2.6 vs 5.4 mo) against HR 1.97 (1.04-3.73) before: direction unchanged, interval now includes 1. Truncating mutations alone, which do not use CNA, give HR 2.56 (1.01-6.50). Randomly relabelling 4 of the 21 all-zero references as hidden LoF gives HR<1 in 1.3% of draws; only relabelling the 3 longest-PFS ones (worst case) flips it. Does not change the method or the label (False), but the result must be described as borderline.

text: REPLY to director Q2 (response grade double counting, bd08-team-b): RESPONSE_GRADE is essentially a banding of PFS_MONTHS, not of RECIST response: Poor = PFS 1.6-4.2 mo (n=22, includes 8 PR and 5 SD), Intermediate = 3.5-11.4 (n=17), Excellent = 7.1-58.9 (n=23), NE = 4 patients; bands overlap only slightly at the edges. label: FINDING
text: FINDING: No published, validated way to infer chromoplexy-type chained rearrangements from copy-number segments alone was found; a 2024 review states chromoplexy has been inferred solely from whole-genome sequencing, and chain methods work on graphs of rearrangement junctions. A 'deletion bridge' is a deleted stretch lying between breakpoints that belong to two DIFFERENT fusions of a chain (copy number shows the loss; junction calls are what show the two edges join to other loci rather than to each other), so in a segment file it looks the same as a simple independent deletion. Reviews describe chromoplexy as largely copy-neutral with bridges only 'occasionally' present (about 60% of chromoplectic Ewing sarcomas had any), and no source read quantifies how specific multi-locus small deletions are for chains, so such a pattern is at most a compatible footprint, not a test of interdependence. The numeric bridge thresholds of the original chain model were not retrieved because they sit in the paper that appears to be this task's source, which was deliberately not opened. QUESTION: Can chained (chromoplexy) events be inferred from copy-number segments alone, what is a deletion bridge and how specific are multi-locus small deletions for chains? label: FINDING
text: FINDING: In ERG break-apart FISH a split of the red (centromeric, 3-prime ERG) and green (telomeric, 5-prime ERG) probe pair means ERG is rearranged with both sides still present in the nucleus ('translocation', also called insertion or Esplit), and a lone red signal with loss of the green one means rearrangement with interstitial deletion of the roughly 3 Mb between ERG and TMPRSS2 ('translocation with deletion', Edel); both classes correspond to TMPRSS2-ERG fusion. Because the two genes lie in the same orientation on 21q, fusing them requires the intervening DNA to leave its place, so in the no-deletion class it has been moved, described as insertion elsewhere in the genome or exchange between the two chromosome 21 homologues; in sequenced tumours such copy-neutral fusions were found inside balanced closed chains of 3 to 4 loci (one on chromosomes 1 and 21, one wholly within chromosome 21). The FISH class alone does not prove more than two breakpoints or another chromosome (an inter-homologue exchange needs two breaks and no other chromosome), cannot see losses smaller than the probe, and the deletion class does not say whether the loss was a simple deletion or part of a chain; it is a coarse per-sample copy-loss versus copy-retaining mechanism variable, not a test of chained origin. QUESTION: What do the ERG FISH classes 'translocation' and 'translocation with deletion' mean mechanistically and what does a fusion without loss of the intervening 3 Mb imply? SOURCE: https://aacrjournals.org/cancerres/article/66/17/8337/526226/TMPRSS2-ERG-Fusion-Associated-Deletions-Provide ; https://www.jmdjournal.org/article/S1525-1578(12)00100-6/pdf ; https://ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pmc/articles/PMC1601467/ ; https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC8126330/ ; https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC3075885/ ; https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC3632390/

question: FINDING FROM THE LAB'S LIBRARY, asked for by the director. QUESTION: Is there any published, validated way to infer chained (interdependent) rearrangement events of the chromoplexy type from copy-number segment profiles alone, without junction-level structural-variant calls? In particular, what is a 'deletion bridge' in the original chain-detection model, how is it defined from copy-number data, and how specific is a pattern of small deletions at multiple loci on different chromosomes for chained rearrangement versus independent events? ANSWER: No such method was found. A 2024 review states that chromoplexy events have so far been inferred solely from whole-genome sequencing data, and the chain methods described in the pages read build graphs from rearrangement junctions (breakpoints as nodes, rearrangements as edges, e.g. clustering breakpoints closer than 10 kb). Reviews describe chromoplexy as leaving little or no copy-number change, so most of a chain is invisible to a segment file. A 'deletion bridge' is a deleted stretch at the junctions of a chain that spans the sequence between breakpoints belonging to two different fusions (equivalently, a looped rearrangement cluster in which a deletion spans two breakpoints, so the paired breakpoints sit further apart than in a precise balanced join). Copy number supplies the loss; the junction calls are what show that the two edges of the loss are joined to other loci rather than to each other. In a segment file a bridge therefore looks the same as a simple, independent two-break deletion. Specificity is not established: no page read gives a figure for how specific small deletions at several loci are for chained versus independent events. Bridges are described as occurring only 'occasionally' alongside mostly copy-neutral junctions, and were present in about 60% (30/52) of chromoplectic Ewing sarcomas. Multi-locus small deletions are at most a compatible footprint, not a test of interdependence, so the teams' rule (segments alone cannot test interdependence) stands on this evidence. Not settled: the numeric bridge criteria of the original chain-detection model (copy-ratio cut-off, maximum bridge length). They are in the methods of the paper that appears to be the source of this task; it came up in search and I did not open it. The reviews I opened do summarise that paper's conclusions; I have not relayed them because they are not evidence from the task's tables. HOW SURE: medium. SOURCES: https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC7616040/, https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC6176908/, https://www.nature.com/articles/s12276-018-0112-3, https://www.mdpi.com/1422-0067/26/8/3826.
