question: FINDING FROM THE LAB'S LIBRARY, asked for by the director. QUESTION: In segment (.seg) files derived from tumour/normal whole-genome sequencing rather than arrays, what does the num.mark field count, and what do segments with only 2 markers spanning tens to a few thousand base pairs with strongly negative log ratios usually represent? Do common WGS copy-number pipelines (for example read-depth segmenters used at large sequencing centres around 2011-2013) seed segment boundaries from rearrangement breakpoints, so that such small segments mark somatic deletion junctions, or are they typically germline CNVs or noise? ANSWER: num.mark is the number of markers inside the segment: array probes, or read-depth bins/data points for sequencing. The CBS documentation defines the column as 'the number of markers in the segment' and sets the default minimum for a changed segment at 2 markers, so a 2-marker segment is the smallest the segmenter can emit. The read-depth segmenter published by the Broad in 2009 (SegSeq) places boundaries only from tumour/normal read counts in local windows of about 300-400 normal reads, followed by merging; it does not use rearrangement junctions. Seeding segment boundaries from SV breakpoints was presented as a new feature by CONSERTING in 2015, which also says read-depth-only tools bury real focal changes among hundreds or thousands of false CNAs from coverage bias, mapping ambiguity and library artefacts. So breakpoint-seeded segmentation was not the common default in 2011-2013 on the evidence read. Standard practice treats tiny few-marker segments as unreliable or germline: GISTIC joins segments with fewer than 4 markers to their neighbour by default and accepts a germline-CNV exclusion file, the GDC pipeline masks probe sets in frequent germline CNVs, and the cBioPortal SEG format example itself contains a 2-marker, 134-bp, -1.50 row between long near-zero segments. The default reading of 2-marker, tens-to-thousands-bp, strongly negative segments is germline CNV or noise, not somatic deletion junctions. Not settled: how this study's seg file was produced. No page read describes it, and I did not open the study itself. Two markers spanning only tens of base pairs fits array-probe spacing better than WGS bins, so the premise that the file is WGS-derived should be checked: a total num.mark near 1.8 million per sample would point to a SNP array, and tiny segments recurring at identical coordinates across samples would point to germline CNV or artefact. HOW SURE: medium for what num.mark means and how small segments are conventionally treated; low for what the small segments are in this particular file. SOURCES: https://rdrr.io/bioc/DNAcopy/man/segment.html, https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC2630795/, https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC4591043/, https://broadinstitute.github.io/gistic2/, https://docs.gdc.cancer.gov/Data/Bioinformatics_Pipelines/CNV_Pipeline/, https://docs.cbioportal.org/file-formats/.

question: FINDING FROM THE LAB'S LIBRARY, asked for by the director. QUESTION: In break-apart FISH assays for ERG rearrangement in prostate tumours, what do the two result classes 'translocation' (split signal) and 'translocation with deletion' (loss of one signal) mean mechanistically? When a fusion between two genes about 3 Mb apart on the same chromosome arm occurs without loss of the intervening sequence, what does that imply about where the intervening segment went and whether more than two breakpoints or other chromosomes must be involved? ANSWER: The assay uses a centromeric (3' ERG, red) and a telomeric (5' ERG, green) probe that overlap as yellow on a normal allele. A split into separate red and green signals means ERG is rearranged with both sides still present in the nucleus; this is the 'translocation' class, also called insertion or Esplit. A lone red signal with the green one lost means rearrangement with interstitial deletion of the roughly 3 Mb between ERG and TMPRSS2; this is the 'translocation with deletion' class, or Edel, and was confirmed on SNP arrays as a hemizygous 21q22.2-3 loss. Both classes correspond to TMPRSS2-ERG fusion; deletion accounted for about 60% of rearranged primaries in the defining study. TMPRSS2 and ERG lie in the same orientation, so fusing them on one chromosome requires the intervening DNA to leave its place. In the no-deletion class it has been moved rather than lost: sources describe insertion of the sequence at separate location(s) in the genome, or exchange between the two chromosome 21 homologues, or microdeletion with concurrent translocation. In an earlier seven-genome sequencing study, copy-neutral TMPRSS2-ERG fusions sat inside balanced 'closed chains': one a quartet of rearrangements over 4 loci on chromosomes 1 and 21, another a trio wholly within chromosome 21. The FISH class alone does not prove more than two breakpoints or involvement of another chromosome: an exchange between the two homologues needs only two breaks and no other chromosome (this step is my inference from the mechanisms listed, not a statement in a source). The assay cannot see losses smaller than the probes, and the deletion class does not say whether the loss was a simple deletion or part of a chain. The column is a per-sample variable for copy-loss versus copy-retaining fusion mechanism; the retaining class is suggestive of a multi-breakpoint balanced rearrangement but does not identify a chain or test interdependence. One paper on retention of the interstitial genes (Murphy 2017) failed to load and was not read. HOW SURE: high for what the two classes mean; medium for what the no-deletion class implies. SOURCES: https://aacrjournals.org/cancerres/article/66/17/8337/526226/TMPRSS2-ERG-Fusion-Associated-Deletions-Provide, https://www.jmdjournal.org/article/S1525-1578(12)00100-6/pdf, https://ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pmc/articles/PMC1601467/, https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC8126330/, https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC3075885/, https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC3632390/, https://www.nature.com/articles/ncponc0945.pdf.

text: REPLY (bd09-team-b) to director Q on platform gap: Checked sample-table classes and MAF tumor_f. Genome-only samples (n=18) median 0.28/Mb vs exome (n=222) 0.63/Mb (Mann-Whitney p=0.003). The gap is NOT in the denominator (covered Mb median 30.3 vs 28.8, p=0.43). It is in the numerator and sits most in silent calls: silent rate 4.1x lower (p=7e-6; silent share of calls 10% genome-only vs 22% exome), nonsilent 1.7x lower (p=0.017), indels no clear difference (p=0.08). tumor_f/read counts are missing for 91% of genome-only calls, so the allele-fraction test can only be run on exome calls: 23-32% of exome calls have VAF<0.2 (WGA has a hard floor at 0.10), and dropping them lowers the exome median to 0.46-0.48/Mb, still 1.7x the genome-only rate, so low-VAF calls explain about half the gap at most. The 10% silent share shows the genome-only call sets are incomplete, so the exome rate is closer to the truth; restoring silent calls at the exome proportion gives genome-only 0.32/Mb. Decision: does not change the method (median per-tumour rate) or label; I now treat exome-only 0.63/Mb (CI 0.57-0.71) as the upper, less biased estimate beside pooled 0.60. Every stratum and every VAF cut is below 1/Mb.

label: REPLY
text: REPLY (bd09-team-b) to director Q on the scale for 'high': Earlier scales were stated loosely ('adult 1-10/Mb, high >=10/Mb') without matching definitions. Redone like-for-like using the library's definitions. Total coding (silent+nonsilent per covered coding Mb): cohort median 0.60 (CI 0.52-0.69; exome-only 0.63) versus adult total-coding 1.8/Mb, paediatric 'highly mutated' tier >=2/Mb, hypermutated >=10/Mb. Nonsilent per covered coding Mb: cohort 0.47-0.49 (CI 0.42-0.55) versus adult nonsilent median 1.5/Mb. Per tumour: 23.7% are >=1/Mb, 2.9% (7/240) >=2/Mb, none >=10/Mb (max 7.3). Sign tests reject a median >=0.79, 1, 1.5, 2/Mb (p from 4e-6 to 1e-60). Smallest threshold the median would cross: 'high' would need to be set at <=0.60/Mb total (<=0.52 to be clear of the CI) or <=0.47/Mb nonsilent. No published scale, adult or paediatric, has a 'high' threshold that low; the lowest is 2/Mb. The one caveat: the cohort median lies above the paediatric pan-cancer average (0.13/Mb) and the top of the per-type range (0.49/Mb) on the total-coding definition, so it is not low among childhood cancers, but that is a relative ranking across studies with different pipelines, and rates in this range are called low in that literature. Changes confidence slightly (down), not the label: False.

text: REPLY (bd09-team-b) to director Q on survival columns and high-risk status: data_clinical_patient.txt has EFS_MONTHS and OS_MONTHS for all 240 patients (0 blank) and no status column. text: REPLY to director Q (in-data yardstick and label rule): Ranked the TERT promoter among all 188 mutated genes by fraction of samples mutated. Rank 1 overall (58/117=50%; BRAF 37%, TP53 26%, NRAS 21%; median gene 0.9%, 95th percentile 6.5%), rank 1 in THAP (73% vs TP53 70%), rank 1 in THPD (40% vs BRAF 33%), rank 1 in primaries and in metastases, rank 1 in P- and s_JF sources and rank 2 in s_JJ (33% vs BRAF 53%). Paired against BRAF across the 117 samples, McNemar p=0.049. Word by word: 'TERT promoter mutations' = 58 samples with 5'Flank C228T/C250T; 'highly prevalent' = rank 1 of 188, no outside level needed; 'clonal' = corrected ratio to BRAF/RAS driver, 40/45 clonal; 'advanced cancers' = all 117 (84 PDTC, 33 ATC); 'compared to PTCs' = no in-data number, there are zero PTC samples. Label rule: the task gives 'Not verifiable' only when the data hold no relevant variables or tables; the variables exist and support both asserted properties, nothing contradicts, so True. If the PTC contrast is treated as essential the files cannot settle it and the label would be Not verifiable; this is a reading choice, not a data result. CHANGES METHOD: no.

label: REPLY
text: REPLY (bd09-team-a) to the director's question on dual-platform samples: three samples have ambiguous platform labels. TARGET-30-PANYGR (PLATFORM 'Exome_WGA,Genome_BCCA', panel WXS/WGS): 24 MAF rows, all Center=broadinstitute.org (the exome caller), no duplicated positions, has read counts like exomes, COVERED_BASES 29.1 Mb, 0.79/Mb (63rd percentile of exomes) - it is an exome call set, not a union; classified exome. TARGET-30-PASLGS ('Genome_BCCA,Genome_CGI', panel WGS): 17 rows, all Center=bcgsc.ca, no duplicates, no read counts, COVERED_BASES 30.7 Mb (CGI-like), 0.52/Mb - one genome call set, not a union; classified genome. TARGET-30-PALAKE (PLATFORM Exome_WGA but panel says WGS): 68 rows all from broadinstitute.org with read counts, COVERED_BASES 27.3 Mb, 2.42/Mb - an exome sample mislabelled in the panel matrix; classified exome. So 222 exome and 18 genome samples by caller (Center column settles it; my earlier '18 genome' count matches, the other team's 17 follows from a different handling of PASLGS/PALAKE). Medians: pooled 0.595/Mb (n=240); dropping the three 0.595 (n=237); exome only 0.63 (n=221-222); genome only 0.28 (n=18; Mann-Whitney p=0.003 vs exome, similar age and MYCN mix, so the gap is a calling-sensitivity difference, not biology). Using exomes as the primary stratum moves the estimate from 0.60 to 0.63/Mb. No change of method or label.

label: REPLY
text: REPLY on library findings: (1) The standard clonal rule (upper 95% bound of CCF reaching 1) was applied to the copy-number-corrected TERT/driver ratio: 40/45 clonal, 5/45 subclonal; the posterior rule P(ratio>0.95)>0.5 gives 35/45 clonal corrected (38/45 uncorrected). (2) The finding that VAF-derived purity makes CCF equal the ratio to the anchor is confirmed in this data: purity = 2 x driver VAF in 71/93 samples. (3) Low-depth explanation for ratios above 1 is not supported here: TERT depth median 335 (min 51), and ratio does not track depth (Spearman 0.07); 16/45 ratios have a lower bound above 1 before and after copy-number correction, so that excess is unexplained by segment copy number.

label: REPLY
text: REPLY (bd09-team-a) to the director's question on benchmarks: definition-matched comparisons for the 240 samples (total = silent+nonsilent per covered coding Mb, median 0.595, CI 0.52-0.69; nonsilent per covered Mb, median 0.476, CI 0.42-0.54). Adult 27-type exome analysis, nonsilent per ~30 Mb covered coding: mean 4.0 -> ratio 0.12, 1/240 above; median 1.5 -> ratio 0.32, 11/240 (4.6%) above. Adult TCGA coding rate from the 914-patient paediatric study, total coding per covered coding base: 1.8 -> ratio 0.33, 13/240 (5.4%) above. Per-tumour thresholds (total coding): 'paediatric highly mutated' 2/Mb -> ratio 0.30, 7/240 (2.9%) above; hypermutated 10/Mb -> ratio 0.06, 0/240 above. Paediatric-only (total coding, same study): pan-paediatric 0.13/Mb -> ratio 4.6, 212/240 (88%) above; highest paediatric cancer-type rate 0.49 -> ratio 1.2, 141/240 (59%) above; medulloblastoma 0.35 nonsilent -> ratio 1.36. I withdrew the 0.17-0.79/Mb paediatric range I quoted before, because it is a genome-wide non-coding SNV rate, not an exonic one. So the matched comparisons do NOT all fall on one side: the cohort is about 3-fold or more below every adult and every threshold-type benchmark, but 4.6-fold above the pooled paediatric coding rate and at the top of the paediatric cancer-type range. I keep the absolute scale as primary because the hypothesis is unqualified, the only numeric definitions of 'high' (2/Mb and 10/Mb) are missed by 3.4- and 17-fold with 97% of tumours below 2/Mb, and the field describes rates of this size as low. Label stays False; the paediatric-relative reading remains the main caveat.

label: REPLY
text: REPLY (bd09-team-a) to the director's question on high-risk scope: coding MYCN_AMP 1=amplified (77), 0 (158), 9 unknown (5); 1p- 54, 11q- 114, 17q+ 193 positive; EFS_MONTHS < OS_MONTHS in 108 patients, equal in 132, never longer. Patients with no positive marker (MYCN not 1, no 1p-/11q-/17q+, EFS not shorter than OS): 13 of 240 (5.4%); 12 of these have no segmental flag in any of the 13 chromosome-arm columns. Median total rate: marked 0.63/Mb (n=227), unmarked 0.10/Mb (n=13), Mann-Whitney p=3e-7. Ignoring survival (which cannot separate 'no event' from 'death as first event' when EFS=OS), 29 patients lack MYCN amplification and 1p-/11q-/17q+: median 0.105/Mb versus 0.66/Mb in the 211 with a genomic marker. The unmarked tumours are almost all flat in every copy-number column and carry about 3 coding mutations each, which looks like low tumour content (neither copy-number changes nor mutations detected) as much as lower-risk biology; all are older than 18 months (1.56-9.96 y). Dropping them raises the cohort median from 0.60 to 0.63 (13 dropped) or 0.66/Mb (29 dropped), still about 3-fold below 2/Mb and the adult 1.8/Mb. The group is small and its removal moves the estimate by 10% at most, so scope and label do not change; I report 0.60 for all 240 and 0.63-0.66 for marker-positive patients.

label: REPLY
text: REPLY (bd09-team-a) on the library findings: (1) survival columns - checked in data: EFS_MONTHS equals OS_MONTHS for 132/240 and is shorter for 108, no status columns exist, so EFS=OS cannot be read as 'event-free'; I used EFS<OS only as a supporting marker and the conclusion does not depend on it. (2) benchmark bases - adopted: total coding rate compared only with total-coding benchmarks, nonsilent with nonsilent, and the non-coding 0.17-0.79 range dropped. (3) thresholds for 'high' - adopted 2/Mb (paediatric highly mutated) and 10/Mb (hypermutated) as the only numeric definitions; 7/240 and 0/240 tumours exceed them and the cohort median is 0.30x and 0.06x of them. SUBSTITUTION and INDEL columns do not sum to the total count in most samples (104/240), so an SNV-only rate cannot be derived cleanly from the sample table; total minus INDEL gives 0.58/Mb.

label: LEARNED
text: LEARNED: The 2018 paediatric pan-cancer study of 961 tumours (24 cancer types, 879 primary tumours) plots 'somatic coding mutation frequencies' against 11 adult TCGA types and marks 'hypermutated' and 'highly mutated' samples with separate dashed lines in its Figure 1; the page fetch was truncated before the numeric thresholds, so the 2/Mb and 10/Mb lines and the 0.13 vs 1.8/Mb figures still rest on the library's reading, not mine. USED FOR: choosing definition-matched (total coding per covered coding Mb) benchmarks for the cohort median. SOURCE: https://www.nature.com/articles/nature25480.

label: REPLY
text: REPLY (bd07-team-a) to director Q1 (copy number at both loci): In all 45 TERT-promoter-mutant samples with a BRAF/RAS hotspot a seg segment spans the driver position; data_cna.txt is 0 at TERT and at the driver gene in all 45 (no discrete amplification/deletion); |seg.mean|>=0.2 at the driver in 10 and at TERT in 7. With multiplicity 1 the corrected ratio is (VAF_TERT*2^seg_TERT)/(VAF_driver*2^seg_driver), in which purity cancels. Using the interval rule (subclonal only if the upper 95% bound of the ratio, with binomial uncertainty from both loci, is below 1): 40 clonal / 5 subclonal before and after adjustment, 0 of 45 change class (under a point rule ratio>=0.75 one sample, P-0002212, moves 0.70->0.82). Excess above 1 remains: 30 above vs 15 below (sign p=0.036, Wilcoxon p=0.011), median 1.08 (raw 1.12; 33 vs 12); it sits in ATC (median 1.38) not PDTC (1.04) and is not tied to low TERT depth (Spearman 0.07). Sensitivity: Landau-style rule P(ratio>0.95)>0.5 gives 35/45 clonal; rounding multiplicity with the (circular) purity column gives 37/45 and removes the excess (25 vs 20). CHANGES: method refined (both loci adjusted, interval rule) and stated count revised from 7 subclonal of 46 to 5 subclonal of 45 (P-0000320 becomes clonal, s_JF_thy_002_P has no independent comparator); conclusion 'clonal in the large majority' and label unchanged.

text: REPLY (bd07-team-a) to director Q2 (PDTC_DEFINITION x pipeline): Caller column maps exactly to batch (mutect = 77 research s_JF/s_JJ samples, empty = 35 P-xxxx-IM3 samples, 5 research samples have no MAF row). TERT promoter prevalence: PDTC-Turin 22/52=42% (CI 29-57), PDTC-MSK 11/31=35% (19-55), Fisher p=0.64; ATC 24/33=73%. By pipeline: Turin IM3 10/19, Turin research 12/33, MSK IM3 2/2, MSK research 9/29, ATC IM3 10/13, ATC research 14/20; within-pipeline Turin vs MSK p=0.49 and 0.79. Clonal (both-loci ratio, interval rule) among those with a driver comparator: Turin 13/15, MSK 9/11, ATC 18/19. The pooled PDTC result is not carried by one definition or one pipeline (every cell >=31% prevalent, >=60% clonal; smallest cell Turin-IM3 3/5). label: REPLY
text: REPLY (bd07-team-a) to director Q3 (in-cohort yardstick and label rule): Ranking all genes in data_mutations.txt by fraction of the 117 samples mutated (TERT promoter = 5'Flank rows kept separate), the TERT promoter is rank 1 of 188 mutated genes overall (49.6%; next BRAF 36.8%, TP53 25.6%, NRAS 21.4%; only 5 genes reach 10%; median gene 0.9%), rank 1 in THPD (40.5% vs BRAF 33.3%) and rank 1 in THAP (72.7% vs TP53 69.7%). As a clonality yardstick, TERT/driver VAF ratio (median 1.09, 85% >=0.75) equals that of all other non-driver mutations (median 1.09, 77% >=0.75) and of EIF1AX (0.96) and TP53 (1.37). Split: 'TERT promoter mutations are clonal' and 'highly prevalent in advanced cancers' are each supported by in-data numbers; 'compared to PTCs' is touched by no in-data number (no PTC samples; the only indirect in-data signal is the gradient PDTC 40% < ATC 73%, p=0.002). Rule applied: the task defines Not verifiable as the data holding NO relevant variables or tables and False as analysed variables contradicting the claim; relevant variables exist and nothing contradicts, so the label is True on the measured clauses. Removing the ~10% benchmark does not change the label (rank 1 replaces it). If the comparative clause is treated as essential, the label would become Not verifiable; that is a reading of the label definitions, not something a data check decides, so it is stated as the weakest point and the label is kept.

label: REPLY
text: REPLY (bd07-team-a) to director Q4 (SAMPLE_TYPE, no-driver cases): Earlier classes by stratum (primary / recurrence+metastasis): clonal 31/8, subclonal 6/1, circular 4/5, purity-missing 2/1 (43 primary, 15 rec/met TERT-mutant). The 7 earlier subclonal: 6 primaries (P-0002212, P-0000320, s_JJ_thy_023, s_JF_thy_017, s_JJ_thy_051, s_JF_thy_002) and 1 metastasis (P-0000415). The 13 TERT-mutant samples without a BRAF/RAS hotspot were: 7 circular (purity = 2x TERT VAF), 3 purity-missing, 2 clonal (P-0000954, P-0002204, both ATC with 5p gain) and 1 subclonal (s_JF_thy_002_P, unmatched, purity 0.22, TERT VAF 0.066); 4 of the 13 carry a fusion in data_sv.txt (CCDC6-RET in P-0000889, P-0000425, s_JJ_thy_042_P; STRN-ALK in s_JJ_thy_026_P), which gives no VAF comparator. Keeping only the 45 samples with an independent BRAF/RAS comparator (both-loci ratio, interval rule): clonal 40/45 = 89% (CI 76-96); primaries 32/36 = 89% (74-97); recurrence+metastasis 8/9 = 89% (52-100). TERT prevalence: primary 43/92 (ATC 20/28, PDTC 23/64), metastasis 12/19, recurrence 3/6. CHANGES: nothing; restricting to primaries or to independently assessable samples leaves the clonal proportion at 85-89%.

label: REPLY
text: REPLY (bd07-team-a) on the three library findings, each checked on the data: (1) CCF rules: applied the interval rule and the P(>0.95)>0.5 rule to the both-loci copy-number-corrected TERT/driver ratio: 40/45 and 35/45 clonal. (2) TERT VAF bias: TERT depth is about half the driver depth (median 335 vs 669, minimum 51) but depth does not predict the ratio (Spearman 0.07, p=0.65; ratio>1 in 17/23 high-depth and 13/22 low-depth calls), so the excess above 1 is not low-depth noise; it is concentrated in ATC and disappears when multiplicity is allowed to exceed 1, consistent with gain/LOH of the mutant allele, which does not make TERT less clonal. (3) Purity: confirmed that TUMOR_PURITY equals 2x VAF of a called mutation in 80 of 94 samples, so purity-based CCF is the same measurement as the ratio; the corrected ratio with multiplicity 1 needs no purity. None of the three changes the label.

text: PRE-REGISTERED CRITERION (bd16-team-a, written before running the director's IDH-wt/non-G-CIMP check): a recorded variable counts as a 'relevant variable' for TERT promoter mutation status only if (1) it is a genotype of the promoter itself (a call at chr5:1295228/1295250 or a clinical TERT-promoter column), or (2) it is a surrogate measured independently of TERT mRNA whose agreement with promoter genotype is known to be high in both directions (sensitivity and specificity both about 90% or more) AND which varies within the cohort. A variable that merely associates with low/zero TERT mRNA in this dataset does not qualify, because defining 'mutant' through TERT expression or its correlates makes a mutation-vs-expression test circular.

text: REPLY (bd16-team-b) to the director's question on whether data_mutations.txt itself shows the promoter was outside the call set: CHECK RUN = cross-tab of Variant_Classification x is_coding/is_flank/categ/original MutSig 'type' per source, plus DISTANCE/gc_content/t_depth for every non-coding row. FINDING: Source A (257 samples, Center=broad.mit.edu, 13,957 rows) has is_coding=1 and is_flank=0 on every row and its original MutSig 'type' column holds only coding classes (Missense, Silent, Nonsense, indels, Splice_Site, Translation_Start_Site); the 158 rows now labelled 5'Flank/5'UTR/3'Flank/3'UTR/Intron/RNA are re-annotations of calls originally typed as coding (e.g. 30 of 37 5'UTR rows were Translation_Start_Site; the 8 5'Flank rows were Missense/Silent/Start_Site in FCAR, GCSH, NOS1 etc., gc_content 0.44-0.66). Maximum gc_content in the whole file is 0.817 and only 14 rows exceed 0.75; t_depth is 0 on every row (uninformative). So the file itself shows source A is coding-only by construction and no upstream GC-rich territory was in its call set. Source B (34 samples, no Center, no helper columns) has 72 non-coding rows: mostly pseudogene/lncRNA 'RNA' exons, 6 5'UTR calls within 145 bp of a start codon, 4 introns, 1 5'Flank in IGHD2-21; the file cannot show whether TERT promoter territory was callable there, but 0 of the 152 RNA-seq samples are in source B (all 146 RNA-seq samples with mutation data are source A), so source B is irrelevant to the expression comparison. LABEL UNDER BOTH READINGS: 'never assayed' -> no promoter variable -> Not verifiable; 'assayed, no mutation in any sample' -> 0 mutants vs 146 wild-type, no group contrast can be formed -> still Not verifiable. CHANGES METHOD: no; it replaces the outside statement about exome capture with in-file evidence.

label: REPLY
text: REPLY (bd16-team-b) to the director's question on proxies within IDH1-wild-type non-G-CIMP tumours: PRE-REGISTERED criterion (prereg_q2.txt, written before the check): a variable is 'relevant' for promoter status only if it is a promoter genotype/status field, or a stand-in whose agreement with true promoter status can be checked inside these files, and it is not defined from TERT mRNA itself. CHECK RUN = TERT log2(RSEM+1) distribution in the 139 IDH1-WT non-G-CIMP RNA-seq samples, Gaussian mixture BIC, and tests of ATRX/DAXX/TERC mRNA, METHYLATION_STATUS, AGE, TERT copy number, ATRX/TP53 mutation against the low group. FINDING: only 7/139 (5%) have zero TERT RSEM; the distribution is unimodal (median 4.09, IQR 2.70-5.29; BIC 578 for 1 component vs 594 for 2), so there is no separable low group. Nothing recorded marks the low/zero samples as promoter-wild-type-like: ATRX mutation 0/139, ATRX mRNA zero-vs-rest p=0.80, TERC p=0.51, AGE p=0.12, METHYLATION_STATUS p=0.96, TERT GISTIC p=0.46, linear CN p=0.69. The only associations are DAXX mRNA (log2<2 group lower, p=4e-4; the opposite direction to an ALT-loss marker would need mutation, not shown) and expression subtype (low group is Mesenchymal/Neural, 0 of 39 Classical, p=2e-4), which are general expression/purity correlates of TERT mRNA, not genotype. No variable meets the pre-registered criterion. WHY THE ASYMMETRY: 'promoter not assayed' no longer rests on outside knowledge (the MAF is coding-only by its own columns), and abstaining only needs 'the files do not record X'; using a proxy needs the positive outside claim 'Y equals X', which the library finding says fails for 15-22% of IDH-WT tumours, with the clean wild-type group being 8 IDH1-mutant samples. CHANGES METHOD: no; label stays Not verifiable.

label: REPLY
text: REPLY (bd16-team-b) to the director's question on TERT copy number and the z-score files: (1) CHECK RUN = leave-out and stratified correlations of TERT linear CN vs log2(RSEM+1) (n=146) and chr5p15.33 segments in data_cna_hg19.seg. FINDING: linear-scale Spearman rho=0.17 (p=0.037) but Pearson r=0.02 (p=0.82); it is NOT carried by a few samples: dropping the 1-8 most extreme samples leaves rho 0.18-0.21, and it persists among the 128 samples with |linear|<0.2 (rho=0.19, p=0.035), i.e. it is a weak rank trend among near-zero noise-level values (73% of samples have |linear|<0.05). It weakens to rho=0.11 (p=0.22) in IDH1-WT non-G-CIMP samples and rho=0.14 (p=0.11) among TERT>0 samples. Real gains do not raise expression: 8 samples with linear>0.2 have median 3.32 vs 4.04 in neutral (p=0.40); the focal amplification TCGA-32-1982-01 (seg 1.02-1.43 Mb, mean 1.11) has TERT log2 1.58, while TCGA-06-2564-01 (focal 0.63 gain ending at chr5:1,300,584, about 5 kb upstream of TERT) has the second-highest TERT (9.27). Copy number is not promoter genotype, so this does not bear on the claim. (2) CHECK RUN = reconstructed both z-score references for TERT. FINDING: ref_all_samples z = (log2(RSEM+1) - 4.112)/1.702, the mean/SD of the 135 tumours with non-zero TERT; ref_diploid z = (raw RSEM - 34.05)/88.4, a raw-scale tumour-cohort mean/SD (max z 9.0, zeros at -0.39). Both are monotone transforms of RSEM (Spearman 1.0 with log2 values) and both references are tumours from this cohort (all 152 RNA-seq samples are primary tumours, no normal brain). 'Elevated' in either file means only 'higher than other GBMs here' (3 samples z>2 in each). No reading can be judged: 'elevated in mutants vs wild-type' needs promoter status, and 'elevated vs normal' needs a normal reference; neither exists. CHANGES METHOD: no.

text: REPLY (bd06-team-a) to the director's question on SIFT/PolyPhen/MutationAssessor/CLIN_SIG for the 4 protein-altering BRCA2 calls: CLIN_SIG is blank for all BRCA2 rows. PGM15 p.E3223G: SIFT deleterious(0.03), PolyPhen probably_damaging(0.94), MA:FImpact medium (FIS 1.995). PGM18 p.G1206A: tolerated(0.28), benign(0.049), MA low (1.735). label: REPLY
text: REPLY (bd06-team-a) to the director's bounding question on blank OS_MONTHS: PGM15 (BRCA2-mutant, LIVING) and PGM56 (wild-type, LIVING) were put back as censored at the cohort's shortest (0 months) and longest (79 months) observed time, in all 4 combinations (4 mutants vs 74 wild-type, 32 deaths, exact test over all 1,426,425 relabellings). Primary result with both dropped: O-E -0.02, log-rank p 0.98, exact p 0.99, HR 0.98. PGM15 at 0: p 0.98-1.00, HR 0.98-1.00. PGM15 at 79: log-rank p 0.49-0.52, exact p 0.47-0.55, HR 0.50-0.53 (95% CI 0.07-3.9), i.e. mutants do better, the opposite of the hypothesis. PGM56's placement barely matters. One-sided exact p for 'mutant worse' is 0.50-0.76 across the bounds. The primary result never approaches significance and never points to shorter survival, so dropping the two blank-time patients stays as the handling.

text: REPLY (bd06-team-a) to the director's question on EBV_STATUS and LOCATION: BRCA2 protein-altering mutants are 3 of 37 EBV-Positive and 1 of 41 EBV-Negative (Fisher p 0.34); by LOCATION 2 Antrum, 1 Body, 1 Cardia of 26 each. Among the 76 evaluable: EBV Positive 36 (15 deaths) vs Negative 40 (17 deaths), log-rank p 0.98, HR 1.01 (95% CI 0.50-2.03), so EBV_STATUS is not associated with overall survival here; LOCATION log-rank p 0.89. Log-rank for BRCA2 stratified by EBV_STATUS: O-E +0.05, p 0.96, HR about 1.06; stratified by LOCATION: p 0.97, HR about 0.96; Cox adjusted for EBV: BRCA2 HR 0.97 (0.13-7.40). Neither EBV nor location confounds the comparison; no change to method or conclusion wording.

text: REPLY (bd06-team-b) to director question on the stage positive control and PGM15: STAGE is a complete integer field (1:2, 2:24, 3:32, 4:20 of 78) while CLIN_T/N/M are blank for 49-50 of 78; every STAGE 4 patient with a recorded CLIN_M_STAGE (8 of 8) is M0, so STAGE 4 here is not distant-metastatic disease. Deaths / KM median OS by stage among 76 evaluable: stage 1 0/2; stage 2 8/24, 68 mo; stage 3 17/31, 24 mo; stage 4 7/19, 45 mo. Stage 4 vs 1-3 is null (HR 0.97, p=0.94) but stage 3-4 vs 1-2 is HR 2.49 (95% CI 1.06-5.81, p=0.036), and deceased patients have shorter OS_MONTHS (median 14) than living (36.5), so the survival fields order early vs late disease as expected; the anomaly is the stage-4 code, not the OS fields. Median follow-up of living patients differs by stage (58.5 mo stage 2 vs about 27 mo stages 3-4), so follow-up is not equal across strata and a stage-stratified exact test is the safer adjusted analysis. Putting carrier PGM15 back as censored at shortest follow-up (0 mo) leaves HR 0.98, log-rank p=0.98; at longest (79 mo) HR 0.50, p=0.49, exact one-sided mutant-worse p=0.76. Changes method: no for the primary comparison; it corrects my earlier wording that stage simply lacked power and that stage 4 marks metastatic disease.

label: REPLY
text: REPLY (bd06-team-a) to the director's question on the truncating-only exact p (PGM63 alone, 76 evaluable patients, one relabelling per patient). Statistic: log-rank O-E for the labelled patient; tied deaths share one risk set (hypergeometric variance); a patient censored before a death time simply leaves the risk set, so early-censored patients score near 0, not extreme. PGM63 died at 6 months, the earliest death time, tied with wild-type PGM17 and PGM59 (71 at risk, O-E = 1 - 3/71 = 0.958). My earlier p = 0.039 = 3/76 ordered relabellings by |Z| with the variance recomputed per relabelling and counted ties as >=; under that ordering nothing in the opposite tail qualifies, so it equals the one-sided p. Under the software-default ordering by |O-E| (R coin style) the two longest survivors PGM16 and PGM1 (O-E -1.02) also count: p = 5/76 = 0.066. Doubling the one-sided tail gives 6/76 = 0.079. So the other team's p above 0.05 is the same data under a different two-sided definition, and my 0.039 was really a one-sided value. Within STAGE = 4 (19 patients, 7 deaths) PGM63 is the unique earliest death: p = 1/19 = 0.053 under every ordering (0.105 doubled); it cannot go below 0.053. Firth-penalised Cox (my own implementation, Breslow ties, profile CI, penalised LR test): all 76 HR 42 (95% CI 3.8-316), p 0.006; stage 4 only HR 45 (2.4-6566), p 0.013; the ordinary Cox MLE is finite under Breslow/Efron ties (HR 35/55, LR p 0.029/0.018) because of the 3-way tie, and monotone within stage 4. The Firth p-values are chi-square approximations resting on one informative patient and are below the floor the exact test can reach, so they add no information. The reconciled result strengthens the statement that this definition is an n=1 artefact; the label stays on the pre-specified primary analysis. Reporting change only: I now quote the coin-style exact p (0.066) and name the definition; the |Z|-with-recomputed-variance ordering is dropped because it misbehaves when a label lands on an early-censored patient (it gave 0.011 vs 0.35 in a 2-patient check).

text: REPLY (bd06-team-b) to director question on exact enumeration of the truncating-only test: replaced the 5000-draw Monte-Carlo with full enumeration. Statistic is the log-rank O-E of the mutant group (sum of log-rank scores; tied deaths share one risk set; relabellings tied with the observed value count as at least as extreme). Single carrier PGM63 among 76: O-E=0.958; PGM63 died at 6 months tied with wild-type PGM17 and PGM59 for the earliest death, so one-sided p=3/76=0.039; two-sided by |O-E| ordering (coin default) is 5/76=0.066 because the two longest-censored patients PGM16 and PGM1 have |score| 1.018; doubling gives 0.079; ordering by the per-relabelling chi-square (variance recomputed) gives 3/76=0.039. So the two teams' numbers differ by definition (my 0.07 was the |O-E| two-sided value, a below-0.05 value is the one-sided or chi-square-ordered one), not by Monte-Carlo error. Within STAGE 4 only (19 patients, 7 deaths) PGM63 is the unique earliest death and p=1/19=0.053 one- and two-sided (0.105 doubled), the smallest value attainable. For three nonsynonymous carriers (70,300 relabellings) one-sided p=0.49, two-sided 0.99; stage-stratified one-sided p=0.33. Ordinary Cox for the single carrier does not converge to a finite estimate (HR about 1e7, Wald p=0.99, LR p=0.019). Changes method: yes for the test (exact enumeration with stated definition replaces Monte-Carlo); no for the label, because the signal is one patient, crosses 0.05 only under the one-sided or chi-square-ordered definition and not within stage.

text: REPLY (bd06-team-a) on the three library findings, checked against the data. (1) In-silico predictors: consistent with the data; only PGM15 is predicted damaging and that patient has no survival time, so the grouping cannot be evaluated beyond the single truncating patient; kept as a labelled sensitivity analysis. (2) Exact log-rank definitions: confirmed numerically; for the one-patient group the p is 3/76 (|Z|, variance recomputed), 5/76 (|O-E|, coin style) or 6/76 (doubled), which fully explains the two teams' disagreement across 0.05. text: REPLY (bd06-team-b) to director question on the adjusted Cox model: STAGE was coded numeric (integer 1-4, linear) and my earlier model used lifelines penalizer=0.01. Unpenalised refits for nonsynonymous BRCA2 (3 carriers, 1 death, n=76), coefficient (SE): unadjusted -0.020 (1.02); +AGE 0.19 (1.09); +STAGE 0.25 (1.04); +logTMB -0.07 (1.03); AGE+STAGE 0.42 (1.10); AGE+STAGE+logTMB 0.35 (1.11), HR 1.42 (0.16-12.4), p=0.75; no convergence warnings with numeric stage. Categorical stage gives coef 0.60 (1.07), HR 1.83, p=0.57 with a lifelines convergence warning because stage 1 has 0 deaths in 2 patients. AGE and STAGE each move the estimate up (the one carrier who died is 55 and stage 4; the two living carriers are 76 and 82, stage 2); logTMB moves it slightly down. Every shift is under 0.6 SE, so the sign change across HR=1 is noise and the model converges but carries no information with one mutant event. Changes method: yes for what is reported as adjusted (a range of HR 0.94-1.83, all p>0.57, plus the stage-stratified exact test one-sided p=0.33, instead of a single three-covariate HR); no for the label.

(3) Firth/monotone likelihood: PGM63's death is tied with two wild-type deaths at the first event time (6 months); lifelines' ordinary Cox still diverges (HR about 1e7, Wald p=0.99, LR p=0.019), so the asymptotic p-values for this one-patient group are not usable and the exact test is the one to report. None of the three changes the label False.

text: REPLY (bd13-team-b) to the director's question on threshold-free checks of 'uncommon'. Check 1, ranking of the 476 genes that have copy-number calls in all 71 ULMS samples (i.e. on all three panel versions): by patients with a truncating mutation ATRX is 1st (17, 23.9%), TP53 2nd (13, 18.3%), RB1 3rd (9, 12.7%); the 4th gene is PTEN with 2 patients (2.8%), every other gene has 0 or 1, and 455 of 476 genes have none. By truncating mutation or deep deletion: RB1 1st (38, 53.5%), TP53 and ATRX tied 2nd (21 each, 29.6%), then PTEN 12 (16.9%), CDKN2A/CDKN2B 7 (9.9%). By any nonsynonymous mutation: TP53 32 (45%), ATRX 22 (31%), RB1 10 (14%), MED12 9 (12.7%). So the three hypothesis genes are the three most frequently inactivated genes in the tumour type, 4.5-fold or more ahead of the next gene on truncating mutations. Check 2: no ULMS sample is hypermutated or MSI-high (TMB max 6.85/Mb, median 2.6; MSI score max 4.95, 9 missing; nothing above Q3+3*IQR), so no patient is removed and the frequencies are unchanged. Both checks agree with label False. Changes method: NO for the label; I do replace my self-chosen 10% cut with the published bands the library gave (<=5% rare, >20% high, 5-20% intermediate) and use the rank check to judge the intermediate band.

label: REPLY
text: REPLY (bd13-team-b) to the director's question on the mutation file alone. Rule stated first (I could not be blind to the numbers, they were already in my records): the claim is conjunctive (all three genes uncommon), so one gene whose frequency is robustly above 20% (lower 95% bound above 20%) is enough to contradict it; a gene between 5% and 20% is 'intermediate' and by itself neither supports nor contradicts, so if all three sat there the band rule gives no label and I would decide from the rank among all panel genes and the share of patients with any of the three; True needs all three at or below about 5-10% with upper bounds under 20%. Numbers from data_mutations.txt only, 71 ULMS patients, exact CIs: (i) truncating classes only: TP53 13/71 = 18.3% (10.1-29.3), RB1 9/71 = 12.7% (6.0-22.7; 7/71 = 9.9% if the two UNKNOWN-status splice calls from unmatched samples are dropped), ATRX 17/71 = 23.9% (14.6-35.5); 34/71 = 48% have a truncating mutation in at least one of the three. (ii) truncating + TP53 missense: TP53 31/71 = 43.7% (31.9-56.0), or 30/71 = 42.3% (30.6-54.6) keeping only DNA-binding-domain missense/in-frame; RB1 and ATRX as in (i); any of three 44-45/71 = 62-63%. Under (ii) TP53 is decisively above 20% (exact one-sided p = 2e-5 against 20%), so the label False holds on the mutation file alone. Under (i) alone no gene is decisively above 20% (ATRX point estimate 24% but CI spans 20%) and none is rare (every lower bound above 5%; p<0.01 against 5% for each), so (i) alone would rest on the rank check (top three genes of 476) rather than on the band rule. Changes method: NO; RB1 by sequence mutation alone (about 10-13%) is the one cell that could be read as 'uncommon', and that is now stated as the weakest point.

label: REPLY
text: REPLY (bd13-team-b) to the director's question on per-patient segment support of deep deletions. All 71 ULMS samples are in the seg file. Of 42 CNA -2 calls (TP53 8, RB1 29, ATRX 5) the lowest segment overlapping the gene has seg.mean <= -1 in 36 (TP53 6/8, RB1 26/29, ATRX 4/5); supported RB1 segments are focal (4-31 marks, seg.mean -1.09 to -3.91, median about -2.3). Six calls are not clearly negative: TP53 P-0006042 (+0.28, 130-mark arm-level segment - no support at all) and P-0000271 (-0.84, 14 marks); RB1 P-0005331 (-0.28, 32 marks), P-0002356 (-0.73, 207 marks) and P-0001564 (-0.91, 26 marks); ATRX P-0001464 (-0.88, 118 marks; this patient also has an ATRX frameshift). One supported RB1 call rests on only 4 marks (P-0003806, -3.52). Strict frequencies (truncating mutation + seg-supported deletion + SV): TP53 20/71 = 28.2% (CI 18.1-40.1), RB1 35/71 = 49.3% (37.2-61.4), ATRX 23/71 = 32.4% (21.8-44.5), versus 31.0%, 53.5%, 32.4% with all -2 calls. By WGD (38 true, 30 false, 3 missing), truncating + seg-supported deletion: RB1 16/30 = 53% non-WGD vs 19/38 = 50% WGD; ATRX 8/30 = 27% vs 11/38 = 29%; TP53 6/30 = 20% vs 13/38 = 34% (with DBD missense 11/30 = 37% vs 26/38 = 68%). RB1 stays far above 20% in both WGD strata; TP53 stays above 20% as a point estimate but its lower bound falls to 18% under the no-missense definition, and is 39% once DBD missense is counted. Changes method: NO; seg-supported counts are now reported as the conservative figure, and the loss is not confined to WGD tumours.

label: REPLY
text: REPLY (bd13-team-b) on the three library findings, each checked against the data. (1) TP53 missense rule (DBD codons 102-292 = likely loss-of-function): applied - 20 of 22 TP53 missense/in-frame calls in ULMS fall in codons 110-282 and are kept; E326K and R337L fall outside and are treated as VUS; this moves TP53 by one to three patients only. (2) Frequency bands (<=5% rare, >20% high, 5-20% intermediate, no support for a 10% cut): adopted in place of my own 10%/20-30% cuts; under them TP53 (42% by mutation, 51-54% with deletions), RB1 (49-54% with deletions) and ATRX (31%) are 'high', and no definition puts any of the three genes at or below 5%. (3) 'Mutations' versus 'alterations' (deep deletions are loss-of-function alterations but not mutations in cBioPortal/OncoKB terms): reported both ways - on sequence mutations alone TP53 is 42%, ATRX 24%, RB1 13%; with deep deletions RB1 is 49-54%. The label False holds under both readings because the claim covers all three genes and TP53 is above 20% even on the strictest literal reading that still follows the knowledge-base definition of TP53 loss of function.

label: REPLY
text: REPLY (bd13-team-a) to the TMB/MSI/WGD question: among the 71 ULMS patients none has TMB above 10 per Mb (ULMS maximum 6.85) and none has an outlying MSI score (ULMS maximum 4.95, far-out Tukey fence 6.0; MSI is missing for 9 ULMS samples, 19 study-wide). The two hypermutated, MSI-high samples in the study (P-0001821 TMB 73/MSI 25 with no TP53/RB1/ATRX call; P-0002812 TMB 21/MSI 18.5 with ATRX frameshift, RB1 frameshift, TP53 R337C) are both epithelioid LMS (UELMS) and were never in the ULMS denominator, so excluding hypermutators leaves every ULMS frequency unchanged. By WGD (38 true, 30 false, 3 missing): TP53 LoF mutation 19/38 = 50% vs 10/30 = 33% (Fisher p 0.22), RB1 truncating 4/38 vs 5/30 (p 0.49), ATRX truncating 9/38 vs 7/30 (p 1.0); union TP53 66% vs 43%, RB1 53% vs 60%, ATRX 34% vs 27%. No gene becomes clearly uncommon in either stratum; TP53 mutation-only lower bound dips to 19.2% in the 30 non-WGD patients only because n is small (point 33%). Does not change the method or the label.

label: REPLY
text: REPLY (bd13-team-a) to the TP53 missense question: ULMS has 21 TP53 missense rows in 21 patients: R110P, R156P, R158P, V173G, V173L, V173A, R175H, Q192L, R213Q, V216M, M237I, C242_M243delinsWL, R248Q x2, R248W, G262V, V274F, C275R, R282G (19 in the DNA-binding domain, codons 102-292) plus E326K and R337L outside it. Allele fractions range 0.19 to 0.96 (none below 10%; depth 156-1764). Three missense patients also carry a TP53 truncating call (R156P, Q192L, R248W) and one (E326K) a deep deletion; 18 patients have missense without truncation. Recounts of TP53 mutation-only: truncating + any DBD missense 29/71 = 40.8% (Wilson 30.2-52.5); truncating + missense at named inactivating residues (broad list of recurrent DBD/zinc-ligand/tetramerization codons, my own list, not an external annotation) 29/71; allele fraction >= 10% changes nothing; truncating + only the six classic hotspot codons 175/245/248/249/273/282 gives 17/71 = 23.9% (15.5-35.0), which is above 20% as a point estimate but no longer 'clearly common' by my lower-bound rule. So the 'clearly common' verdict for TP53 on mutations alone depends on accepting non-hotspot DBD missense as loss of function, which the library's OncoKB finding supports. Changes the method only in that the label must not rest on TP53 missense alone; label unchanged.

label: REPLY
text: REPLY to the director's question on candidate stand-ins for the WES side (bd18-team-a, checks in q1_standins.py): no construction survives as a relevant variable, method unchanged, label stays Not verifiable. (A) Second TMB column: MUTATION_RATE and TMB_NONSYNONYMOUS are both integer counts over a fixed per-panel footprint and their ratio is constant within panel (1.087, 1.037, 1.055 for IMPACT341/410/468) in 84, 90 and 70 percent of samples, so it is the same panel call set rescaled. (B) Wider variant class: only 22 of 2517 rows are outside the nonsynonymous classes (12 are TERT promoter, 1 Silent in the whole file), all in panel genes; all-variant count vs nonsynonymous count has Pearson 0.9994 and is part-whole; a WES call set would carry many silent calls and thousands of genes. (C) Split-half of the 385 mutated panel genes, 20 random disjoint halves: Spearman median 0.62 (range 0.59 to 0.70); both halves are subsets of the same panel calls and every gene is a panel gene, so this is the panel's internal consistency and no exome value enters it. (D) FGA: recomputed from data_cna_hg19.seg (|seg.mean| >= 0.2) it matches the supplied FGA at Pearson 1.000; the seg file has the same 240 panel sample IDs and a median of 6925 markers per sample rising with panel version (6308, 6925, 7722), i.e. panel probes not exome; FGA is a copy-number quantity (Spearman 0.30 with TMB) and not a mutation count. (E) Outcome: panel TMB is higher with durable clinical benefit (median 8.8 vs 6.9, p=0.007, n=227) but this pairs panel TMB with outcome, not with an exome value. (F) Every table (mutations, CNA, seg, SV, panel matrix) uses only the 240 clinical sample IDs, all with IM3/IM5/IM6 suffixes, one per patient. Data-based reason for rejecting all: none is independent of the panel assay and none measures territory outside the panel.

label: REPLY
text: REPLY to the director's question on a label-independent depth check (bd18-team-a, q2_depth.py): nothing indicates a second sequencing source, method unchanged. All 2517 rows have tumour and normal depths. Per-sample median tumour depth: 5th to 95th percentile 226 to 1247, median 691; per-sample median normal depth: minimum 120, median 414, maximum 800 (no sample has an exome-like normal near or below 100x). Seven samples have median tumour depth below 200 (lowest: one single-call sample at 29x, and P-0002758-T01-IM3 at 101x over 30 calls) but their normals are 207 to 648x, so these are low-yield tumour libraries on the panel, not exome data; only 29 of 2517 rows have tumour depth under 100 and they are scattered across 13 samples. No sample shows a two-block depth profile (largest within-sample gap in log10 depth is under 1 and comes from single outlier rows). The 35 rows with Matched_Norm_Sample_Barcode = NORMAL are all of sample P-0003132-T01-IM5 (IMPACT410, LUSC): tumour depth median 976 (range 279 to 1471), normal median 176, all 35 calls in panel genes (12 in MGA), 31 rows have Center MSKCC and Score MSK-IMPACT and the 4 blank rows are its 4 deletions; the block differs from the rest of the file only in the normal-barcode and normal-allele fields being filled, which fits a different conversion path (vcf2maf placeholder) and not a different assay. The one mutated gene outside the 517-gene CNA list is INSRR, one missense call (p.V1129I, chr1:156811916) in P-0003034-T01-IM5 at 1144x tumour and 593x normal, the same depth as that sample's other 13 panel calls; INSRR is not an MSK-IMPACT gene but lies inside the genomic span of the panel gene NTRK1, so it is a call in captured panel territory annotated to an overlapping gene, not an exome call.

label: REPLY
text: REPLY (bd13-team-a) to the ranking question: among the 476 genes with non-NA copy-number values on all three panels (IMPACT341/410/468) in the 71 ULMS patients, ranking by patients with any truncating mutation gives ATRX 17 (24%), TP53 13 (18%), RB1 9 (13%) as ranks 1, 2, 3; the next gene is PTEN at 2 (3%), then 17 genes at 1 patient each, and the median gene is 0. Ranking by truncating mutation or deep deletion gives RB1 38 (54%), ATRX 21 and TP53 21 (30%), then PTEN 12 (17%), CDKN2A/CDKN2B/PDCD1 7 (10%). Only these three genes reach 10% for truncating mutations. The cut-off-free ranking agrees with the label False: TP53, RB1 and ATRX are the most frequent loss-of-function events in the cohort, 4-fold or more above the next gene, so they cannot be called uncommon. I changed the method by adding this within-cohort ranking as a second, threshold-free criterion beside the absolute cut-offs.

label: REPLY
text: REPLY to the director's question on why MUTATION_RATE is not reproduced in about 9 percent of samples (bd18-team-a, q3_mismatch.py): the mismatch is scattered, not concentrated, and does not point to a different assay; conclusion and method unchanged. MUTATION_RATE times the panel footprint (0.98, 1.06, 1.22 Mb) is an exact integer in all 240 samples, and it is an integer multiple of 1/30 or 1/38 Mb in none, so it is a panel count and not an exome rate. Against the nonsynonymous count from data_mutations.txt, 219 of 240 match exactly and 21 differ: +1 in 10 samples, +2 in 9, +3 in 1, -1 in 1 (maximum 3 mutations; implied and file counts both range 1 to 90; Pearson 0.9991). Mismatch share by GENE_PANEL: IMPACT341 12.5 percent (7 of 56), IMPACT410 7.3 percent (12 of 164), IMPACT468 10 percent (2 of 20), chi-square p=0.49; by IRB: Clinical trial 11.1 percent (6 of 54), Commercial 8.1 percent (15 of 186), p=0.67; by tumour number: T01 9.0 percent (19 of 212), T02 7.4 percent (2 of 27), T03 0 of 1, p=0.92. Mismatched samples have more mutations (median 12 vs 7), as expected if a few calls were merged or dropped after the rate was computed. The direction is almost always MUTATION_RATE slightly higher than the file, which fits a slightly earlier or less filtered version of the same panel call list (for example adjacent variants later merged, or calls removed in curation); what exactly was removed cannot be recovered from the tables.

label: REPLY
text: REPLY (bd13-team-a) to the narrowest-reading question: with truncating point mutations only (no missense, deep deletion or SV) among 71 ULMS patients, TP53 is 13/71 = 18.3% (Wilson 11.0-28.8), RB1 9/71 = 12.7% (6.8-22.4), ATRX 17/71 = 23.9% (15.5-35.0). Under my pre-recorded rule every gene is 'in between': none clearly common (lower bound > 20%), none clearly uncommon (upper bound < 10%), and the rule as written returns no label in that case. So the submitted False, as derived from that rule, depended on counting TP53 DNA-binding-domain missense (29/71) or deep deletions. The label still survives this reading on other evidence: all three are significantly above the published 5% 'rare' level (exact binomial p 5e-5, 0.009, 6e-8), TP53 and ATRX are significantly above 10% (p 0.023, 0.0005), 34/71 patients (48%) carry a truncating mutation in at least one of the three, and they are the top three truncated genes of 476. Method changed: the decision now uses the ranking and tests against 5% in addition to the 10%/20% rule; label stays False; confidence lowered from high to about 0.85 because the strict reading shows 'intermediate to high', not unambiguously common.

label: FINDING
text: FINDING: The formal test for two non-nested Cox models on the same patients is Fine's (2002, Biometrika 89:635) partial-likelihood-ratio test, the Cox analogue of Vuong's (1989) test: null = the two models are equidistant from the truth in Kullback-Leibler distance on the rank (partial) likelihood; it is valid when both models are misspecified, and it is sequential: step 1 a variance test (H0: models indistinguishable), step 2 a normal z test of the partial log-likelihood difference (H1A model 1 closer, H1B model 2 closer, two-sided). It is implemented in R only, in the GitHub package thomashielscher/nonnestcox: plrtest(fit1, fit2, nested=FALSE, adjusted='none'|'AIC'|'BIC') on coxph objects fitted with x=TRUE, y=TRUE on identical rows in identical order; adjusted='AIC' subtracts (p1-p2) from the log-likelihood difference, 'BIC' uses log(number of events). CRAN nonnest2 (vuongtest, icci) and pscl::vuong do NOT accept coxph objects; no Python implementation was found. Interpretation: 'pick the lower AIC' can never conclude equal fit and is unstable across samples; under Vuong theory, when the z test is non-significant or the confidence interval for the AIC difference includes zero, the documented reading is 'the model fits are sufficiently close that neither can be preferred over the other', so an AIC or LR chi-square edge whose paired interval crosses zero, with concordance tied, does not count as one model outperforming the other. Caveat: this reading is documented for Vuong-theory intervals; nonparametric bootstrap intervals for information-criterion differences are reported as not fully characterising their variability, so Fine's test is the better-founded check. QUESTION: What formal tests exist for comparing two non-nested Cox models on the same patients, which packages implement them, and how should an AIC or LR chi-square difference be read when its paired bootstrap interval includes zero? SOURCE: https://doi.org/10.1093/biomet/89.3.635 ; https://raw.githubusercontent.com/thomashielscher/nonnestcox/master/R/plrtest.R ; https://cran.r-project.org/web/packages/nonnest2/vignettes/nonnest2.pdf ; https://cran.r-project.org/web/packages/nonnest2/nonnest2.pdf ; https://arxiv.org/abs/1402.6720 ; https://stats.stackexchange.com/questions/484649/comparing-non-nested-cox-models-aic-partial-likelihood-test

label: FINDING
text: FINDING: No source read gives a published number for the optimism of a 3-class risk grouping selected from 100+ candidate features with a few hundred events; the web gives estimators and reference magnitudes only. (a) Heuristic shrinkage (van Houwelingen-le Cessie): s = (LR chi-square - p)/LR chi-square, because the part of the model chi-square bought by estimating p parameters has expectation p under the null; p must be the number of CANDIDATE predictor parameters considered before any selection (anything screened against the outcome has 'spent' degrees of freedom that cannot be retrieved; a k-level factor counts k-1), not the 2 df of the final grouping. Sample-size guidance asks for s >= 0.9. Levelling rule: subtract the df from each chi-square before comparing models. (b) Reference magnitudes for a PRE-SPECIFIED 8-parameter Cox model with no selection: C-index optimism about 0.07 at about 6 events per parameter, 0.044 at 9, 0.028 at 14, 0.018 at 25, 0.010 at 43, 0.005 at 86; supervised selection from many candidates makes it worse, and resubstitution statistics for survival risk classifiers built from high-dimensional data are described as highly biased. (c) Bootstrap optimism and cross-validation need the whole supervised pipeline re-run in every resample, so they cannot be applied when the fitting procedure is unknown; only the heuristic (needs p and the observed LR) or a permutation null through a surrogate pipeline (answer depends on the surrogate) remain. Library's inference, not a quoted source: the optimism in LR chi-square is bracketed between the grouping's nominal df (2, no selection effect) and roughly p (the full candidate df), so with p near 100 or more and an observed LR chi-square of similar or smaller size the heuristic shrinkage is near zero or negative and a small apparent edge over an externally defined index cannot be told apart from resubstitution optimism. QUESTION: How large is the expected optimism in apparent concordance and LR chi-square for a 3-class grouping derived by supervised selection from 100+ candidate features and scored on the same cohort, and which estimators apply when the candidate count is known but the fitting procedure is not? SOURCE: https://med-study-rpg.com/biostats/en/methods/b5-02-shrinkage/ ; https://doi.org/10.1002/sim.7992 ; https://hbiostat.org/rmsc/multivar ; https://scispace.com/pdf/tutorial-in-biostatistics-multivariable-prognostic-models-4auy6032o6.pdf ; https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC3105299/

label: FINDING
text: FINDING: The web does not give a rule that picks a winner when two risk systems rank differently at early and late horizons under non-proportional hazards; what the methods literature does state is: (1) the time horizon must be decided for the model's practical use (disease-specific, clinically motivated, fixed in advance) and follow-up must be sufficient to assess performance over it (STRATOS guidance, which uses 5 years in a cohort with full 5-year follow-up); (2) for risk by a fixed horizon t the C-index is NOT a proper measure (it scores the order of event times, not event status at t, and can rank a misspecified model above the correct one), whereas time-dependent AUC at t is proper; (3) a C-statistic is a global summary over event times, Harrell's version depends on the study's censoring distribution, and the censoring-free version is Uno's C restricted to a fixed, prespecified window (0, tau); estimators derived under proportional hazards are biased if PH fails; (4) C statistics do not measure prediction accuracy, the (integrated) Brier score does, and evaluation is confined to the period where censoring still leaves information. Consequence: rest the comparison on a horizon justified before looking at which model it favours and lying where most events have occurred and enough patients remain at risk, reporting time-dependent AUC plus Brier score at that horizon and Uno's C / integrated Brier over (0, tau]; a late-horizon-only advantage in a thin risk set, or a ranking that flips between horizons, is mixed evidence and not proof that one system predicts better. No DLBCL-specific horizon convention was looked up. QUESTION: When two risk systems both violate proportional hazards and their ranking differs between early and late horizons, which summary measure and horizon are recommended, and how should the horizon be chosen relative to event timing and numbers at risk? SOURCE: https://www.stratos-initiative.org/wp-content/uploads/2023/07/McLernonetal-2023.pdf ; https://doi.org/10.1093/biostatistics/kxy006 ; https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC3079915/ ; https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC10660575/

text: PRE-STATEMENT (bd28-team-a, written before running the gene-level recurrence check): an excess of samples with protein-altering ARAF mutations over the chance expectation from the cohort's own non-silent rate and ARAF's coding length could indicate positive selection on ARAF (driver rather than passenger). It could NOT tell the direction of effect on signalling: selection is equally expected for RAS-independent activating, kinase-impaired RAS-dependent, or other functional classes, and with 2 different residues in 8 samples it is not a hotspot test. It is a genotype-recurrence statistic, not a pathway-output variable, so by itself it would not make part (b) 'leads to pathway activation' testable; no excess would also not contradict activation. It would change what I report as context (strength of driver evidence), not the label rule, unless combined with a functional variable.

question: FINDING FROM THE LAB'S LIBRARY, asked for by the director. QUESTION: What formal tests exist for comparing two non-nested Cox proportional-hazards models fitted to the same patients (for example a Vuong-type or Fine partial-likelihood-ratio test for non-nested Cox models), which R or Python packages implement them, and how do methods papers say an AIC or likelihood-ratio chi-square difference between two non-nested survival models should be interpreted when a paired bootstrap interval for that difference includes zero? ANSWER: TEST. The defined test is Fine's partial-likelihood-ratio test (Fine 2002, Biometrika 89:635-647), the Cox analogue of Vuong's (1989) non-nested likelihood-ratio test. Its null hypothesis is that the two models are equidistant from the truth in Kullback-Leibler distance applied to the rank (partial) likelihood; neither model has to be correct, and the statistic is consistent for the model closer to the truth. It is a sequential procedure: step 1 is a variance test (H0: the two fitted models are indistinguishable); step 2 is a standard-normal z test of the scaled partial log-likelihood difference, with one-sided alternatives (model 1 fits better / model 2 fits better) and a two-sided p. PACKAGES. R only: the GitHub package thomashielscher/nonnestcox, function plrtest(object1, object2, nested=FALSE, adjusted='none'). Both coxph fits need x=TRUE and y=TRUE and must use identical rows in identical order (the function stops otherwise). adjusted='AIC' subtracts (p1 - p2) from the log-likelihood difference; adjusted='BIC' subtracts log(number of events)/2 * (p1 - p2); the default is no adjustment. CRAN nonnest2 (vuongtest, icci) lists lm, glm, glm.nb, clm, hurdle, zeroinfl, mlogit, nls, polr, rlm, lavaan, vglm, mirt and OpenMx as supported classes, not coxph; pscl::vuong also does not take coxph. The search turned up no Python implementation. INTERPRETATION. Merkle, You and Preacher (2016) state that 'select the model with the lowest' information criterion is problematic because it can never conclude equal fit and the preferred model often changes in new samples; Vuong-type tests allow three conclusions (one model fits better, equal fit, or indistinguishable). The nonnest2 vignette reads a 95% interval for the AIC difference that overlaps zero as 'the model fits are sufficiently close that neither can be preferred over the other'. An accepted CrossValidated answer reads a significant variance test with a non-significant LR test as: the models differ, but neither can be shown to be closer to the truth. So an AIC or LR chi-square advantage whose paired interval includes zero, with concordance tied, is 'fits not distinguishable', not 'one model outperforms the other'. LIMITS. That reading is documented for Vuong-theory intervals, not specifically for a paired bootstrap interval; Merkle et al. note that nonparametric bootstrap procedures did not fully characterise the sampling variability of BIC, so Fine's test is the better-founded check. I read only the abstract of Fine's paper (full text not retrieved) plus the plrtest source code; I found no survival-specific methods paper on bootstrap intervals for AIC differences. HOW SURE: high for the test and its R implementation; medium for the interpretation of a bootstrap interval that includes zero (by analogy with Vuong-theory intervals). SOURCES: https://doi.org/10.1093/biomet/89.3.635, https://github.com/thomashielscher/nonnestcox/, https://raw.githubusercontent.com/thomashielscher/nonnestcox/master/R/plrtest.R, https://cran.r-project.org/web/packages/nonnest2/nonnest2.pdf, https://cran.r-project.org/web/packages/nonnest2/vignettes/nonnest2.pdf, https://arxiv.org/abs/1402.6720, https://stats.stackexchange.com/questions/484649/comparing-non-nested-cox-models-aic-partial-likelihood-test, https://stats.stackexchange.com/questions/310925/compare-non-nested-cox-models.

It is a sequential procedure: step 1 is a variance test (H0: the two fitted models are indistinguishable); step 2 is a standard-normal z test of the scaled partial log-likelihood difference, with one-sided alternatives (model 1 fits better / model 2 fits better) and a two-sided p. QUESTION: When a categorical risk grouping (three classes) has been derived by supervised selection from on the order of a hundred or more candidate molecular features in a cohort with a few hundred events, and is then scored on that same cohort against an externally defined clinical index, how large is the expected optimism in apparent concordance and likelihood-ratio chi-square, and what estimators can be applied when the candidate-feature count is known but the fitting procedure is not (for example the van Houwelingen-le Cessie heuristic shrinkage factor, Harrell's bootstrap optimism, or permutation of the outcome through a surrogate pipeline)? ANSWER: NOT SETTLED AS A NUMBER. No source I read gives the expected optimism for this exact configuration. The web gives estimators and reference magnitudes. (a) Heuristic shrinkage (van Houwelingen and le Cessie): s = (LR chi-square - p) / LR chi-square. The rationale given is that the part of the model chi-square bought by estimating p parameters has expected value p under the null. p has to count every candidate predictor parameter considered before selection, not the 2 df of the final three-class grouping: Riley et al. define 'candidate' as considered before any variable selection and count a k-category predictor as k-1 parameters; Harrell's course notes say degrees of freedom are 'spent' by anything examined against the outcome and cannot be retrieved, and recommend subtracting the df from a chi-square to correct for chance. Riley et al. set s >= 0.9 as the target for a model not to be materially overfitted. (b) Reference magnitudes, from a teaching simulation of a pre-specified 8-parameter Cox model with no selection: apparent-minus-held-out C-index was about 0.069 at 5.7 events per parameter, 0.044 at 8.6, 0.028 at 14, 0.018 at 25, 0.010 at 43 and 0.005 at 86; the heuristic factor tracked the held-out calibration slope (0.59 predicted vs 0.53 measured at the smallest size). These are a floor for a pipeline that also selects features. Simon et al. (2011) describe resubstitution separation of survival curves, time-dependent ROC and Harrell's C for classifiers built from high-dimensional data as 'highly biased'. (c) Bootstrap optimism and cross-validation require re-running the whole supervised pipeline in each resample, so they are not available when the fitting procedure is unknown. That leaves the heuristic (needs only p and the observed LR chi-square) and a permutation null through a surrogate pipeline, whose answer depends on how well the surrogate mimics the real procedure. MY INFERENCE (not a quoted source): the optimism in LR chi-square lies between the grouping's nominal 2 df (no selection effect) and roughly p, the full candidate df. With p around 100 or more, an observed LR chi-square of similar or smaller size gives a heuristic shrinkage near zero or negative, so a small apparent edge over an externally defined index cannot be separated from resubstitution optimism. The heuristic was derived for full pre-specified models, so using p = all candidates is a conservative upper bound. LIMITS. The retrieval tool returned only the opening part of each page. The formula itself was read on a secondary teaching page, not in the original 1990 paper. The statement in (c) that every supervised step must be repeated inside the resampling was not reached in this session's page text; it rests on the department's earlier finding from the Simon et al. paper. question: FINDING FROM THE LAB'S LIBRARY, asked for by the director. QUESTION: In the prognostic-model literature, when two risk systems both violate proportional hazards and their ranking differs between early and late time horizons, which summary measure and which horizon are recommended for deciding which system predicts prognosis better (for example Uno's truncated C, integrated Brier score over a pre-set window, time-dependent AUC at a clinically chosen landmark), and how is the horizon supposed to be chosen relative to when most events occur and to the numbers still at risk? ANSWER: NOT SETTLED AS A DECISION RULE. No source I read says which horizon wins when rankings flip under non-proportional hazards. What the sources do state: (1) Horizon. The STRATOS guidance (McLernon et al. 2023) says a time horizon must be decided for the model's practical use, that follow-up must be sufficient to assess performance over that disease-specific horizon, and that performance can be assessed either at the fixed end of the horizon or over the whole follow-up within it; its case study uses 5 years. The horizon is therefore a clinical choice fixed in advance, not the one at which a model looks best. (2) Measure at a fixed horizon. Blanche, Kattan and Gerds (2019) show the C-index is not proper for t-year risk: it scores the order of event times rather than event status at t and can rank a misspecified model above the correct one. Time-dependent AUC at t is proper. (3) Measure over a window. Uno et al. (2011) describe the C-statistic as a global assessment rather than a t-year measure, show that Harrell's C estimates a quantity that depends on the study's censoring distribution, and define the censoring-free alternative as C restricted to a fixed, prespecified period (0, tau); they note estimators derived under proportional hazards are biased when that model is wrong. (4) Accuracy. Wang et al. (2023) state that C statistics do not quantify prediction accuracy and that the integrated Brier score does; in their example evaluation stops where censoring leaves 'minimal information'. CONSEQUENCE FOR THE TEAMS. Rest the comparison on a horizon justified before seeing which model it favours and placed where most events have occurred and enough patients remain at risk. Report time-dependent AUC and Brier score at that horizon, plus Uno's C and integrated Brier score over (0, tau]. A late-only advantage in a thin risk set, or a ranking that flips between horizons, is mixed evidence rather than one system predicting better. LIMITS. The retrieval tool returned only the opening part of each page: the STRATOS sentences on choosing the horizon came from a search excerpt of the Annals version of the paper whose PDF I opened; the PDF text I received stops at the start of the Methods. The numbers-at-risk criterion rests on the department's earlier finding (Kaplan-Meier estimates are unstable where the risk set is small), not on a page read in this session. No DLBCL-specific horizon convention was looked up. HOW SURE: medium for which measures suit which target and that the horizon must be prespecified with sufficient follow-up; low for which horizon should decide a ranking that flips. SOURCES: https://www.stratos-initiative.org/wp-content/uploads/2023/07/McLernonetal-2023.pdf, https://doi.org/10.7326/m22-0844, https://doi.org/10.1093/biostatistics/kxy006, https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC3079915/, https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC10660575/.

The STRATOS guidance (McLernon et al. 2023) says a time horizon must be decided for the model's practical use, that follow-up must be sufficient to assess performance over that disease-specific horizon, and that performance can be assessed either at the fixed end of the horizon or over the whole follow-up within it; its case study uses 5 years. The horizon is therefore a clinical choice fixed in advance, not the one at which a model looks best. (2) Measure at a fixed horizon. Blanche, Kattan and Gerds (2019) show the C-index is not proper for t-year risk: it scores the order of event times rather than event status at t and can rank a misspecified model above the correct one. Time-dependent AUC at t is proper. (3) Measure over a window. Uno et al. (2011) describe the C-statistic as a global assessment rather than a t-year measure, show that Harrell's C estimates a quantity that depends on the study's censoring distribution, and define the censoring-free alternative as C restricted to a fixed, prespecified period (0, tau); they note estimators derived under proportional hazards are biased when that model is wrong. (4) Accuracy. Wang et al. (2023) state that C statistics do not quantify prediction accuracy and that the integrated Brier score does; in their example evaluation stops where censoring leaves 'minimal information'. CONSEQUENCE FOR THE TEAMS. Rest the comparison on a horizon justified before seeing which model it favours and placed where most events have occurred and enough patients remain at risk. Report time-dependent AUC and Brier score at that horizon, plus Uno's C and integrated Brier score over (0, tau]. A late-only advantage in a thin risk set, or a ranking that flips between horizons, is mixed evidence rather than one system predicting better. LIMITS. The retrieval tool returned only the opening part of each page: the STRATOS sentences on choosing the horizon came from a search excerpt of the Annals version of the paper whose PDF I opened; the PDF text I received stops at the start of the Methods. The numbers-at-risk criterion rests on the department's earlier finding (Kaplan-Meier estimates are unstable where the risk set is small), not on a page read in this session. No DLBCL-specific horizon convention was looked up. HOW SURE: medium for which measures suit which target and that the horizon must be prespecified with sufficient follow-up; low for which horizon should decide a ranking that flips. SOURCES: https://www.stratos-initiative.org/wp-content/uploads/2023/07/McLernonetal-2023.pdf, https://doi.org/10.7326/m22-0844, https://doi.org/10.1093/biostatistics/kxy006, https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC3079915/, https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC10660575/.

text: REPLY from bd28-team-b to the director's question on RIN1 fusions. My pathway gene list did not contain RIN1, so the per-sample driver table could not have caught it. data_sv.txt has RIN1 as the 5' gene in 3 of 8 samples (ICC12 RIN1-IGLL5, ICC14 RIN1-IGLJ3, ICC8 RIN1-IGLJ3), every partner an immunoglobulin-lambda segment, all DNA_support No and RNA_support Yes, and RIN1 has no row in the MAF; it is the only 5' gene recurring across samples, and two other rows have mitochondrial partners (SERINC2-MT-RNR1, NTM-MT-ATP6), the same class of highly expressed partner. My earlier statement that the ARAF-mutant samples have no other pathway alteration does not stand as written; the supported statement is that ICC12 and ICC18 have no SNV call in any RAS/RAF/MAPK/FGFR gene (a wider name-pattern scan found none either) and that ICC12 carries an RNA-only RIN1-IGLL5 call of unknown significance. text: REPLY from bd28-team-b to the director's question on scaling recurrence. Written before reading the result: an excess of hits in ARAF could indicate positive selection but not whether the variants raise or lower signalling, and a mutation count is not a pathway-activity variable, so it cannot move the label. Result: the cohort has 148 nonsilent SNVs over 8 x 30 Mb (TMB_NONSYNONYMOUS x 30 reproduces my per-sample counts in 7 of 8 samples, ICC24 is 10 vs 9), a rate of 6.2e-7 per base. Using coding lengths recalled from memory, not from the data (ARAF 1.8 kb, MUC16 43.5 kb, ACAN 7.6 kb), expected samples hit and P(at least 2 of 8) are ARAF 0.009 and 3.4e-5, ACAN 0.037 and 5.8e-4, MUC16 0.21 and 0.017; about 0.5 genes of typical length among 20,000 would reach 2 hits by chance, so one such gene is not surprising cohort-wide. ARAF hits are two different residues (N217I, G322S, neither in dbSNP); MUC16 hits are two different variants in a very long gene; ACAN is the identical variant p.A1099T (rs563511597) in ICC8 and ICC10, which looks like a polymorphism or recurrent artefact. The recurrence is weak evidence of selection at most and says nothing on direction; method and label unchanged.

text: REPLY (bd15-team-b) to the genome-wide calibration question: ran the truncating-share binomial test, a truncating-vs-silent test and a nonsynonymous-vs-silent test on all 1,341 genes with >=10 protein-altering rows (strict truncating definition, background 9.2%). The test is calibrated and separates drivers from passengers: 47 genes reach p<0.05 (67 expected by chance), top ranks are FAT1, CDKN2A, ARID2, NOTCH1, PTPN14, CHUK, RB1, TPO, USP28, TP53, CASP8; TTN, MUC16, RYR2, CSMD3 and all 15 tested olfactory receptors fail (p 0.41-1.0); HRAS fails by design (missense hotspot oncogene, 0 truncating). Target genes: CHUK 7/12 truncating, p=2.9e-5, rank 6/1341, BH q=0.006; USP28 7/14, p=1.0e-4, rank 9, q=0.016; EP300 5/19, p=0.025, rank 31, q=0.99; PBRM1 3/10, p=0.057, rank 59, q=1.0 (truncating-vs-silent: PBRM1 p=0.005 rank 21 q=0.29, EP300 p=0.026 rank 48 q=0.70). So only CHUK and USP28 survive genome-wide FDR; EP300 and PBRM1 are nominal only (EP300 additionally has 6 of 14 missense within aa 1399-1485 of the HAT domain, permutation p=0.001 for a 90-aa window, but the window was chosen after seeing the data). Changes method: yes for what the label rests on. The label True now rests on descriptive prevalence (each gene protein-altered in >=10% of tumours, comparable to HRAS 12%, RB1 11%, CREBBP 14% in the same data), with genome-wide-significant selection as corroboration for CHUK and USP28 only, not for all four.

text: REPLY (bd15-team-b) on the library findings, checked against cscc-ucsf-2021: (1) Funcotator Splice_Site finding is confirmed by the data: 1,757 of 3,681 Splice_Site rows carry a protein change (1,197 missense, 511 synonymous, 49 nonsense), so only rows without a protein change were kept as truncating; this removed one EP300 and one PBRM1 row. (2) Composition finding: I cannot compute gene-specific neutral nonsense expectations because no reference sequence is in the data; as a bound, doubling the neutral truncating expectation to 18.4% leaves CHUK p=0.002 and USP28 p=0.007 but EP300 p=0.26 and PBRM1 p=0.27; 4 of 5 EP300 nonsense calls are at Gln codons, consistent with the Gln-rich warning, so EP300 truncating enrichment is not reliable. (3) Convention finding: I fix 'frequently' as descriptive prevalence (>=10% of tumours with a protein-altering mutation, set in my plan before analysis) and report the background-aware result beside it: prevalence 19-22%, 12%, 12-13%, 11% for EP300, PBRM1, USP28, CHUK; genome-wide-significant excess for CHUK and USP28 only. By raw prevalence the genes rank 133, 808, 633, 1019 of 15,393 genes, i.e. about 1,000 genes are mutated as often, most of them UV passengers.
